In the 1980s a different model of the mind gathered force, and it is called connectionism.

Connectionism is the view that mental activity arises from the combined action of many simple units connected together, loosely inspired by the brain's networks of nerve cells.

Instead of one central processor following rules one step at a time, a connectionist system is a web of many simple units that pass signals to one another all at once.

Each connection between units has a strength, called a weight, and the system learns not by being programmed but by gradually adjusting these weights through experience.

A weight, in this setting, means a number that says how strongly one unit influences another, and learning is the slow tuning of many such numbers.

These systems came to be known as neural networks, meaning networks of simple units modelled very loosely on the neurons, or nerve cells, of the brain.

A landmark was a two volume work published in 1986 by David Rumelhart, James McClelland, and a group of collaborators who called their approach parallel distributed processing.

Parallel distributed processing means that many computations happen at the same time, in parallel, and that knowledge is spread across the whole network rather than stored in one tidy place.

In systems terms this was a rival architecture, not just a rival theory: it replaced the serial central processor with massively parallel hardware, replaced explicit stored rules with tuned connection weights, and replaced programming with training on data.

Connectionism was attractive because it learned gracefully, handled messy real world input well, and degraded gently, still working even when parts were damaged, much as a brain can.

It sparked sharp debates with the older symbol based view, and experts still disagree about how much of the mind is best described by rules and symbols and how much by networks and weights.

That very debate, unresolved to this day, kept the field honest and set the stage for the powerful learning systems we see now.


2.5.2 The turn to the brain and the birth of cognitive neuroscience

For most of its early life, cognitive psychology studied the mind by watching behaviour, largely leaving the physical brain to one side.

That changed dramatically as new tools made it possible to watch the living, working brain in action.

The key advances were brain imaging methods, which are techniques for producing pictures of brain activity in a living person without surgery.

The most important of these is functional magnetic resonance imaging, usually shortened to fMRI, which detects changes in blood flow to reveal which brain areas are more active during a task.

The idea is simple to grasp: brain regions doing more work call for more oxygen rich blood, and the scanner can track where that extra blood goes.

With such tools, researchers could finally connect mental processes described by cognitive psychology to specific machinery in the brain, which in systems terms means the field finally gained instrumentation on the hardware layer instead of inferring everything from the system's external behavior.

Out of this marriage a new field was born, called cognitive neuroscience, which is the study of how the brain gives rise to mental processes.

The name itself began to be used in the late 1970s, and the field flowered through the 1980s and 1990s as the scanners improved.

Cognitive neuroscience also drew on older evidence from patients with brain injuries, whose specific losses had long hinted that particular abilities depend on particular regions.

A famous example is a patient known by the initials H. M., who after brain surgery for epilepsy lost the ability to form new lasting memories, while his older memories and his intelligence stayed intact.

That heartbreaking case showed that the ability to lay down new memories is a distinct function, tied to specific brain structures: in systems terms his write path to long term storage was severed while the existing archive and the processor stayed intact, a dissociation that shaped memory research for decades.

We should be careful, though, not to expect a neat single spot for every mental function, because most abilities depend on many regions working together in networks.

Cognitive neuroscience is now one of the most active areas of the whole science of mind, and it fills a substantial part of this book.


2.5.3 The Bayesian and probabilistic synthesis of the 2000s

Around the turn of the twenty first century, a powerful new way of describing the thinking mind gained ground.

It rests on the idea that the mind is, in effect, always dealing with uncertainty and making its best guesses about a doubtful world.

The tools for this come from probability, the branch of mathematics that measures how likely things are.

At its heart sits a rule known as Bayes theorem, named after Thomas Bayes, an English minister and mathematician who lived from about 1701 to 1761.

Bayes theorem is a precise recipe for updating a belief when new evidence arrives, combining what you already expected with what you have just observed.

In plain terms, it says you should weigh your prior expectations against fresh evidence, and shift your belief by an amount that reflects how strong that evidence is.

The word prior here means the belief you held before seeing the new evidence, and updating means adjusting that belief in light of it.

Researchers proposed that the brain works in a broadly similar way, constantly combining its prior expectations with incoming sense data to arrive at its best interpretation of the world.

This is often called the Bayesian brain, or predictive processing, the idea that the brain is a prediction machine that guesses what is coming and pays special attention to its errors.

Predictive processing means that the brain continually generates expectations about its own inputs and updates itself chiefly when those expectations are wrong.

In systems terms this reframed the mind's core loop: the input is noisy evidence, the state is a probability distribution over possible worlds, the update rule is Bayes theorem, and the output is the current best estimate, published to perception and action alike.

This viewpoint elegantly explains many puzzles, such as why we can act on blurry or incomplete information, since a good prior can fill the gaps that the senses leave open.

It also ties together perception, learning, and action under a single mathematical idea, which is part of why it drew so much excitement.

Not everyone agrees that the brain is literally Bayesian, and experts debate how seriously to take the mathematics as a description of real neural machinery, so this remains an active and open question.


2.5.4 The deep-learning and foundation-model era and its challenge to the field

We arrive, finally, at our own moment, which has been reshaped by a dramatic advance in artificial intelligence.

Beginning around 2012, a form of connectionism called deep learning began to achieve results that astonished even its own researchers.

Deep learning means training neural networks that have many layers of units stacked one after another, so that each layer builds on the patterns found by the layer before it.

The word deep here simply refers to the large number of stacked layers, which allow the network to learn very rich and abstract patterns from vast amounts of data.

Fed enormous quantities of examples and running on powerful computers, these deep networks learned to recognize images, understand speech, and translate languages with remarkable skill.

In the years around 2018 to the early 2020s, a further leap produced what are now called foundation models.

A foundation model is a very large network trained on an enormous and broad body of data, which can then be adapted to a wide range of different tasks.

The best known foundation models are large language models, which are systems trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word and, in doing so, learn to produce fluent language.

A large language model, often shortened to LLM, is a system that generates and understands human language by having learned the statistical patterns in a vast collection of writing.

These systems now write essays, answer questions, and hold conversations, and the assistant helping to shape this very book is one of them.

Their arrival poses a genuine challenge to the science of mind, and thoughtful researchers disagree about what it means.

On one hand, here at last are working systems that use language flexibly, which is exactly what behaviourism said could never be explained and what the cognitive revolution set out to understand.

On the other hand, these systems learn from far more data than any child ever sees, and it is fiercely debated whether they think in anything like the way a person does, or merely imitate the surface of thought.

In systems terms the two sides predict differently: if these networks share the mind's design, their internal representations should line up with human ones under careful comparison, while if they only imitate the surface, the input-output match should break down off the beaten path of their training data, and both predictions are being actively tested.

Some scholars see them as a powerful new model of the mind, while others warn against mistaking fluent output for real understanding, and this disagreement is entirely unsettled today.

What is clear is that the old questions from the start of this chapter, about where knowledge comes from and what it means to understand, are alive and urgent once again.

The science of mind, then, is not a finished story but an ongoing conversation, and you are joining it at a moment of unusual excitement.


We close the chapter by treating its best measured discovery, the memory system Ebbinghaus benchmarked, as this chapter's system, since it was the first cognitive process ever specified with real numbers.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Study episodes: items presented for learning, arriving through perception, together with the time and effort spent on each.

◦ Rehearsal events: repetitions and reviews of previously learned items, whether massed together or spaced over time.

◦ Retrieval requests: prompts, such as a test or a real world need, asking the store to reproduce what it holds.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Recall performance: the proportion of learned material reproduced on demand, consumed by the tasks and decisions that need it.

◦ Savings: the reduction in effort needed to relearn material, which was Ebbinghaus's sensitive measure of hidden residual memory.

◦ Reconstructions: schema-shaped retellings of stored material, as Bartlett showed, consumed by communication and further remembering.

• STATE.

◦ Memory traces: stored records of the learned items, each with a current strength.

◦ Trace stability: a durability value per trace that grows with each spaced review and governs how fast the trace decays.

◦ Schemas: the frameworks of prior knowledge that compress new material at encoding and fill gaps at retrieval.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Decay rate: how quickly an unrehearsed trace loses strength.

◦ Spacing gain: how much each successful spaced review multiplies trace stability.

◦ Meaningfulness: how well the material fits existing schemas, which lowers the effective learning cost, the very variable Ebbinghaus removed with nonsense syllables.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Initial rapid forgetting: much of the loss occurs within the first hour, with roughly two thirds of Ebbinghaus's savings gone within about a day.

◦ Slow residual decay: the surviving remainder fades only gradually over days to a month.

◦ Spaced review benefit: reviews separated by hours to days flatten the decay curve relative to the same reviews massed into one session.

• MODES.

◦ Encoding mode: active study writes new traces, engaged whenever material is attended and processed.

◦ Retention mode: traces decay passively between uses, the default when the material is untouched.

◦ Reconstruction mode: retrieval rebuilds material from gist plus schema, engaged whenever recall is requested, especially after long delays.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Rapid early loss: unreviewed material is mostly gone within a day, the practical failure that defeats cramming.

◦ Systematic distortion: schema-driven reconstruction drops odd details and inserts expected ones, producing confident but altered memories.

◦ Measurement failure in the science itself: introspection could not observe these processes, which is why the field needed savings scores and behavioral measures.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called stability with initial value one.
Create a number variable called strength with initial value one.
Create a list variable called review_days containing the days on which reviews occur.
Create a number variable called previous_day with initial value zero.
For each day from one to thirty, do the following.
    Set a number variable called elapsed to one.
    Multiply the strength by the exponential of the negative of the elapsed value divided by the stability.
    If the day is in the review_days list, then do the following.
        Set the strength to one.
        Multiply the stability by two.
    Record the day and the strength in a results list.
Print the results list so the forgetting curve and the spacing effect can be read.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for the exponential function
import math

# Define a function that simulates memory strength over a number of days given review days
def forgetting_simulation(days, review_days):
    # Create a number variable called stability with initial value one, in days
    stability = 1.0
    # Create a number variable called strength with initial value one, meaning fully learned
    strength = 1.0
    # Create an empty list variable called results
    results = []
    # For each day from one to the number of days, do the following
    for day in range(1, days + 1):
        # Multiply the strength by the exponential of negative one day divided by the stability
        strength = strength * math.exp(-1.0 / stability)
        # If the day is in the review_days list, refresh and stabilise the trace
        if day in review_days:
            # Set the strength back to one, modelling a successful review
            strength = 1.0
            # Multiply the stability by two, modelling the spacing effect
            stability = stability * 2.0
        # Append the day and the rounded strength to the results list
        results.append((day, round(strength, 3)))
    # Return the results list
    return results

# Create a list variable called crammed with no later reviews after day one
crammed = forgetting_simulation(30, [])
# Create a list variable called spaced with reviews on day one, day three, day seven, and day fourteen
spaced = forgetting_simulation(30, [1, 3, 7, 14])
# Print the retained strength after thirty days without spaced reviews
print("no reviews, day 30 strength:", crammed[-1][1])
# Print the retained strength after thirty days with spaced reviews
print("spaced reviews, day 30 strength:", spaced[-1][1])


CHAPTER 3. THE THEORETICAL PARADIGMS (FRAMEWORK)

Welcome to the part of the story where we meet the big competing ideas about how the mind actually works.

A paradigm, in plain words, is a whole way of seeing a problem: a shared set of assumptions, favourite examples, and preferred tools that a community of researchers uses to make sense of things.

In the science of the mind there is not one single agreed paradigm but several, and each one paints thinking in a different light.

For a systems reader the cleanest way to hold this chapter is to treat the four paradigms as four rival system designs for the same requirements document: each proposes a different architecture, a different data format, a different update rule, and a different account of where the system's power and its failures come from.

This chapter introduces four of the most important of these ways of seeing, explains what each one gets right and where each one struggles, and then asks how they fit together.

By the end you should be able to hear a claim about the mind and guess which paradigm it grew out of.

3.1 Symbolic computationalism

The first big idea is that thinking is a kind of calculation carried out on symbols, much like the steps a person follows when doing arithmetic on paper.

This section explains what a symbol is in this setting, how a mind built from symbols would work, and why this picture was the dominant one for the early decades of cognitive science.

3.1.1 The physical symbol system hypothesis

Let us start with the single boldest claim in this whole area, so you can see what everything else is reacting to.

A symbol, here, simply means a token that stands for something else: the way the letters c, a, t stand for a small furry animal, or the way a red light stands for stop.

Symbolic computationalism is the view that thinking is what happens when a physical system shuffles such symbols around according to rules, and that this shuffling is literally computation, the same kind of thing a computer does.

The formal version of this claim is called the physical symbol system hypothesis, and it was stated by two American scientists, Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, in a 1976 lecture and paper.

Their hypothesis says that a physical symbol system, meaning any physical machine that can create, combine, and transform symbol structures, has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action.

In plainer words, they were claiming that if something is genuinely intelligent then it must be manipulating symbols, and that any system rich enough to manipulate symbols in the right way could, in principle, be intelligent.

The word necessary means you cannot have intelligence without it, and the word sufficient means having it is enough, on its own, to make intelligence possible.

An everyday image helps here: think of thinking as being like following a recipe, where the ingredients are symbols and the instructions are rules for combining them.

Just as the recipe does not care whether your kitchen is large or small, the hypothesis says intelligence does not care whether the symbols live in a brain, in a computer, or in some other machine, as long as the symbol shuffling is the same.

As a system design, this paradigm specifies discrete tokens as the data format, explicit rules as the processing, a working memory of symbol structures as the state, and serial rule application as the execution model.

This idea was powerful because it suggested that the mind could be studied as software, separately from the particular hardware, whether that hardware is made of neurons or of silicon chips.

3.1.2 Production systems and the language of thought

Now let us look at two concrete ways this symbol idea was turned into working theories, because a slogan is not yet a model.

A production system is a way of building intelligent behaviour out of many small if-then rules, where each rule, called a production, says if such and such a condition holds, then take such and such an action.

For example, one rule might say if the goal is to make tea and there is no hot water, then boil the kettle, and the system keeps matching its rules against the current situation and firing whichever one applies.

In systems terms a production system's inputs are the current contents of a working memory, its output is the action of whichever rule fires, its state is that working memory plus the rule base, and its characteristic cycle time in human modelling is about 50 milliseconds per rule firing.

Newell and Simon used production systems to model human problem solving, and this style later grew into large architectures of the mind such as ACT-R, meaning Adaptive Control of Thought - Rational, built by John Anderson, and SOAR, an architecture whose name was originally an acronym for State, Operator, And Result.

The second concrete idea is the language of thought, proposed by the American philosopher Jerry Fodor in a 1975 book of that name.

Fodor argued that thinking happens in an inner mental language, sometimes nicknamed Mentalese, which has words and a grammar just as spoken languages do, so that a thought is literally a sentence written in the head.

Jargon check: syntax means the rules for how symbols may be arranged, the grammar, while semantics means what those symbols mean, their content.

The appeal of the language of thought is that it explains why thoughts, like sentences, can be built up from parts in endless new combinations, a point we turn to next.

3.1.3 Strengths in compositionality and systematicity, weaknesses in learning and grounding

Every paradigm has things it explains beautifully and things it handles badly, and being honest about both is how you judge one fairly.

The great strength of the symbolic view is that it naturally explains two features of thought called compositionality and systematicity.

Compositionality means that the meaning of a whole is built from the meanings of its parts and the way they are put together, so that knowing the words dog, bites, and man lets you understand both the dog bites the man and the man bites the dog.

Systematicity, a term stressed by Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn in a much cited 1988 paper, means that minds that can think one thought can usually think closely related ones: anyone who can grasp the dog bites the man can also grasp the man bites the dog, because thoughts share reusable parts.

Symbols handle this effortlessly, because rearranging tokens according to a grammar is exactly what a symbol system does.

The weaknesses, though, are just as real, and in systems terms they are both interface problems.

The first weakness is learning: classic symbolic systems are often handed their rules and symbols by a human designer, and they are not naturally good at discovering new ones for themselves from messy experience, which means the design lacks a credible training pipeline from raw data to rule base.

The second weakness is called the symbol grounding problem, a phrase from the cognitive scientist Stevan Harnad in 1990.

Grounding is the question of how a symbol ever comes to mean anything at all, rather than being just a meaningless token defined only by other meaningless tokens, which in systems terms is the missing connection between the symbol store and the sensors and actuators.

The worry is like trying to learn Chinese from a Chinese only dictionary with no pictures and no experience of the world: you could shuffle the symbols forever and never connect the word for apple to any actual apple.

So the symbolic paradigm is strong on structure and meaning making sense, but shakier on where knowledge comes from and how it touches the real world.

3.2 Connectionism and parallel distributed processing

The second big idea takes its inspiration not from logic and language but from the brain itself, with its billions of simple cells working at once.

This section explains how networks of simple units can represent and learn, and why this approach became the ancestor of today's artificial intelligence.

3.2.1 Distributed representation and learning from data

Let us begin with the basic building block, so the later ideas have somewhere to stand.

Connectionism is the view that thinking arises from the cooperation of many very simple units, loosely modelled on brain cells, that pass signals to one another through connections of varying strength.

The fuller name, parallel distributed processing, was made famous by a two volume book of that title edited by David Rumelhart and James McClelland in 1986, and the word parallel means many units are active at the same time rather than one step following another.

Each connection carries a weight, which is just a number saying how strongly one unit pushes or pulls on another, and learning in these systems means gradually adjusting those weights.

A key idea is distributed representation, which means a concept is not stored in one single place but is spread across the pattern of activity over many units at once.

Contrast this with a symbolic system, where the idea of a grandmother might sit in one labelled slot; in a distributed system the idea of a grandmother is a whole pattern lit up across thousands of units, and no single unit is the grandmother.

These networks learn from data by example: you show the network many cases, it makes a guess, you tell it how wrong it was, and it nudges its weights to do better next time.

The most influential method for this nudging is called backpropagation, short for backward propagation of errors, popularised in that same 1986 work, which is a mathematical recipe for spreading the blame for a mistake back through the connections so each weight knows which way to move.

As a system design, this paradigm specifies continuous activation vectors as the data format, weighted sums and thresholds as the processing, the weight matrix as the long-lived state, the learning rate as the key parameter, and parallel update as the execution model.

This learning from examples is the direct ancestor of the neural networks behind modern speech recognition, image labelling, and language tools.

3.2.2 Graceful degradation and content-addressable memory

Now for two lovely properties that fall out of the distributed design almost for free, and that feel very lifelike.

The first is graceful degradation, which means that when the system is damaged or fed messy input, its performance gets a little worse rather than collapsing all at once.

Because knowledge is spread over many units, losing a few units is like smudging a few pixels of a photograph: the picture dims a little but is still recognisable, unlike a filing cabinet where losing one card loses one fact completely.

This matches how real brains and real people behave, since we can often still think and remember reasonably well even when tired, distracted, or mildly injured.

The second property is content-addressable memory, which means you can retrieve a whole memory from just a piece of it.

Ordinary computer memory is address based: you must know the exact slot number to fetch what is stored there.

Human memory is content based instead: a few notes of a song, or a whiff of a smell, can call up an entire scene, and connectionist networks reproduce this by settling into the full stored pattern when given only a fragment.

In systems terms the retrieval interface takes a partial pattern as input and publishes the completed pattern as output, with the network's settling process doing the lookup without any address ever being computed.

An everyday example is recognising a friend from just their walk seen at a distance, with no face and no voice, because the partial cue is enough to complete the pattern.

3.2.3 Strengths in learning and pattern, weaknesses in structure and binding

As before, we weigh the gains against the costs so the comparison stays honest.

The clear strengths of connectionism are the mirror image of the symbolic weaknesses.

These networks are excellent at learning from raw data, at recognising patterns, at coping with noise and damage, and at grounding, since their units can be wired directly to sensors and so connect to the world.

But the weaknesses are also the mirror image, and they cluster around structure.

Connectionist systems have historically struggled with compositionality and systematicity, the very things symbols do so well, because it is not obvious how a blurry pattern of activity keeps the parts of a complex thought neatly separable and recombinable.

A sharp form of this difficulty is the binding problem, which is the question of how a system keeps track of which features belong together.

Imagine a network sees a red circle and a blue square, and it lights up units for red, blue, circle, and square all at once: how does it remember that red goes with circle and blue with square, rather than mixing them into a blue circle and a red square?

In systems terms this is a missing tagging mechanism: the design publishes feature signals on a shared bus without an agreed scheme for marking which signals belong to the same object.

Critics such as Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn pressed exactly this point in 1988, arguing that without built in structure a network cannot guarantee the systematic, rule respecting character of thought.

Defenders reply that networks can learn approximate structure, and much recent research tries to get the best of both worlds, a theme we return to at the end of the chapter.

3.3 Dynamical, embodied, and enactive approaches

The third family of ideas challenges something both earlier paradigms took for granted: that thinking is basically computation happening inside the head.

This section introduces a looser cluster of views that treat the mind as an unfolding process spread across brain, body, and world.

3.3.1 Cognition as continuous dynamics rather than discrete computation

Let us first meet the mathematical mood of this approach, because it changes the very language used to describe thought.

The dynamical approach says that the mind is better understood as a continuously changing physical system than as a step by step manipulation of symbols.

The key piece of jargon is a dynamical system, which simply means any system whose state changes smoothly over time according to fixed laws, the way the swing of a pendulum, the sloshing of water, or the weather all evolve moment by moment.

On this view, instead of asking what computational steps the mind takes, we ask how its state flows and settles, using the mathematics of change rather than the mathematics of logic.

As a system design, this paradigm specifies a continuous state vector as the data format, differential change laws as the processing, and real physical time as a first-class citizen: timing is part of the specification, not an implementation detail.

A vivid example comes from the psychologist Esther Thelen and colleagues studying how babies learn to reach and to walk, where behaviour emerges from the shifting balance of muscle, gravity, and practice rather than from a stored program.

The point is not that no computing happens, but that treating the mind as a bunch of discrete symbol steps may miss the smooth, timed, whole body nature of much real behaviour.

Where a symbolic model tends to ignore timing, a dynamical model puts timing at the very centre.

3.3.2 The body and the environment as parts of the cognitive system

Now for the even bolder move, which is to let the mind spill out beyond the skull.

Embodied cognition is the view that the shape and workings of the body deeply influence and even constitute thinking, so that we think with our bodies and not only with our brains.

Enactive cognition, a term from Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch in their 1991 book The Embodied Mind, adds that a creature brings forth its world through its own activity, so that knowing and doing are woven together rather than separate.

There is also the extended mind idea, argued by Andy Clark and David Chalmers in a 1998 paper, that tools like a notebook or a phone can literally be part of the thinking system, not just aids to a thinking that happens only inside.

In systems terms this whole family redraws the system boundary: where the other paradigms draw the box around the brain, these views draw it around the closed loop of brain, body, and environment, so the paper you scribble on is inside the system's state and the sensing-acting cycle is the system's main loop.

An everyday example: when you work out a hard sum by jotting figures on paper, the paper is doing part of the remembering, so the calculation is really happening across you and the page together.

Another example is that we often gesture with our hands while speaking, and evidence suggests the gestures help the thinking along rather than merely decorating it.

The shared message of these embodied and enactive views is that a mind is not a lonely computer in a box but a living body actively coupled to its surroundings.

Not everyone accepts the strongest versions of these claims, and critics argue that much of thought, such as planning a holiday or doing algebra, still looks like internal computation, so this remains a lively and unsettled debate.

3.4 Bayesian and probabilistic approaches

The fourth big idea returns to the head but changes what it thinks the head is doing: not shuffling certain facts, but weighing uncertain bets.

This section explains how treating the mind as a machine for reasoning under uncertainty has become one of the most influential frameworks in recent decades.

3.4.1 The mind as an engine of inductive inference under uncertainty

Let us start with the core insight, which is that the world rarely tells us anything for sure.

The Bayesian approach says the mind works like an engine of inference under uncertainty, constantly forming best guesses about hidden causes from limited, noisy evidence.

Inductive inference means reasoning from particular observations to general conclusions that go beyond the evidence, such as concluding from a few white swans that swans tend to be white, a leap that can never be perfectly certain.

The approach is named after Thomas Bayes, an eighteenth century English clergyman, whose rule, called Bayes theorem, is a formula for updating your confidence in an idea when new evidence arrives.

In plain terms, the rule says: start with how likely you thought something was, called the prior, then adjust it in light of how well it predicted the new evidence, to reach an updated belief, called the posterior.

A homely example is a doctor who starts with a hunch about what is wrong, called the prior, then updates that hunch as test results come in, arriving at a revised diagnosis, the posterior.

As a system design, this paradigm specifies probability distributions as the data format, Bayes theorem as the update rule, the prior as the persistent state carried between updates, and evidence strength as the gain that decides how far each observation moves the belief.

The claim of Bayesian cognitive science, developed by researchers such as Joshua Tenenbaum, Thomas Griffiths, and colleagues from the early 2000s onward, is that perception, learning, and reasoning all look, at the level of the whole task, like this kind of rational updating.

Perception itself can be seen this way: your eye receives an ambiguous smear of light, and your brain settles on the most probable scene that could have produced it, which is why optical illusions fool us in systematic, predictable ways.

3.4.2 Structured probabilistic knowledge and learning-to-learn

Now for the part that lets this approach reach beyond simple guessing games toward the richness of real knowledge.

The newer Bayesian models do not treat the mind as juggling loose probabilities in a vacuum; they give it structured knowledge, meaning organised background assumptions about how the world tends to work.

For instance, a child learning words seems to assume in advance that a new word probably labels a whole object of a familiar kind, and this built in expectation lets the child learn a word from very few examples, sometimes just one.

Learning from very few examples is a real human talent, and the Bayesian answer is that strong prior structure does the heavy lifting that scarce data cannot.

There is also learning to learn, sometimes called forming a hierarchical model, which means that while solving specific problems you also learn the more general shape of that kind of problem, so the next one comes faster.

A concrete case: after learning to read a few different alphabets, you get better at learning any new alphabet, because you have learned what alphabets in general are like.

In systems terms a hierarchical model is a stack of update loops running at different speeds: the fast loop updates beliefs about the current problem in seconds, while the slow loop updates beliefs about the whole class of problems over days and years, and the slow loop's output becomes the fast loop's prior.

This blend of structure and probability is deliberately trying to marry the strengths of the symbolic paradigm, which loves structure, with the strengths of the statistical paradigm, which loves learning from data, and that ambition points us straight to the final section.

3.5 How the paradigms relate

Having met the four ways of seeing, we now step back and ask the natural question: are they enemies, teammates, or something in between?

This section describes how the paradigms have competed and cooperated, and then explains the particular stance that this book, and the konnectome project it belongs to, chooses to take.

3.5.1 Rivalry, division of labour, and attempts at reconciliation

Let us be honest that the history here has often been combative, because that is part of understanding where we are now.

For a long stretch the paradigms were rivals, each presented as the one true account, and the sharpest clash was the debate between symbolic and connectionist camps in the late 1980s, with Fodor and Pylyshyn on one side arguing that networks lacked real structure.

Over time many researchers softened into a division of labour, the idea that different paradigms simply suit different jobs: symbols for language and reasoning, networks for perception and skill, dynamics for real time movement, probability for judgement under uncertainty.

In systems terms that division assigns each design to the layer where its assumptions hold: discrete serial processing for slow deliberate tasks, parallel pattern completion for fast perceptual tasks, continuous control for the motor loop, and probabilistic updating wherever evidence is noisy.

Others have pushed for outright reconciliation, building hybrid or neurosymbolic systems, a term meaning systems that deliberately combine neural networks with symbolic rules so as to get learning and structure at once.

The Bayesian program can itself be read as a peace treaty, since its structured probabilistic models put symbol like structure and data driven learning inside a single framework.

Yet no grand unified theory of the mind has won general agreement, and thoughtful researchers still disagree about whether one paradigm is fundamental or whether the mind is genuinely many kinds of process at once, so this remains open.

3.5.2 Why konnectome treats them as complementary constraints rather than competitors

Finally, here is the attitude this book adopts, and the reason for it, stated plainly.

Konnectome is the name of the larger project this book belongs to, and its working stance is that the paradigms are best treated not as competitors fighting for a single throne but as complementary constraints.

A constraint, in plain words, is a requirement that any good answer has to respect, like the walls of a maze that any correct path must stay within.

An engineer will recognize this as reading the four paradigms not as four finished designs but as four sections of one requirements document that the true design must satisfy simultaneously.

The thought is that each paradigm has discovered something true that a complete account of the mind must honour: thought really is systematic and structured, as the symbolists insist; it really is learned, robust, and pattern rich, as the connectionists show; it really is timed, embodied, and world coupled, as the dynamical and enactive thinkers argue; and it really is a matter of sensible inference under uncertainty, as the Bayesians demonstrate.

Seen this way, a mind is whatever manages to satisfy all of these constraints at once, and the job of the science is to find the design that meets every demand rather than to crown one demand as the only one.

This is a deliberately humble and integrative posture: instead of asking which paradigm is right, konnectome asks what each one is telling us that must be kept, and treats the disagreements as clues to a richer picture rather than as a contest to be settled.

Keep this stance in mind as you read on, because the chapters ahead will keep drawing on all four ways of seeing rather than betting everything on one.


We close the chapter by writing the interface that all four rival designs are trying to implement: the belief-updating engine that takes evidence in and puts revised beliefs and choices out.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Evidence: observations from perception, noisy and incomplete, arriving as a stream over time.

◦ Task context: the current goal and situation, which determines which beliefs and rules are relevant.

◦ Feedback: the outcomes of past choices, which grade the quality of previous updates.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Updated beliefs: revised estimates of what is true, consumed by reasoning, perception, and planning.

◦ Selected actions: the rule firings or choices the current beliefs and goals recommend, consumed by the action system.

◦ Uncertainty estimates: how confident the system is, consumed by processes that decide whether to gather more evidence.

• STATE.

◦ The knowledge base: rules and symbol structures on the symbolic reading, a weight matrix on the connectionist reading, priors on the Bayesian reading.

◦ Working contents: the currently active facts, patterns, or hypotheses being processed.

◦ Slow structural knowledge: the learned shape of whole problem classes, the learning-to-learn layer.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Learning rate: how far one experience moves the knowledge base.

◦ Prior strength: how heavily existing expectations outweigh fresh evidence.

◦ Rule specificity and conflict resolution settings: which rule fires when several match, in production system terms.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ One production rule firing in human cognitive architectures: about 50 milliseconds.

◦ One elementary recognition or pattern completion step: on the order of 100 milliseconds.

◦ Belief revision across a task: seconds to minutes as evidence accumulates.

◦ Settling time of a dynamical account of an arbitrary thought process: REFUSED, because settling times are specific to each modelled system and no general literature value exists.

• MODES.

◦ Structure-driven mode: explicit rule application dominates, engaged for novel, verbal, or logical tasks.

◦ Pattern-driven mode: learned associations dominate, engaged for familiar, fast, perceptual tasks, with practice shifting tasks from the first mode to the second.

◦ Exploration versus exploitation: gathering more evidence when uncertainty is high, acting on current beliefs when it is low.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Symbolic failure: brittleness and groundlessness, where rules break outside their designed cases and tokens fail to connect to the world.

◦ Connectionist failure: binding errors and loss of systematic structure, where features are mixed across objects.

◦ Bayesian failure: bad priors, where an overweighted expectation makes the system see what it expects rather than what is there, the mechanical signature of many biases and illusions.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called prior with initial value zero point five, the belief that the coin is biased.
Create a number variable called likelihood_biased with value zero point eight, the chance a biased coin shows heads.
Create a number variable called likelihood_fair with value zero point five, the chance a fair coin shows heads.
Create a list variable called observations containing the observed coin flips.
For each observation in the observations list, do the following.
    If the observation is heads, then do the following.
        Set a number variable called evidence_biased to the likelihood_biased value.
        Set a number variable called evidence_fair to the likelihood_fair value.
    Otherwise, do the following.
        Set the evidence_biased variable to one minus the likelihood_biased value.
        Set the evidence_fair variable to one minus the likelihood_fair value.
    Set a number variable called numerator to the product of the evidence_biased and the prior.
    Set a number variable called denominator to the numerator plus the product of the evidence_fair and one minus the prior.
    Set the prior to the numerator divided by the denominator.
    Print the observation and the updated prior.
If the final prior is greater than zero point five, then print that the system believes the coin is biased.
Otherwise, print that the system believes the coin is fair.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Define a function that updates a belief about a biased coin from a list of flips
def bayesian_coin_judge(observations):
    # Create a number variable called prior with initial value zero point five
    prior = 0.5
    # Create a number variable called likelihood_biased with value zero point eight
    likelihood_biased = 0.8
    # Create a number variable called likelihood_fair with value zero point five
    likelihood_fair = 0.5
    # For each observation in the observations list, do the following
    for observation in observations:
        # If the observation is heads, use the heads likelihoods
        if observation == "heads":
            # Set evidence_biased to the likelihood of heads under the biased hypothesis
            evidence_biased = likelihood_biased
            # Set evidence_fair to the likelihood of heads under the fair hypothesis
            evidence_fair = likelihood_fair
        # Otherwise, use the tails likelihoods
        else:
            # Set evidence_biased to one minus the likelihood of heads under the biased hypothesis
            evidence_biased = 1.0 - likelihood_biased
            # Set evidence_fair to one minus the likelihood of heads under the fair hypothesis
            evidence_fair = 1.0 - likelihood_fair
        # Set numerator to the product of evidence_biased and the prior
        numerator = evidence_biased * prior
        # Set denominator to the numerator plus the product of evidence_fair and one minus the prior
        denominator = numerator + evidence_fair * (1.0 - prior)
        # Set the prior to the numerator divided by the denominator, which is Bayes theorem
        prior = numerator / denominator
        # Print the observation and the updated belief
        print(observation, "-> belief coin is biased:", round(prior, 3))
    # Return the final belief
    return prior

# Create a list variable called flips containing a run of observed coin flips
flips = ["heads", "heads", "tails", "heads", "heads", "heads"]
# Call the bayesian_coin_judge function on the flips list
final_belief = bayesian_coin_judge(flips)
# If the final belief is greater than zero point five, report a biased verdict
if final_belief > 0.5:
    # Print that the system believes the coin is biased
    print("verdict: the coin is probably biased")
# Otherwise, report a fair verdict
else:
    # Print that the system believes the coin is fair
    print("verdict: the coin is probably fair")


CHAPTER 4. LEVELS OF ANALYSIS AND EXPLANATION (FRAMEWORK)

Welcome to a chapter about a simple but powerful idea: that a thinking system can be understood at several different heights at once, and that each height answers a different kind of question.

Imagine you are trying to understand a pocket calculator.

You could ask what job it does, or how it does that job step by step, or what it is physically made of.

Those are three separate questions, and confusing them causes most of the muddles in the study of the mind.

Every engineer already knows this distinction by other names: the specification says what the system must do, the algorithm and data structures say how it does it, and the hardware says what physically runs it, and no one would debug a program by measuring the temperature of the chip.

This chapter gives you a set of lenses - ways of looking - that let you keep those questions apart, and then shows you how leading thinkers argued about which lens matters most.

4.1 Marr's three levels

The most famous version of this idea comes from David Marr, a British scientist who studied vision in the 1970s and wrote a book, published after his early death in 1982, called simply Vision.

Marr proposed that any system that processes information should be understood at three levels at the same time, and that a full explanation needs all three.

The sections below walk through each level in turn, and then look at how the levels relate to one another.

4.1.1 The computational level: the problem and why it must be solved

The computational level asks a plain question: what problem is the system actually trying to solve, and why is that a sensible problem to solve?

Here the word computational does not mean a computer chip; it means the abstract job of turning some input into some useful output.

In engineering language this level is the specification: the contract that names the inputs, the required outputs, and the reason the mapping matters, while saying nothing about how it is achieved.

Think of a cash register at a shop: at this top level, its job is to take a list of prices and return the correct total.

Notice that this description says nothing about buttons, wiring, or the exact method of adding.

It only names the goal and the logic of the goal - the what and the why, not the how.

Marr argued that this level is the one people most often skip, and that skipping it is a serious mistake.

His reason was that you cannot understand a device by studying its parts if you do not first know what the device is for.

As an everyday example, he pointed out that studying the feathers of a bird will never, on its own, explain flight; you first have to understand the problem of staying up in the air.

For vision, the computational question is something like: given the pattern of light hitting the eye, what in the outside world produced that pattern?

That is a genuinely hard problem, because many different scenes can produce the same image, and the brain must make a good guess.

Stating the problem clearly, at this level, tells you what a solution would even look like.

4.1.2 The algorithmic and representational level: the representations and processes

The second level asks how the problem is solved: what recipe, or step by step procedure, does the system follow, and what form does the information take along the way?

A step by step procedure for solving a problem is called an algorithm, and a representation is simply a chosen way of writing down information so it can be worked on.

For an engineer this level is the algorithms and data structures layer: the same specification can be met by many implementations, and choosing the data format largely decides which algorithms are cheap.

Consider adding two numbers.

You could represent them as everyday decimal numerals, the ones with digits 0 through 9, or as Roman numerals like IX and IV, or as the strings of 0s and 1s that a computer uses, called binary.

The problem being solved is the same in every case, namely finding the sum, but the representation differs, and the algorithm you use to add differs with it.

That is the key insight of this level: the same top level goal can be reached by different methods, and choosing the representation and the method is a real design decision with real consequences.

Some representations make a task easy and some make it clumsy; adding is simple with decimal numerals and painful with Roman ones.

For vision, this level would describe the particular steps the brain might take to find the edges of objects, and the particular way it stores what it has found so far.

The important thing for a beginner to hold onto is that this level is about method and format, sitting underneath the goal and above the physical hardware.

4.1.3 The implementational level: the physical realisation

The third level asks the most concrete question: what physical stuff actually carries out the procedure, and how?

This is called the implementational level, where to implement something means to build it in real material that obeys the laws of physics.

In a calculator, this level is the silicon chips, the electrical currents, and the tiny switches called transistors.

In a person, this level is the living nerve cells, called neurons, and the chemical and electrical signals that pass between them.

Marr's point was that the very same algorithm could be run on very different hardware.

The rules of addition can be carried out by a wet human brain, by a metal and silicon computer, by beads on an abacus, or even by water flowing through pipes if you were patient enough.

Because of this, knowing the physical details alone does not tell you the algorithm, and knowing the algorithm alone does not tell you the physical details.

Each level has facts of its own that the others do not fix, though the hardware does set the timing budget: a neuron signals in about a millisecond, a transistor switches in under a nanosecond, and that difference constrains which algorithms each substrate can afford to run.

4.1.4 The independence and the interaction of the levels

Having separated the three levels, we now have to be careful, because they are partly independent and partly tangled together.

They are independent in the sense that you can describe one without fully describing the others, which is why the same goal can have many algorithms and the same algorithm can have many physical builds.

This independence is genuinely useful, because it lets a psychologist study the method of thinking without first mapping every neuron, and lets a neuroscientist study brain tissue without first solving the whole puzzle of the mind.

In engineering terms the levels are an abstraction stack, and abstraction is precisely the discipline of working at one layer while trusting the interfaces to the layers above and below.

But the levels also interact, and this is where careful thinkers disagree.

The physical hardware can make some algorithms fast and cheap and others slow and expensive, so the choice of hardware quietly pushes on the choice of method, just as a chip's memory layout quietly pushes a programmer toward certain data structures.

Likewise, the problem you are trying to solve shapes which algorithms are even worth considering.

So the honest picture is a loose hierarchy, meaning a ranking of levels that constrain each other without any one level completely dictating the others.

Marr himself stressed the top down direction, believing that understanding the problem should guide everything below it, but he did not claim the levels were sealed off from one another.

4.2 Companion tri-level schemes

Marr was not the only thinker to slice the mind into levels, and it helps a beginner to see that several respected schemes rhyme with his.

Seeing the family resemblance makes the underlying idea clearer, and seeing the differences shows where the real debates live.

The following sections introduce four other well known frameworks, each from a major figure in the cognitive sciences.

4.2.1 Chomsky's competence and performance

Noam Chomsky, an American linguist whose work reshaped the study of language starting in the late 1950s, drew a line between competence and performance.

Competence is the underlying knowledge a person has of their language, the silent set of rules that tells them which sentences are well formed.

Performance is what the person actually does in real time, complete with slips of the tongue, forgotten words, coughs, and false starts.

Here is an everyday example: you know, deep down, that a very long sentence with many clauses stacked inside it can still be grammatical, yet in practice you would lose track of it halfway through.

Your competence says the sentence is fine; your performance breaks down.

An engineer would say competence is the specification of the language system and performance is the runtime behavior of its implementation, complete with buffer limits and dropped packets, so the two can legitimately disagree.

Chomsky argued that the science of language should aim first at competence, the clean underlying knowledge, rather than at the noisy surface of performance.

This maps loosely onto Marr, because competence is close to a computational level description of what the language system knows, while performance leans toward the algorithmic and physical business of producing speech under real world limits.

4.2.2 Newell's bands and time scales, from the biological to the social

Allen Newell, an American researcher who helped found the field of artificial intelligence, offered a scheme organised by time rather than by abstraction.

Artificial intelligence, often shortened to AI, is the effort to build machines that carry out tasks we would call intelligent in a human.

In his 1990 book Unified Theories of Cognition, Newell described human action as a stack of bands, where each band is a range of time scales at which different things happen.

At the fastest, the biological band, events in single neurons take roughly thousandths of a second.

Above that sits the cognitive band, where basic mental steps take on the order of tenths of a second to a few seconds.

Higher still is the rational band, covering minutes to hours, where a person pursues goals in a way that looks sensibly planned.

At the top is the social band, spanning days, years, and generations, where whole communities shape behaviour.

Newell's message was that phenomena at each time scale call for their own kind of explanation, and that you should not expect the vocabulary of milliseconds to explain the vocabulary of years.

This is a levels idea told through the clock, and every systems engineer uses the same trick: hardware clock cycles, request latencies, deployment cycles, and product lifetimes are analysed with different tools precisely because they live in different bands.

It pairs naturally with Marr's more abstract ladder, and this book's TIME CONSTANTS blocks are Newell's idea applied one process at a time.

4.2.3 Pylyshyn's functional architecture and cognitive penetrability

Zenon Pylyshyn, a Canadian cognitive scientist, gave us two ideas that sharpen the boundary between Marr's middle and bottom levels.

The first is functional architecture, which means the fixed, built in operations of the mind that are not themselves changed by what you happen to believe or want.

Think of it as the basic instruction set of the mind, the primitive moves that everything else is built out of, exactly as a processor's instruction set is fixed while the programs running on it change freely.

The second idea is cognitive penetrability, which is a test for telling which processes belong to that fixed architecture and which do not.

A process is cognitively penetrable if your beliefs, goals, or knowledge can reach in and change how it works.

In systems terms the test asks whether a component exposes a configuration interface to the rest of the system: penetrable processes accept runtime reconfiguration by beliefs and goals, while architectural processes run the same way no matter what the higher layers know.

Here is the classic example: certain visual illusions do not go away even after you are told, and fully believe, that the two lines are the same length.

Because your knowledge cannot penetrate and fix the illusion, Pylyshyn argued that the part of vision producing it is part of the fixed architecture rather than part of ordinary reasoning.

This gives researchers a practical way to draw the line between the changeable software of thought and the fixed machinery beneath it.

4.2.4 Dennett's physical, design, and intentional stances

Daniel Dennett, an American philosopher, approached levels from the side of the observer, asking not what a system is but what stance you should take to predict it best.

A stance here just means a viewpoint you adopt in order to make sense of something.

The physical stance predicts a thing purely from its material and the laws of physics; you use it when you expect a dropped rock to fall.

The design stance predicts a thing from what it was built or evolved to do, without worrying about its physics; you use it when you assume an alarm clock will ring because that is what alarm clocks are for.

The intentional stance predicts a thing by treating it as if it had beliefs and desires and acted rationally on them; you use it when you say the chess program moved its bishop because it wanted to protect its king.

Dennett's clever point is that the intentional stance can be wildly useful even for systems that do not literally have minds, because it lets us predict complex behaviour quickly.

An engineer switches stances all day without noticing: debugging a burned board is the physical stance, reading an interface contract is the design stance, and saying the load balancer wants to drain that node is the intentional stance, each chosen for predictive convenience.

These three stances echo Marr's levels, with the physical stance near implementation, the design stance near the algorithm and the problem, and the intentional stance sitting at the highest, most goal focused view.

4.3 The debate over levels

So far the levels have looked tidy, but researchers have argued hard about how they fit together and which one deserves priority.

These disagreements are not idle; they shape how billions are spent on brain research and how findings are interpreted.

The following sections lay out three of the central arguments in plain terms.

4.3.1 The claim that algorithm constrains computation

One line of argument pushes back on Marr's top down spirit by insisting that the middle level, the algorithm, actually limits what counts as the right problem description.

The idea is that a purely abstract statement of the problem is too loose, because it ignores that the brain has finite time and finite resources.

Once you take those limits seriously, the argument goes, the set of realistic algorithms narrows the sensible problem descriptions rather than the other way round.

For example, describing vision as finding the single mathematically perfect interpretation of an image may be the wrong top level goal, because no fast algorithm could ever compute it.

A better top level description might be finding a good enough answer quickly, precisely because that is what an achievable algorithm can deliver.

Every engineer has lived this argument: a specification that no implementation can meet within the latency budget is a wrong specification, and requirements get rewritten to match what the platform can actually deliver.

On this view the levels talk back to each other from the bottom up, and computation cannot be settled in splendid isolation from the methods available.

4.3.2 The warning that neuroscience needs behaviour

A second and much discussed argument warns that studying the brain's physical level without a clear account of behaviour can fail to explain anything.

This point was made vividly by Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording in a 2017 paper with a memorable setup.

They took a microprocessor, a simple computer chip whose every wire is already fully understood, and applied to it the very methods neuroscientists use on brains.

Despite having complete access to the chip, those methods failed to recover how the chip actually worked, or what program it was running.

The lesson they drew is that mountains of physical detail do not, by themselves, add up to understanding, and that without a firm grip on the higher levels the data can mislead.

In systems terms: probing voltages on a running chip, with no concept of instructions, programs, or tasks, produces data without a decoder, because the meaning of the hardware activity lives at the levels above it.

In Marr's language, this is a plea not to drown at the implementational level while ignoring the computational and algorithmic questions that give the data meaning.

Not everyone agrees the analogy is airtight, since brains and chips differ in important ways, but the warning is widely taken to heart.

4.3.3 Reverse engineering versus mechanistic explanation

A third debate is about what kind of explanation we are even after, and here two camps use different words for the goal.

Reverse engineering means starting from what a system does and working backward to figure out the design that would achieve it, much as one might take apart a rival's gadget to learn its trick.

This way of thinking is very comfortable with Marr's top down order, since it begins from the problem and the function.

The rival view prizes mechanistic explanation, which means describing the actual parts of a system and showing, concretely, how their arrangement and activity produce the behaviour.

A mechanism, in this sense, is a set of real components whose organised interaction makes something happen, like the gears and springs that together make a watch tell time.

Supporters of mechanistic explanation worry that reverse engineering can drift into just so stories, tidy tales of what the system might be for that are never grounded in real parts.

Supporters of reverse engineering reply that a heap of parts explains nothing until you know the function they serve.

In systems terms the two camps would deliver different documents: the reverse engineers a specification with a proposed design, the mechanists a verified wiring diagram with traced causal paths, and a complete explanation plainly needs both documents to agree.

Many researchers now try to hold both, seeking accounts that are both function first and honestly tied to the machinery, and this blended aim leads directly into the next section.

4.4 Cognitive computational neuroscience as the level-bridging programme

There is now a research programme whose whole purpose is to connect the levels rather than choose among them, and it goes by the name cognitive computational neuroscience.

The phrase stacks three ideas: cognitive, meaning about the mind and its tasks; computational, meaning built from precise, runnable models; and neuroscience, meaning grounded in the biology of the brain.

The aim is to build models that answer the what and why, spell out the how, and still match what real brains do.

The following two sections describe the main tools this programme uses to stitch the levels together.

4.4.1 Model classes that span the levels

A model, in this setting, is a working system, usually a computer program, that is meant to stand in for some part of the mind or brain so that its behaviour can be tested against reality.

Different families of models sit at different heights, and the programme deliberately uses several so that the levels can be linked.

At the top sit task models, which capture only the goal and the ideal solution, close to Marr's computational level.

In the middle sit process models and, importantly, neural network models, which are systems of many simple units loosely inspired by neurons that learn to perform a task by adjusting the strengths of their connections.

These network models are prized here precisely because a single model can both perform a real task, honouring the top level, and produce internal activity that can be compared with brain activity, reaching toward the bottom level.

At the most detailed end sit biophysical models, which try to reproduce the electrical and chemical behaviour of actual neurons.

In systems terms the programme maintains one model per abstraction layer and checks that the layers stay consistent, the way an engineering team keeps a specification, a reference implementation, and a hardware design in sync.

By moving deliberately among these classes, researchers can ask how a change at one level shows up at another, which is exactly the bridging that earlier debates found so hard.

4.4.2 Representational comparison between models and brains

The final tool is a way of checking whether a model and a brain are handling information in a similar way, even when they are built of utterly different stuff.

The trick is to compare representations, meaning the internal patterns of activity that stand for things, rather than comparing the hardware directly.

A widely used version of this is called representational similarity analysis, which works on a clever principle.

Instead of asking whether a model and a brain light up in the same physical spots, it asks whether they treat the same things as similar and the same things as different.

For instance, if a brain treats a cat and a dog as more alike than a cat and a car, a good model of that brain should do the same, sorting the items into the same web of similarities.

Because this method compares patterns of sameness and difference, it can line up a computer model against living brain tissue despite their having nothing physical in common.

In systems terms it is a hardware-independent conformance test: instead of diffing the internals byte for byte, it checks that two implementations induce the same similarity structure over the same inputs, which is a test any two realisations of one algorithm should pass.

That is a direct, practical bridge between Marr's algorithmic level, where representations live, and his implementational level, where brains do their work.

With this tool, the old question of how the levels connect stops being only a matter of argument and becomes something researchers can measure.


We close the chapter by writing the levels framework itself as a system: the analysis engine a researcher runs when explaining any information-processing device.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ The target system's behaviour: input-output records from experiments, the evidence every level must answer to.

◦ The target system's physical measurements: recordings and images of the hardware in action.

◦ Candidate task descriptions: proposed statements of what problem the system is solving and why.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A computational level account: the specification, naming the problem and its logic, consumed by theorists and model builders.

◦ An algorithmic level account: the proposed representations and procedures, consumed by process modellers and by artificial intelligence builders.

◦ An implementational level account: the mapping from procedure to physical machinery, consumed by neuroscientists and engineers.

• STATE.

◦ The current best hypothesis at each level, held simultaneously and revised as evidence arrives.

◦ The recorded constraints each level currently places on the others, such as timing budgets and resource limits.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Direction of emphasis: how strongly top down problem-first reasoning is weighted against bottom up mechanism-first reasoning.

◦ Resource realism: how strictly candidate specifications are required to be computable within the hardware's time and energy budget.

◦ Penetrability threshold: the evidence required to classify a process as fixed architecture rather than changeable strategy.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Biological band events in single neurons: on the order of 1 millisecond.

◦ Cognitive band elementary steps: on the order of 100 milliseconds to a few seconds.

◦ Rational band goal pursuit: minutes to hours.

◦ Social band change: days to generations.

◦ A characteristic duration for the analysis process itself: REFUSED, because how long it takes a research community to settle a levels question is not a quantity the literature supports with a number.

• MODES.

◦ Top down mode: analysis starts from the task and works toward the machinery, triggered when the function is clear and the mechanism is obscure.

◦ Bottom up mode: analysis starts from the machinery and works toward the task, triggered when rich physical data exist but the function is uncertain.

◦ Bridging mode: models at several levels are run and compared at once, triggered when both kinds of account exist and must be reconciled, as in cognitive computational neuroscience.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Level confusion: answering a question posed at one level with facts from another, the root of most muddles this chapter warns about.

◦ Drowning in implementation: collecting physical detail without higher level accounts, the failure the microprocessor study dramatised.

◦ Just so storytelling: accepting an elegant top level account that is never checked against the parts, the failure the mechanists warn about.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called prices containing the input numbers, the shared computational level problem.
Define a function called sum_left_to_right that takes a list of numbers.
    Create a number variable called total with initial value zero.
    For each price in the list, add the price to the total.
    Return the total.
Define a function called sum_by_pairing that takes a list of numbers.
    Copy the list into a working list.
    While the working list has more than one item, do the following.
        Remove the first two items from the working list.
        Calculate their sum.
        Append the sum to the end of the working list.
    Return the single remaining item.
Call the sum_left_to_right function on the prices list and store the result.
Call the sum_by_pairing function on the prices list and store the result.
If the two results are equal, then print that two different algorithms satisfied the same computational level specification.
Otherwise, print that an implementation has a bug.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Define a function that sums a list left to right, the first algorithmic level design
def sum_left_to_right(numbers):
    # Create a number variable called total with initial value zero
    total = 0
    # For each price in the numbers list, add the price to the total
    for price in numbers:
        # Add the price to the total
        total = total + price
    # Return the total
    return total

# Define a function that sums a list by repeated pairing, a second algorithmic level design
def sum_by_pairing(numbers):
    # Copy the numbers list into a working list
    working = list(numbers)
    # While the working list has more than one item, do the following
    while len(working) > 1:
        # Remove the first item from the working list
        first = working.pop(0)
        # Remove the next item from the working list
        second = working.pop(0)
        # Append the sum of the two removed items to the end of the working list
        working.append(first + second)
    # Return the single remaining item
    return working[0]

# Create a list variable called prices, the input named by the computational level specification
prices = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
# Call the sum_left_to_right function on the prices list and store the result
result_one = sum_left_to_right(prices)
# Call the sum_by_pairing function on the prices list and store the result
result_two = sum_by_pairing(prices)
# If the two results are equal, the two algorithms meet the same specification
if result_one == result_two:
    # Print that two different algorithms satisfied the same computational level specification
    print("same spec, two algorithms, one answer:", result_one)
# Otherwise, an implementation has a bug
else:
    # Print that an implementation has a bug
    print("implementations disagree:", result_one, result_two)

CHAPTER 5. THE METHODS OF COGNITIVE SCIENCE (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter is about the toolbox.

Cognition happens inside the head, where nobody can watch it directly, so the science of the mind lives or dies by the cleverness of its methods for measuring something invisible.

This chapter walks through those methods, from the simple stopwatch experiment to brain scanners and computer models, and it asks a plain but important question about each one: how do we know it is telling us the truth?

The tag (FRAMEWORK) means this chapter does not describe a mental capacity itself.

Instead it describes the tools and rules that let us study those capacities carefully, so that the later chapters can rest on solid ground.

Read as a systems engineer would, every method in this chapter is a measurement channel: it takes hidden internal state as input, produces an observable number as output, and adds its own noise and bias along the way, so the recurring engineering question is how to recover the hidden signal from the corrupted reading.


5.1 The logic of the behavioural experiment

Before any fancy equipment, the oldest and still the most powerful tool in the field is the controlled experiment.

The idea is simple: change one thing on purpose, hold everything else steady, and watch what happens to behaviour.

This section lays out the basic grammar of that method, the vocabulary and the safeguards that turn a casual observation into evidence.

In systems terms, an experiment is a probe of a black box: the experimenter drives one input line while clamping the others, and reads the output to infer the transfer function inside.


5.1.1 Independent, dependent, and control variables; within and between designs

An experiment is a way of asking nature a yes-or-no question by deliberately changing something and measuring the result.

The thing the researcher deliberately changes is called the independent variable, which just means the input that the experimenter sets, for example whether a word is shown for a short time or a long time.

The thing the researcher measures is called the dependent variable, which means the outcome that is allowed to vary and that presumably depends on the input, for example how many words a person later remembers.

A control variable is anything the researcher holds constant on purpose so that it cannot muddy the result, for example keeping the room equally bright for every person.

The logic is that if only the independent variable was allowed to change, then any change in the dependent variable can be blamed on it and on nothing else.

There are two broad ways to arrange the people in a study.

In a within-subjects design, the same person experiences every condition, so each person is compared against themselves, which is efficient and cancels out the fact that people naturally differ.

In a between-subjects design, different groups of people each experience only one condition, which avoids the problem that doing one condition might teach or tire a person before they reach the next.

Neither design is universally better, and choosing between them is one of the first real decisions a researcher makes.

As a system, the design maps directly onto signal processing: the independent variable is the controlled input, the dependent variable is the measured output, control variables are clamped inputs, and the within versus between choice is a choice between reusing one noisy channel repeatedly or averaging across many parallel channels.


5.1.2 Confounds, counterbalancing, and the validities

A confound is a hidden second thing that changed at the same time as the thing you meant to change, so that you cannot tell which of the two caused the result.

For example, if the hard problems were always shown in the morning and the easy problems always in the afternoon, then tiredness is a confound, because time of day sneaked in alongside difficulty.

Counterbalancing is the standard cure for one common confound, the confound of order.

It means giving different people the conditions in different sequences, so that being first or last is spread evenly across conditions and cannot favour any one of them.

Researchers also worry about several kinds of validity, which is a word for the different ways a study can be trustworthy or not.

Internal validity is the confidence that the change you made, and not some confound, really caused the result.
