Attention enters as a bias, an extra push that favours the neurons representing the attended object, so that they win the competition and the attended object comes to dominate the neuron's response.

Single-cell recordings in monkeys supported this directly: when two stimuli sat in a cell's receptive field the response was intermediate, but when the animal attended to one of them the response shifted toward the value that stimulus would produce on its own.

The systems reading is that selection is implemented not by a separate router but by weighting an existing winner-take-most competition: the inputs are competing stimulus drives plus a small top-down bias term, and the output is a neural response drawn toward the biased stimulus, all unfolding within tens to a few hundred milliseconds of stimulus onset.

The appeal of biased competition is that it explains selection without any separate spotlight mechanism, treating attention instead as a thumb on the scale of an ordinary neural contest.


14.3.2 Attentional modulation of neural gain

Gain is an engineering word for how strongly a system amplifies its input, like the volume knob that sets how loudly a faint signal comes through, and gain modulation means attention turning that knob.

The central finding is that attending to a stimulus increases the responses of the neurons that represent it, effectively amplifying the attended signal relative to the ignored background.

This shows up in several ways: attended stimuli produce larger neural responses, the baseline activity of relevant neurons can rise even before a stimulus appears, and the sharpness with which neurons distinguish stimuli can improve.

One useful way to summarise the effect is that attention improves the signal-to-noise ratio, meaning it makes the wanted signal stand out more clearly against random background activity.

In systems terms, gain modulation is a multiplicative control input: the attended channel's output equals its input times a gain slightly above one, the ignored channel's gain sits at or below one, and the pre-stimulus baseline shift is the controller warming up the selected channel before data arrive.

Gain modulation and biased competition are not rivals so much as two descriptions of the same underlying process, since boosting the gain of the attended neurons is one natural way to bias the competition in their favour.

Together they give the field a mechanistic account of selection, connecting the everyday experience of concentrating on something to concrete, measurable changes in how brain cells fire.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Retinotopic feature maps: location-tagged sensory activity from early visual cortex.

◦ Exogenous events: abrupt onsets and salient changes, delivered bottom-up to the ventral network.

◦ Endogenous goals: task instructions and learned cue meanings, delivered top-down from executive control to the dorsal network.

◦ Warning signals: temporal alerts that raise readiness via the alerting network.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A spatial priority pointer: the current attended location and focus width, consumed by perception, binding (Chapter 15), and the eye-movement system.

◦ Gain commands: multiplicative amplification of neurons coding the attended region, raising their signal-to-noise ratio.

◦ Reaction-time benefits and costs: faster responses at attended locations, slower at unattended ones, the behavioural signature read out in cueing tasks.

◦ Interrupt notifications: ventral-network alerts that force reorienting to unexpected relevant events.

• STATE.

◦ Current pointer coordinates and zoom width.

◦ A decaying inhibition-of-return map tagging recently visited locations.

◦ Baseline gain profile across the visual field, including pre-stimulus warm-up of the selected region.

◦ Global alertness level.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Attentional gain factor for the selected region.

◦ Zoom trade-off constant linking focus area to resolution.

◦ Interrupt threshold: how salient and how task-relevant an event must be for the ventral network to pre-empt the dorsal plan.

◦ Inhibition-of-return strength and decay rate.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Exogenous orienting: benefit peaks within roughly 100 milliseconds of an abrupt cue.

◦ Endogenous orienting: deliberate shifts take roughly 200 to 300 milliseconds to deploy.

◦ Inhibition of return onset: the cueing benefit reverses to a cost at cue-to-target intervals beyond about 200 to 300 milliseconds, and the inhibition can persist for a second or more.

◦ Magnitude of single-neuron gain change: REFUSED, because reported firing-rate increases vary widely across areas, tasks, and species, and no single canonical value is supported.

• MODES.

◦ Overt orienting: attention moves with an eye movement; triggered when the target justifies foveation.

◦ Covert orienting: attention moves while gaze stays fixed; triggered by task demands that forbid or precede eye movements.

◦ Endogenous (goal-driven) mode: the dorsal network sets the pointer from current goals; the default during purposeful tasks.

◦ Exogenous (stimulus-driven) mode: a salient event captures the pointer via the ventral network; triggered by abrupt, unexpected, potentially relevant onsets.

◦ Wide versus narrow zoom: focus width set by task precision demands, trading coverage for resolution.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Attentional capture: salient but irrelevant events hijack the pointer through the exogenous route.

◦ Spatial neglect: right-hemisphere ventral damage leaves patients failing to attend to the left side of space despite intact vision.

◦ Invalid-cue cost: misdirected expectation slows responses to targets appearing away from the cued location.

◦ Search perseveration when inhibition of return fails: attention revisits already-checked locations and search becomes inefficient.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called base_rt with initial value three hundred.
Create a number variable called cue_benefit with initial value forty.
Create a number variable called invalid_cost with initial value forty.
Create a number variable called ior_cost with initial value twenty.
Create a number variable called ior_onset with initial value two hundred fifty.
Create an empty list variable called results.
For each trial in the trial list, perform the following steps.
    Read the cue location, the target location, and the cue-to-target interval of the trial.
    Create a number variable called rt with initial value equal to base_rt.
    If the target location equals the cue location, perform the following steps.
        If the interval is less than ior_onset, subtract cue_benefit from rt.
        Otherwise, add ior_cost to rt.
    Otherwise, add invalid_cost to rt.
    Add a random noise value drawn from a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation twenty to rt.
    Append the trial description and rt to results.
Return results.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module for reaction-time noise and trial construction.
import random

# Create the baseline reaction time in milliseconds.
BASE_RT = 300
# Create the benefit for a validly cued target at short intervals.
CUE_BENEFIT = 40
# Create the cost for an invalidly cued target.
INVALID_COST = 40
# Create the inhibition-of-return cost at long intervals.
IOR_COST = 20
# Create the interval in milliseconds at which inhibition of return begins.
IOR_ONSET = 250

# Define a function that simulates one Posner cueing trial.
def cueing_trial(cue_side, target_side, interval_ms):
    # Start the reaction time at the baseline value.
    rt = BASE_RT
    # If the target appears on the cued side, apply benefit or inhibition.
    if target_side == cue_side:
        # If the interval is short, attention is still there, so subtract the benefit.
        if interval_ms < IOR_ONSET:
            rt = rt - CUE_BENEFIT
        # Otherwise, inhibition of return has set in, so add its cost.
        else:
            rt = rt + IOR_COST
    # Otherwise the cue was invalid, so add the reorienting cost.
    else:
        rt = rt + INVALID_COST
    # Add Gaussian noise with mean zero and standard deviation twenty.
    rt = rt + random.gauss(0, 20)
    # Return the simulated reaction time.
    return rt

# Define a function that averages many trials for one condition.
def mean_rt(cue, target, interval, n):
    # Calculate the mean of n simulated trials for the condition.
    return sum(cueing_trial(cue, target, interval) for _ in range(n)) / n

# For each cue-to-target interval, print valid and invalid mean reaction times.
for interval in [100, 200, 400, 800]:
    # Compute the mean reaction time when the cue is valid.
    valid = mean_rt("left", "left", interval, 2000)
    # Compute the mean reaction time when the cue is invalid.
    invalid = mean_rt("left", "right", interval, 2000)
    # Print the interval and both means rounded to whole milliseconds.
    print("interval", interval, "ms: valid", round(valid),
          "ms, invalid", round(invalid), "ms")


CHAPTER 15. ATTENTION, BINDING, AND ITS FAILURES (PROCESS)

This chapter is about one of attention's least obvious but most important jobs: gluing separate features into whole objects, and about the striking ways attention fails.

When you see a red ball, your brain processes its colour and its shape in partly different places, yet you experience one unified red ball, and the puzzle of how that unity is achieved is called the binding problem.

In systems terms the problem is one of correct address association: features are computed on separate maps, and the system must guarantee that the colour at a location gets attached to the shape at the same location and not to a neighbour.

This chapter explains the leading theory that attention is the glue, the evidence for a distinct binding step, and then the dramatic failures that reveal how much of the visual world we miss.


15.1 Attention and the binding of features

This section presents the theory that binding features into objects requires attention, and traces how that theory was tested and refined.


15.1.1 Feature integration theory and the preattentive to attentive transition

Feature integration theory (FIT), proposed by Anne Treisman and Garry Gelade in 1980, is the influential claim that separate features are combined into objects only where attention is directed.

The theory divides vision into two stages.

In the first, preattentive stage, meaning the stage before attention is applied, basic features such as colour, orientation, and motion are registered automatically, in parallel, across the whole scene at once and effortlessly.

In the second, attentive stage, attention moves to a location and binds together the features present there into a single object, and this stage is serial, meaning it handles one location at a time.

The evidence comes from visual search, the task of finding a target among distractors.

When the target differs from the distractors by a single basic feature, such as a red item among green ones, it seems to pop out instantly, and the time to find it barely changes as you add more distractors, which fits automatic parallel processing.

When the target is defined by a combination of features, such as a red vertical bar among red horizontal bars and green vertical bars, search becomes slow and the time rises steadily with each added distractor, as if attention must visit items one at a time to bind their features.

The systems signature is in the slopes: feature search shows a search time nearly flat in the number of items, while conjunction search shows a linear rise of roughly 20 to 40 milliseconds per additional item, which is the fingerprint of a parallel front end feeding a serial binding stage.

This contrast between flat and rising search times is the core support for the idea that binding needs attention.


15.1.2 Illusory conjunctions as evidence of a binding step

An illusory conjunction is a perceptual mistake in which features from different objects are wrongly combined, so that you might report seeing a red X when the display actually contained a red O and a green X.

Treisman and colleagues demonstrated these errors by showing people displays very briefly, or by loading their attention elsewhere, so that attention could not be properly directed to each item.

Under those conditions people reliably reported these wrong combinations, mixing up which colour went with which shape.

The importance of this finding is that it is exactly what feature integration theory predicts: if attention is the glue that binds features to the right object, then removing attention should let features float free and recombine incorrectly.

In systems terms, an illusory conjunction is an address-association fault: the feature values are read correctly, but with the binding process starved of its attention input, the pointers linking values to locations are assigned wrongly, and the system outputs a well-formed object description that corresponds to nothing in the input.

Illusory conjunctions therefore provide positive evidence that binding is a real, separable step in perception rather than something that happens automatically for free.

They also gently unsettle our confidence in perception, showing that without attention the visual system can assemble an object that was never actually there.


15.1.3 Guided search as a refinement

Guided search is a revision of feature integration theory, developed chiefly by Jeremy Wolfe from the late 1980s onward, that keeps the two-stage idea but makes the search smarter.

The problem with the original theory was that it implied combination searches were essentially blind, with attention wandering from item to item at random until it stumbled on the target.

Real search is more efficient than that, so guided search proposes that the fast preattentive stage does more than just register features: it also builds a rough map of where the promising items are and steers attention toward them.

For example, when looking for a red vertical bar, the preattentive stage can flag all the red things and all the vertical things, and attention is then guided to locations that score high on both, which are the likely targets.

This means attention is not random but biased toward candidates that share features with the target, which explains why combination search, though slower than pop-out, is far more efficient than pure item-by-item checking would be.

As a system, guided search inserts a priority map between the two stages: the parallel front end outputs an activation score per location, summing bottom-up salience and top-down feature matches, and the serial binder visits locations in descending score order rather than at random, cutting expected search time sharply.

Guided search is now one of the most developed and well-tested models of visual search, and it is best seen as an extension that preserves the core of feature integration theory while making it realistic.


15.2 The failures of attention

This section turns to what happens when attention is absent or overloaded, and the results are surprising demonstrations of how much of the world goes unnoticed.


15.2.1 Inattentional and change blindness

Inattentional blindness is the failure to see a fully visible object simply because your attention was occupied elsewhere.

The most famous demonstration is the invisible gorilla study by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris in 1999, which built on earlier work by Ulric Neisser.

Viewers watched a video and counted how many times players in white shirts passed a basketball, and while they were absorbed in counting, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the scene, faced the camera, thumped its chest, and walked off.

About half of the viewers, deeply focused on counting, never saw the gorilla at all.

Change blindness is a related failure: the difficulty people have noticing large changes to a scene when the change happens during some interruption such as a brief blank, a cut in a film, or a blink.

In striking demonstrations, people fail to notice that a conversation partner has been swapped for a different person during a momentary interruption.

The systems reading of both failures is that conscious scene representation is sparse and demand-driven: the input is the full scene, but the output to awareness contains only what the attentional binder has actually visited, and the interruption in change blindness deletes the transient signal that would otherwise flag the changed location for a visit.

Both phenomena carry the same lesson: we feel as though we take in the whole rich scene before us, but in truth we consciously register far less than we think, and attention is required to notice even obvious things.

This is humbling and practically important, for example in eyewitness reports and in the danger of distracted driving.


15.2.2 The attentional blink

The attentional blink is a brief lapse in attention that follows the successful detection of one target, during which a second target is likely to be missed.

It is studied with a method called rapid serial visual presentation, in which a stream of items, such as letters, is flashed one after another at the same spot very quickly, roughly ten per second.

The viewer must spot two targets embedded in the stream, for example two letters of a particular colour among other letters.

The finding is that if the second target appears very soon after the first, within about half a second, it is often missed entirely, as if attention had briefly blinked.

Curiously, if the second target comes immediately after the first, with no gap at all, it is usually caught, and if it comes after a longer delay it is also caught, so the failure is worst at an intermediate lag.

The blink is not a failure of the eyes, since they are open the whole time, but a limit of central processing: consolidating the first target into a form that can be reported ties up attention for a moment, leaving the second target vulnerable.

In systems terms the blink is a busy period on the consolidation server: encoding the first target into reportable working-memory format occupies the server for roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds, and any second target arriving in that window is overwritten by the ongoing stream before it can be served, while a target arriving in the same batch as the first rides through on the first target's service.

The attentional blink is valuable to researchers because it exposes the timing of the bottleneck between merely perceiving something and turning it into a reportable, conscious item.


15.3 The binding problem in general

This section widens the lens from perception to a problem that runs through all of cognition and through artificial intelligence: how a system represents which things go with which.


15.3.1 Feature binding and the unity of the percept

Feature binding is the specific problem of how the separately processed features of an object become tied together into a single unified perception.

The puzzle is real because the brain analyses different attributes in partly different regions, for instance colour and motion are handled by distinct areas, yet we never experience a scene as a loose soup of free-floating colours and motions.

Instead we see whole, coherent objects, each with its colour, shape, and motion correctly assigned, and something must be doing the assigning.

One leading proposal is temporal synchrony, an idea developed by Christoph von der Malsburg and others, that neurons representing features of the same object fire in time with one another, while neurons for different objects fire out of step, so that being in sync marks features as belonging together.

In systems terms synchrony is a time-multiplexed tagging scheme: instead of a dedicated wire announcing which features go together, co-membership is signalled by shared firing phase, which requires no extra hardware but limits how many objects can be kept apart at once by the number of distinguishable phases.

This idea is elegant and has some experimental support, but it remains debated, and there is no consensus that synchrony is the brain's actual solution.

The honest state of the science is that feature binding is a recognised, deep problem with several candidate answers, of which attention and neural synchrony are the most discussed, and none is settled.


15.3.2 The variable-binding problem for symbolic and connectionist systems

Variable binding is the more abstract cousin of feature binding, and it is the problem of temporarily tying a role to a filler, for instance binding the role agent to the filler John in the thought that John chased the dog.

The word variable here is borrowed from mathematics and computing, where a variable is a slot that can hold different values at different times.

Symbolic systems, meaning the classical approach to artificial intelligence that manipulates language-like symbols according to rules, handle variable binding naturally, because assigning a value to a named slot is exactly what such systems are built to do.

This is often cited as a strength of the symbolic approach, since it makes structured, compositional thought, such as understanding who did what to whom, straightforward.

Connectionist systems, meaning neural networks that represent information as patterns of activity spread across many simple units, find variable binding much harder, because there is no obvious built-in way to keep track of which pattern is currently filling which role.

This difficulty was a central point in a long-running debate, sparked by a 1988 critique from Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn, over whether neural networks can support the systematic, structured character of human thought.

The two sides predict differently in systems terms: a symbolic architecture predicts effortless, error-free re-use of a structure with new fillers, since binding is a pointer assignment, while a plain connectionist architecture predicts degraded or interference-prone generalisation to novel role-filler combinations unless a dedicated binding mechanism is added.

Researchers have proposed various fixes, including the temporal synchrony idea mentioned above and specialised network designs, and modern deep-learning systems address related challenges with mechanisms such as attention layers.

The broad lesson for konnectome is that binding, whether of visual features or of abstract roles, is one of the genuine hard problems that any complete architecture of mind, natural or artificial, must solve, and it is not yet fully solved by anyone.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Parallel feature maps: location-indexed maps of colour, orientation, motion, and other basic features from early vision.

◦ The spatial attention pointer: the current attended location from the orienting system of Chapter 14, which selects where binding occurs.

◦ Target template: the sought feature combination from working memory, used to weight the priority map in guided search.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Bound object files: unified object descriptions with features correctly assigned, forwarded to recognition, working memory, and report.

◦ Search decisions: target present or absent judgements with reaction times whose slope over set size reveals the search mode.

◦ Consolidated targets: reportable items handed to working memory, one at a time, through the consolidation stage exposed by the attentional blink.

• STATE.

◦ The priority map: per-location activation combining bottom-up salience and top-down template matches.

◦ The set of currently open object files and their feature assignments.

◦ Consolidation-stage occupancy: whether the binder is busy encoding a just-found target.

◦ A record of locations already visited in the current search.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Per-item inspection time of the serial binder.

◦ Weights on each feature dimension in the priority map.

◦ Consolidation duration for a detected target.

◦ Guidance quality: how sharply the priority map separates targets from distractors.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Serial inspection rate: conjunction search costs roughly 20 to 40 milliseconds per additional item, versus a near-zero slope for feature pop-out.

◦ Attentional blink window: a second target is missed most often 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first.

◦ Rapid serial visual presentation rate in blink studies: roughly ten items per second, about 100 milliseconds per item.

◦ Duration of the preattentive stage as a separate interval: REFUSED, because the parallel feature stage runs continuously rather than for a fixed measurable period, and the literature supports no single value.

• MODES.

◦ Preattentive parallel mode: features registered across the whole field at once; always on, no trigger needed.

◦ Attentive serial mode: one location bound at a time; triggered whenever the task requires feature conjunctions or object identity.

◦ Guided mode: serial visits ordered by the priority map; engaged whenever a target template is available to weight the map.

◦ Blink (busy) mode: new targets refused while consolidation of a previous target is in progress; triggered by successful target detection, released after consolidation completes.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Illusory conjunctions: features from different objects wrongly combined when attention is diluted or displays are too brief.

◦ Inattentional blindness: fully visible objects never reach awareness because the binder never visits them.

◦ Change blindness: large scene changes missed when the transient cue is masked by an interruption.

◦ The attentional blink: the second of two rapid targets lost during consolidation of the first.

◦ Balint syndrome: bilateral parietal damage producing severe binding failure, with patients able to see only one object at a time.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called per_item_time with initial value thirty.
Create an empty list variable called display.
For each item to be displayed, append its colour, its orientation, and its location to display.
Read the target colour and the target orientation from the task instructions.
Create an empty list variable called priority_map.
For each item in display, perform the following steps.
    Create a number variable called score with initial value zero.
    If the item colour equals the target colour, add one to score.
    If the item orientation equals the target orientation, add one to score.
    Add a random guidance noise value between zero and one point five to score.
    Append the item and its score to priority_map.
Sort priority_map from highest score to lowest score.
Create a number variable called elapsed with initial value zero.
For each entry in priority_map, perform the following steps.
    Add per_item_time to elapsed.
    If the entry colour equals the target colour and the entry orientation equals the target orientation, return target found and elapsed.
Return target absent and elapsed.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module for building random search displays.
import random

# Create the serial inspection time per item in milliseconds.
PER_ITEM_MS = 30

# Define a function that runs one guided conjunction search.
def guided_search(display, t_colour, t_orient):
    # Create an empty list variable called priority_map.
    priority_map = []
    # For each item, score it by how many target features it shares.
    for item in display:
        # Start the score at zero.
        score = 0
        # If the item colour matches the target colour, add one.
        if item["colour"] == t_colour:
            score = score + 1
        # If the item orientation matches the target orientation, add one.
        if item["orient"] == t_orient:
            score = score + 1
        # Add guidance noise between zero and one point five to the score.
        score = score + random.uniform(0, 1.5)
        # Append the score and the item to the priority map.
        priority_map.append((score, random.random(), item))
    # Sort the map from highest score to lowest, breaking ties randomly.
    priority_map.sort(reverse=True)
    # Create a number variable called elapsed with initial value zero.
    elapsed = 0
    # Visit items in priority order, binding one at a time.
    for score, tiebreak, item in priority_map:
        # Add the per-item inspection time to the elapsed clock.
        elapsed = elapsed + PER_ITEM_MS
        # If both features match, the conjunction is bound and found.
        if item["colour"] == t_colour and item["orient"] == t_orient:
            return "found", elapsed
    # If no item matched, report the target absent with the total time.
    return "absent", elapsed

# Define a function that builds a display with one target and many distractors.
def make_display(n):
    # Build distractors sharing exactly one feature with the target.
    items = []
    # For each distractor slot, choose red horizontal or green vertical.
    for i in range(n - 1):
        if random.random() < 0.5:
            items.append({"colour": "red", "orient": "horizontal"})
        else:
            items.append({"colour": "green", "orient": "vertical"})
    # Append the red vertical target itself.
    items.append({"colour": "red", "orient": "vertical"})
    # Return the completed display.
    return items

# For increasing set sizes, print the mean search time over many runs.
for n in [4, 8, 16, 32]:
    # Average the elapsed time across five hundred simulated searches.
    times = [guided_search(make_display(n), "red", "vertical")[1]
             for _ in range(500)]
    # Print the set size and the mean search time in milliseconds.
    print("set size", n, ": mean search time", round(sum(times) / len(times)), "ms")
