PART FOUR. MEMORY: RETAINING AND RECONSTRUCTING

================================================================================

CHAPTER 16. SENSORY AND SHORT-TERM STORES (PROCESS)

This chapter begins the study of memory, and it starts at the front door, with the very brief and very short stores that hold information for moments rather than for a lifetime.

Memory is not a single thing but a set of systems that operate over different time scales, and this chapter covers the fastest of them.

In systems terms these front-end stores are buffers: high-capacity but rapidly decaying holding areas whose job is to keep raw input alive just long enough for slower stages to read what they need.

Understanding these early stores matters because everything that ends up in lasting memory has to pass through them first, so they set the terms on which the rest of memory operates.


16.1 The modal model

This section describes the classic overall picture of memory as a flow of information through a series of stores, a picture so widely adopted that it earned the name modal, meaning the standard or most common model.


16.1.1 The sensory, short-term, and long-term stores

The modal model, laid out by Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin in 1968, pictures memory as three stores arranged in sequence, through which information passes.

The first is sensory memory, a very brief, high-capacity hold that keeps a faithful sensory copy of what just hit the senses for a fraction of a second.

The second is short-term memory, a limited store that holds a small amount of information for a matter of seconds, roughly what you are consciously thinking about right now.

The third is long-term memory, a vast and durable store that can hold information for years or a lifetime.

Information flows from sensory memory into short-term memory if it is attended to, and from short-term into long-term memory if it is processed enough, often through rehearsal, meaning the repeating or working-over of material to keep it alive and pass it along.

The model is called a structural account because it proposes distinct storage boxes, and it also describes control processes, the strategies such as rehearsal that the person uses to move information between the boxes.

As a system, the modal model is a three-tier cache hierarchy: a huge, sub-second front buffer, a small, seconds-long working tier, and a vast, slow-writing archive, with attention as the read policy from tier one to tier two and rehearsal as the write policy from tier two to tier three.

This three-store framework has been revised heavily over the decades, but it remains the shared starting point for almost all later theories of memory, which is why it is worth learning first.


16.1.2 The transfer between stores and its controversies

This sub-section examines the arrows in the model, the claimed movement of information between stores, which turned out to be more contentious than the boxes themselves.

The original model leaned heavily on rehearsal as the engine of transfer, proposing that the longer an item sat in short-term memory being rehearsed, the more likely it was to enter long-term memory.

This simple idea ran into trouble.

Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart argued in 1972 that sheer repetition is a poor predictor of lasting memory, and that what matters instead is the depth of processing, meaning whether you engage with the meaning of material rather than just its surface.

Merely repeating a word over and over, which they called maintenance rehearsal, does surprisingly little to build long-term memory, while thinking about its meaning, called elaborative rehearsal, does far more.

A further controversy concerns whether short-term and long-term memory are genuinely separate stores at all, since some theorists argue that short-term memory is simply the currently activated portion of long-term memory rather than a separate box.

The evidence usually cited for a real separation includes patients whose long-term memory is devastated while their short-term memory is spared, and the opposite pattern in other patients, a double pattern that suggests two distinct systems.

In systems terms the debate is between two architectures with different predictions: separate stores predict that damage can knock out one tier while sparing the other, exactly the double pattern seen in patients, while an activation account predicts that short-term failures should always track the state of the underlying long-term representations.

The reasonable modern position is that the distinction between short-term and long-term memory is real and useful, but that the neat one-way flow of the original diagram is too simple, and the systems interact richly in both directions.


16.2 Sensory memory

This section zooms in on the first and briefest store, the fleeting sensory trace that holds a rich copy of the world for a moment before it fades.


16.2.1 Iconic memory and the partial-report advantage

Iconic memory is the visual form of sensory memory, a brief snapshot-like store that holds a large amount of visual detail for roughly a quarter to a half of a second.

The word icon here just means a visual image, and the store is named for that fleeting image.

The classic evidence comes from George Sperling's experiments in 1960, which cleverly measured a store that vanishes too fast to report in full.

Sperling flashed a grid of letters, for example three rows of four, for a fraction of a second, and when he asked people to report as many as they could, the whole-report condition, they managed only about four or five.

The trick was the partial-report condition, in which a tone sounded just after the grid disappeared, high, medium, or low, telling the person to report only the top, middle, or bottom row.

Because the tone came after the grid was gone, people could only succeed by reading the answer off a lingering mental image, and they did well on whichever row was cued, showing that nearly the whole grid was briefly available.

This gap, between the many letters momentarily available and the few that survive long enough to report, is called the partial-report advantage, and it proves that iconic memory briefly holds far more than we can report before it fades.

Sperling further showed that the advantage shrinks as the tone is delayed, disappearing after about a second, which measures how fast the icon decays.

The systems reading of Sperling's method is a race between decay and readout: the buffer holds the full grid but its contents decay in well under a second, the readout channel into short-term memory transfers only a few items in that window, and the delayed cue measures the buffer's decay curve directly by moving the readout start time.


16.2.2 Echoic memory

Echoic memory is the auditory form of sensory memory, the brief store that holds a trace of what you just heard, and it is the reason a sound seems to linger for a moment after it stops.

The word echoic comes from echo, capturing the way the sound seems to persist.

Echoic memory lasts noticeably longer than iconic memory, on the order of a few seconds rather than a fraction of a second, which makes sense because sound unfolds over time and must be held long enough to be interpreted.

A familiar everyday sign of echoic memory is the experience of not quite catching what someone said, asking what, and then finding you can suddenly replay and understand the words after all, because the trace was still available.

Laboratory studies use methods analogous to Sperling's partial-report technique but with sounds presented to different locations, and they find a similar brief, high-capacity auditory store that fades over a few seconds.

In systems terms echoic memory is a rolling audio buffer holding the last few seconds of input: its input is the raw auditory stream, its output is replayable material for speech and music interpretation, and its longer time constant matches the temporal structure of the signal it serves.

Echoic memory is especially important for understanding speech and music, because both require holding recent sounds in mind long enough to relate them to what comes next.


16.3 Short-term memory

This section covers the second store, the small workspace that holds the handful of items you are actively aware of, and the questions of how much it holds, how its contents are ordered, and why they are lost.


16.3.1 Capacity, the magical number, and chunking

This sub-section is about how much short-term memory can hold, one of the most famous questions in all of psychology.

In 1956 George Miller wrote a celebrated paper titled The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, observing that people can typically hold about seven items in short-term memory, give or take a couple.

Miller himself treated the number partly with humour and did not mean it as an exact law, but it became one of the best-known figures in the field.

The crucial refinement is that the limit is measured not in raw items but in chunks, a chunk being a meaningful unit that groups several pieces of information into one.

For example, the string of letters F B I C I A can be held as six separate letters or, if you recognise them, as two familiar chunks, FBI and CIA, which is far easier.

Chunking is powerful because it lets long-term knowledge repackage information into fewer, denser units, which is a large part of why experts can seem to hold so much in mind within their field.

More recent work, especially by Nelson Cowan in 2001, argues that when chunking and rehearsal are prevented so that pure capacity is measured, the real limit is closer to about four chunks rather than seven.

In systems terms the capacity limit counts slots, not bits: the store holds roughly three to five chunk pointers, each pointer referencing an arbitrarily rich structure in long-term memory, so chunking is a compression scheme that raises effective throughput without changing slot count.

The reasonable summary is that the honest number is smaller than Miller's famous seven, roughly three to five chunks under strict conditions, and that chunking is the trick by which people seem to exceed it.


16.3.2 Serial position, primacy, and recency

This sub-section is about a reliable pattern in how well we remember a list depending on where an item sat in it.

When people try to recall a list of items in any order, their success depends strongly on position, and plotting accuracy against position gives a U-shaped curve called the serial position curve.

The primacy effect is the better memory for items at the beginning of the list, thought to arise because those early items received more rehearsal and had a better chance of entering long-term memory.

The recency effect is the better memory for items at the end of the list, thought to arise because those last items are still sitting in short-term memory, freshly available, when recall begins.

A classic piece of evidence that these two effects have different causes is that delaying recall by a filled interval, such as counting backward for half a minute, wipes out the recency effect while leaving the primacy effect intact.

This makes sense because the delay lets the fragile short-term contents fade, removing recency, while the durably stored early items survive, preserving primacy.

The systems reading is that recall draws on two stores with different time constants: the recency portion is read from the fast, decaying buffer and vanishes after roughly 30 seconds of distraction, while the primacy portion is read from the durable archive that the early items reached through extra rehearsal.

The serial position curve is important because it offers behavioural support for the distinction between a short-term and a long-term store, since the two ends of the curve seem to draw on different systems.


16.3.3 Decay against interference as the cause of loss

This sub-section addresses a basic question: when something slips out of short-term memory, why does it go.

There are two classic answers, and they have competed for decades.

The decay account says that memory traces simply fade with the passage of time if they are not refreshed, so forgetting is caused by time itself, like a footprint smoothed away.

The interference account says that time as such is not the culprit, and that items are lost because other items crowd them out or overwrite them, so forgetting is caused by competition, not by the clock.

Interference comes in two directions: proactive interference, where older material disrupts memory for newer material, and retroactive interference, where newer material disrupts memory for older material.

The two accounts predict differently in systems terms: pure decay predicts loss that grows with elapsed time even in an empty channel, while pure interference predicts no loss in a silent delay and loss proportional to the amount of competing material, whatever the clock says.

Distinguishing decay from interference is genuinely hard, because in ordinary situations time and competing material go together, so a delay during which more items arrive could hurt memory for either reason.

The debate is not fully resolved, and honest reviews note that the evidence is mixed, but many researchers lean toward interference, and some influential accounts argue that pure time-based decay plays little or no role once interference is controlled.

For a builder of cognitive systems the practical point stands regardless of which side is right: a small, fast store loses its contents quickly unless they are actively maintained or protected from competing information.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Raw sensory streams: the full visual and auditory input, written automatically into the iconic and echoic buffers.

◦ Attention selections: the pointer from Chapters 13 to 15 choosing which buffered items are read into short-term memory.

◦ Long-term knowledge: chunk definitions that let incoming material be recoded into fewer, denser units.

◦ Rehearsal commands: control-process instructions to refresh or elaborate held items.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ The current short-term contents: the handful of active chunks available to thought, report, and response.

◦ Transfer candidates: items forwarded toward long-term memory, with success governed more by depth of processing than by repetition count.

◦ Recall output: reported items whose accuracy by list position traces the serial position curve.

• STATE.

◦ The decaying iconic and echoic traces with their onset times.

◦ The occupied short-term slots and the identity of each held chunk.

◦ The rehearsal loop's current refresh order.

◦ Accumulated interference from prior and subsequent material.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Sensory buffer capacity (large: essentially the whole display for the icon's brief life).

◦ Short-term capacity in chunks (roughly three to five under strict measurement).

◦ Rehearsal refresh rate and its type, maintenance versus elaborative.

◦ Interference weights for proactive and retroactive competition.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Iconic memory decay: the partial-report advantage fades within roughly 250 to 500 milliseconds and is gone by about 1 second.

◦ Echoic memory persistence: on the order of 2 to 4 seconds.

◦ Unrehearsed short-term retention: severe loss within roughly 15 to 30 seconds of filled delay, as in counting-backward studies.

◦ A pure time-based decay rate for short-term memory: REFUSED, because the field has not separated decay from interference cleanly enough to certify a rate for time alone.

• MODES.

◦ Passive registration: sensory buffers fill automatically from input; always on, no trigger.

◦ Whole-report readout: unguided transfer that salvages only about four items before the icon fades.

◦ Partial-report readout: cue-guided transfer that reads any requested subset while the trace survives; triggered by a selection cue arriving before decay completes.

◦ Maintenance rehearsal: cyclic refresh that keeps items alive without deepening them; triggered by the goal of holding material briefly.

◦ Elaborative rehearsal: meaning-based processing that builds durable long-term traces; triggered by the goal of lasting retention.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Buffer expiry: unattended sensory detail is lost within a second, the everyday miss of what was just seen.

◦ Overflow displacement: new items push out old ones once the three to five chunk slots are full.

◦ Interference corruption: proactive and retroactive competition overwrite held items.

◦ Recency wipe-out: a filled delay before recall erases the short-term tail of a list.

◦ Rehearsal futility: maintenance rehearsal gives an illusion of learning while building little durable memory.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called icon_half_life with initial value zero point three.
Create a number variable called span with initial value four.
Create an empty list variable called iconic_buffer.
For each element on the display, append the element and the current time to iconic_buffer.
Create an empty list variable called short_term.
For each time step in the simulation, perform the following steps.
    For each element in iconic_buffer, calculate its surviving strength as one half raised to the power of its age divided by icon_half_life.
        If the surviving strength is less than a random number between zero and one, remove the element from iconic_buffer.
    If an attention cue is present, perform the following steps.
        Select the cued element from iconic_buffer if it still survives.
        If short_term already holds span items, remove the oldest item from short_term.
        Append the selected element to short_term.
    If rehearsal is active, move the oldest item in short_term to the newest position, refreshing it.
    Otherwise, remove each item in short_term with a small random probability, representing loss.
Return the final contents of short_term.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for exponential decay and the random module for chance.
import math
import random

# Create the iconic half life in seconds.
ICON_HALF_LIFE = 0.3
# Create the short-term span in chunks.
SPAN = 4
# Create the per-step loss probability when rehearsal is off.
LOSS_P = 0.08

# Define a function that simulates the icon, readout, and rehearsal.
def run_buffer(display, cue_times, rehearse):
    # Stamp every displayed element into the iconic buffer at time zero.
    iconic = [(element, 0.0) for element in display]
    # Create an empty list for the short-term store.
    short_term = []
    # Step the clock forward in ticks of one tenth of a second.
    for step in range(1, 21):
        # Calculate the current time in seconds.
        now = step * 0.1
        # Create an empty list of surviving iconic elements.
        survivors = []
        # For each buffered element, test whether its trace survives this tick.
        for element, onset in iconic:
            # Calculate survival probability from exponential decay over the tick.
            p = math.exp(-math.log(2) * 0.1 / ICON_HALF_LIFE)
            # Keep the element only if a random draw falls under that probability.
            if random.random() < p:
                survivors.append((element, onset))
        # Replace the iconic buffer with the survivors.
        iconic = survivors
        # If attention cues a readout at this tick, transfer one element.
        if step in cue_times and iconic:
            # Take the first surviving element from the icon.
            element, onset = iconic.pop(0)
            # If the store is full, evict the oldest chunk.
            if len(short_term) >= SPAN:
                short_term.pop(0)
            # Append the element to the short-term store.
            short_term.append(element)
        # If rehearsal is on, refresh the oldest item by moving it to the end.
        if rehearse and short_term:
            short_term.append(short_term.pop(0))
        # Otherwise, each held item risks loss this tick.
        elif short_term:
            short_term = [x for x in short_term if random.random() > LOSS_P]
    # Return what remains in the short-term store.
    return short_term

# Build a twelve-letter display like Sperling's grid.
letters = list("KLBYNXFDJSRT")
# Cue readouts on the first six ticks, while the icon is still alive.
cues = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
# Print what survives after two seconds with rehearsal on and off.
print("with rehearsal:", run_buffer(letters, cues, True))
print("without rehearsal:", run_buffer(letters, cues, False))

CHAPTER 17. WORKING MEMORY (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the small mental workspace you use to hold and juggle information for the few seconds you are actually using it.

Working memory is the name for the system that keeps a phone number alive in your head while you dial it, or holds the first half of a sentence while you read the second half.

It matters because almost everything else the mind does, from understanding speech to solving a puzzle, depends on being able to keep a few things in mind and work on them at the same time.

The older term for this idea was short-term memory, which mostly meant simple storage, and working memory is the richer modern idea that adds the active manipulation of what is stored.

Seen as an engineered system, working memory is a small, fast, volatile buffer: it accepts inputs from perception and from long-term memory, holds a handful of active representations as its state, refreshes them against loss, and publishes their contents to reasoning, language, and action systems on demand.


17.1 The multicomponent model

The most influential picture of working memory says it is not one thing but a team of parts that each do a different job.

This picture was proposed by Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch in 1974, and it is usually called the multicomponent model.

In systems terms, it is a modular architecture: two specialised storage buffers, a later-added binding buffer, and a controller that allocates a limited attentional resource among them.

The following sub-sections walk through each member of that team in turn.


17.1.1 The central executive

The central executive is the boss of the working memory system, the part that decides what to pay attention to and how to coordinate the other parts.

In plain terms, it is the mental manager that directs your limited attention, chooses which task to work on, and switches between jobs.

Baddeley described it as a control system with limited attentional capacity, meaning it can only supervise so much at once before it becomes overloaded.

It does not store information itself in the original model; instead it steers the storage parts and shares out attention among them.

As a mechanism, its inputs are current task goals and the states of the storage buffers, its outputs are allocation and switching commands, and its characteristic timescale is the task-switch cost of a few hundred milliseconds that appears whenever it must reconfigure from one job to another.

Because it was defined mostly by what it does rather than by a clear mechanism, critics complained that the central executive was a bit like a homunculus, which means a little person inside the head doing all the clever work without being explained.

In response, later versions broke the executive down into more specific abilities, such as focusing attention, dividing attention between tasks, and switching between tasks.

Researchers today often link these executive abilities to what are called executive functions, a set of control skills covered in a later chapter, and this connection is one of the model's most fruitful legacies.


17.1.2 The phonological loop and its behavioural signatures

The phonological loop is the part of working memory that holds sound-based and speech-based information for a short time.

You can think of it as an inner voice combined with an inner ear that lets you silently repeat and briefly store words and numbers.

Baddeley proposed that it has two pieces, a store that holds speech sounds for a couple of seconds before they fade, and a rehearsal process that refreshes those sounds by silently repeating them, which is often called subvocal rehearsal.

The systems reading is a decaying buffer plus a refresh loop: input is speech-coded material from hearing or from reading recoded into sound, output is ordered verbal content for recall or language processes, and the critical time constant is a trace lifetime of roughly two seconds unless rehearsal rewrites the trace first.

A behavioural signature means a reliable pattern in people's performance that reveals a hidden mechanism at work, and the phonological loop has several famous ones.

The first is the word-length effect, which is the finding that people remember fewer long words than short words, because long words take longer to rehearse and so more of them fade before they can be refreshed.

The second is the phonological similarity effect, which is the finding that lists of words that sound alike, such as cat, cap, and mat, are harder to recall in order than words that sound different, because the sound-based store confuses similar sounds.

The third is articulatory suppression, which is what happens when you force a person to say something irrelevant out loud, such as repeating the word the again and again, and this blocks rehearsal and wipes out the other effects, showing that the inner voice really is doing the rehearsing.

The fourth is the irrelevant speech effect, where unattended background speech disrupts recall because it intrudes into the same sound-based store.

Together these findings are strong evidence that verbal short-term memory really does rely on a sound-based code kept alive by silent rehearsal.


17.1.3 The visuospatial sketchpad

The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that holds visual and spatial information, such as what things look like and where they are.

In everyday terms, it is the mental scratch pad you use to picture a route, imagine how furniture would fit in a room, or keep track of where a moving object is.

Baddeley and later colleagues suggested it can be divided into a visual part, which handles form and colour, and a spatial part, which handles location and movement, though the exact split is still debated.

As a mechanism, its inputs are visual features and locations from perception or from imagery generation, its outputs are object and position estimates consumed by navigation, mental rotation, and action planning, and its capacity limit of about three or four objects is reached within a few hundred milliseconds of display onset.

The evidence that this system is separate from the phonological loop comes from the finding that a visual or spatial task and a verbal task interfere with each other far less than two visual tasks do, which suggests they draw on different stores.

For example, you can often repeat a string of numbers out loud while also tracking a moving dot, because each task uses a different subsystem, but tracking two moving dots at once is much harder.

This subsystem is important for navigation, for mechanical reasoning, and for mental imagery, which is the ability to picture things in the mind's eye.


17.1.4 The episodic buffer

The episodic buffer is a part that Baddeley added to the model much later, in the year 2000, to fix two gaps the original three parts could not fill.

The first gap was that the sound-based store and the picture-based store use different codes with no shared format, so nothing in the old model explained how a single united experience, such as remembering a person's face together with their name, could be held at once.

The second gap was that the old model did not explain how working memory talks to long-term memory, which is your vast permanent store of knowledge.

The episodic buffer is described as a limited store that binds information from the different subsystems, and from long-term memory, into single integrated chunks, called episodes, that you can be consciously aware of.

You can picture it as a mental meeting room where sounds, images, and stored knowledge are brought together into one combined scene.

In systems terms it is a multiplexing buffer: inputs arrive in incompatible codes from the loop, the sketchpad, and long-term memory, and the output is a small number of bound, multimodal chunks in a common format that consciousness and the central executive can read.

It is thought to be controlled by the central executive and to be the workspace where conscious, unified experience in working memory is assembled.

Fifty years on, the multicomponent model remains one of the field's most cited frameworks, and its authors continue to refine it, though as the next section shows it is not the only way to think about working memory.


17.2 The alternative frameworks

The multicomponent model treats working memory as a set of dedicated boxes, but other researchers describe it quite differently, and it is honest to say there is no single agreed theory.

Several major alternatives see working memory not as separate stores but as a special state of attention or of long-term memory.

In systems language, the debate is whether working memory is dedicated hardware, separate buffers with their own storage, or a privileged access mode over the long-term store, the same memory addressed with elevated activation.

The following sub-sections lay out the main rivals so you can see where they agree and disagree.


17.2.1 Working memory as activated long-term memory and the focus of attention

One influential alternative says there is no separate short-term store at all, and that working memory is simply the currently activated portion of your long-term memory.

On this view, associated most closely with Nelson Cowan and with earlier ideas from theorists such as James Nairne and Anders Ericsson, remembering something for a moment is just a matter of that stored knowledge being switched on and made temporarily more active.

Cowan added an important refinement called the focus of attention, which is a very narrow spotlight that holds only a handful of items in a state of direct, immediate access.

Inside this framework, items in the broader activated store are quickly available, but only the few items inside the focus of attention are being directly used right now.

The systems reading is a two-ring cache: a wide outer ring of activated long-term representations with fast but indirect access, and an inner focus holding about four items with immediate access, with attention deciding which items are promoted inward or demoted outward from moment to moment.

This picture is attractive because it explains neatly how working memory and long-term knowledge are connected, since they are, in effect, the same store seen in two states.

It also gives a natural home for the well-supported estimate, discussed later, that the focus of attention holds only about four items at once.


17.2.2 Working memory as executive attention and its link to fluid intelligence

A closely related framework, developed by Randall Engle, Michael Kane, and their colleagues, argues that the heart of working memory is executive attention, meaning the ability to control attention and keep a goal in mind despite distraction.

On this account, what really varies between people is not the size of a storage box but how well they can hold information in an active state while resisting interference and intrusion.

The striking finding that drove this view is that measures of working memory capacity correlate strongly with measures of fluid intelligence, which is the ability to reason and solve new problems that do not depend on prior knowledge.

In plain terms, people who are better at holding and protecting information in mind also tend to score higher on tests of on-the-spot reasoning.

Because this sub-section describes a theoretical position rather than a distinct mechanism, the systems statement of the difference is this: a pure storage account predicts that individual differences should appear only when item count is high, while the executive attention account predicts that they should appear whenever distraction must be resisted, even at low loads, and the data favour the second prediction.

The proposed explanation is that both abilities lean on the same underlying skill of controlling attention, especially the skill of keeping a relevant goal active while pushing away distractions and unwanted thoughts.

This is one of the most robust and important results in the study of individual differences, though researchers still debate exactly which ingredient of attention control does the work.


17.2.3 Time-based resource sharing and interference accounts

A third family of theories asks a more basic question, which is why the contents of working memory are lost at all, and the answers split into two camps.

The time-based resource sharing model, developed by Pierre Barrouillet and Valerie Camos, proposes that memory traces fade with time unless attention is used to refresh them, and that attention must be shared between refreshing old items and processing new ones.

On this view, the more of your time is taken up by other processing, the less time is left to refresh the fading memories, and so more is lost, which is why the pace and difficulty of a task matters so much.

The rival interference account argues that time itself is not the enemy, and that forgetting instead comes from items overwriting, blurring, or competing with one another.

In an interference account, a memory is lost not because it faded on the clock but because other similar items degraded it or crowded it out.

The two camps make different systems predictions: a decay-plus-refresh system predicts that loss should scale with the fraction of time attention is occupied elsewhere, regardless of what the distracting material is, while an interference system predicts that loss should scale with the similarity between old and new material, regardless of elapsed time.

This debate between decay-with-time and interference is genuinely unsettled, and careful experiments have been used to support each side, so the current honest position is that both processes may contribute.


17.3 The nature of the capacity limit

Everyone agrees that working memory can hold only a little at once, but there is real disagreement about what form that limit takes.

This section looks at how much fits, and at whether the limit is best described as a fixed number of slots or a shared pool that can be spread thin.

In systems terms, the question is whether the buffer is quantised, a fixed count of discrete slots, or continuous, a fixed budget of representational resource that can be divided ever more thinly.


17.3.1 The slots against continuous-resource debate

The oldest famous claim about capacity came from George Miller in 1956, who suggested the limit was about seven items, plus or minus two, a figure he half-jokingly called the magical number seven.

Later work by Nelson Cowan, published in 2001, argued that once you strip away tricks like rehearsal and grouping, the true limit is smaller, roughly four chunks of information, a figure sometimes called the magical number four.

Beyond the exact number lies a deeper argument about the very shape of the limit, and this is the slots against continuous-resource debate, most sharply studied in visual working memory.

The slot theory says working memory has a fixed, small number of discrete slots, so it can hold about three or four items with good detail, and anything beyond that is simply not stored and must be guessed.

The continuous-resource theory says instead that working memory is a shared pool of a limited resource that can be spread across any number of items, so that the more items you try to hold, the less precisely each one is remembered.

The practical difference is testable, because slot models predict some items are remembered sharply and the rest not at all, while resource models predict that everything gets fuzzier as the load grows.

Stated as system behaviour, a slot store fails by dropping items when demand exceeds the slot count, while a resource store fails by degrading precision on every item as demand rises, and measured error distributions show elements of both.

Neither pure version fits all the data perfectly, and many current researchers favour hybrid models, in which there is both a limit on the number of items and a graded loss of precision, so this remains an active and unresolved question.


17.3.2 Compression, chunking, and expertise

If capacity is so small, the natural question is how anyone manages to hold complex material in mind, and the answer is that the mind repackages information to make each unit count for more.

Chunking is the process of grouping separate items into a single meaningful unit, so that a chunk, rather than a raw item, is what fills a slot.

For example, the letters F, B, and I are three items, but for someone who knows the agency, FBI is a single familiar chunk, and the digit sequence one, seven, seven, six can become one date for someone who recognises it.

Chunking works by drawing on long-term knowledge, which is why the same string is easier to hold for a person who finds meaning in it, and this directly links capacity to what you already know.

Compression is a broader term for any way the mind recodes information into a more efficient form, squeezing out redundancy so that more fits within the same limit.

In systems terms, chunking is a compression codec that runs at encoding: input is a raw item stream, the codebook is the pattern library in long-term memory, and the output is a shorter stream of pointers to known patterns, so effective capacity is the slot count multiplied by the average chunk size the codebook affords.

This is why expertise matters so much, because an expert has a large store of learned patterns and can package incoming information into a few large, meaningful chunks that a novice would have to hold as many small ones.

The classic demonstration is that chess masters can glance at a real game position and reproduce it almost perfectly, far outperforming novices, but this advantage vanishes when the pieces are placed at random, showing that the skill is meaningful chunking rather than raw memory power.


17.4 The neural basis

Working memory is not just a psychological idea; it corresponds to real activity in the brain, and studying that activity has both confirmed and complicated the psychological picture.

This section looks at how the brain seems to hold information over short delays, and at a lively recent debate about the mechanism.

In systems terms, the question is how a volatile buffer is physically implemented: by keeping a signal actively cycling, or by briefly rewriting the hardware itself.


17.4.1 Persistent activity in prefrontal cortex

The classic neural account of working memory is that certain neurons keep firing steadily during the delay while information is being held, and this steady firing is called persistent activity.

The prefrontal cortex, which is the front part of the brain just behind the forehead and is heavily involved in control and planning, is the region where this was first and most famously observed.

In pioneering studies with monkeys, researchers such as Joaquin Fuster and Patricia Goldman-Rakic found neurons that fired continuously during the gap between seeing a cue and having to respond, as though the cell were holding the memory alive by its own ongoing activity.

The natural interpretation is that a memory is kept in mind by a self-sustaining loop of neural firing, sometimes described using the mathematics of attractor networks, which are stable patterns of activity that maintain themselves.

The systems reading is dynamic storage that must be continuously refreshed, like a memory chip that loses its contents the moment power is interrupted: input is a transient cue, state is the ongoing firing pattern sustained across delays of seconds, and output is the reinstated code at response time.

This view dominated for decades and fits nicely with the idea of an active, effortful workspace, since holding the activity going takes continuous energy and can be disrupted by distraction.


17.4.2 Activity-silent and synaptic accounts

More recent work has challenged the assumption that a memory must be held by continuous firing, and has proposed that information can be stored in a hidden, activity-silent form.

The activity-silent idea, developed prominently by Mark Stokes and colleagues from around 2013, is that during a delay the relevant neurons can fall quiet, yet the memory survives in temporary changes to the connections between neurons.

The proposed storage mechanism is short-term synaptic plasticity, which means rapid, brief changes in the strength of synapses, the junctions where neurons pass signals to one another.

In this account a memory can rest silently in briefly strengthened synapses, perhaps through leftover calcium building up at the connections, and can be read back out later by a pulse of activity, rather than needing to be held aloud the whole time.

As a system, this is passive storage with an explicit read operation: the write briefly reconfigures connection weights, the state persists for seconds without any signal on the wires, and a nonspecific ping of activity reads the pattern back out.

Evidence for this comes from findings that the pattern of brain activity holding a memory is often dynamic and can even disappear and then be revived, which is hard to square with a simple steady loop.

The current consensus is not that one account is right and the other wrong, but that both persistent activity and activity-silent synaptic storage occur, and the brain may use whichever suits the moment, so the two mechanisms are best seen as complementary rather than rivals.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Perceptual codes: speech-coded verbal material from audition and reading, and visual object and location codes from vision, delivered as the outputs of the short-term sensory stores of Chapter 16.

◦ Retrieved content: chunks and pattern codes pulled up from long-term memory when needed for the current task.

◦ Task goals: the current goal and priority signals from executive control, which determine what is admitted, refreshed, and dropped.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ The active contents: a small set of bound chunks in a common format, readable by reasoning, language comprehension and production, planning, and action systems.

◦ Rehearsal traffic: refreshed verbal codes recycled internally through the phonological loop.

◦ Encoding candidates: active items handed to long-term memory for possible storage.

• STATE.

◦ About four active chunks, each with its current activation level and its binding of features into a unit.

◦ The current allocation of attention across items and subsystems, including which item sits in the focus of attention.

◦ The rehearsal queue order for verbal material.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Capacity: about 4 chunks in the focus of attention; about 7 plus or minus 2 when rehearsal and grouping are allowed.

◦ Refresh rate: how often attention revisits each stored item, set by the free time the concurrent task leaves.

◦ Chunk size: how much raw material each chunk compresses, set by expertise and the long-term pattern library.

◦ Displacement policy: which item is dropped when a new item arrives at full capacity, typically the least recently refreshed.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Phonological trace lifetime: about 2 seconds without rehearsal.

◦ Focus of attention shift and task switch: on the order of a few hundred milliseconds.

◦ Maintenance duration: seconds to tens of seconds with active refresh, after which content must be re-encoded or handed to long-term memory.

◦ Decay rate of a single unrefreshed trace as an exact exponential constant: REFUSED, because the decay against interference debate means no agreed pure decay constant exists.

• MODES.

◦ Maintenance mode: attention is devoted to refreshing stored items, triggered when the concurrent task leaves free time.

◦ Processing mode: attention is captured by ongoing computation and refreshing pauses, triggered by task demands, at the cost of stored items fading or suffering interference.

◦ Manipulation mode: stored items are actively transformed, reordered, or combined rather than merely held, triggered by task instructions that require updating.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Overload: items beyond capacity are displaced or degraded, producing omissions and guesses.

◦ Similarity confusion: sound-alike or look-alike items swap or blur, as in the phonological similarity effect.

◦ Distraction loss: interruption of rehearsal or attention capture wipes fragile content, as in articulatory suppression and the irrelevant speech effect.

◦ Clinical breakdowns: reduced span after prefrontal or parietal damage, and the working memory deficits seen in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and schizophrenia.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called capacity with initial value four.
Create an empty list variable called store.
Define a procedure called encode that takes an item.
    If the item is already in the store, move the item to the end of the store and stop.
    If the length of the store equals the capacity, remove the first item from the store.
    Add the item to the end of the store.
Define a procedure called rehearse that takes an item.
    If the item is in the store, move the item to the end of the store.
Define a procedure called recall that takes a probe item.
    If the probe item is in the store, return true.
    Otherwise, return false.
For each incoming item in the input stream, call encode with the incoming item.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a number variable called CAPACITY with initial value four.
CAPACITY = 4

# Define a class called SlotStore to model a slot-limited working memory.
class SlotStore:
    # Define the initialiser, which takes no arguments beyond the store itself.
    def __init__(self):
        # Create an empty list attribute called slots, ordered oldest first.
        self.slots = []

    # Define a method called encode that takes an item.
    def encode(self, item):
        # If the item is already held, refresh it by moving it to the newest position, then stop.
        if item in self.slots:
            # Remove the item from its old position.
            self.slots.remove(item)
            # Add the item at the newest position.
            self.slots.append(item)
            # Return from the method.
            return
        # If the store is full, displace the least recently refreshed item.
        if len(self.slots) == CAPACITY:
            # Remove the oldest item and remember it as the displaced item.
            displaced = self.slots.pop(0)
            # Print a message naming the displaced item.
            print("displaced:", displaced)
        # Add the new item at the newest position.
        self.slots.append(item)

    # Define a method called recall that takes a probe and returns whether it is held.
    def recall(self, probe):
        # Return true when the probe is among the slots, and false otherwise.
        return probe in self.slots

# Create a SlotStore instance called wm.
wm = SlotStore()

# Create a list of nine digit strings to present, more than the store can hold.
digits = ["3", "1", "4", "1", "5", "9", "2", "6", "5"]

# For each digit in the list, encode the digit into working memory.
for d in digits:
    # Call encode with the digit.
    wm.encode(d)

# Print the final contents of the store, oldest first.
print("held:", wm.slots)

# For each digit from the original list, print the digit and whether recall succeeds.
for d in digits:
    # Print the digit and the recall result.
    print(d, wm.recall(d))


CHAPTER 18. LONG-TERM MEMORY SYSTEMS (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the mind's vast and lasting store, the memory that holds your knowledge, your past, and your skills for days, years, or a lifetime.

Long-term memory is not a single warehouse but a set of different systems that store different kinds of information in different ways.

Understanding that it comes in distinct kinds matters because damage or disease can knock out one kind while leaving another untouched, which tells us the systems are genuinely separate.

In systems terms, long-term memory is a family of persistent stores with different write paths, different read interfaces, and different hardware, some readable by consciousness and some readable only through behaviour.

This chapter maps those systems, then looks at two special corners of memory, the memory of your own life and the memory for things you still intend to do, and finally at the surprising discovery that remembering the past and imagining the future share the same machinery.


18.1 The taxonomy of long-term memory

A taxonomy is simply an organised classification, a way of sorting things into named groups, and long-term memory has a well-developed one.

The main division separates memory you can consciously bring to mind and put into words from memory that shows up only in behaviour, and the sub-sections below unpack that scheme.

The engineering criterion behind the taxonomy is the read interface: declarative stores support explicit query and verbal report, while non-declarative stores are write-only from the point of view of consciousness and expose their contents only as changed performance.


18.1.1 Declarative against non-declarative memory

The broadest split in long-term memory is between declarative memory and non-declarative memory, a distinction associated especially with Larry Squire.

Declarative memory is memory for facts and events that you can consciously recall and, as the name suggests, declare or state in words, such as knowing that Paris is a city or recalling what you ate this morning.

Non-declarative memory, also called implicit memory, is memory that shapes your behaviour without conscious recollection, such as knowing how to ride a bicycle or being unconsciously influenced by something you saw earlier.

As mechanisms, the two differ in every interface property: declarative memory takes a single experience as input and can be written in one exposure, while most non-declarative learning takes many repetitions as input and its output is a gradual change in speed, accuracy, or response tendency rather than a reportable fact.

The reason to believe these are truly different systems comes largely from patients with amnesia, which is severe memory loss usually from brain damage.

The most famous case is a patient known for decades by his initials H. M., later revealed as Henry Molaison, who after surgery to his medial temporal lobes could no longer form new declarative memories, yet could still learn new motor skills while having no conscious memory of the practice sessions.

This double pattern, a devastated declarative memory alongside a preserved skill-learning ability, is powerful evidence that the two kinds of memory rely on different brain systems.

Declarative memory depends heavily on the hippocampus and nearby structures in the medial temporal lobe, while various non-declarative forms depend on other regions such as the basal ganglia and cerebellum.


18.1.2 Episodic against semantic memory

Within declarative memory there is a further important split, proposed by Endel Tulving in 1972, between episodic memory and semantic memory.

Episodic memory is memory for specific personal experiences tied to a particular time and place, such as remembering your last birthday or where you left your keys.

Semantic memory is memory for general facts and knowledge about the world that is not tied to any particular occasion of learning, such as knowing that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, or that a dog is an animal.

In systems terms, an episodic record carries a spatiotemporal index, a stamp of when and where, and is retrieved by reconstructing that context, while a semantic record has had its index stripped away and is retrieved by content alone, which makes it faster to query but impossible to trace to its source.

Tulving argued that episodic memory involves a special kind of conscious re-experiencing, a mental time travel back into the remembered event, which he called autonoetic awareness, meaning a self-knowing awareness that this happened to you.

Semantic memory, by contrast, feels more like simply knowing something, without any sense of reliving the moment you learned it.

The two are connected, since repeated episodes can feed into general knowledge, and much of what you know began as specific experiences whose individual details have faded.

Evidence for the split again comes from patients, since some people with brain damage lose the ability to recall personal events while keeping their general knowledge relatively intact, and the reverse pattern also occurs.


18.1.3 Procedural memory, priming, and conditioning

Non-declarative memory is not one thing either, and it includes at least three important kinds worth naming.

Procedural memory is the memory for skills and habits, the knowing-how that lets you perform actions such as typing, swimming, or reading fluently without consciously recalling the rules.

A hallmark of procedural memory is that it is hard to put into words, since a skilled cyclist cannot easily explain the fine adjustments that keep them upright, yet their body performs them reliably.

As a mechanism, procedural memory takes repeated practice as input, stores compiled sensorimotor routines, and outputs faster and smoother performance over a timescale of many sessions, which is the learning curve treated in Chapter 33.

Priming is a subtler form, in which recent exposure to something makes you faster or more likely to recognise or produce it later, even when you have no conscious memory of the exposure.

For example, if you have just seen the word doctor, you will complete the fragment nur followed by a blank and an e as nurse more readily, without realising why, which is priming at work.

In systems terms priming is a short-lived bias written into perceptual and lexical pathways by a single exposure, raising the readiness of the exposed representation for minutes to days.

Conditioning is the third kind, and it refers to simple learned associations of the sort studied by Ivan Pavlov, in which a neutral signal that reliably precedes an important event comes to trigger a response on its own.

The classic example is a dog that learns to salivate at a bell that has repeatedly preceded food, an association that forms and operates without any need for conscious, declarative recollection.

These non-declarative forms are evolutionarily ancient and widely shared across animals, and they run quietly beneath awareness, which is exactly why they survive when conscious memory is destroyed.


18.2 Autobiographical and prospective memory

Beyond the basic taxonomy, two kinds of memory are especially close to daily life and deserve their own treatment.

One is the memory of your own life story, and the other is memory for the future, the ability to remember to carry out plans, and the sub-sections take each in turn.


18.2.1 The self across time in autobiographical memory

Autobiographical memory is the memory for the events and facts of your own life, and it is what gives you a continuous sense of who you are across time.

It is a blend of episodic and semantic memory, combining specific remembered episodes, such as a particular family holiday, with general personal facts, such as which town you grew up in.

Researchers describe it as organised in layers, from broad lifetime periods, such as your school years, down through general events, down to specific single episodes, and recall usually works top down through these layers.

In systems terms it is a hierarchical index: a query enters at the lifetime-period level, narrows through general events, and resolves to a specific episode, which is why retrieving a particular memory often takes several seconds of deliberate search rather than the instant pop-out of a semantic fact.

One robust finding is the reminiscence bump, which is the tendency of older adults to recall a disproportionate number of memories from roughly their teens to their late twenties, perhaps because this is a formative period rich in novel, identity-defining experiences.

Another is that autobiographical memory is not a neutral record but is shaped by your current self, since your present beliefs, mood, and goals colour which events come to mind and how they are remembered.

Because it links memory to identity, damage to autobiographical memory can be deeply disorienting, robbing a person not just of facts but of the felt story of their own life.


18.2.2 Remembering to act in prospective memory

Prospective memory is the memory for actions you intend to carry out in the future, such as remembering to take medicine at night or to pass on a message when you see a friend.

It is different from ordinary memory because the challenge is not to recall a fact when asked, but to remember, at the right moment and without any prompt, that there was something you meant to do.

Researchers distinguish two types, event-based prospective memory, where a cue in the world reminds you, such as seeing the friend, and time-based prospective memory, where you must act at a certain time with no external cue, which is generally harder.

Prospective memory has two ingredients, a prospective part, which is remembering that there is an intention at all, and a retrospective part, which is remembering what the intended action actually was.

As a mechanism, it is a deferred trigger system: the input is a stored intention paired with a trigger condition, the system must match ongoing perception or elapsed time against that condition over minutes to days, and the output is an interrupt that injects the intended action into current behaviour.

There is an ongoing debate about how the right moment is caught, between accounts that say it takes continuous effortful monitoring of the environment and accounts that say a suitable cue can trigger the intention more automatically, and in systems terms the first predicts a measurable cost on the ongoing task while an intention is pending and the second predicts no cost, with evidence for a situation-dependent mixture of both.

Failures of prospective memory are among the most common and consequential everyday memory lapses, ranging from the harmless, such as forgetting to post a letter, to the tragic, such as forgetting a child in a car.


18.3 The convergence with imagination

One of the most striking discoveries in memory science is that memory is not only about the past, and this section explains why.

It turns out that recalling what happened and imagining what might happen draw on much the same mental and neural machinery.


18.3.1 The shared machinery of remembering the past and simulating the future

For a long time memory was pictured as a kind of recording of the past, but evidence now shows that the very same brain network is active whether you remember a past event or imagine a future one.

Brain imaging studies, along with observations of patients, revealed that a common core network, including the hippocampus and connected midline regions, lights up both when people recall autobiographical events and when they imagine plausible personal futures.

Tellingly, some amnesic patients who cannot recall their past also cannot construct vivid imagined future scenes, which suggests the two abilities depend on one shared system rather than two separate ones.

Daniel Schacter and Donna Rose Addis captured this in what they called the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis, proposed in 2007.

The core idea is that episodic memory is not a faithful playback but a flexible process of pulling apart and recombining stored details, and that this same recombining ability is exactly what is needed to build a novel imagined future.

In systems terms, one generative engine serves two calls: given a query about the past it retrieves and reassembles stored fragments into a remembered scene, and given a query about the future it recombines the same fragments into a simulated scene, so the input differs only in the direction of the request while the assembly machinery is identical.

In this view, remembering and imagining are two uses of a single constructive system, one aimed backward in time and one aimed forward.


18.3.2 Memory as a tool for prospection rather than a record

This convergence leads to a deeper rethinking of what memory is for, and the proposal is that memory evolved less to preserve the past than to help us prepare for the future.

Prospection is the general term for thinking about and mentally simulating the future, and the argument is that the adaptive payoff of memory lies here.

An animal that can recombine fragments of past experience into simulations of what might happen can rehearse plans, weigh options, and anticipate outcomes without having to try them out in the risky real world.

On this account the flexible, reconstructive nature of memory is not a design flaw but the very feature that makes future simulation possible, since a rigid, tape-like record could not be freely recombined into new scenarios.

Stated in systems terms, the design trade is explicit: a lossless append-only log maximises fidelity but supports no recombination, while a fragment store with a constructive assembler supports planning and simulation at the cost of occasional wrong reassembly.

The same flexibility, however, comes at a price, because a system that recombines details can also stitch them together wrongly, which is one root of the memory errors covered in Chapter 20.

So the honest summary is that memory's usefulness for imagining the future and its vulnerability to distortion are two sides of the same coin.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Encoding candidates: bound chunks and episodes handed over from working memory, tagged with context.

◦ Practice traffic: repeated sensorimotor and perceptual exposures that drive procedural learning, priming, and conditioning without explicit hand-over.

◦ Retrieval queries: cues from working memory, perception, and ongoing thought that request stored content.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Retrieved declarative content: facts and reconstructed episodes delivered back into working memory for report and reasoning.

◦ Performance changes: faster, smoother, or biased responding that expresses procedural memory, priming, and conditioned associations.

◦ Simulations: recombined episodic fragments assembled into imagined future or hypothetical scenes for planning.

• STATE.

◦ The semantic knowledge base: content-addressed facts and concepts with no source stamp.

◦ The episodic store: context-stamped event records indexed by the hippocampus.

◦ Compiled skill routines, primed pathway biases, and learned signal-outcome associations in their separate substrates.

◦ Pending intentions with their trigger conditions, for prospective memory.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Write threshold: how much attention, depth, and emotional weight an experience needs before a durable declarative trace is laid down.

◦ Activation decay rate: how fast an unused declarative trace loses retrievability, the parameter d in activation models.

◦ Association strength gain per pairing, for conditioning and priming.

◦ Monitoring allocation: how much attention is spent checking for prospective memory triggers.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Declarative write: a single exposure of seconds can create a lasting episodic trace.

◦ Procedural learning: improvement accrues over many sessions spanning days to years.

◦ Priming persistence: minutes to days depending on the task.

◦ Retention span: hours to decades for consolidated declarative content.

◦ A single universal decay constant for all long-term forgetting: REFUSED, because measured retention depends on material, cueing, and interference, and no one constant fits.

• MODES.

◦ Explicit retrieval mode: a deliberate query reconstructs declarative content, triggered by a question or a goal.

◦ Implicit expression mode: stored learning shapes behaviour without any query, the default for non-declarative forms.

◦ Simulation mode: the episodic machinery runs forward to imagine futures, triggered by planning and prospection demands.

◦ Prospective watch mode: stored intentions are matched against ongoing events and time, triggered by holding an uncompleted intention.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Anterograde amnesia: loss of the declarative write path after medial temporal damage, with non-declarative learning spared, as in patient H. M.

◦ Retrograde amnesia: loss of access to already stored declarative content, typically worst for the most recent memories.

◦ Dissociations: episodic loss with semantic sparing or the reverse, and semantic dementia eroding the knowledge base itself.

◦ Prospective lapses: intentions whose triggers are never matched, from missed medicine doses to catastrophic omissions.

◦ Recombination errors: the constructive engine stitching fragments into scenes that never occurred, the seed of the false memories of Chapter 20.
