But the model soon ran into trouble.

It could not explain the typicality effect, that people confirm "a robin is a bird" faster than "a penguin is a bird" even though both are one step away.

It also mispredicted some distances, since people verify "a dog is an animal" surprisingly fast, and its strict tree could not easily hold the messy, criss-crossing associations of real knowledge.


22.1.2 Spreading activation

To fix these problems Collins, now working with Elizabeth Loftus, published a revised model in 1975 based on spreading activation.

The picture is still a network of concept nodes joined by links, but the tidy hierarchy is abandoned in favour of a web organised by relatedness, where the length of a link reflects how closely two ideas are associated in your experience.

Closely related ideas such as "red" and "fire" sit on short links; loosely related ones sit on long links.

Spreading activation is the core mechanism: when you think of a concept, that node lights up, and the activation flows outward along its links to neighbouring nodes, lighting them up too, more strongly for near neighbours than for distant ones.

As a system, this is a graph with a numeric activation level held at every node: the input is a probe that injects activation at one node, the process is iterative propagation along weighted links with decay at each step, and the output is a pattern of raised activations that makes related concepts faster to retrieve for the next second or so before the boost fades.

This elegantly explains typicality, because a strong short link runs from "bird" to the well-connected "robin" and a weaker one to "penguin".

It also explains a famous laboratory finding called semantic priming: people recognise the word "nurse" faster if they have just seen the related word "doctor", because seeing "doctor" has already sent activation flowing to "nurse", giving it a head start.

The cost of this flexibility is that a network you can reshape at will is harder to prove wrong, but spreading activation remains one of the most durable and widely used ideas in the psychology of memory.


22.2 The feature and space models

A different tradition sets aside the picture of nodes and links and asks instead what a meaning is made of.

Perhaps the meaning of a word is a bundle of smaller features, or perhaps it is a location in a vast mental space.

This section covers both, ending with the modern computational version that now powers much of artificial intelligence.


22.2.1 Semantic feature comparison

In 1974 Edward Smith, Edward Shoben, and Lance Rips proposed that a concept is not a point in a network but a list of features, and that categorising works by comparing the features of two things.

They drew a useful distinction between two kinds of feature.

Defining features are the ones essential to a category, the ones every member must have, such as "has feathers" for birds.

Characteristic features are ones that are merely typical, common but not required, such as "can fly", which most birds have but ostriches and penguins do not.

To judge a statement like "a robin is a bird", the model runs in two stages: first a quick, rough comparison of all features of both kinds, and if that gives a clear yes or a clear no the person answers at once.

Only if the first stage is ambiguous does a slower second stage kick in that checks the defining features alone.

In systems terms this is a two-stage pipeline with an early exit: stage one computes overall feature overlap and answers fast when the overlap is clearly high or clearly low, and only intermediate overlap values trigger the slower stage-two check, which is what adds the extra response time for atypical members.

This two-stage design neatly explains the typicality effect: a robin shares both defining and characteristic features with birds, so it passes the fast first stage and gets a quick "yes", while a penguin lacks characteristic features like flying, fails the fast stage, and forces the slow careful check, producing the observed delay.

The feature-comparison model faded as a standalone theory, partly because it is hard to say which features are truly "defining" for everyday concepts, the very problem that sank the classical definitional view, but its idea that meaning is built from features lives on.


22.2.2 Distributional semantics and vector-space meaning

Distributional semantics is a powerful modern idea about meaning that turned out to be the engine behind much of today's artificial intelligence, and its slogan is memorably simple.

The linguist John Rupert Firth put it in 1957 as "you shall know a word by the company it keeps", meaning you can learn what a word means just by watching which other words it tends to appear near.

The word "dog" keeps company with "bark", "leash", "tail", and "vet", and that pattern of company is, on this view, most of what "dog" means.

The method turns each word into a vector, which is just a long list of numbers recording how often the word co-occurs with every other word, so that a word becomes a point in a space with hundreds of dimensions.

Words used in similar contexts end up as nearby points, so "dog" and "cat" sit close together while "dog" and "democracy" sit far apart, and closeness in the space captures similarity of meaning.

In systems terms the pipeline is clear: the input is a large body of text, the process is counting co-occurrences and compressing the counts, the state is one vector per word, and the output for any query pair of words is a similarity score, usually the cosine of the angle between their vectors.

An early version was Latent Semantic Analysis in the 1990s, which used linear algebra to compress large bodies of text into such a space.

A famous later version was word2vec, introduced by Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google in 2013, which used a neural network and could even do rough analogies by arithmetic on the vectors, so that the vector for "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands near "queen".

The great strength of this approach is that meaning is learned automatically from ordinary text with no human hand-labelling, and it is the direct ancestor of the word representations inside modern large language models.

Its much-debated weakness returns us to a theme of the next chapter: a system that has only ever seen words next to other words, and never touched a dog or seen the sky, may capture how words relate to each other without capturing what they are actually about.


22.3 The neural organisation of meaning

The models so far are about the mind's software; this section turns to the brain's hardware and asks where and how meaning is physically stored.

The evidence comes largely from what happens to knowledge when specific parts of the brain are damaged, which offers rare, if sad, natural experiments.


22.3.1 The hub-and-spoke model and the semantic hub

A central question about the brain is whether meaning lives in one place or is scattered.

The hub-and-spoke model, developed by Karalyn Patterson, Matthew Lambon Ralph, and colleagues, offers a "both" answer that has become the leading account.

The spokes are the scattered, modality-specific brain regions that hold the different kinds of sensory and motor knowledge about a thing: what a banana looks like sits near the visual areas, what it tastes like near the taste areas, how you peel it near the movement areas.

The term modality just means a channel of experience, such as sight, sound, or touch.

But scattered features are not enough, because knowing a banana means pulling all those strands into a single unified concept, and that is the job of the hub.

The hub is a region in the anterior temporal lobe, the front part of the temporal lobes which sit low on each side of the brain roughly behind the ears, and it draws the spokes together into a general, sense-independent meaning that captures the deep similarities between things.

In systems terms the hub is an integration layer: it subscribes to feature signals from every modality-specific spoke, computes a shared cross-modal code, and publishes that unified concept back out so that any single cue, a smell, a word, a picture, can retrieve the whole.

The strongest evidence comes from a condition called semantic dementia, in which the anterior temporal lobes gradually waste away.

Patients with semantic dementia lose meaning itself in a broad, even way across all categories and all senses, which is exactly what you would expect if the shared hub, rather than any single spoke, were breaking down; they come to sort things by shallow appearance rather than deep meaning, for instance grouping all four-legged animals together.


22.3.2 Category-specific semantic deficits as evidence of structure

One of the most surprising discoveries in this field is that brain damage can rob a person of knowledge about one category of things while leaving other categories almost intact.

Elizabeth Warrington and Tim Shallice reported the landmark cases in 1984.

Some patients could recognise and name non-living objects like tools and furniture perfectly well, yet were badly impaired at living things such as animals and fruits, and, more rarely, other patients showed the opposite pattern.

When two patients show opposite patterns like this, researchers call it a double dissociation, and it is powerful evidence that the two abilities rest on at least partly separate machinery rather than one lumped-together store.

Warrington and Shallice offered an explanation called the sensory-functional theory.

Their idea was that we tell living things apart mainly by their sensory features, that is, by fine differences in shape, colour, and texture, whereas we identify non-living tools mainly by what they are for and how we act with them, their functional features.

In systems terms the two accounts predict different fault maps: a single undivided store predicts uniform degradation under damage, while a store partitioned by feature type predicts exactly the category-selective outages that were observed.

If sensory knowledge and functional knowledge live in different parts of the brain, then damage to the sensory part would hit living things hardest, and damage to the functional part would hit tools hardest, which is roughly the observed pattern.

The theory is not the last word, and rival accounts stress other factors such as how familiar or how visually crowded the categories are, but the basic finding stands: the fact that knowledge can fracture along the seam between living and non-living things tells us semantic memory has real internal structure rather than being one undivided mass.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Retrieval probes: words, images, or thoughts that name or cue a concept, arriving from perception, language comprehension, and ongoing reasoning.

◦ New facts and associations to be stored, arriving from episodic memory through consolidation.

◦ Contextual priming input: recently active concepts whose residual activation biases what is retrieved next.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Retrieved facts, properties, and associations, formatted as activated concept representations, consumed by language, reasoning, and imagery.

◦ Graded activation levels over related concepts, consumed as priming by word recognition and by fluency of thought.

◦ Verification signals, yes or no with a confidence level, for queried statements, consumed by decision and response systems.

• STATE.

◦ The long-term knowledge graph itself: concept nodes, weighted links, feature lists, and distributed vector-like codes, plus the short-lived pattern of current activation across the network.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Link strengths between concepts; an activation decay rate; a spreading fraction governing how much activation passes to neighbours; a retrieval threshold a node must exceed to enter awareness.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Sentence verification of familiar facts completes in roughly 1 second, with each extra hierarchical step adding on the order of 75 milliseconds for category statements and about 225 milliseconds for property statements in the Collins and Quillian data.

◦ Automatic semantic priming is strongest when the related word appears within roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds before the target and largely dissipates over the following seconds.

◦ A universal decay half-life for spreading activation: REFUSED, because published estimates vary widely with task and model and no single agreed value exists.

• MODES.

◦ Automatic retrieval mode, fast spreading of activation without effort, against strategic search mode, deliberate cue-generation when automatic retrieval fails, with the switch triggered by a retrieval failure such as a tip-of-the-tongue state.

◦ Read mode against write mode, with writing gated by consolidation processes that slowly add new links to the store.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Tip-of-the-tongue states and retrieval blocks; false confirmations of plausible but wrong facts through overlapping associations; semantic dementia, a broad cross-modal loss of meaning when the anterior temporal hub degenerates; and category-specific deficits when particular feature regions are damaged.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary variable called network where each concept name maps to a list of pairs of a neighbouring concept name and a link strength between zero and one.
Create a dictionary variable called activation where every concept name maps to the number zero.
Receive a concept name called probe as input.
Set the activation of probe to one.
Create a number variable called decay with value zero point six.
Create a list variable called frontier containing only the probe.
Repeat three times:
    Create an empty list called next frontier.
    For each concept in frontier:
        For each pair of neighbour and strength linked to the concept:
            Calculate the product of the concept's activation, the strength, and decay.
            If the result is greater than the neighbour's current activation:
                Set the neighbour's activation to the result.
                Add the neighbour to next frontier.
    Set frontier to next frontier.
Sort the concepts by activation from highest to lowest.
Return the sorted list as the pattern of primed concepts.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a dictionary mapping each concept to its neighbours and link strengths
network = {
    # Link the concept doctor to its associates
    "doctor": [("nurse", 0.9), ("hospital", 0.8), ("stethoscope", 0.6)],
    # Link the concept nurse to its associates
    "nurse": [("doctor", 0.9), ("hospital", 0.8), ("uniform", 0.5)],
    # Link the concept hospital to its associates
    "hospital": [("doctor", 0.8), ("nurse", 0.8), ("ambulance", 0.7)],
    # Link the concept ambulance to its associates
    "ambulance": [("hospital", 0.7), ("siren", 0.8)],
    # Link the concept siren to its associates
    "siren": [("ambulance", 0.8), ("fire", 0.4)],
    # Link the concept stethoscope to its associates
    "stethoscope": [("doctor", 0.6)],
    # Link the concept uniform to its associates
    "uniform": [("nurse", 0.5)],
    # Link the concept fire to its associates
    "fire": [("siren", 0.4), ("red", 0.7)],
    # Link the concept red to its associates
    "red": [("fire", 0.7)],
}

# Define a function that spreads activation outward from a probe concept
def spread(probe, steps=3, decay=0.6):
    # Create an activation dictionary with every concept set to zero
    activation = {name: 0.0 for name in network}
    # Set the activation of the probe concept to one
    activation[probe] = 1.0
    # Create a frontier list containing only the probe
    frontier = [probe]
    # Repeat the propagation for the requested number of steps
    for _ in range(steps):
        # Create an empty list for the next frontier
        next_frontier = []
        # For each active concept in the current frontier
        for concept in frontier:
            # For each neighbour and link strength of the concept
            for neighbour, strength in network[concept]:
                # Calculate the activation passed along the link with decay
                passed = activation[concept] * strength * decay
                # If the passed activation exceeds the neighbour's current level
                if passed > activation[neighbour]:
                    # Set the neighbour's activation to the passed value
                    activation[neighbour] = passed
                    # Add the neighbour to the next frontier
                    next_frontier.append(neighbour)
        # Replace the frontier with the next frontier
        frontier = next_frontier
    # Return the concepts sorted from most to least activated
    return sorted(activation.items(), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])

# Spread activation from the concept doctor and print the primed concepts
for concept, level in spread("doctor"):
    # Print each concept with its activation level rounded to three places
    print(concept, round(level, 3))


CHAPTER 23. GROUNDED, EMBODIED, AND DISTRIBUTED MEANING (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter steps back from the machinery of memory to ask a deep and stubborn question: what makes a thought about something actually be about that thing.

It is tagged as a framework because it supplies ideas and arguments that sharpen and constrain the process chapters around it, rather than describing a single mental capacity.

The question sounds abstract but it has become urgent in the age of artificial intelligence, because a chatbot can produce fluent sentences about apples without ever having seen, held, or tasted one.

The worry running through this chapter is whether meaning can live purely inside a system of symbols, or whether it must somehow be anchored, or grounded, in real experience of the world, in a real body acting in a real environment.

In systems terms the question is about the interface between the symbol store and the world: a purely symbolic system has inputs and outputs only in symbol format, while a grounded system also subscribes to sensor streams and publishes motor commands, and the debate is over whether the first kind of interface can ever carry meaning on its own.


23.1 The symbol grounding problem

This section sets out the core problem plainly and traces it to the two thinkers who framed it, then surveys the main proposed escape routes.


23.1.1 Harnad's formulation and the Chinese Room

The symbol grounding problem was named and sharpened by the cognitive scientist Stevan Harnad in 1990.

The problem is this: if the meaning of a symbol in your head is given only by other symbols, the way a dictionary defines each word using more words, then the whole system seems to spin in a closed circle, with meaning never touching the world at all.

Harnad's own image is of trying to learn Chinese from a Chinese-to-Chinese dictionary alone: every definition sends you to more Chinese words you also do not know, and you could circle forever without ever learning what a single word means.

So the question is how any symbol inside a mind or a machine gets to be about a real thing out in the world, rather than just pointing at yet more symbols.

Harnad built directly on a famous earlier thought experiment by the philosopher John Searle in 1980, called the Chinese Room.

Searle imagined himself locked in a room with a huge rulebook, receiving slips of paper covered in Chinese characters and using the rulebook to send back other Chinese characters.

To the Chinese speakers outside, the room gives perfect answers and seems to understand Chinese, yet Searle inside understands nothing; he is just shuffling shapes by their form according to rules.

Searle's point was that manipulating symbols by their shape, which is what he argued a computer does, can never by itself add up to genuine understanding of what the symbols mean.

In systems terms the room is a pure input-output transducer over symbol strings, and the two sides predict differently: Searle predicts that no amount of internal symbol shuffling changes what the system is about, while his critics predict that aboutness can emerge from the right functional organisation regardless of the medium.

Harnad accepted the force of this and turned it into a constructive challenge: rather than just denying that machines understand, he asked how symbols could be given real meaning, and he suggested the answer must involve connecting symbols to the world through the senses.


23.1.2 Grounding by sensorimotor experience and by multimodal learning

Harnad's proposed way out of the circle is to tie at least some symbols directly to the world through sensory and motor experience, so that they are not defined by other words but by contact with the things themselves.

Sensorimotor means having to do with sensing and moving, that is, with perceiving the world and acting on it with a body.

The idea is that a basic word like "red" or "cup" gets its meaning grounded because the system can pick out red things and cups by seeing and handling them, and richer words can then be built on top of these grounded basics.

Harnad specifically proposed a hybrid system, one that joins a symbol-manipulating part to a pattern-learning neural network that connects those symbols to sensory images of the world, so you get the best of both.

In systems terms grounding is an added input channel: the base symbols subscribe directly to perceptual classifiers trained on sensor data, and every higher symbol inherits its connection to the world through composition over those grounded bases.

A modern echo of this idea is multimodal learning in artificial intelligence, where "multimodal" means using several channels of input at once, such as pictures and text together rather than text alone.

Recent artificial intelligence systems that are trained on images paired with their captions learn to connect the word "dog" to actual pictures of dogs, which many researchers see as a partial, practical form of grounding that a text-only system lacks.

Whether this truly solves Harnad's problem or merely connects one set of symbols, words, to another, patterns of pixels, is still genuinely debated, and reasonable experts disagree, so it is fair to call this an open question rather than a settled one.


23.2 Grounded and perceptual symbol systems

This section presents the strongest positive theory in this area, the claim that concepts are not abstract at all but are re-enactments of experience, and then weighs the evidence honestly.


23.2.1 Concepts as simulations rather than amodal symbols

The traditional view in cognitive science held that concepts are amodal symbols.

Amodal means stripped of any particular sense, an abstract code standing for "dog" that is no more visual than it is auditory, like a word written in an internal language of thought.

The psychologist Lawrence Barsalou challenged this head-on in 1999 with his theory of perceptual symbol systems, part of a broader movement called grounded or embodied cognition.

Barsalou's proposal is that concepts are not abstract codes but simulations, partial re-enactments of the very brain states that occur when you actually perceive or act.

On this view, to think about a hammer you unconsciously and partly reactivate the visual experience of seeing a hammer and the motor experience of swinging one; the concept is a rehearsal of the experience rather than a description of it.

Barsalou calls the full stored capacity to run such re-enactments for a category a simulator, and any single running instance a simulation, so your "car" simulator can generate a simulation of a specific red sports car when needed.

In systems terms a simulator is a stored generative model whose input is a conceptual query and whose output is a partial replay of sensory and motor activity, so that thinking reuses the perception and action hardware rather than a separate symbol processor.

The appeal of this theory is that it dissolves the grounding problem at a stroke: if concepts just are reactivated perception and action, they are grounded in the world automatically, with no gap to bridge.


23.2.2 The evidence for and against grounding

The evidence for grounded cognition is real but has been contested, so it is worth laying out both sides plainly.

On the supporting side, many experiments show that understanding language stirs up sensory and motor brain systems.

For example, reading action words like "kick", "pick", and "lick" activates the very regions of the motor cortex that control the foot, hand, and mouth, as if you faintly simulate the action to understand the word.

In behavioural studies, people are faster to judge a sentence sensible when the hand movement they must make to respond matches the movement the sentence describes, a result known as the action-sentence compatibility effect.

On the sceptical side, critics raise two main points.

First, activation is not the same as necessity: the fact that motor areas light up when you read "kick" does not prove that you need those areas to understand the word, since the activation might be a side effect that follows understanding rather than causing it.

Second, grounded theories struggle to explain abstract concepts like "justice", "seven", or "tomorrow", which have no obvious look, sound, or feel to simulate.

In systems terms the two camps predict differently under intervention: if simulation is load-bearing, disabling the motor channel should slow or impair understanding of action words, while if it is a side effect, understanding should proceed unchanged when the channel is removed.

The current balanced view among many researchers is a middle position: sensory and motor simulation genuinely contributes to meaning, especially for concrete words, but it probably works alongside more abstract, language-based, and word-co-occurrence knowledge rather than replacing it entirely.

In short, the mind may be neither purely grounded nor purely abstract, but a blend, and pinning down that blend is active research.


23.3 Schemas, frames, and mental models

The final section of this chapter turns from single concepts to larger packages of structured knowledge, the ready-made mental frameworks that let you make sense of whole situations quickly.


23.3.1 Frames and scripts as structured knowledge

Much of the knowledge you use is not about lone objects but about how things typically hang together in familiar situations, and researchers proposed structured packages to capture this.

The artificial-intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky introduced the idea of a frame in 1974.

A frame is a data structure for a stereotyped situation, made of slots that expect certain kinds of filler, with sensible default values ready when the details are missing.

Your "kitchen" frame has slots for a stove, a sink, and cupboards, and if someone mentions a kitchen you have not seen, you automatically assume it has these things unless told otherwise; that is a default value at work.

Closely related is the script, an idea from Roger Schank and Robert Abelson in 1977, which is a frame for a routine sequence of events.

Their famous example is the restaurant script: you know without being told that you enter, are seated, read a menu, order, eat, pay, and leave, in that order, with roles for the waiter and the cook.

In systems terms a frame is a record with typed slots and defaults and a script is the same structure ordered in time: the input is a mention of the situation, the process is slot filling from evidence with defaults for the gaps, and the output is a complete situation model produced within the second or two it takes to read a sentence.

Scripts explain why stories can leave so much unsaid, since if a tale says "she ate at the cafe and left a big tip", you effortlessly fill in the ordering and the eating from your script, and they also explain a memory quirk: people often misremember a story as having included typical script events that were never actually mentioned, because the script quietly supplied them.

Frames and scripts are important both as theories of human knowledge and as early blueprints for getting machines to reason about ordinary situations.


23.3.2 Mental models as manipulable internal representations

A mental model is a small working replica of some part of the world that you build in your head and can then run or manipulate to figure things out, rather than a static store of facts.

The idea was developed in depth by the psychologist Philip Johnson-Laird, building on an older insight from Kenneth Craik in 1943 that the mind works by carrying a small-scale model of reality that it can use to try out actions in imagination before committing to them in the flesh.

The key feature is that a mental model has a structure that mirrors the structure of the thing it represents, so relationships in the model line up with relationships in the world, which is what lets you "read off" new conclusions by inspecting the model.

In systems terms a mental model is a runnable simulation: its inputs are premises or observations, its state is a structural replica whose parts map to parts of the world, and its output is whatever new relation becomes visible when the model is inspected or stepped forward in time.

Johnson-Laird applied this powerfully to reasoning: he argued that when people work through a logic problem they do not follow formal rules of logic but instead imagine concrete example situations, that is, build mental models of the possibilities, and then check what holds across them.

This theory neatly predicts why people make certain reasoning errors, because they tend to build only one or a few models and overlook other possibilities that a fuller search would reveal, so the errors come from limited model-building rather than from broken logic.

Mental models also explain everyday understanding, such as how you predict what a set of gears will do by mentally turning them, and the idea connects outward to the broader theme of Chapter One, that a mind works largely by building and running internal models of its world.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Symbol streams: words and sentences arriving from language comprehension, whose meanings are the thing to be grounded.

◦ Sensor streams: visual, auditory, tactile, taste, and smell input from perception, plus proprioceptive feedback from the body.

◦ Motor efference copies: records of one's own actions, which tie words like "grasp" to the experience of grasping.

◦ Situation cues that trigger frames, scripts, and mental-model construction.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Grounded concept representations: symbols bound to perceptual classifiers and motor routines, consumed by semantic memory and reasoning.

◦ Running simulations: partial re-enactments of sensory and motor states, consumed by imagery, comprehension, and planning.

◦ Filled situation models: frames and scripts with slots resolved, consumed by discourse comprehension and memory encoding.

◦ Predictions read off from mental models, consumed by decision and action systems.

• STATE.

◦ The learned mappings from symbols to sensorimotor patterns; the library of frames, scripts, and simulators; and the currently constructed mental model of the situation at hand.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ The blend weight between grounded simulation and distributional word-co-occurrence knowledge; the strength of frame default values; the number of alternative mental models a reasoner will build before answering.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Motor-cortex activation by action words appears within roughly 200 milliseconds of word onset in electrophysiological studies, fast enough to be part of comprehension rather than an afterthought.

◦ Script-based inference completes within normal reading time, on the order of a few hundred milliseconds to a couple of seconds per sentence.

◦ A characteristic time constant for constructing or updating a full mental model: REFUSED, because construction time varies with model complexity and the literature reports no single standard value.

• MODES.

◦ Grounded simulation mode against symbolic shortcut mode, with concrete familiar content favouring simulation and abstract or highly practised content favouring language-based association, the depth demanded by the task switching between them.

◦ Default mode against evidence mode within a frame, with each slot switching from its default value to an observed value the moment the input specifies it.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Ungrounded fluency, producing well-formed talk with no anchoring in experience, as critics allege of text-only artificial intelligence; script-driven false memory, recalling typical events that never occurred; default-value errors when a situation silently violates the frame; and reasoning errors from building too few mental models of the possibilities.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary variable called word vectors where each word maps to a list of numbers describing the contexts the word appears in.
Receive two words called word a and word b as input.
Look up the vector for word a and the vector for word b.
Create a number variable called dot product with initial value zero.
For each position in the vectors, calculate the product of the paired values and add the result to dot product.
Create a number variable called norm a with initial value zero.
For each value in the vector of word a, calculate the square of the value and add the result to norm a.
Set norm a to the square root of norm a.
Create a number variable called norm b with initial value zero.
For each value in the vector of word b, calculate the square of the value and add the result to norm b.
Set norm b to the square root of norm b.
Calculate the quotient of dot product divided by the product of norm a and norm b, and store the result in a variable called cosine similarity.
Return cosine similarity as the closeness of meaning between the two words, noting that it measures only the company the words keep, not contact with the world.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for the square root function
import math

# Create a dictionary of word vectors built from counts of context company kept
word_vectors = {
    # Record how often dog co-occurs with the contexts bark, leash, purr, vote, and law
    "dog": [8.0, 7.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0],
    # Record the same context counts for cat
    "cat": [2.0, 1.0, 9.0, 0.0, 0.0],
    # Record the same context counts for puppy
    "puppy": [7.0, 6.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0],
    # Record the same context counts for democracy
    "democracy": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 8.0, 9.0],
    # Record the same context counts for election
    "election": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 9.0, 7.0],
}

# Define a function that returns the cosine similarity of two words
def cosine(word_a, word_b):
    # Look up the vector for each word
    a, b = word_vectors[word_a], word_vectors[word_b]
    # Calculate the dot product by summing the products of paired values
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    # Calculate the length of the first vector
    norm_a = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    # Calculate the length of the second vector
    norm_b = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    # Return the dot product divided by the product of the two lengths
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b)

# Create a list of word pairs to compare
pairs = [("dog", "puppy"), ("dog", "cat"), ("dog", "democracy"), ("democracy", "election")]
# For each pair of words in the list
for w1, w2 in pairs:
    # Print the pair with its cosine similarity rounded to three places
    print(w1, "and", w2, "have similarity", round(cosine(w1, w2), 3))


CHAPTER 24. MENTAL IMAGERY AND ANALOG REPRESENTATION (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the pictures in your head.

Mental imagery is the experience of perceiving something in its absence, most familiarly "seeing" something with your mind's eye, as when you picture your front door or count the windows on your house from memory.

Almost everyone has some version of this experience, and it raises a genuinely deep question about the mind: when you picture something, is there really a picture-like thing in your head, or is that just a figure of speech for a process that is actually more like describing.

That question drove one of the longest and most instructive debates in cognitive science, and this chapter lays out the striking experiments first and then the debate they fed.

The word analog in the chapter title means a representation that varies smoothly and resembles what it stands for, the way the length of a mercury thermometer's column varies in step with the temperature, as opposed to a digital or symbolic code that stands for things by arbitrary labels.

Viewed as a system, imagery is a generator and a workspace: it takes a request from thought, loads a spatial representation from memory, applies continuous transformations such as rotation and scanning, and publishes the transformed image back for inspection, with a processing time that grows in a lawful way with the size of the transformation.


24.1 The phenomena of imagery

Before the theories, this section presents the two classic experimental findings that made imagery a respectable scientific topic, because both produced clean, orderly numbers rather than mere reports of private experience.


24.1.1 Mental rotation and its linear signature

The most celebrated imagery experiment was carried out by Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler in 1971, and its result is beautifully simple.

They showed people pairs of drawings of three-dimensional shapes built from little cubes, and the task was just to decide whether the two shapes were the same object seen from different angles, or genuinely different mirror-image shapes.

The crucial trick was that when the two shapes were the same, one was shown rotated by some amount relative to the other, anywhere from zero up to 180 degrees.

The striking finding was a straight-line relationship: the more one shape was rotated away from the other, the longer people took to decide they matched, and the increase was remarkably steady, adding a roughly constant amount of time for each extra degree of rotation.

This orderly straight-line pattern is the "linear signature" of the chapter title.

The natural interpretation, and the one Shepard and Metzler drew, is that people literally rotate a mental image of one shape, smoothly and at a fairly constant speed of very roughly 60 degrees per second, until it lines up with the other and they can compare them.

In systems terms the rotation module takes an image and a target orientation as inputs and publishes an aligned image, and its time cost is the angular disparity divided by a rotation rate of roughly 60 degrees per second, so a 180 degree rotation costs about 3 seconds on top of the fixed time to encode the shapes and press the button.

The importance of this result is that the timing behaves as if a real object were being physically turned in space, which is hard to explain if the mind were only shuffling abstract symbols, and it strongly suggested that imagery is an analog process that preserves the spatial structure of what it represents.


24.1.2 Image scanning and the preservation of metric structure

The second classic finding came from Stephen Kosslyn in the 1970s, and it concerns not rotating an image but scanning across one.

Kosslyn had people memorise a map of a made-up island dotted with landmarks such as a hut, a tree, and a well, and then, with eyes closed, picture the map and mentally move their attention from one named landmark to another.

The result mirrored the rotation studies: the greater the real distance between two landmarks on the original map, the longer people took to scan between them in their mind's eye.

Again the times rose in a steady, straight-line fashion with distance.

The phrase "preservation of metric structure" means that the mental image keeps the actual distances of the real thing, so that things far apart on the map are far apart in the image and take longer to travel between.

In systems terms the scanning module moves an attention pointer across a stored spatial layout at a roughly constant internal speed, so its output latency is a linear function of represented distance, which is precisely the behaviour of a pointer traversing a genuine spatial medium.

Kosslyn argued that this is exactly what you would expect if a mental image is genuinely laid out like a picture in a space, with the mind's eye moving across it much as real eyes move across a real scene.

Taken together with mental rotation, image scanning built a strong case that mental images are not just vague inner talk but structured, space-like representations you can move around in, which set up the great debate that follows.


24.2 The imagery debate

The experiments above were dramatic, but they did not by themselves settle what a mental image really is, and for decades two camps drew opposite conclusions from the same data.

This section lays out the two positions and then gives an honest account of what was and was not resolved.


24.2.1 The depictive account

The depictive account, championed by Stephen Kosslyn, takes the experiments largely at face value.

Depictive means picture-like, representing by resemblance the way a photograph does, so that parts of the representation correspond to parts of the thing and spatial layout is genuinely preserved.

On this view a mental image really is a special kind of picture in the head, displayed on an internal space-like medium that Kosslyn compared to a screen, which the rest of the mind can inspect much as an eye inspects a scene.

This account explains the rotation and scanning results very naturally: they take time in an orderly, distance-dependent way precisely because a real spatial layout is being traversed step by step, just as it would take you longer to walk across a bigger room.

In systems terms the depictive claim is a claim about the storage format: the image buffer is an array-like medium in which adjacency in the representation mirrors adjacency in the world, so transformation cost necessarily scales with represented distance.

Kosslyn's stronger claim, developed later, was that these mental pictures are actually laid out on the maps in the early visual areas of the brain, the same regions that light up when you really see, so that imagining and seeing share hardware.


24.2.2 The propositional account

The opposing view was pressed hardest by Zenon Pylyshyn, and it denies that there is any real picture in the head at all.

A proposition is an abstract, language-like description of a fact, something like "the hut is north of the tree", with no pictorial quality of its own.

Pylyshyn argued that all knowledge, including so-called images, is really stored in this abstract propositional form, and that the feeling of seeing a picture is just that, a feeling, not evidence of an actual internal picture doing the work.

His sharpest objection was ingenious.

He suggested that the scanning and rotation results might come not from any picture but from what he called tacit knowledge, meaning people's unconscious knowledge about how real objects behave.

The idea is that participants know, without realising they are using it, that in the real world scanning a longer distance or rotating a larger angle takes more time, and they unconsciously reproduce that expected timing when asked to imagine, so the neat results reflect their beliefs about the world rather than the mechanics of a mental image.

In systems terms the two accounts predict differently under a change of instructions: a fixed depictive medium should yield the same time-per-degree regardless of what participants believe, whereas a tacit-knowledge simulation should shift its timing when expectations are changed.

Pylyshyn backed this with the finding that the results can change when you change the instructions or what people expect, which is awkward for the idea that you are simply reading off a fixed internal picture.


24.2.3 What the debate settled and what it did not

After decades of argument, the imagery debate reached a partial and honest resolution rather than a clean victory for either side.

What the newer evidence, especially brain imaging, did settle for many researchers is that imagery is not purely abstract description.

When people form vivid visual images, the early visual areas of the brain, including the primary visual cortex that also processes real sight, often become active, and the pattern of activity even reflects the size and shape of what is imagined, which fits the depictive account and is hard to square with a purely propositional one.

Damage to visual brain areas can impair imagery in ways that parallel its effect on perception, further tying the two together.

What the debate did not fully settle is the deeper philosophical point, and Pylyshyn and his allies were never entirely refuted, because one can always insist that the brain activity is a by-product and that the real computations underneath are still symbol-like.

There is also a genuine puzzle the debate did not anticipate: people vary enormously in their imagery, and some individuals, described only in recent years under the name aphantasia, report no conscious visual imagery at all yet can still do many imagery tasks, which suggests the vivid inner picture may not be doing all the work we once assumed.

In systems terms aphantasia looks like a missing or silent display channel with the underlying spatial computation intact, a dissociation between the workspace and its conscious readout that neither original camp predicted.

The lasting lesson is a good one for a beginner to carry away: two careful camps looked at the same solid data and disagreed for years, and progress came less from winning the argument than from inventing new methods, here brain imaging, that could see past the private nature of the experience.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Generation requests from thought and language: a description or memory cue naming what to imagine.

◦ Stored visual and spatial long-term memories, supplying the content that the image is built from.

◦ Transformation commands from executive control: rotate, scan, zoom, or recompose the current image.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ The current image state, a space-preserving representation, consumed by inspection processes that read off shape, size, and spatial relations.

◦ Comparison verdicts, for example same object or mirror image, with response times that grow linearly with the transformation applied, consumed by decision and response systems.

◦ Reactivation of early visual cortex that can prime or interfere with concurrent real seeing.

• STATE.

◦ The contents of the visual buffer: the currently generated image, its position, scale, and orientation, plus the location of the attention pointer within it.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Rotation rate in degrees per second; scanning speed across the represented layout; buffer resolution and extent; image vividness, which varies enormously between individuals.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Mental rotation proceeds at very roughly 60 degrees per second for the Shepard and Metzler block figures, adding roughly 1 second of decision time per 60 degrees of angular disparity.

◦ Image scanning time grows linearly with represented distance in Kosslyn's map studies, with scanning a full map taking on the order of 1 to 2 seconds.

◦ Image generation time for a simple familiar object: REFUSED, because reported values vary widely with image complexity and no single standard figure is agreed.

◦ Unrehearsed image maintenance fades within a few seconds without active refreshing, consistent with visual short-term store limits.

• MODES.

◦ Generation mode, building an image from memory, against inspection mode, reading properties off the current image, against transformation mode, rotating or scanning it, with executive commands switching between the three.

◦ Perception-coupled against decoupled operation: the same early visual machinery serves real seeing or imagery, with sensory input normally dominating and imagery running when input is absent or gated.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Aphantasia, the absence of conscious voluntary imagery; imagery loss after damage to visual cortex that parallels perceptual loss; confusing vividly imagined events with perceived ones, a source of false memory; and experimenter-expectation effects in which tacit knowledge shapes the measured timings.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called rotation rate with value sixty, representing degrees rotated per second.
Create a number variable called base time with value one, representing the fixed seconds needed to encode the shapes and respond.
Create a list variable called disparities containing the angles zero, thirty, sixty, ninety, one hundred twenty, one hundred fifty, and one hundred eighty.
Create an empty list called predicted times.
For each angle in disparities:
    Calculate the quotient of the angle divided by rotation rate.
    Calculate the sum of base time and the quotient, and store the result as the predicted response time.
    Add a small random amount of noise to the predicted response time.
    Add the predicted response time to predicted times.
For each pair of angle and predicted response time, print the angle and the time.
Calculate the difference between the last predicted time and the first predicted time.
Calculate the quotient of that difference divided by one hundred eighty, and store the result as the estimated slope in seconds per degree.
Print the estimated slope to show the linear signature of mental rotation.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module for response-time noise
import random

# Create a variable for the mental rotation rate in degrees per second
rotation_rate = 60.0
# Create a variable for the fixed encoding and response time in seconds
base_time = 1.0

# Define a function that predicts the response time for one trial
def predict_response_time(angle):
    # Calculate the rotation time as the angle divided by the rotation rate
    rotation_time = angle / rotation_rate
    # Calculate a small random noise value between minus and plus a tenth of a second
    noise = random.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)
    # Return the sum of the base time, the rotation time, and the noise
    return base_time + rotation_time + noise

# Create a list of angular disparities from zero to one hundred eighty degrees
disparities = [0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180]
# Create an empty list for the predicted times
times = []
# For each angle in the list of disparities
for angle in disparities:
    # Predict the response time for this angle
    rt = predict_response_time(angle)
    # Add the predicted time to the list
    times.append(rt)
    # Print the angle and the predicted response time rounded to two places
    print("disparity", angle, "degrees -> response time", round(rt, 2), "seconds")

# Calculate the estimated slope as the rise over the run of the line
slope = (times[-1] - times[0]) / (disparities[-1] - disparities[0])
# Print the slope in milliseconds per degree to show the linear signature
print("estimated slope:", round(slope * 1000, 1), "milliseconds per degree")

PART SIX. LANGUAGE

CHAPTER 25. THE STRUCTURE AND FACULTY OF LANGUAGE (PROCESS)

Language is the system that lets one mind put a thought into another mind using sound, sign, or written marks.

Viewed as an engineered system, language is a layered protocol stack: each layer consumes the output of the layer below it, applies its own rules, and publishes a richer representation to the layer above.

This chapter is about what language is made of and whether the ability to use it is a special piece of mental machinery all its own.

We will start with the layers that every language is built from, then look at the features that make human language so powerful, and finish by asking whether language is a separate faculty or just ordinary thinking put to use.

The reason any of this matters is simple: understanding how language is structured is the first step toward understanding how a mind, human or machine, could ever produce and understand it.


25.1 The levels of linguistic structure

Language looks like a single smooth stream, but underneath it is organised into separate layers, each with its own rules.

Linguists find it useful to peel these layers apart, because a problem at one layer can be studied without solving the others.

In systems terms this is classic modular decomposition: each layer exposes a clean interface to its neighbours, so an engineer, or a scientist, can debug one layer while treating the others as black boxes.

The sections below walk up from the smallest pieces, the sounds, to the largest, whole conversations.


25.1.1 Phonology and morphology

Phonology is the study of the sound system of a language, meaning the set of sounds it uses and the rules for how those sounds may be combined.

The smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word is called a phoneme, and swapping one phoneme for another turns "bat" into "pat" or "cat".

A phoneme is not a letter and not an exact acoustic recording; it is a category of sound that speakers of a language treat as the same, even when the actual noise varies from person to person and moment to moment.

Different languages carve the sound world up differently, so a distinction that matters in one language can be invisible in another.

For example, English treats the "r" and "l" sounds as two different phonemes, while Japanese does not draw that line in the same way, which is why the contrast is famously hard for some Japanese learners of English.

Phonology also covers rules about which sound sequences are allowed, so an English speaker senses that "blick" could be a word but "bnick" could not, even though neither is real.

Morphology is the study of the internal structure of words, meaning how words are built out of smaller meaningful pieces.

The smallest unit that carries meaning is called a morpheme, and a single word can contain several of them.

The word "cats" contains two morphemes, the root "cat" and the plural marker "s", and the word "unhappiness" contains three, namely "un", "happy", and "ness".

Morphemes come in two broad kinds, free morphemes that can stand alone as words, like "dog", and bound morphemes that must attach to something else, like the past-tense "ed".

Morphology is why you can hear a brand new word like "to google" and instantly know that "googled" means it happened in the past, without anyone teaching you that specific form.

Together, phonology and morphology handle the raw materials of language, the sounds and the word-parts, before any sentence is built.

As a system, the phonological layer takes a continuous acoustic or articulatory signal as input, outputs a discrete sequence of phoneme categories, and operates at the timescale of ordinary speech, which runs at roughly five syllables per second, so its units turn over every few hundred milliseconds; the morphological layer takes that phoneme sequence as input and outputs structured words tagged with their meaningful parts.


25.1.2 Syntax

Syntax is the set of rules that govern how words are combined into phrases and sentences.

It is the reason "the dog chased the cat" and "the cat chased the dog" mean different things even though they contain exactly the same words.

Syntax shows that meaning does not live in words alone; it lives partly in the arrangement, in who is placed where.

A key idea in syntax is that sentences are not flat strings of words but have hidden hierarchical structure, meaning words group into phrases, and phrases group into larger phrases, like nested boxes.

In "the old man in the corner smiled", the words "the old man in the corner" form one group that acts as a single unit, the thing that did the smiling.

This grouping is invisible in the sound but real in the grammar, and it is what lets us understand sentences we have never heard before.

Syntax also captures the fact that some strings of words are well formed and others are not, so "she quickly ran home" is fine while "quickly she home ran" feels broken to an English ear.

A grammar, in the technical sense, is a finite set of such rules that can describe an unlimited number of possible sentences.

Noam Chomsky, the linguist whose work reshaped this field starting in the 1950s, argued that the deep patterns of syntax are surprisingly similar across the world's languages, hinting at a shared underlying design.

Syntax is often treated as the engine room of language, the part that assembles small meaningful pieces into the endless variety of things we can say.

In systems terms the syntactic layer takes an ordered stream of tagged words as input, outputs a hierarchical tree structure over them, and must do its work incrementally at the pace of incoming speech, committing to structure within a few hundred milliseconds of each word.


25.1.3 Semantics, pragmatics, and discourse

Semantics is the study of meaning: what words, phrases, and sentences actually refer to and how their meanings combine.

At the word level, semantics asks what "dog" picks out in the world, and at the sentence level it asks how the meanings of the parts add up to the meaning of the whole.

A central principle here is compositionality, the idea that the meaning of a sentence is built up in a regular way from the meanings of its words and the way they are arranged.

Compositionality is why, once you know the words and the grammar, you can understand "the purple elephant sneezed" even though no one has ever said it to you.

Pragmatics is the study of meaning in context, meaning what a speaker actually intends beyond the literal words.

If someone at the dinner table says "can you pass the salt?", the literal question is about your ability, but the intended meaning is a polite request, and pragmatics is what explains the gap.

Pragmatics covers things like sarcasm, hinting, politeness, and the way "it is cold in here" can be a request to close the window.

Discourse is the level above the single sentence, the study of how sentences link together into a coherent stretch of language, such as a paragraph, a story, or a conversation.

At the discourse level we track things like who "she" refers to three sentences later, and how one sentence sets up an expectation that the next one fulfils.

These three levels, semantics, pragmatics, and discourse, are where language stops being a formal puzzle and starts being about communication between real people with intentions and shared history.

As a system, the semantic layer takes syntactic trees as input and outputs propositions, the pragmatic layer takes propositions plus a model of the speaker and the situation as input and outputs intended meanings, and the discourse layer maintains a running state across sentences, holding referents and expectations open over seconds to minutes.


25.2 The defining properties

Having seen the layers, we can now ask what makes human language special compared with other communication systems in nature.

The properties in this section are the features most often named as the signature of human language, the things a honeybee's dance or a vervet monkey's alarm call does not fully share.


25.2.1 Generativity, productivity, and recursion

Generativity, also called productivity, is the ability of a language to produce and understand an unlimited number of new sentences from a limited set of words and rules.

You are almost certainly reading sentences right now that you have never encountered before, and you understand them effortlessly, which is generativity in action.

This is what separates human language from a fixed list of calls or signals, where an animal has, say, a few dozen fixed messages and no way to make new ones.

In engineering language, generativity means the system's output space is unbounded while its program, the grammar, is finite, which is only possible if the rules can be applied repeatedly and in combination.

Recursion is a specific and powerful trick that helps make this openness possible: it is the ability to place a structure inside another structure of the same kind.

For example, you can put a sentence inside a sentence, as in "she said that he thought that they knew that it would rain".

Because recursion can in principle be repeated without a fixed limit, it lets a finite grammar describe an infinite range of possible sentences, exactly as a recursive function in software lets a few lines of code handle inputs of any depth.

In an influential 2002 paper in the journal Science, Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky, and W. Tecumseh Fitch proposed that recursion might be the one core ingredient of the language faculty that is uniquely human.

This claim became the centre of a heated debate, because in 2005 the linguist Daniel Everett argued that Piraha, a language of the Amazon, lacks recursive embedding, which he attributed to the culture rather than to a different brain.

Critics replied on several fronts, some disputing Everett's data, and others pointing out that Piraha speakers readily learn Portuguese, a language that clearly uses recursion, so their minds must be capable of it even if their own language rarely displays it.

In systems terms the two sides predict different things: if recursion is a built-in core capability, every human language processor ships with a call stack and only culture decides whether it is exercised, whereas if it is a cultural construction, some processors might genuinely lack the stack.

The honest current state of the matter is that the special status of recursion is still contested, and experts have not reached full agreement, though the broader point that human language is open ended in a way animal signals are not is widely accepted.


25.2.2 Competence against performance

Competence and performance is a distinction, introduced by Chomsky, between what a speaker knows about their language and how they actually use it in real time.

Competence is the idealised underlying knowledge, the internal grammar that in principle allows a speaker to produce and judge an unlimited set of sentences.

Performance is the actual behaviour, the messy real-world talking and listening that is shaped by memory limits, tiredness, distractions, and slips of the tongue.

A computer systems analogy makes the distinction crisp: competence is the specification, the abstract program, while performance is the program running on real hardware with finite memory, interrupts, and noise.

The distinction matters because our performance often falls short of our competence, and a scientist must decide which one is the real target of study.

Consider a sentence like "the cat the dog the rat bit chased ran", which is grammatical by the rules yet almost impossible to understand because it overloads memory.

By the competence view, that sentence is a legitimate product of the grammar, and its difficulty is a performance problem about the limited working memory of a real brain, not a flaw in the grammar itself.

Chomsky argued that linguistics should aim first at describing competence, the pure knowledge, treating performance factors as a separate matter.

Many psychologists pushed back, arguing that the limits of real-time processing are not a nuisance to be set aside but a central fact about how the mind actually works.

In systems terms the two camps predict differently: a pure competence theory says difficulty should track only grammatical complexity, while a performance theory says difficulty should track resource load, such as how many unfinished structures must be held open at once, and the nested-cat sentence favours the resource account.

This tension runs through the whole field, and it is one reason cognitive scientists and formal linguists sometimes talk past one another, since they are aiming at different targets.


25.3 The modularity question

We now reach the deepest question of the chapter: is the ability to use language a special, dedicated system in the mind, or is it just general intelligence applied to words?

This is called the modularity question, and how you answer it shapes how you would try to build or model a language user.

For an engineer the question is whether language runs on a dedicated coprocessor with its own firmware, or as one more application on the general-purpose central processor.


25.3.1 Language as a distinct faculty

A faculty, in this context, means a distinct mental capacity with its own dedicated machinery, as opposed to a general-purpose ability used for many things.

The claim that language is a distinct faculty says that the mind contains specialised equipment for language that is not simply the same equipment we use for vision, memory, or reasoning.

The philosopher Jerry Fodor sharpened this idea in 1983 with the notion of a mental module, a processing system that is specialised for one kind of input and runs somewhat automatically and independently of the rest of thought.

A module, in Fodor's sense, is fast, mandatory, and informationally encapsulated, meaning it does its job without waiting for the rest of your knowledge and beliefs to weigh in.

Encapsulation is a systems property: the module reads only its own input channel and its own internal database, and no signal path exists by which general beliefs can reach inside and alter its computation mid-run.

The classic evidence for encapsulation is that you cannot help understanding a sentence in your native language when you hear it, just as you cannot choose to stop seeing an optical illusion.

On the strongest version of this view, associated with Chomsky, humans are born with a language-specific endowment, sometimes called universal grammar, that guides how any child acquires whatever language surrounds them.

The opposing camp holds that language is built out of more general abilities, such as learning statistical patterns, imitating others, and reading intentions, rather than from a dedicated grammar organ.

The two views predict differently in systems terms: a dedicated module predicts sharp input selectivity and immunity to belief, while the general-abilities view predicts that language performance should rise and fall with the same resources that drive other learning.

This disagreement is genuine and ongoing, and researchers of good faith line up on both sides, so the fair summary is that the question of a distinct language faculty remains open.


25.3.2 The evidence from dissociation and development

Two main streams of evidence are used to argue that language is at least partly its own system: dissociation and development.

A dissociation, in this field, is a case where one ability is damaged while another is spared, which suggests the two rely on at least partly separate machinery.

The strongest form is a double dissociation, where in one group ability A is lost but ability B survives, and in another group the reverse is true, which is powerful evidence that A and B are separate, exactly as two software services that can each fail independently must be running on separate components.

Language provides a striking dissociation between grammar and general intelligence, and between different parts of language itself.

In a condition called Broca's aphasia, caused by damage usually toward the front of the left side of the brain, people can often still understand meaning but produce halting, grammatically stripped-down speech, a pattern called agrammatism.

In another pattern linked to damage further back, people may produce fluent, smoothly structured speech that is oddly empty of correct meaning, roughly the mirror image.

Recent brain-mapping studies have supported a genuine double dissociation of this sort, with grammatical production and meaning leaning on partly different tissue, which many take as evidence that the language system has separable internal parts.

There is also a developmental disorder called developmental language disorder, once widely known as specific language impairment, in which children struggle with grammar despite otherwise typical intelligence and hearing.

Cases like this, where language lags while general reasoning proceeds normally, are used to argue that language draws on some machinery of its own rather than riding entirely on general smarts.

It is important to be careful here, because the brain regions involved are not neat single-purpose boxes, and later research has shown these areas also take part in other tasks, so the evidence points to specialisation of degree rather than to a perfectly sealed language organ.

The developmental evidence adds a second angle: children the world over acquire language on a broadly similar timetable, rapidly and without formal teaching, which supporters of a language faculty read as a sign of built-in guidance.

Skeptics answer that powerful general learning, plus the rich social input children receive, could produce the same regularities, so this evidence too is read in more than one way.

Taken together, the dissociation and development findings make a serious case that language has some dedicated machinery, while stopping well short of proving that it is a fully separate and self-contained organ of mind.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Acoustic speech signal, a continuous air-pressure waveform delivered by the auditory system, or visual marks delivered by the visual system for reading and sign.

◦ Conceptual intentions, the preverbal thoughts to be expressed, delivered by general cognition to the production side of the stack.

◦ Contextual and social information, including the situation and a model of the interlocutor, delivered by memory and social cognition to the pragmatic layer.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Structured meaning, propositions and speaker intentions, delivered to reasoning, memory, and decision systems.

◦ Articulated utterances, motor commands for speech or sign, delivered to the motor system.

◦ Grammaticality signals, fast judgements of whether an input is well formed, available to metalinguistic thought.

• STATE.

◦ The lexicon, a long-term store of tens of thousands of words with their sounds, meanings, and grammatical properties.

◦ The grammar, a long-term store of combinatorial rules at each layer, phonological, morphological, syntactic.

◦ A running discourse state holding current referents, topics, and expectations across sentences.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Vocabulary size, on the order of tens of thousands of words for an adult.

◦ Embedding depth tolerance, the number of unfinished structures the processor can hold open, in practice about two before comprehension collapses.

◦ Degree of encapsulation, how much general knowledge can penetrate the fast parsing machinery, the tuning knob the modularity debate is about.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Syllable turnover in ordinary speech is roughly 150 to 250 milliseconds, since speakers produce about five syllables per second.

◦ Word-level processing commits within a few hundred milliseconds of each word, as the electrophysiological signatures in Chapter 27 show.

◦ Timescale of the competence grammar itself: REFUSED, because competence is a timeless body of knowledge and assigning it a latency would be a category error.

• MODES.

◦ Comprehension mode against production mode, switched by whether the system is currently receiving signal or executing an intention to speak.

◦ Native fluent mode against effortful learner mode, switched by proficiency, with the fluent mode fast, mandatory, and automatic and the learner mode slow and attention-hungry.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Agrammatism in Broca's aphasia, halting speech stripped of grammar with meaning relatively spared.

◦ Fluent but empty speech after more posterior damage, the mirror dissociation.

◦ Developmental language disorder, grammar lagging behind otherwise typical intelligence.

◦ Performance overload on centre-embedded sentences that the grammar licenses but working memory cannot hold.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called layers with the values phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics.
Create a variable called signal with the raw input stream as its initial value.
For each layer in the layers list, perform the following steps.
    Retrieve the rule set stored for the current layer.
    Create a list variable called units with no items.
    For each segment of the signal, check the segment against the rule set.
        If the segment is licensed by a rule, add the resulting structured unit to the units list.
        If the segment is not licensed by any rule, mark the segment as ill formed and add a repair request to the units list.
    Replace the signal with the units list, so the output of this layer becomes the input of the next layer.
Return the final signal as the structured meaning.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a dictionary mapping each word to the letters that support it.
words = {"cat": "cat", "car": "car", "can": "can", "bat": "bat"}
# Create a dictionary of word activations, each starting at zero.
act = {w: 0.0 for w in words}
# Create the bottom-up letter evidence, with the middle letter ambiguous.
evidence = [{"c": 1.0}, {"a": 1.0}, {"t": 0.6, "r": 0.4}]
# Set the excitation gain to 0.1 and the inhibition gain to 0.04.
excite, inhibit = 0.1, 0.04
# Repeat the interactive-activation cycle twenty times.
for step in range(20):
    # Create a dictionary to hold the change in each word's activation.
    delta = {w: 0.0 for w in words}
    # For each word, gather excitation from every matching letter position.
    for w, spelling in words.items():
        # For each letter position, add evidence times gain if the letter matches.
        for pos, letter in enumerate(spelling):
            # Add the letter evidence at this position, scaled by the excitation gain.
            delta[w] += excite * evidence[pos].get(letter, 0.0)
        # Words feed activation back down, sharpening their own letters (top-down flow).
        for pos, letter in enumerate(spelling):
            # Increase the supported letter's evidence by a small fraction of the word's activation.
            evidence[pos][letter] = evidence[pos].get(letter, 0.0) + 0.01 * act[w]
    # Apply lateral inhibition, so each word suppresses its rivals.
    for w in words:
        # Subtract the inhibition gain times the total activation of all other words.
        delta[w] -= inhibit * sum(act[v] for v in words if v != w)
    # Update every activation, keeping it at or above zero.
    for w in words:
        # Add the change and clip the result at zero from below.
        act[w] = max(0.0, act[w] + delta[w])
# Report the winning word, the one with the highest activation.
print("recognised:", max(act, key=act.get), {w: round(a, 3) for w, a in act.items()})


CHAPTER 26. SPEECH PERCEPTION AND WORD RECOGNITION (PROCESS)

When someone speaks to you, your ears receive nothing but a continuously changing wave of air pressure, yet you hear crisp, separate words.

This chapter is about the remarkable and largely unconscious work that turns that smeared, noisy sound stream into recognised words.

In systems terms the task is a decoding problem: recover a discrete symbol sequence from a continuous, noisy, speaker-dependent channel, in real time, with no possibility of asking the transmitter to slow down.

We look first at how the mind hears individual speech sounds, then at how it identifies spoken words as they unfold in time, and finally at how the same recognition problem plays out for written words on a page.

The theme throughout is that recognition is an active guessing process, not a passive recording, because the raw signal is far too messy to read off directly.


26.1 Speech perception

Speech perception is the process by which the sounds of speech are mapped onto the units of language, such as consonants and vowels.

It is harder than it sounds, because the acoustic signal for a given speech sound is never exactly the same twice.

The two sections here cover the mind's tidy solution to that messiness and the surprising fact that seeing a speaker's face changes what you hear.


26.1.1 Categorical perception and the lack of invariance

The lack of invariance problem is the fact that there is no single fixed acoustic pattern that always corresponds to a given speech sound.

The exact sound waves for the consonant "d" differ depending on the vowel that follows it, the speaker's voice, the speed of talking, and the surrounding words, yet listeners hear "d" every time.

This is a deep puzzle, because it means the mind cannot simply match incoming sound against a stored template, since there is no one true template to match.

Categorical perception is part of the mind's answer, and it means we tend to hear speech sounds as belonging to distinct categories rather than as points on a smooth continuum.

The classic demonstration uses a cue called voice onset time, which is the gap between when a sound is released and when the vocal cords start buzzing.

A short voice onset time near zero milliseconds is heard as "b", while a longer one around forty milliseconds is heard as "p", with a fairly sharp boundary near twenty milliseconds.

The striking finding is that if you slowly slide the voice onset time from zero upward, listeners do not hear a gradual blend; they hear a clear "b" right up to the boundary and then abruptly a clear "p".

Two sounds that sit on the same side of the boundary are hard to tell apart, while two sounds the same physical distance apart but straddling the boundary are easy to tell apart.

The practical effect is that the mind throws away fine within-category detail and keeps only the category identity, which is exactly what you want if your goal is to recover the intended word rather than the exact noise.

In systems terms this stage is a quantiser: input, a continuous acoustic cue such as voice onset time; output, a discrete phoneme label; characteristic timescale, tens of milliseconds, since the "b" to "p" boundary sits near twenty milliseconds of voice onset time.

Later research has softened the original strict picture, showing listeners retain more graded, within-category sensitivity than once believed, and can use it when the task demands, so the perception is less all-or-nothing than the early studies suggested.

Even so, the core insight stands: speech perception imposes stable categories on an unstable signal, which is a large part of how we cope with the lack of invariance.


26.1.2 The multimodal nature of speech and the McGurk effect

Speech perception is multimodal, meaning it uses more than one sense at once, in particular sight as well as hearing.

We are usually unaware of it, but when we can see a talker's lips, we use that visual information to help decide what we heard, which is why a noisy phone call is harder than a face-to-face chat.

The most famous demonstration is the McGurk effect, first reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 1976.

In the classic setup, a listener hears the sound "ba" while watching a video of a mouth silently articulating "ga", and the surprising result is that most people report hearing "da", a third sound that matches neither the ears nor the eyes exactly but splits the difference.

The effect is compelling because closing your eyes instantly restores the true "ba", proving that vision was actively shaping what felt like a purely auditory experience.
