The systems reading: habituation is a stimulus-specific gain that decays with each repetition and recovers with rest, on timescales from seconds to minutes for short-term forms and days for long-term forms, while sensitisation is a global gain raised by a strong aversive input and decaying back over minutes to hours.


30.2 Classical conditioning

Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning in which an animal learns that one event predicts another.

Associative learning means learning a link between two things, so that one comes to stand for or signal the other.

This kind of learning lets an animal use a cue in the world to prepare for something important that reliably follows it, which is enormously adaptive.

As a mechanism, its inputs are paired events, a cue and an outcome, its state is the learned strength of the cue-to-outcome link, and its output is an anticipatory response emitted to the cue alone, typically established over tens of pairings.


30.2.1 The Pavlovian paradigm and its phenomena

Classical conditioning is also called Pavlovian conditioning after the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov, who discovered it around the turn of the twentieth century while studying digestion in dogs.

Pavlov noticed that his dogs began to salivate not just when food arrived but at signals that food was coming, such as the footsteps of the person who fed them.

The basic setup uses four terms that are worth defining clearly.

The unconditioned stimulus is something that naturally triggers a response without any learning, such as food in the mouth.

The unconditioned response is the natural, unlearned reaction to it, such as salivating to food.

The conditioned stimulus is a neutral signal, such as a bell, that the animal learns to associate with the unconditioned stimulus.

The conditioned response is the learned reaction to that signal, such as salivating to the bell alone.

After the bell is paired with food many times, the animal salivates to the bell by itself, which shows it has learned that the bell predicts food.

Several further phenomena flesh out the picture.

Acquisition is the gradual building up of the conditioned response over repeated pairings.

Extinction is the fading of the conditioned response when the signal is presented many times without the food, so the animal learns the bell no longer predicts anything.

Spontaneous recovery is the surprising reappearance of the response after a rest, which shows that extinction does not erase the original learning but rather overlays it with new learning.

Generalisation means the animal responds to signals similar to the trained one, while discrimination means it learns to respond only to the specific signal and not to others.

In systems terms, acquisition and extinction are both the same update process running on different data: the state variable is association strength, acquisition drives it toward a positive ceiling over tens of trials, extinction drives it back toward zero, and spontaneous recovery shows that extinction writes a second, competing memory rather than deleting the first.


30.2.2 The Rescorla-Wagner model and prediction error

The Rescorla-Wagner model, published by Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner in 1972, is one of the most important theories in the whole of learning science.

Before it, people often assumed that learning happened simply because two things occurred close together in time, an idea called contiguity.

The Rescorla-Wagner model made a deeper and more powerful claim: learning is driven by surprise, not merely by togetherness.

The central idea is prediction error, which is the gap between what actually happens and what the animal expected to happen.

When an outcome is fully expected, the prediction error is zero, and no new learning occurs, because there is nothing to update.

When an outcome is surprising, either better or worse than expected, the prediction error is large, and learning is strong, because the animal must revise its expectations.

In plain terms, you learn about a cue only to the extent that the outcome it predicts caught you off guard.

The model can be stated as a simple rule: the change in the strength of an association depends on how salient the cue and outcome are, multiplied by the difference between the maximum possible learning and how much has already been learned.

Crucially, when several cues are present at once, the expectation is the sum of all their strengths, and the shared prediction error is divided among them, which is what gives the model its distinctive predictions.

This one idea, that learning tracks prediction error, turned out to be extraordinarily fruitful, and as later chapters show, it became the bridge between animal conditioning and modern theories of how the brain and artificial systems learn from rewards.

As a mechanism, the model's inputs on each trial are the set of cues present and the outcome, its state is one strength number per cue, its parameters are the salience-based learning rates, and its output is the updated strengths, converging over tens of trials at typical learning rates.


30.2.3 Blocking, overshadowing, and the primacy of contingency over contiguity

Blocking is the single most important piece of evidence for the prediction-error view of learning, and it was discovered by Leon Kamin around 1969.

In a blocking experiment, an animal first learns that one cue, say a light, reliably predicts a shock.

Then a second cue, say a tone, is added, so the light and tone appear together and are followed by the same shock.

Common sense might expect the animal to learn that the tone also predicts shock, since the tone was always paired with it.

Instead, the animal learns little or nothing about the tone, because the shock was already fully predicted by the light, so there was no surprise and no prediction error to drive learning about the tone.

The prior learning about the light "blocks" learning about the tone, which is exactly what the Rescorla-Wagner model predicts and what a simple contiguity account cannot explain.

Overshadowing is a related effect: when two cues of unequal salience are trained together from the start, the more noticeable cue captures most of the learning and overshadows the weaker one.

Together these findings establish the primacy of contingency over contiguity.

Contiguity means two things merely occurring close together in time.

Contingency means one thing genuinely predicting another, that is, the outcome being more likely when the cue is present than when it is absent.

Rescorla showed in a classic experiment that animals learn about a cue only when it actually changes the odds of the outcome, not simply when the cue and outcome happen to co-occur.

The lesson, which reshaped the field, is that brains are not passive recorders of what happens together but active predictors that learn from the mismatch between expectation and reality.

The systems reading of blocking is direct: because the shared prediction error is computed from the summed expectation of all present cues, a cue added after the error has already been driven to zero receives no update, so blocking is not an anomaly but a mathematical consequence of the update rule.


30.3 Instrumental conditioning

Instrumental conditioning, also called operant conditioning, is learning from the consequences of your own actions.

In classical conditioning the animal learns a relationship between two events it does not control, but in instrumental conditioning the animal learns that its own behaviour produces outcomes.

This is the kind of learning behind training a dog to sit for a treat, or a person forming a habit because it pays off, and it is central to how goals and rewards shape behaviour.

As a mechanism, its input is the outcome that follows the animal's own action, its state is a value attached to each action, and its output is a shifted probability of emitting each action, changing over tens to hundreds of trials.


30.3.1 The law of effect and schedules of reinforcement

The law of effect was formulated by the psychologist Edward Thorndike around 1898, based on experiments with cats learning to escape from puzzle boxes.

The law states, in plain form, that actions followed by satisfying outcomes become more likely to be repeated, while actions followed by unpleasant outcomes become less likely.

Thorndike's cats did not solve the box in a flash of insight but gradually got faster over many trials, as successful actions were stamped in by their rewarding consequences.

Reinforcement is anything that makes a behaviour more likely in the future, while punishment is anything that makes it less likely.

The psychologist B. F. Skinner built an entire research programme on these ideas, using a device now called the Skinner box in which an animal presses a lever for food.

A key discovery was that the pattern, or schedule, on which reinforcement is delivered has powerful and predictable effects on behaviour.

A fixed-ratio schedule gives a reward after a set number of responses, such as one treat per five lever presses, and produces high, steady rates of responding.

A variable-ratio schedule gives a reward after an unpredictable number of responses, and produces very high and persistent responding, which is why slot machines, built on exactly this schedule, are so compelling.

A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time has passed, producing a burst of responding as the deadline approaches.

A variable-interval schedule rewards the first response after an unpredictable amount of time, producing slow, steady responding.

These schedules matter because they reveal that behaviour is finely tuned to the statistics of reward, a theme that connects directly to the reinforcement-learning theories of the next chapter.

In systems terms, a schedule is the environment's reward function, and the observed response rates are the learner's policy adapting to that function, which is why each schedule produces its own characteristic response curve.


30.3.2 Goal-directed against habitual control

A crucial insight of modern learning science is that instrumental behaviour is not one thing but is controlled by two different systems.

Goal-directed control means acting because you expect the action to lead to a specific outcome that you currently want.

If you press a lever because you know it delivers a particular food and you are hungry for that food, your behaviour is goal-directed.

Habitual control means acting out of ingrained routine, triggered by the situation, without weighing the current value of the outcome.

If you keep pressing the lever automatically even after the food has been made worthless, your behaviour has become a habit.

Researchers tease these apart with a clever manipulation called outcome devaluation.

They make the reward worthless, for example by letting the animal eat it to full satiation or by making it mildly sickening, and then see whether the animal still performs the action.

A goal-directed animal immediately stops, because it no longer wants the outcome, while a habitual animal keeps going, because its behaviour is no longer tied to the outcome's value.

A central finding, associated with researchers such as Anthony Dickinson, is that behaviour tends to start out goal-directed and become habitual with extended practice.

This distinction is deeply important, because it maps onto the difference between flexible, thoughtful action and automatic routine, and, as the next chapter describes, onto two computational strategies known as model-based and model-free learning.

The systems reading: goal-directed control consults a stored action-to-outcome map plus the outcome's current value at decision time, so it updates instantly when value changes, while habitual control consults only a cached action strength, so it updates only through slow retraining over many trials.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ A stream of stimuli, meaning cues such as tones and lights, arriving from the perceptual systems.

◦ Outcome signals, such as food, shock, or their omission, arriving from the body's reward and pain systems.

◦ For instrumental learning, a copy of the animal's own emitted action, so that consequences can be credited to behaviour.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Anticipatory conditioned responses, such as salivation to a bell, sent to the autonomic and motor systems.

◦ Updated association strengths and action values, consumed by the decision and reinforcement-learning systems of the next chapter.

◦ A prediction-error signal, the difference between expected and received outcome, broadcast as a teaching signal.

• STATE.

◦ One association strength per cue, summed across present cues to form the current expectation.

◦ One value per action for instrumental learning, plus a record of which controller, goal-directed or habitual, currently dominates.

◦ A separate extinction memory that competes with the original learning rather than erasing it, as spontaneous recovery shows.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Cue salience, the learning-rate factor determined by how noticeable a cue is.

◦ Outcome salience, the learning-rate factor determined by how important the outcome is.

◦ The asymptote, the maximum association strength a given outcome can support.

◦ The reinforcement schedule, the environment-side rule mapping responses and time to rewards.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Conditioned eyeblink responses form best when the cue leads the outcome by roughly 250 to 500 milliseconds, a classic optimal-interval finding.

◦ Acquisition of a reliable conditioned response typically takes on the order of tens of pairings, though single-trial learning occurs for taste aversion.

◦ Taste-aversion learning tolerates cue-to-outcome delays of minutes to hours, a striking exception to short-interval contiguity.

◦ Short-term habituation decays over seconds to minutes, while long-term habituation in Aplysia can persist for days to weeks after repeated training sessions.

◦ Transfer from goal-directed to habitual control emerges with extended training, REFUSED as a single number because the trial count at which it occurs varies widely with task, schedule, and species.

• MODES.

◦ Acquisition mode, active while the prediction error is positive and the association is growing toward its asymptote.

◦ Extinction mode, triggered when the cue repeatedly occurs without the outcome, driving expression of the response back down.

◦ Goal-directed mode, dominant early in instrumental training, in which actions are chosen by expected outcome value.

◦ Habitual mode, reached after extended repetition on a stable schedule, in which actions are triggered by the situation itself; outcome devaluation is the diagnostic switch test.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Blocking and overshadowing, in which perfectly correlated cues fail to be learned because other cues already absorb the prediction error.

◦ Phobias, in which a single traumatic pairing creates a fear association that resists extinction.

◦ Relapse after apparently successful extinction, through spontaneous recovery, renewal in a new context, or reinstatement by a stress or reminder.

◦ Compulsive habit, in which behaviour persists despite a devalued or harmful outcome, a laboratory model for aspects of addiction.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary variable called strength with an entry for light with value zero and an entry for tone with value zero.
Create a number variable called learning rate with initial value zero point two.
Create a number variable called asymptote with initial value one.
Create a list variable called phase one containing sixty trials, each with the cue list containing only light and with the outcome present.
Create a list variable called phase two containing sixty trials, each with the cue list containing light and tone and with the outcome present.
Create a list variable called all trials by joining phase one and phase two.
For each trial in all trials, do the following.
    Create a number variable called expectation with initial value zero.
    For each cue in the trial's cue list, add the strength entry for the cue to expectation.
    If the trial's outcome is present, set target to asymptote; otherwise set target to zero.
    Calculate the prediction error as target minus expectation.
    For each cue in the trial's cue list, add the product of learning rate and the prediction error to the strength entry for the cue.
Return the strength entries for light and tone.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a dictionary variable called strength with entries for light and tone, both zero.
strength = {"light": 0.0, "tone": 0.0}

# Create a number variable called learning_rate with initial value zero point two.
learning_rate = 0.2
# Create a number variable called asymptote with initial value one.
asymptote = 1.0

# Create a list of phase-one trials: sixty trials of light alone followed by shock.
phase_one = [(["light"], True)] * 60
# Create a list of phase-two trials: sixty trials of light plus tone followed by shock.
phase_two = [(["light", "tone"], True)] * 60
# Create a list variable called all_trials by joining phase one and phase two.
all_trials = phase_one + phase_two

# For each trial in all_trials, apply the Rescorla-Wagner update.
for cues, outcome_present in all_trials:
    # Create a number variable called expectation with initial value zero.
    expectation = 0.0
    # For each cue in the trial's cue list, add its strength to expectation.
    for cue in cues:
        # Add the strength entry for the cue to expectation.
        expectation = expectation + strength[cue]
    # If the outcome is present, set target to the asymptote; otherwise set target to zero.
    target = asymptote if outcome_present else 0.0
    # Calculate the prediction error as target minus expectation.
    prediction_error = target - expectation
    # For each cue present, nudge its strength by the shared prediction error.
    for cue in cues:
        # Add the product of learning_rate and prediction_error to the cue's strength.
        strength[cue] = strength[cue] + learning_rate * prediction_error

# Print the final strengths, showing the light near one and the tone blocked near zero.
print("Light strength:", round(strength["light"], 3))
print("Tone strength (blocked):", round(strength["tone"], 3))


CHAPTER 31. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING AS A THEORY OF COGNITION (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter presents one of the most successful bridges ever built between artificial intelligence, psychology, and neuroscience.

Reinforcement learning is a mathematical framework for how an agent should learn to act in order to maximise reward over time, through trial and error.

It began as an engineering method for training machines, but it turned out to describe, with startling accuracy, how real brains learn from reward, using the very prediction-error idea introduced in the last chapter.

In systems terms, a reinforcement-learning agent is a control loop: it reads the current state, emits an action, receives a reward and a new state, and updates an internal table of values, cycling continuously for the lifetime of the agent.

Because it is precise, testable, and shared across biological and artificial minds, reinforcement learning is a central framework for konnectome's aim of understanding humanlike intelligence.


31.1 The formal framework

This section lays out the basic mathematical machinery of reinforcement learning in plain terms.

The goal is to give you the core concepts, an agent, states, actions, rewards, and value, without heavy equations, so the later sections make sense.

Do not worry if the vocabulary is new; each term names a simple, intuitive idea.


31.1.1 Markov decision processes and value functions

A Markov decision process is the standard formal description of the situation a learning agent faces.

It sounds technical, but the idea is simple: it is a way of describing a world made of situations you can be in, actions you can take, and rewards you can receive.

A state is the situation the agent is currently in, such as a particular square on a game board.

An action is a choice the agent can make, such as moving left or right.

A reward is a number signalling how good the immediate outcome was, such as plus one for finding food or minus one for hitting a wall.

The word Markov refers to a simplifying assumption: that the future depends only on the present state, not on the whole history of how you got there.

In other words, if you know where you are now, you know everything you need to decide what to do next, and the path you took to get there does not add information.

The agent's job is to find a policy, which is a rule that says which action to take in each state.

To choose well, the agent needs to think beyond the immediate reward, because a small reward now might lead to a big reward later, or a tempting reward now might lead to disaster.

This is captured by the value function, which is the heart of the framework.

The value of a state is the total amount of reward the agent can expect to collect in the long run, starting from that state and following its policy.

Value is distinct from immediate reward: a state can feel unrewarding right now yet have high value because it leads somewhere good.

Because future rewards are less certain and less pressing than present ones, they are usually discounted, meaning a reward far in the future counts for a little less than the same reward now.

The systems reading: the Markov decision process is the interface contract between agent and world, specifying the input format as a state and reward pair, the output format as an action, and the discount factor as the parameter that sets the agent's effective planning horizon.

Learning good value estimates is the key to acting well, and the next sub-section describes the elegant trick that makes such learning possible.


31.1.2 Temporal-difference learning and its variants

Temporal-difference learning is the central algorithm of reinforcement learning, developed largely by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto in the 1980s.

It solves a hard problem: how can an agent learn the long-run value of situations when the rewards may come much later, without waiting to see the entire future?

The clever answer is to learn from the difference between successive predictions, which is where the name temporal difference comes from.

Here is the idea in plain words.

At each step, the agent has a prediction of how much reward is coming.

A moment later, it has a new, slightly better-informed prediction, plus whatever reward it just received.

If the new estimate is higher than the old one, the agent was pleasantly surprised, and it nudges the earlier prediction upward; if lower, it nudges it downward.

This nudge is the temporal-difference error, and it is a form of the very same prediction error we met in classical conditioning.

The beauty of this method is that the agent learns continually, step by step, using each prediction to correct the one before it, without ever needing to know the full outcome in advance.

There are several variants worth naming.

In one variant, called Q-learning, the agent learns the value of taking a particular action in a particular state, which directly tells it which action is best.

Q-learning is called off-policy because it can learn about the best possible actions even while behaving more cautiously or randomly.

Another variant, called SARSA, which stands for state, action, reward, state, action, learns the value of the actions the agent actually takes, and is called on-policy.

As a mechanism, temporal-difference learning takes the current reward and the next state's value estimate as input, holds a table of value estimates as state, and outputs an updated estimate every step of the loop, so learning happens at the same tempo as behaviour itself.

The deep significance of temporal-difference learning, spelled out later in this chapter, is that the brain appears to use exactly this kind of error signal, carried by the chemical dopamine.


31.1.3 The exploration and exploitation trade-off

The exploration-exploitation trade-off is a fundamental dilemma that every learning agent, biological or artificial, must face.

Exploitation means using what you already know to get the best reward you can right now.

Exploration means trying something new and uncertain, giving up guaranteed reward now for the chance of discovering something better.

The tension is easy to feel in everyday life.

Imagine you have a favourite restaurant you know is good; going there is exploitation.

Trying a new restaurant that might be wonderful or might be terrible is exploration.

If you only ever exploit, you may never discover a better option and get stuck in a rut.

If you only ever explore, you never settle down to enjoy what you have found, and you waste chances on bad options.

A good learner must balance the two, exploring more when it is ignorant and exploiting more as it grows confident.

Researchers have formalised several strategies for striking this balance.

One simple method is to act greedily most of the time but occasionally choose at random, ensuring the agent keeps sampling alternatives.

A widely used refinement is the softmax rule, which turns the learned values into choice probabilities so that better actions are chosen more often but weaker actions still get sampled, with a single temperature parameter controlling how random the choices are.

More sophisticated methods add a bonus for uncertainty, deliberately favouring options the agent knows little about, an idea sometimes summarised as optimism in the face of uncertainty.

In systems terms, the exploration policy is a tunable gain between value estimates and action output: high temperature or high random-choice rate spreads choices widely early in learning, and annealing that parameter downward over time shifts the agent from exploration to exploitation.

This trade-off is not just an engineering concern; it describes real dilemmas that animals and people navigate constantly, from foraging for food to choosing a career, and it reappears in the chapter on decision making.


31.2 Model-free and model-based control

This section describes a deep division within reinforcement learning that mirrors the psychological distinction between habits and goal-directed action from the previous chapter.

The two approaches, model-free and model-based, represent two fundamentally different ways of using experience to choose actions.

Understanding their trade-offs illuminates both how brains work and how to build flexible artificial agents.


31.2.1 The two systems and their behavioural dissociation

Model-free control is learning by directly storing the value of actions, based on how much reward they have produced in the past, without any understanding of how the world works.

It is like memorising, through repetition, that a certain route gets you home quickly, without knowing why or being able to reason about detours.

Model-free learning is computationally cheap and fast to use once learned, but it is inflexible, because if the world changes, it must relearn slowly through many new experiences.

This maps neatly onto habitual behaviour: efficient, automatic, but slow to update.

Model-based control, by contrast, builds an internal model of how the world works, a map of which actions lead to which states, and then uses that model to plan by imagining the consequences of different choices.

It is like having a real map of the city, so that when a road is closed you can immediately reason out a new route.

Model-based learning is flexible and updates quickly when circumstances change, but it is computationally expensive, because planning takes effort and time.

This maps onto goal-directed behaviour: flexible, thoughtful, but costly.

The two systems can be told apart in the laboratory using tasks designed to separate them.

A widely used tool is the two-step task, developed by Nathaniel Daw and colleagues, in which the pattern of a person's choices after surprising outcomes reveals whether they are relying on stored action values or on an internal model of the task's structure.

The evidence shows that people use a blend of both systems, leaning more on the effortful model-based system when it is worth the cost and falling back on the cheap model-free system when under time pressure, stress, or fatigue.

The systems reading: model-free control answers a value query in a single table lookup, while model-based control answers it by simulating futures through its stored map, so the two differ chiefly in their time constant at decision time, milliseconds for the lookup versus a slower, effortful search for the simulation.


31.2.2 The successor representation as a middle ground

The successor representation is an elegant idea that sits between the model-free and model-based extremes, offering some of the flexibility of planning at much of the speed of habit.

The problem it solves is that model-free learning is too rigid while model-based planning is too slow, so the mind may use a clever compromise.

The core idea, originally proposed by Peter Dayan in 1993 and revived strongly in recent years, is to store not the full model of the world, and not just cached values, but a predictive map of where you are likely to go.

In plain terms, the successor representation records, for each situation, which other situations you tend to end up in later.

Instead of memorising raw values or simulating every step, the agent keeps a summary of its expected future whereabouts and combines that with current reward information to compute values quickly.

This gives a useful pattern of strengths: the successor representation adjusts quickly when the rewards in the world change, because reward information is kept separate, but it adjusts slowly when the very structure of the world changes, because the predictive map must be relearned.

That specific signature, flexible to reward changes yet rigid to structural changes, has been found in human behaviour by researchers such as Ida Momennejad and colleagues, supporting the idea that the brain uses something like a successor representation.

It is also attractive because it connects to how the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and navigation, appears to represent maps of space and experience in a predictive way.

In systems terms, the successor representation factorises the value computation into two stored components, a predictive occupancy map and a reward vector, so value queries stay cheap while reward updates propagate in a single step and structural updates still require slow relearning of the map.


31.3 The neuroscience of reward

This section turns from mathematics and behaviour to the brain itself.

It presents one of the great success stories of computational neuroscience: the discovery that a specific brain signal implements the abstract prediction-error idea with remarkable precision.

The key player is a chemical messenger called dopamine.


31.3.1 The dopamine reward-prediction-error hypothesis

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter, which is a chemical that nerve cells use to signal to one another, produced by a small group of cells deep in the midbrain.

For a long time dopamine was loosely described as a "pleasure chemical", but the modern and better-supported view is quite different and more precise.

The dopamine reward-prediction-error hypothesis holds that these dopamine cells signal not pleasure itself but the prediction error, the gap between the reward received and the reward expected.

This was established through recordings of monkey dopamine neurons by Wolfram Schultz and colleagues, interpreted in light of temporal-difference learning by Peter Dayan, Read Montague, and Terrence Sejnowski in a landmark 1997 paper.

The findings are strikingly clean.

When a monkey receives an unexpected reward, its dopamine cells fire a burst, signalling a positive prediction error.

When a cue reliably predicts the reward, the dopamine burst shifts backward in time from the reward to the cue, exactly as temporal-difference learning says it should.

When a fully predicted reward arrives, the cells show no burst at all, because there is no surprise and no error.

And when an expected reward is omitted, the cells briefly dip below their baseline, signalling a negative prediction error, a disappointment signal.

As a signal, the phasic dopamine response is fast: the burst begins roughly 100 milliseconds after the triggering event and lasts on the order of 100 to 200 milliseconds, a timing consistent with a step-by-step teaching signal.

This match between a theory born in artificial intelligence and the behaviour of real neurons is one of the most celebrated results in neuroscience, and it firmly linked the abstract framework of reinforcement learning to the machinery of the brain.


31.3.2 The basal ganglia as an actor-critic

The basal ganglia are a set of structures deep in the brain that are heavily involved in selecting actions and in learning from reward.

A popular and productive way to understand their role uses a design from reinforcement learning called the actor-critic architecture.

In an actor-critic system, the work is split between two cooperating parts.

The critic learns to evaluate situations, computing the value of states and generating the prediction-error signal.

The actor learns the policy, that is, which actions to take, and it is trained by the critic's prediction-error signal, strengthening actions that turned out better than expected and weakening those that turned out worse.

Mapped onto the brain, the dopamine signal plays the role of the critic's teaching signal, broadcast to the striatum, which is the main input structure of the basal ganglia.

Within this scheme, parts of the striatum help evaluate states like a critic, while other parts help select actions like an actor, and dopamine adjusts the connections in both according to prediction error.

This account is attractive because it links anatomy, chemistry, and computation into one coherent story, and it helps explain disorders such as Parkinson's disease, in which the loss of dopamine cells impairs both movement and reward-based learning.

It should be said that the actor-critic mapping is a useful model rather than a fully settled fact, and researchers continue to debate the precise division of labour within the basal ganglia.

The systems reading: the critic subscribes to state and reward, publishes a scalar error, and the actor subscribes to that error to adjust its action weights, a two-module loop closed on every behavioural step.


31.3.3 Distributional codes for value

Distributional reinforcement learning is a recent and important refinement of the classic picture.

The traditional theory assumes that the brain learns a single average value for each situation, a single best guess of expected reward.

Distributional reinforcement learning proposes instead that the brain learns the whole spread of possible rewards, that is, the full range of good and bad outcomes and how likely each is, not just the average.

The idea came first from artificial intelligence, where representing the full distribution of possible returns was found to make learning agents perform better.

Then a 2020 study by Will Dabney, Naoshige Uchida, and colleagues reported evidence that real dopamine neurons do something similar.

They found that different dopamine cells are tuned to be optimistic or pessimistic to varying degrees, some firing mainly for better-than-expected outcomes and others mainly for worse-than-expected ones.

Taken together, this population of cells with different outlooks can represent the entire distribution of expected rewards rather than a single number.

This matters because knowing the range of possible outcomes, not just the average, supports better decisions under risk and uncertainty, and it is a fine example of an insight flowing from artificial intelligence back into neuroscience.

In systems terms, the change is in the output format of the value system: instead of publishing one scalar per state, the population publishes a set of estimates at different optimism settings, from which downstream systems can read off both the average and the risk.

As a recent finding, its full scope is still being worked out, but it has already reshaped how researchers think about what dopamine represents.


31.4 Extensions

This section surveys three ways the basic reinforcement-learning framework has been extended to capture more of the richness of real behaviour.

Each addresses a limitation of the simple picture: how to handle complex nested goals, how to learn faster by learning how to learn, and how to decide not just what to do but how hard to try.

Together they show reinforcement learning maturing from a narrow model into a broad theory of adaptive action.


31.4.1 Hierarchical reinforcement learning and subgoals

Hierarchical reinforcement learning addresses a serious weakness of the basic framework: it struggles with tasks that require long sequences of actions to reach a distant goal.

The problem is that if reward comes only at the very end of a long task, it is extremely slow to figure out which of the thousands of small actions along the way deserve credit.

The solution is to organise behaviour into a hierarchy, with big goals broken down into smaller subgoals, and those into individual actions.

Consider making breakfast: the overall goal decomposes into subgoals like "make toast" and "brew coffee", and each of those into concrete steps.

In hierarchical reinforcement learning, the agent learns reusable chunks of behaviour, sometimes called options or skills, that accomplish subgoals, and then it can plan at the level of these chunks rather than every tiny step.

This dramatically speeds up learning, because a subgoal reached becomes a milestone that can carry reward information, and because skills learned for one task can be reused in another.

In systems terms, the hierarchy inserts an extra control layer whose actions are whole sub-policies, so credit assignment operates over a handful of chunk-level steps instead of thousands of primitive steps.

This connects directly to the psychology of skill and to the way people plan by setting intermediate targets, and it is an active area where artificial intelligence and cognitive science inform each other.


31.4.2 Meta-reinforcement learning and learning to learn

Meta-reinforcement learning is the idea of learning how to learn.

Ordinary reinforcement learning masters a single task, but a human or animal placed in a new but related task does not start from zero; it draws on the general lessons of similar past tasks and adapts quickly.

Meta-reinforcement learning captures this by training an agent across many related tasks so that it acquires a general learning strategy, not just the solution to one task.

After such training, the agent can adapt to a fresh task within that family in just a few trials, because it has, in effect, learned the shape of the problems it tends to face.

An influential proposal by Jane Wang, Matthew Botvinick, and colleagues suggested that the brain implements something like this, with the slow dopamine-based learning system gradually shaping a faster learning process housed in the prefrontal cortex, the front part of the brain involved in flexible control.

In this view, one learning system trains another, so that the prefrontal network becomes able to adapt rapidly on its own, which would help explain the striking flexibility of human and animal learning.

The systems reading is a two-timescale design: a slow outer loop adjusts connection weights over many tasks, and a fast inner loop adapts within a task over a few trials using activity rather than weight change.

This is a frontier idea rather than an established fact, but it is a promising attempt to explain why real minds learn so much faster than a naive learning algorithm would.


31.4.3 Vigour, opportunity cost, and tonic dopamine

This final extension addresses a question the basic framework ignores: not just which action to take, but how fast or how hard to perform it.

Vigour refers to the energy or speed with which an animal acts, such as how quickly it presses a lever or how fast it moves toward a goal.

The key insight, developed by Yael Niv, Nathaniel Daw, Peter Dayan, and colleagues, is that the right level of vigour depends on the opportunity cost of time.

Opportunity cost is what you give up by spending time on one thing instead of another.

When rewards are plentiful in the environment, time is precious, because dawdling means missing out on all the reward you could be earning, so it pays to act quickly and vigorously.

When rewards are scarce, there is less to lose by taking your time, so slower, more leisurely action is appropriate.

The proposal links this to a distinction between two modes of dopamine signalling.

Phasic dopamine refers to brief bursts that, as we saw, carry the reward-prediction-error signal used for learning which actions are good.

Tonic dopamine refers to the slow, steady background level of dopamine, which this theory suggests represents the average rate of reward available, and thus sets how vigorous behaviour should be.

In systems terms, tonic dopamine is a slowly varying gain, integrating reward rate over seconds to minutes, that scales the speed of every action, while phasic dopamine is the fast error channel operating over roughly a tenth of a second.

This helps make sense of clinical observations, such as the slowed movement and reduced motivation seen when dopamine is depleted in Parkinson's disease, by tying dopamine not only to learning but to the energising of action.

Like the other extensions, this is an actively researched proposal that enriches the simple framework rather than a closed question.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ The current state, a description of the situation the agent is in, from the perceptual systems.

◦ A scalar reward signal after each action, from the environment via the body's reward systems.

◦ The next state that follows each action, closing the step of the control loop.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ An action selected on each step, sent to the motor systems.

◦ A prediction-error signal, the temporal-difference error, broadcast as the teaching signal that in the brain is carried by phasic dopamine.

◦ Learned values and policies, consumed by the decision-making and planning systems of later chapters.

• STATE.

◦ A table or function of action values, one entry per state and action pair, for the model-free controller.

◦ An internal model of state transitions for the model-based controller, or a predictive occupancy map under the successor representation.

◦ A running estimate of the average reward rate, the proposed content of tonic dopamine, used to set vigour.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ The learning rate, controlling how far each prediction error moves the stored values.

◦ The discount factor, controlling how strongly future rewards count relative to present ones and thus the planning horizon.

◦ The softmax temperature or random-choice rate, controlling the balance of exploration against exploitation.

◦ An arbitration weight setting how much control the model-based system gets relative to the model-free system.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Phasic dopamine bursts begin roughly 100 milliseconds after an unexpected reward and last on the order of 100 to 200 milliseconds, per recordings in the Schultz tradition.

◦ The control loop updates once per behavioural step, from hundreds of milliseconds upward depending on the task.

◦ Tonic dopamine and the average-reward estimate change over seconds to minutes, the vigour timescale.

◦ Convergence time of value learning, REFUSED as a single number because it scales with the size of the state space, the learning rate, and the reward sparsity of the task.

• MODES.

◦ Exploration mode, dominant when values are uncertain or the temperature parameter is high, producing varied action sampling.

◦ Exploitation mode, dominant once value estimates are confident, producing consistent choice of the best-known action.

◦ Model-based mode, engaged when stakes are high and cognitive resources are available, computing values by simulation.

◦ Model-free mode, engaged under time pressure, stress, fatigue, or after extensive practice, reading cached values directly; the arbitration between the two is itself learned.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Addiction-like persistence, in which drug-inflated dopamine signalling stamps in action values that no longer track real outcomes.

◦ Impaired reward learning and slowed, unenergetic movement in Parkinson's disease, when dopamine cells are lost.

◦ Getting stuck in local habits through premature exploitation, when exploration is shut down too early.

◦ Perseverative choice after reward contingencies reverse, the signature of an agent relying on stale cached values.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called number of arms with initial value three.
Create a list variable called true rewards containing the values zero point two, zero point five, and zero point eight.
Create a list variable called action values containing one zero for each arm.
Create a number variable called learning rate with initial value zero point one.
Create a number variable called temperature with initial value zero point two.
Repeat the following five hundred times.
    Create a list variable called preferences with no items.
    For each value in action values, calculate the exponential of the value divided by temperature, and append the result to preferences.
    Calculate the preference total as the sum of the items in preferences.
    Create a list variable called probabilities by dividing each item in preferences by the preference total.
    Choose an arm at random, weighted by probabilities, and call it chosen arm.
    Draw a random number between zero and one; if it is less than the true rewards entry for chosen arm, set reward to one, otherwise set reward to zero.
    Calculate the prediction error as reward minus the action values entry for chosen arm.
    Add the product of learning rate and the prediction error to the action values entry for chosen arm.
Return action values.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Bring in the mathematics and randomness modules from the standard library.
import math
import random

# Create a list variable called true_rewards holding each arm's real payoff probability.
true_rewards = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]

# Create a list variable called action_values containing one zero for each arm.
action_values = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]

# Create a number variable called learning_rate with initial value zero point one.
learning_rate = 0.1
# Create a number variable called temperature with initial value zero point two.
temperature = 0.2

# Repeat the learning loop five hundred times.
for trial in range(500):
    # For each value, calculate the exponential of the value divided by temperature.
    preferences = [math.exp(value / temperature) for value in action_values]
    # Calculate the preference total as the sum of the preferences.
    preference_total = sum(preferences)
    # Create the choice probabilities by dividing each preference by the total.
    probabilities = [preference / preference_total for preference in preferences]
    # Choose an arm at random, weighted by the softmax probabilities.
    chosen_arm = random.choices(range(len(action_values)), weights=probabilities)[0]
    # Draw a random number and pay out one if it falls under the arm's true probability.
    reward = 1.0 if random.random() < true_rewards[chosen_arm] else 0.0
    # Calculate the prediction error as reward minus the stored value of the chosen arm.
    prediction_error = reward - action_values[chosen_arm]
    # Add the product of learning_rate and prediction_error to the chosen arm's value.
    action_values[chosen_arm] = action_values[chosen_arm] + learning_rate * prediction_error

# Print the learned values, which should approximate the true payoff probabilities.
print("Learned action values:", [round(value, 2) for value in action_values])
# Print the arm the agent now prefers, which should be the best arm.
print("Preferred arm:", action_values.index(max(action_values)))


CHAPTER 32. STATISTICAL AND IMPLICIT LEARNING (PROCESS)

This chapter is about the quiet learning that happens all the time without our noticing.

Much of what we know we never deliberately studied; we simply absorbed the patterns in our environment through exposure.

Statistical learning is the mind's ability to soak up the regularities and probabilities in what we encounter, and implicit learning is the acquisition of knowledge without awareness of having learned it.

In systems terms, this chapter describes an always-on background process: its input is whatever structured stream the senses deliver, its state is a table of learned transition statistics, and its output is faster and more accurate processing of predictable input, delivered without any conscious report.

These forms of learning are foundational, underlying everything from finding words in speech to picking up the unspoken rules of a game or a social setting, which is why they matter for understanding both human minds and the machines meant to resemble them.


32.1 Statistical learning

Statistical learning is the process by which the mind detects patterns in the frequencies and co-occurrences of events, usually automatically and without effort.

It is how a mind extracts structure from a stream of experience, discovering which things tend to go together and which tend to follow which.

This section explains the core mechanism and then shows how broadly it operates across the senses and across the lifespan.


32.1.1 The extraction of transitional probabilities

The clearest demonstration of statistical learning concerns how we find the boundaries between words in continuous speech.

When you listen to someone talk, the sound is a nearly continuous stream, with no reliable silences marking where one word stops and the next begins.

Yet somehow, especially as infants, we carve that stream into words, and a key tool for doing so is tracking transitional probabilities.

A transitional probability is simply the likelihood that one element follows another; in speech, it is how likely a given syllable is to be followed by a particular next syllable.

The insight is that within a single word, the sequence of syllables is highly predictable, because the same syllables always occur in the same order.

Across a word boundary, though, the next syllable is much less predictable, because many different words could come next.

So a sudden drop in predictability is a good clue that a word has just ended and a new one is beginning.

The pioneering study by Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin, and Elissa Newport in 1996, described earlier in the language chapter, showed that eight-month-old infants use exactly this cue.

After only two minutes of listening to a stream of nonsense syllables with no pauses, the infants treated syllable groups with high internal predictability as words and reacted to the low-predictability boundaries as breaks.

This showed that the mind is running a kind of automatic statistics engine, computing probabilities from mere exposure, without instruction and without conscious effort.

As a mechanism, the engine's input is the element stream, its state is a co-occurrence count table, its output is a predictability estimate for each transition, and its measurable learning timescale in the infant studies is about two minutes of exposure.

It was a profound result because it demonstrated a powerful learning mechanism that could get language acquisition off the ground using nothing but sensitivity to patterns.


32.1.2 Statistical learning across domains and ages

A striking feature of statistical learning is that it is not special to speech; it operates across many kinds of input and throughout life.

The word "domain" here means an area or type of information, such as sounds, sights, or touches.

Research after the 1996 speech study quickly showed that the same kind of probability tracking works with tone sequences that are not speech, demonstrating it is not tied to language.

It also works in vision: people can learn the regularities in sequences of shapes or in the spatial arrangement of visual scenes, which helps explain how we come to know where things are likely to be.

It even appears in the sense of touch, suggesting statistical learning is a general property of how the brain processes any structured stream of input.

This breadth has led many researchers to see statistical learning as a domain-general ability, meaning one broad mechanism rather than many separate ones, though there is ongoing debate about how unified it really is.

Some evidence suggests the learning in different senses may rely partly on separate, sense-specific processes rather than one central engine, so the "one mechanism or many" question is not fully settled.

Because that is a debate, the systems reading is a pair of predictions: a single central engine predicts that learning ability in one sense should correlate strongly with learning ability in another within the same person, while separate sense-specific engines predict weak cross-sense correlations, and current data lean toward the weaker correlations.

Statistical learning also spans ages.

It is present very early, in infants only a few months old, and even newborns show sensitivity to some regularities, which suggests it is a foundational learning ability available from the start of life.

It continues to operate in children and adults, quietly shaping our knowledge of language, music, visual environments, and routines throughout the lifespan.

Its early availability and wide reach are precisely why it is considered such an important building block: it is a mechanism the mind can rely on before it has language, instruction, or deliberate strategies.


32.2 Implicit learning

Implicit learning is learning that happens without conscious awareness, producing knowledge you possess and use but cannot fully describe.

It is closely related to statistical learning but the emphasis is different: statistical learning stresses what is learned, namely patterns and probabilities, while implicit learning stresses how it is learned, namely without awareness.

Much of our practical competence, from riding a bike to sensing the rhythm of our native language, is implicit in this sense, and this section examines how it is studied and how it relates to the knowledge we can consciously state.


32.2.1 Sequence learning and artificial grammar learning

Two laboratory tasks have done most to reveal implicit learning, and both are worth understanding.

The first is artificial grammar learning, introduced by Arthur Reber in the 1960s.

An artificial grammar is a made-up set of rules that decides which strings of letters are "legal", such as which sequences of the letters can follow which.

Participants first study a batch of legal letter strings without being told there are any rules; they are simply asked to memorise the strings.

Later they are told that the strings followed rules, and are asked to judge whether new strings are legal or not.

Remarkably, people judge new strings well above chance, showing they absorbed something about the grammar, yet they typically cannot state the rules they used.

That gap, good performance with poor ability to explain it, is the signature of implicit learning.

The second task is the serial reaction time task, developed by Marvin Nissen and Peter Bullemer in 1987.

In it, participants press buttons in response to targets that appear at various locations, and, unknown to them, the sequence of locations secretly follows a repeating pattern.

People get faster and faster on the repeating sequence, and then slow down abruptly when the pattern is changed to random, proving they had learned the sequence.

Yet many participants cannot report the pattern or even that there was one, again showing knowledge acquired without awareness.

Together these tasks establish that people can learn complex structure implicitly, extracting regularities they cannot consciously articulate.

The systems reading of the serial reaction time task: the input is the sequence of target locations, the state is a set of learned transition expectations, the output is a motor response whose reaction time drops by tens of milliseconds for predictable transitions, and the diagnostic is the abrupt slow-down when the hidden structure is removed.


32.2.2 The relation between implicit and explicit knowledge

The deepest and most debated question in this area is how implicit and explicit knowledge relate.

Explicit knowledge is knowledge you are aware of and can state in words, such as knowing that Paris is the capital of France.

Implicit knowledge is knowledge you have and use but cannot fully put into words, such as the feel of balancing on a bicycle.

The strong claim, associated with Arthur Reber, is that implicit learning is a genuinely separate mode of learning that acquires abstract knowledge unconsciously, largely independent of conscious thought.

This claim is supported by findings that implicit learning seems relatively robust, changing little with age and holding up in some patients with amnesia, a condition in which conscious memory is impaired.

But the strong claim has been seriously challenged, most notably by Pierre Perruchet and colleagues.

Their critique is that much of what looks like abstract, unconscious rule learning can be explained more simply by fragments of concrete knowledge, such as familiarity with small chunks of letters that appeared often, rather than by grasping the underlying grammar.

On this view, participants may be relying on remembered pieces and surface similarity rather than on any deep, hidden rule.

A further difficulty is methodological: it is genuinely hard to prove that knowledge is completely unconscious, because the tests used to measure awareness may be too insensitive to detect the fragments of conscious knowledge people actually have.

Because this is a debate, the two sides predict differently in systems terms: a separate unconscious rule-learning system predicts transfer of grammar knowledge to strings written in entirely new letters, since the abstract rules carry over, while the fragment account predicts that performance collapses when the familiar letter chunks are replaced, and the experimental record shows partial transfer, which is why the debate persists.

The current, cautious consensus is that learning without full awareness is real and important, but that many tasks involve a mixture of implicit and explicit knowledge, and that the sharp separation Reber originally proposed is more blurred than it first appeared.

This honest uncertainty matters for building humanlike minds, because it warns against assuming a clean split between conscious and unconscious learning when the reality is a continuum.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Any structured sequential stream from the senses: syllables, tones, shapes, spatial locations, or touches, delivered element by element.

◦ Timing information about element order and adjacency, since the learned content is which element follows which.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Predictability estimates for upcoming elements, consumed by perception to speed processing of expected input and by motor systems to pre-prepare responses.

◦ Segmentation of continuous streams into chunks, such as words from speech, consumed by the language-acquisition system of the earlier chapter.

◦ Above-chance familiarity judgments about pattern-conforming items, available to decision systems even when no verbal rule report is available.

• STATE.

◦ A table of element-to-element transition counts, accumulated automatically from exposure.

◦ Stored fragments or chunks of frequently co-occurring elements, the alternative currency emphasised by the Perruchet critique.

◦ Expectation strength for the next element, updated on every step of the stream.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Exposure amount, the number of elements observed, which sets the reliability of the statistics.

◦ A chunking threshold, the internal predictability level above which a group of elements is treated as a unit.

◦ Attention to the stream, which modulates but does not abolish learning, since learning proceeds under passive listening.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Statistical segmentation measurable after about 2 minutes of exposure to an artificial speech stream in eight-month-old infants, per Saffran, Aslin, and Newport 1996.

◦ Reaction-time savings in the serial reaction time task build over tens of minutes of practice, with tens of milliseconds of speed-up on predictable transitions.

◦ Above-chance grammar judgments after a study phase of minutes in artificial grammar learning, typically around 60 to 70 percent correct against a 50 percent chance level.

◦ Durability of implicitly learned knowledge, REFUSED as a single number because retention spans from days to a year across studies depending on task and amount of training.

• MODES.

◦ Passive absorption mode, the default, in which statistics accumulate from mere exposure without intent to learn.

◦ Expression mode, in which the stored statistics show themselves as faster reaction times, familiarity feelings, and segmentation, without verbal access.

◦ Explicit discovery mode, entered when a learner notices the pattern and can begin to describe it, converting implicit knowledge into reportable knowledge; noticing is the trigger, and many learners never enter this mode.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Learning false patterns from biased samples, so that accidental regularities in experience become confident expectations, a root of stereotype formation.

◦ Overinterpreting streaks in genuinely random input, since the statistics engine has no off switch for unstructured streams.

◦ Inflexibility of implicitly acquired routines, which are hard to correct verbally precisely because they were never verbally represented.

◦ Measurement failure in the laboratory: insensitive awareness tests can misclassify partly explicit knowledge as implicit, the central methodological trap of the field.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called sequence containing a long stream of location labels generated by repeating a hidden pattern.
Create a dictionary variable called transition counts with no entries.
Create a dictionary variable called context counts with no entries.
Create a list variable called reaction times with no items.
Create a number variable called base time with initial value five hundred.
Create a number variable called maximum saving with initial value one hundred.
For each position from the second element to the last element in sequence, do the following.
    Set previous to the element before the position.
    Set current to the element at the position.
    Create a number variable called expectation with initial value zero.
    If the context counts entry for previous is greater than zero, set expectation to the transition counts entry for the pair of previous and current divided by the context counts entry for previous, treating a missing entry as zero.
    Calculate the simulated reaction time as base time minus the product of maximum saving and expectation.
    Append the simulated reaction time to reaction times.
    Add one to the context counts entry for previous, creating the entry with value zero if it is absent.
    Add one to the transition counts entry for the pair of previous and current, creating the entry with value zero if it is absent.
Calculate the early average as the mean of the first fifty reaction times.
Calculate the late average as the mean of the last fifty reaction times.
Return the early average and the late average.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a list variable called sequence by repeating a hidden location pattern forty times.
sequence = ["A", "C", "B", "D", "C", "A", "D", "B"] * 40

# Create a dictionary variable called transition_counts with no entries.
transition_counts = {}
# Create a dictionary variable called context_counts with no entries.
context_counts = {}

# Create a list variable called reaction_times with no items.
reaction_times = []
# Create a number variable called base_time with initial value five hundred milliseconds.
base_time = 500.0
# Create a number variable called maximum_saving with initial value one hundred milliseconds.
maximum_saving = 100.0

# For each position from the second element to the last, respond and then learn.
for i in range(1, len(sequence)):
    # Set previous to the element before the position.
    previous = sequence[i - 1]
    # Set current to the element at the position.
    current = sequence[i]
    # Create a number variable called expectation with initial value zero.
    expectation = 0.0
    # If the context has been seen, set expectation to the learned transitional probability.
    if context_counts.get(previous, 0) > 0:
        # Divide the pair count by the context count, treating a missing pair as zero.
        expectation = transition_counts.get((previous, current), 0) / context_counts[previous]
    # Calculate the simulated reaction time as the base time minus the expectation saving.
    simulated_reaction_time = base_time - maximum_saving * expectation
    # Append the simulated reaction time to reaction_times.
    reaction_times.append(simulated_reaction_time)
    # Add one to the context count for previous, creating the entry at zero if absent.
    context_counts[previous] = context_counts.get(previous, 0) + 1
    # Add one to the transition count for the pair, creating the entry at zero if absent.
    transition_counts[(previous, current)] = transition_counts.get((previous, current), 0) + 1

# Calculate the early average as the mean of the first fifty reaction times.
early_average = sum(reaction_times[:50]) / 50
# Calculate the late average as the mean of the last fifty reaction times.
late_average = sum(reaction_times[-50:]) / 50

# Print the averages, showing responses speeding up as the hidden pattern is absorbed.
print("Early average reaction time:", round(early_average, 1), "ms")
print("Late average reaction time:", round(late_average, 1), "ms")

CHAPTER 33. SKILL ACQUISITION, EXPERTISE, AND TRANSFER (PROCESS)

This chapter is about how people get good at things.

A skill is any ability that improves with practice, from tying a shoelace to reading an X-ray or playing the violin.

We will look at how a beginner slowly turns into a smooth performer, what makes a true expert different from the rest of us, and the tricky question of whether being good at one thing helps you at another.

This matters because almost everything a mind does well, it once did badly, and understanding that change tells us a great deal about how learning actually works.

Viewed as an engineered system, skill acquisition is a compiler: it takes slow, instruction-following behaviour as input and, through repetition, outputs fast, automatic routines that no longer need step-by-step supervision.

The tag (PROCESS) means this chapter describes a real human capacity that any complete model of the mind would have to reproduce.


33.1 The stages of skill

When you learn something new, you do not stay the same kind of learner all the way through.

Researchers have long noticed that early practice feels very different from later practice, and they have tried to describe the recognisable phases you pass through.

This section lays out the classic picture of those phases and the simple mathematical law that describes how fast you speed up.

In systems terms, the learner moves through distinct operating modes, each with its own resource demands, error profile, and speed, and practice is the signal that drives the transitions.


33.1.1 The cognitive, associative, and autonomous stages

The most influential description of how a skill grows was proposed by two psychologists, Paul Fitts and Michael Posner, in 1967.

They suggested that learning a skill passes through three stages, which they named the cognitive, the associative, and the autonomous.

The cognitive stage is the very beginning, when you are working out what to do at all.

Here you lean heavily on instructions, you talk yourself through each step, and you make many large, clumsy errors.

Think of the first time behind the wheel of a car, when you have to consciously remember which pedal is the brake.

This stage is called cognitive because it leans so hard on conscious thought, which is the effortful, deliberate kind of thinking you are aware of doing.

The associative stage is the long middle period of practice.

By now you know roughly what to do, and the work shifts to doing it better, smoother, and with fewer mistakes.

The name associative refers to the strengthening of links between the situation and the right response, so that the correct action starts to come more reliably.

Errors become smaller and rarer, and the movements or steps begin to flow together instead of being performed one careful piece at a time.

The autonomous stage is the destination, where the skill runs almost by itself.

The word autonomous means self-governing, and here the skill needs very little conscious attention.

An experienced driver can hold a conversation while steering through traffic, because the driving has become nearly automatic, meaning it runs without deliberate control.

A useful sign of this stage is that you can do the skill and something else at the same time without the skill falling apart.

The psychologist John Anderson later gave this three-stage picture a more precise, mechanical explanation inside his computer model of the mind called ACT, short for Adaptive Control of Thought.

In his account, the beginner solves the task slowly by looking up remembered facts and instructions, which is why it is so effortful at first.

With practice, the mind builds direct rules, sometimes called productions, that fire off the right response to a situation without any looking-up, which is what makes an expert fast and seemingly effortless.

The systems reading of the three stages is a change of controller: the input is the same task situation throughout, but the output is generated first by a slow interpretive loop that consults declarative memory on every step, then by a mixed loop, and finally by compiled condition-action rules, each of which fires in roughly 50 milliseconds in production-system models such as ACT-R, the Adaptive Control of Thought - Rational architecture.

One caution is worth stating plainly.

These stages are a helpful description, not sharp lines with fences between them.

Learning is gradual, the boundaries blur, and a person can be at different stages for different parts of the same skill.


33.1.2 Proceduralisation and the power law of practice

Two ideas describe what is happening under the surface as a skill matures: proceduralisation, and the power law of practice.

Proceduralisation is the name for the shift from knowing about something to simply doing it.

At the start you hold the skill as declarative knowledge, which means facts and instructions you could state out loud, such as the written rules of a card game.

With repetition this turns into procedural knowledge, which means know-how that is embedded in action and is hard to put into words, such as the feel of when to play a card.

A telling clue that proceduralisation has happened is that skilled performers often cannot explain what they do; a fluent speaker of a language usually cannot recite its grammar rules.

As a mechanism, proceduralisation takes traces of successful step-by-step solutions as input and outputs new compiled rules, trading away flexibility and verbal access in exchange for speed and low attentional cost, over a timescale of hundreds to thousands of repetitions.

The power law of practice describes how quickly performance improves as you keep practising.

The core finding is simple and very robust: you improve fastest at the start, and then improvement slows down, even though it never quite stops.

The first hour of practice buys you a huge jump, while the thousandth hour buys you only a tiny sliver more.

This pattern was studied early by George Snoddy in 1926 and later made famous as a general law by Allan Newell and Paul Rosenbloom around 1981.

They called it a power law because the mathematics that fits the slowing-down curve is a power function, which is just a particular equation that produces exactly this fast-then-slow shape.

In that equation the time to perform the task equals a floor that can never be beaten, plus a learnable component that shrinks as the number of practice trials is raised to a negative exponent, so each doubling of practice cuts the remaining learnable time by a constant fraction.

There is an honest scientific dispute here that is worth knowing about.

Later researchers, including Andrew Heathcote and colleagues in 2000, argued that when you look at individual people rather than averages, an exponential curve, which is a different equation, often fits better than a power curve.

Averaging across many learners can, by itself, bend an exponential shape into something that looks like a power law, which may have fooled the earlier studies.

In systems terms the two sides predict different things: a power law predicts a learning rate that slows in proportion to how much practice has accumulated, while an exponential predicts a constant proportional gain per trial, and only careful fits to single learners can tell the two curves apart.

So the deep truth is agreed - practice brings large early gains and shrinking later ones - while the exact equation is still argued over.


33.2 Expertise

An expert is someone who performs at a very high level in a particular field after long practice, such as a chess master, a surgeon, or a concert pianist.

Studying experts is a clever research strategy, because they show us the far end of learning and reveal what the mind can build when it is pushed to its limits.

This section looks at what actually makes experts special, and at the fierce debate over how much of expertise is practice and how much is something else.

Read as a system, expertise is not a faster processor but a vastly larger and better-indexed pattern database, queried by recognition in well under a second.


33.2.1 Chunking and pattern recognition in experts

The single most important discovery about expertise is that experts do not have better general memories or faster minds; they have better-organised knowledge of their own field.

The classic demonstration came from chess.

In the 1940s the Dutch psychologist and chess master Adriaan de Groot found that when masters and weaker players were shown a chess position, the masters were far better at reconstructing it from memory - but only when the position came from a real game.

William Chase and Herbert Simon confirmed and extended this in 1973, and added the crucial twist.

When the chess pieces were placed at random, so that the arrangement made no sense as a game, the masters were no better than beginners at remembering it.

This shows the master's advantage is not a bigger memory in general; it is a memory stocked with meaningful patterns.

The explanation is called chunking.

A chunk is a group of individual items bound together into a single meaningful unit, so that the mind can hold and handle it as one thing.

Where a beginner sees twenty separate chess pieces, a master sees a handful of familiar formations, and holding a few chunks is far easier than holding twenty scraps.

The systems reading is a compression scheme: the input is a raw scene, the stored codebook of patterns re-encodes it into a few chunks that fit within a working memory span of about four chunks, and the output is both an economical description of the scene and a set of retrieved candidate actions.

Because experts have stored thousands of these patterns through years of practice, they can also recognise a situation at a glance and know what it calls for, which is why a master's good move often comes to mind almost instantly.

Later theories, such as the long-term working memory account of Anders Ericsson and Walter Kintsch in 1995, and a detailed template theory by Fernand Gobet and Simon in the late 1990s, refined this picture, but the central lesson has held up for decades.

Expertise is largely a matter of having built, through practice, a huge and well-indexed library of patterns in one domain.


33.2.2 Deliberate practice and its limits

If experts are made by storing patterns through practice, a natural question follows: is any practice enough, or does it have to be a special kind?

The psychologist Anders Ericsson argued that the kind matters enormously, and he named the effective kind deliberate practice.

Deliberate practice is not just repeating what you can already do; it is effortful, focused work aimed squarely at your weaknesses, guided by feedback, with clear goals and constant stretching beyond your comfort zone.

A pianist drilling the exact bars she keeps fumbling, slowly and with a teacher's correction, is doing deliberate practice; a pianist happily playing pieces she has mastered is not.

In systems terms deliberate practice is a closed control loop: the input is a performance sample, an external or internal critic compares it against a target, the error signal selects the next drill, and the output is a targeted update to exactly the weakest component, whereas mere repetition runs the loop open with no error signal.

Ericsson's studies of violinists in 1993 found that the best performers had accumulated far more hours of this kind of practice than the good-but-not-great performers.

The writer Malcolm Gladwell later popularised a rounded version of this as the ten thousand hour rule, the idea that roughly ten thousand hours of practice makes a world-class expert.

It is important to be clear that this catchy rule is a simplification that Ericsson himself did not fully endorse; there is no magic number, and the hours were an average, not a threshold everyone must hit.

The limits of the practice-is-everything view were sharpened by a large analysis by Brooke Macnamara and colleagues in 2014.

Pooling eighty-eight studies, they found that the amount of deliberate practice did predict skill, but explained only part of the differences between people - about twenty-six percent in games, twenty-one percent in music, and eighteen percent in sports.

That leaves most of the variation between people to be explained by other things, which may include starting age, working memory capacity, personality, and quite possibly inborn aptitude.

Ericsson pushed back, arguing that many of the pooled studies measured practice loosely, counting mere hours played rather than true deliberate practice, which would understate its real power.

In systems terms the debate is about how much of the variance in final performance the practice input alone controls, and the two camps predict different outcomes when practice quality is measured strictly: the strong practice view predicts the explained share should rise sharply, while the multi-factor view predicts a large residual will remain.

The honest current position is a middle one.
