Sustained, well-designed practice is necessary for high expertise and is the largest single lever most people can pull, but it is not the whole story, and the claim that practice alone explains greatness is not supported by the evidence.


33.3 Transfer

Transfer is the question of whether learning one thing helps, or hinders, your learning or performance of another thing.

It is one of the most practically important topics in all of psychology, because education, training, and the popular hope of brain-training games all rest on the assumption that skills spread from where you learned them to somewhere new.

This section explains how far skills really travel, and the mechanisms that let them travel at all.

In systems terms, transfer asks how much of a trained module can be re-used by a different task, and the answer depends on how much of the module's internal machinery the two tasks genuinely share.


33.3.1 Near and far transfer and the theory of identical elements

Psychologists divide transfer by distance.

Near transfer is when a skill helps on a new task that closely resembles the one you trained on, such as touch-typing on a slightly different keyboard.

Far transfer is when training on one task is supposed to help a very different one, such as playing chess making you better at planning your finances.

The general and sobering finding across a century of research is that near transfer is common, while far transfer is rare and often absent.

The classic explanation was given by Edward Thorndike and Robert Woodworth in 1901 and is called the theory of identical elements.

Their claim is that training on task A helps task B only to the extent that the two tasks share specific components - the same movements, facts, or mental steps.

If two tasks overlap in their actual parts, transfer follows; if they merely feel similar or are both called reasoning, there is little or nothing to carry over.

The systems reading is component re-use: the amount of transfer is predicted by the overlap between the two tasks' processing components, so the input to a transfer prediction is a component-by-component comparison of the tasks, and the output is an expected saving proportional to the shared parts.

Thorndike's work overturned a popular older idea called formal discipline, the belief that studying hard subjects like Latin or geometry strengthens the mind in general, the way lifting weights strengthens a muscle for any task.

The modern echo of this is the disappointing record of commercial brain-training programmes.

Large reviews, including a consensus statement by many scientists in 2014 and careful studies since, have found that practising such games mostly makes you better at those games and at very similar tasks, with little convincing evidence of far transfer to everyday intelligence or memory.

The practical lesson is that if you want to be good at something, the surest route is to practise that thing, or tasks that genuinely share its parts.


33.3.2 Analogical and metacognitive transfer

If transfer by shared surface parts is so limited, is far transfer ever possible, and if so, how?

Research points to two routes that can, under the right conditions, carry learning across genuinely different situations: analogy and metacognition.

Analogical transfer means noticing that a new problem shares its deep structure with a problem you already know how to solve, even when the two look nothing alike on the surface.

A famous study by Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak in 1980 and 1983 showed both the promise and the difficulty of this.

People who had read a story about a general capturing a fort by sending small groups of soldiers along many roads at once could, in principle, use the same idea to solve a medical puzzle about destroying a tumour with many weak rays converging from different directions.

The catch was that most people did not spot the connection on their own; they needed a hint to see that the two problems shared the same underlying trick.

This tells us far transfer is possible but fragile, because people tend to notice surface features and miss deep structure unless something helps them look.

As a mechanism, analogical transfer takes the current problem as a retrieval cue, searches memory for a structurally matching prior case, maps the old solution onto the new elements, and outputs a candidate solution; the retrieval step is the bottleneck because the cue is dominated by surface features.

Metacognitive transfer is the second route, and metacognition means thinking about your own thinking - monitoring how you learn and choosing strategies for it.

The idea is that even when specific content does not transfer, general habits of learning can, such as planning before you start, checking your own understanding, and knowing when to switch approach.

Teaching people to compare cases and to abstract the general principle for themselves, rather than handing them one worked example, tends to improve the chance that they will transfer it later.

The overall verdict is cautiously hopeful.

Far transfer does not happen automatically, but it can be encouraged by teaching for deep structure, by using several varied examples, and by building the learner's awareness of the principles behind what they are doing.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Task situations and goals, delivered as perceptual descriptions from perception and as goal states from executive control.

◦ Instructions and worked examples, held as declarative facts supplied by semantic and episodic memory.

◦ Feedback signals, that is error and reward information from the environment, a teacher, or an internal critic.

◦ A practice counter, the accumulated history of repetitions that drives the learning curve.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Executed actions and solutions, delivered to the motor system or to downstream reasoning.

◦ Compiled production rules, condition-action pairs written into procedural memory for future automatic use.

◦ Chunked pattern codes, compressed re-descriptions of familiar situations published to working memory and to recognition-based action selection.

◦ Performance statistics such as speed and error rate, consumed by metacognitive monitoring to steer further practice.

• STATE.

◦ Declarative task knowledge, the stated rules and facts of the skill.

◦ Procedural rule store, the growing set of compiled productions and their strengths.

◦ Pattern library, the accumulated chunks and templates of the domain.

◦ Current stage mixture, the proportion of performance handled by the interpretive route versus the compiled route.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Learning rate, the size of the strength update per successful repetition.

◦ Power-law exponent, the steepness of the speed-up curve, typically fitted between about 0.2 and 0.6 across tasks.

◦ Asymptotic floor, the irreducible minimum time set by perceptual and motor limits.

◦ Practice quality gain, the multiplier by which feedback-guided deliberate practice outpaces unguided repetition.

◦ Chunk capacity, the number of chunks working memory can hold at once, about four.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Production rule firing cycle: about 50 milliseconds per rule in production-system models.

◦ Expert pattern recognition: familiar configurations are recognised within roughly the first second of viewing, as in brief-exposure chess studies using about 5 second presentations.

◦ Skill compilation: hundreds to thousands of trials over days to months before a component runs automatically.

◦ Elite expertise horizon: on the order of 10 years or roughly ten thousand hours of sustained practice in demanding domains, stated as an average and not a threshold.

◦ Single-trial speed-up magnitude: REFUSED, because the gain per trial depends on the task, the learner, and the disputed power versus exponential form, so no honest general number exists.

• MODES.

◦ Cognitive mode, interpretive step-by-step control from declarative instructions; entered whenever the task is novel or the compiled rules fail.

◦ Associative mode, mixed control while rules are being compiled and tuned; entered as repetitions accumulate and errors shrink.

◦ Autonomous mode, recognition-driven automatic execution; entered when compiled rules cover the task, and exited back toward deliberate control when errors, novelty, or deliberate self-monitoring intervene.

◦ Deliberate practice mode, a training regime in which an error signal selects drills at the edge of competence; switched on by a coach or by metacognitive intent, as opposed to plain performance mode.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Choking under pressure, where attending consciously to an automated skill disrupts it.

◦ Arrested development, where performance plateaus because practice continues without an error signal.

◦ Negative transfer, where old compiled habits fire in a new task that looks similar but demands different responses.

◦ Overconfident far transfer, the mistaken expectation that training one task will improve unrelated abilities, as in brain-training claims.

◦ Loss of verbal access, where the expert can no longer explain or teach what the compiled skill does.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called floor with initial value 0.4.
Create a number variable called learnable with initial value 1.6.
Create a number variable called exponent with initial value 0.5.
Create an empty list called times.
For each trial number from 1 to 1000, do the following.
    Calculate the learnable component as learnable multiplied by the trial number raised to the power of negative exponent.
    Calculate the predicted time as floor plus the learnable component.
    Draw a random noise value from a normal distribution with mean 1 and standard deviation 0.05.
    Calculate the observed time as the predicted time multiplied by the noise value.
    Append the observed time to the list called times.
Calculate the early gain as the first element of times minus the tenth element of times.
Calculate the late gain as the hundredth element of times minus the thousandth element of times.
Report the times at trials 1, 10, 100, and 1000, the early gain, and the late gain.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Load the random module for noise generation.
import random

# Create a number variable called floor with initial value 0.4, the seconds no practice can remove.
floor = 0.4
# Create a number variable called learnable with initial value 1.6, the seconds practice can remove.
learnable = 1.6
# Create a number variable called exponent with initial value 0.5, the power-law learning rate.
exponent = 0.5

# Seed the random number generator so the run is repeatable.
random.seed(33)

# Create an empty list called times to hold one observed time per trial.
times = []

# For each trial number from 1 to 1000, do the following.
for trial in range(1, 1001):
    # Calculate the learnable component as learnable times the trial number raised to negative exponent.
    component = learnable * trial ** (-exponent)
    # Calculate the predicted time as floor plus the learnable component.
    predicted = floor + component
    # Draw a random noise value from a normal distribution with mean 1 and standard deviation 0.05.
    noise = random.gauss(1.0, 0.05)
    # Calculate the observed time as the predicted time multiplied by the noise value.
    observed = predicted * noise
    # Append the observed time to the list called times.
    times.append(observed)

# Report the observed time at four milestone trials.
for milestone in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    # Print the milestone trial number and its observed time in seconds.
    print("trial", milestone, "time", round(times[milestone - 1], 3), "seconds")

# Calculate the early gain as the time at trial 1 minus the time at trial 10.
early_gain = times[0] - times[9]
# Calculate the late gain as the time at trial 100 minus the time at trial 1000.
late_gain = times[99] - times[999]
# Print the early gain, nine trials of practice at the start of learning.
print("gain from 9 early trials", round(early_gain, 3), "seconds")
# Print the late gain, nine hundred trials of practice late in learning.
print("gain from 900 late trials", round(late_gain, 3), "seconds")

PART EIGHT. THINKING: REASONING, JUDGMENT, AND DECISION

================================================================================

CHAPTER 34. DEDUCTIVE AND INDUCTIVE REASONING (PROCESS)

This chapter is about reasoning, which means drawing conclusions from what you already know or observe.

Psychologists study two great families of reasoning.

Deduction moves from general rules to certain conclusions, as in a mathematical proof, while induction moves from specific observations to likely but uncertain conclusions, as when you guess a general pattern from a few examples.

The surprising and important theme running through the chapter is that ordinary human reasoning often departs from the rules of formal logic, and the deep question is whether that makes us irrational or whether logic was simply the wrong yardstick.

Viewed as a system, the reasoner takes premises and observations as input, holds candidate possibilities in a limited working memory, and outputs conclusions with confidence levels, and its characteristic errors reveal the machinery inside.

The tag (PROCESS) marks this as a description of a genuine human capacity a model of the mind must reproduce.


34.1 Deductive reasoning

Deductive reasoning is reasoning where the conclusion follows with certainty from the premises, the starting statements you take as given.

If the premises are true and the reasoning is valid, the conclusion simply must be true - that is the special power of deduction.

This section looks at how well ordinary people actually handle such reasoning, and the results are humbling.


34.1.1 Conditional reasoning and the selection task

Conditional reasoning is reasoning about if-then statements, such as if it rains, then the ground is wet.

These statements are the backbone of logic and of everyday planning, so how well we handle them matters a great deal.

The most famous test of it was invented by Peter Wason in 1966 and 1968 and is called the selection task.

In the classic version you see four cards, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other, showing for example A, K, 4, and 7.

You are told a rule - if a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other - and asked which cards you must turn over to check whether the rule holds.

The logically correct answer is to turn the A and the 7, because only these can possibly break the rule.

You check the vowel to see if it hides an odd number, and you check the odd number to see if it hides a vowel.

Yet most people, typically only around ten percent get it right, choose the A alone or the A and the 4.

They correctly look for confirming cases but fail to look for the case that could prove the rule false, which is the 7.

In systems terms the task exposes the test-selection policy of the reasoner: the input is a rule and a set of partially hidden cases, the required output is the subset of cases that could falsify the rule, and the observed output is instead the subset of cases that match the terms named in the rule.

This is a striking result because the logic is simple, and it suggests that people do not reason by pure formal logic, and that they have a bias toward seeking confirmation rather than disproof.


34.1.2 Content effects and pragmatic reasoning schemas

The selection task took an even more interesting turn when researchers changed not the logic of the puzzle but its content, the everyday subject matter it was dressed in.

The abstract letters-and-numbers version is very hard, but a version with the same logical form set in a familiar real-world situation can suddenly become easy.

In a well-known example, people are told a rule such as if a person is drinking alcohol, then they must be over eighteen, and are shown cards representing drinkers of various ages and drinks.

Now most people correctly choose to check the person drinking alcohol and the person who is underage, which is exactly the logically right pattern they missed with letters and numbers.

This is called a content effect, meaning that the subject matter of a problem, not just its logical skeleton, changes how well people reason about it.

Patricia Cheng and Keith Holyoak offered an influential explanation in 1985 called pragmatic reasoning schemas.

A schema here means a package of general rules that the mind has abstracted from recurring real-life situations, such as situations of permission and obligation.

The drinking rule fits a permission schema - you may do this only if you meet that condition - and people reason well because they are using practical social know-how, not abstract logic.

There is a rival explanation worth noting, from Leda Cosmides and John Tooby, who argued that we have a specialised mental ability for detecting cheaters in social exchanges, sharpened by evolution.

In systems terms the two accounts predict differently: the schema view predicts good performance whenever any familiar permission or obligation structure is recognised, while the cheater-detection view predicts the boost specifically when the content involves a social exchange where someone could take a benefit without paying the cost.

Experts still debate which account is right, but they agree on the core fact: human reasoning is powerfully shaped by the familiar meaning of a problem, not by its bare logical form alone.


34.1.3 Syllogisms and belief bias

A syllogism is a classic form of logical argument with two premises and a conclusion, for example: all birds can fly; a robin is a bird; therefore a robin can fly.

Syllogisms let researchers test whether people can tell a valid argument, where the conclusion truly follows, from an invalid one, where it does not, regardless of whether the statements happen to be true.

Here a revealing error appears, called belief bias.

Belief bias is the tendency to judge an argument by whether its conclusion is believable rather than by whether it is logically valid.

People tend to accept a conclusion that sounds true even when the argument is invalid, and to reject a conclusion that sounds false even when the argument is perfectly valid.

For example, given a valid argument leading to an unbelievable conclusion, many people wrongly call it invalid, because the conclusion clashes with what they know of the world.

The effect is strongest, researchers have found, on invalid arguments with believable conclusions, where belief and logic pull in opposite directions and belief often wins.

In systems terms belief bias is a signal from a fast plausibility checker leaking into the output of a slow validity checker: the plausibility channel evaluates only the conclusion against world knowledge, the validity channel evaluates the whole argument structure, and under time pressure or load the plausibility channel dominates the shared output.

Belief bias shows again that people do not reason as pure logicians.

Instead, prior knowledge and the felt plausibility of a conclusion intrude on the judgment, which is efficient in daily life but can lead us to endorse bad arguments that reach comfortable conclusions.


34.2 The theories of deduction

Given that people reason imperfectly, psychologists want to know what mental machinery they actually use.

Two big theories have competed for decades, and a third, probabilistic view has more recently reframed the whole question.

This section lays out that contest.


34.2.1 Mental logic against mental models

The first theory is called mental logic.

It holds that the mind contains something like a built-in set of logical rules, and that we reason by applying these rules step by step to the statements we are given, rather as a mathematician applies rules of proof.

On this view, errors happen because some rules are missing, or because long chains of steps overload us, not because we lack logic in principle.

The rival theory, developed principally by Philip Johnson-Laird from the 1980s onward, is called mental models.

It holds that we do not manipulate logical rules at all; instead we imagine concrete possible situations - little mental pictures of how the world could be - and read our conclusions off these imagined situations.

For example, to reason about a statement you build a model of a world in which it is true, and check whether the conclusion holds there.

A key prediction of the mental models theory is that problems requiring you to juggle several possible situations at once should be harder, because holding many models strains our limited working memory, the small mental workspace where we keep information active.

This prediction is broadly supported: arguments that force people to consider multiple possibilities do produce more errors, which is a point in favour of mental models.

The systems contrast is sharp: mental logic predicts difficulty proportional to the number and length of rule applications, while mental models predicts difficulty proportional to the number of possibilities that must be held simultaneously, a load bounded by a working memory span of about four chunks.

The debate has never been settled outright, but the mental models approach became the more influential of the two, partly because it neatly explains why certain problems are hard and why people so often consider too few possibilities.


34.2.2 The probabilistic reinterpretation of reasoning

A more recent movement argues that the whole tradition may have been judging people against the wrong standard.

Classical logic treats statements as simply true or false and demands certainty, but everyday life is full of uncertainty, and everyday if-then statements usually express likelihood rather than guarantee.

When you say if you water the plant, it will grow, you mean it will probably grow, not that growth is logically guaranteed.

The probabilistic approach, associated with Mike Oaksford and Nick Chater and their 2007 book, proposes that people treat reasoning problems as matters of probability and useful information, not strict logic.

On this view, behaviour that logicians called errors can look sensible once you assume people are reasoning about what is probable and informative in a normal, uncertain world.

Their bold reanalysis of the Wason selection task argued that the card choices most people make are actually a reasonable strategy for gathering the most useful information, given ordinary assumptions about how rare things are.

In systems terms this swaps the reference standard against which the reasoner is scored: the logical standard scores outputs by falsification coverage, while the probabilistic standard scores them by expected information gain under realistic rarity assumptions, and the same observed behaviour ranks poorly on the first and well on the second.

Not everyone accepts this reinterpretation, and it remains debated.

But it marks an important shift in the field, from asking why people are bad at logic to asking whether people are instead pretty good at reasoning under uncertainty, which is the problem real life actually poses.


34.3 Inductive reasoning

Inductive reasoning moves from specific cases to general or uncertain conclusions.

When you see several white swans and conclude that swans are white, or meet a friendly dog and expect the next dog to be friendly, you are reasoning inductively.

Induction can never give certainty - the next swan might be black - but it is how we learn about the world and predict what we have not yet seen, so it is arguably even more important than deduction.

This section covers how people generalise, how they test their ideas, and how mathematics has been used to model good induction.


34.3.1 Category-based induction

Category-based induction is reasoning about which properties spread from one category of things to another.

If you learn that robins have some new property, say a certain enzyme in their blood, how confident are you that sparrows have it, or that ostriches do, or that all birds do?

Douglas Medin, Edward Smith, Daniel Osherson and colleagues studied this carefully around 1990 and found orderly patterns in how people make such leaps.

One pattern is similarity: people project a property more readily to things similar to the original case, so learning it about robins makes you more confident about sparrows than about ostriches.

Another pattern is diversity: an argument feels stronger when the known cases are varied, so finding the property in both robins and ostriches makes people more willing to believe all birds have it than finding it in two similar birds.

This diversity effect is interesting because it matches good scientific practice, where varied evidence is genuinely more convincing than repetitive evidence.

A further pattern involves the breadth of the conclusion category, and how typical the examples are of it.

In systems terms the inductive engine takes premise categories and a candidate conclusion category as input, computes similarity and coverage over a structured category space held in semantic memory, and outputs a graded argument strength within a second or two of reading the argument.

These findings show that human induction is not random guessing; it follows sensible principles, weighing similarity, variety, and typicality, even though people cannot state the principles they are using.


34.3.2 Hypothesis testing and confirmation bias

When people form an idea about how the world works, how do they check it?

Ideally, good testing means actively trying to prove your idea wrong, because a hypothesis that survives serious attempts to break it has really earned your confidence.

In practice, people show a strong tendency to do the opposite, called confirmation bias.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek, notice, and remember evidence that fits what you already believe, while overlooking or dismissing evidence that would count against it.

Wason demonstrated this in 1960 with a task in which people had to discover a hidden rule behind a sequence of three numbers, such as two, four, six.

Most people guessed a rule like even numbers increasing by two and then only tested examples that fit their guess, which kept confirming it, when the real rule was simply any three increasing numbers.

Because they never tried sequences that would break their pet hypothesis, they clung to a wrong rule while feeling sure they were right.

As a mechanism, the tester holds a current favourite hypothesis as state, generates probe queries as output, and updates on the world's yes-or-no answers as input; the bias is a skewed query generator that samples almost entirely from the region where the favourite hypothesis predicts a yes.

Confirmation bias matters far beyond the laboratory.

It helps explain why people cling to first impressions, why superstitions persist, and why opposing groups can look at the same evidence and each come away more certain they were right.

Understanding it also points to a remedy: deliberately asking what would prove me wrong is one of the most powerful thinking habits a person can build.


34.3.3 Bayesian models of induction

Mathematicians and psychologists have developed a precise framework for how a rational mind ought to reason from evidence, named after the eighteenth century clergyman and mathematician Thomas Bayes.

Bayesian reasoning, in plain terms, is a recipe for updating your beliefs by combining what you already thought with what new evidence tells you.

It has three ingredients: a prior, which is your degree of belief before the evidence; the evidence itself and how likely it would be under different hypotheses; and the posterior, which is your updated belief after taking the evidence into account.

The rule says, sensibly, that strong prior beliefs should shift only under strong evidence, and that a hypothesis under which the observed evidence would be very likely gains support.

Researchers such as Joshua Tenenbaum and Thomas Griffiths, from around 2000 onward, showed that Bayesian models can capture human induction strikingly well in many settings.

For instance, when people are shown a few examples of a concept and asked how far it extends, their guesses often track what a good Bayesian calculation would recommend, balancing how specific the examples are against how common such things are.

A key attraction of the Bayesian approach is that it explains where good priors come from and how learning at one level can guide learning at another, sometimes called learning to learn.

In systems terms a Bayesian inductive module subscribes to a hypothesis space with priors and to incoming evidence, holds a posterior distribution as its state, and publishes graded predictions; the open question is whether the brain implements the full update or a cheap approximation such as sampling a few hypotheses.

It is important to be balanced here.

Bayesian models describe how an ideal reasoner should combine evidence and often match human behaviour, but there is genuine debate over whether the mind literally carries out such calculations or merely approximates them with simpler shortcuts.

Either way, the Bayesian framework has become one of the most powerful tools we have for saying precisely what good inductive reasoning would look like, and for measuring how close people come to it.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Premises and rules, structured statements delivered by language comprehension.

◦ Observed cases and evidence, category examples and outcomes delivered by perception and memory retrieval.

◦ World knowledge and priors, plausibility signals supplied by semantic memory.

◦ Task framing, the stated goal of the reasoning episode, whether to test validity, discover a rule, or estimate likelihood.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Conclusions with validity or strength judgments, consumed by decision making and language production.

◦ Test selections, the chosen probes or cards or experiments, consumed by action systems.

◦ Updated beliefs, revised degrees of confidence written back to memory.

◦ A felt confidence signal, consumed by metacognitive monitoring.

• STATE.

◦ The current set of mental models, the possibilities being held and inspected in working memory.

◦ The current favourite hypothesis in a discovery task.

◦ The running posterior, the graded belief distribution over hypotheses.

◦ The premise text itself, held verbatim long enough to be re-inspected.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Working memory model capacity, the number of possibilities that can be held at once, about four chunks.

◦ Belief bias weight, the gain on the plausibility channel relative to the validity channel.

◦ Prior strength, how heavily existing belief resists new evidence.

◦ Confirmation sampling ratio, the fraction of tests drawn from the expected-yes region.

◦ Similarity and coverage weights in category-based induction.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Simple conditional inference: verified in roughly 1 to 3 seconds for easy one-model arguments in reaction-time studies.

◦ Multi-model syllogism evaluation: slower by seconds as the number of required models rises, with reliably longer latencies and more errors for multiple-model problems.

◦ Belief bias intrusion: present even at fast deadlines and reduced when several extra seconds of evaluation time are allowed.

◦ Exact latency per additional mental model: REFUSED, because the per-model cost varies widely with materials and individuals and no single supported value exists.

• MODES.

◦ Model-inspection mode, building and reading off one possibility at a time; the default for deduction.

◦ Search-for-counterexample mode, deliberately constructing alternative models to break a tentative conclusion; triggered by instruction, high stakes, or metacognitive doubt.

◦ Heuristic plausibility mode, accepting or rejecting by believability alone; triggered by time pressure, load, or low motivation.

◦ Probabilistic mode, treating premises as uncertain and reasoning about likelihoods; triggered when content signals an uncertain everyday domain rather than a formal puzzle.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Confirmation bias, testing only where the favourite hypothesis predicts success.

◦ Belief bias, endorsing invalid arguments with believable conclusions and rejecting valid ones with unbelievable conclusions.

◦ Matching bias in the selection task, choosing the cards named in the rule instead of the cards that could falsify it.

◦ Model shortfall, considering too few possibilities and so missing counterexamples.

◦ Base-rate neglect in induction, projecting from resemblance while ignoring how common categories are.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list called cards containing the visible faces A, K, 4, and 7.
Create an empty list called logical_choice.
For each card in the list called cards, do the following.
    If the visible face is a vowel, then the hidden face could be an odd number, so the card can falsify the rule; append it to logical_choice.
    Otherwise, if the visible face is an odd number, then the hidden face could be a vowel, so the card can falsify the rule; append it to logical_choice.
    Otherwise, the card cannot falsify the rule, so do not append it.
Create an empty list called matching_choice.
For each card in the list called cards, do the following.
    If the visible face is a vowel or an even number, meaning it matches a term named in the rule, then append the card to matching_choice.
Report the logical choice and the matching choice.
For each card in the list called cards, test every possible hidden face and report whether any hidden face would make the card break the rule.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Define a function that reports whether a character is a vowel.
def is_vowel(face):
    # Return whether the face is one of the vowel letters.
    return face in "AEIOU"

# Define a function that reports whether a character is an odd digit.
def is_odd(face):
    # Return whether the face is a digit and that digit is odd.
    return face.isdigit() and int(face) % 2 == 1

# Define a function that reports whether a character is an even digit.
def is_even(face):
    # Return whether the face is a digit and that digit is even.
    return face.isdigit() and int(face) % 2 == 0

# Create a list called cards containing the four visible faces.
cards = ["A", "K", "4", "7"]

# Create the logical choice as the cards whose hidden side could break the rule.
# A vowel could hide an odd number, and an odd number could hide a vowel.
logical_choice = [c for c in cards if is_vowel(c) or is_odd(c)]

# Create the matching choice as the cards that match a term named in the rule.
# The rule names vowels and even numbers, so those faces attract attention.
matching_choice = [c for c in cards if is_vowel(c) or is_even(c)]

# Print the logically correct selection.
print("logical reasoner turns:", logical_choice)
# Print the typical human selection driven by matching bias.
print("matching reasoner turns:", matching_choice)

# For each card, test every possible hidden face for a rule violation.
for card in cards:
    # Assume at first that no hidden face can make this card break the rule.
    can_falsify = False
    # For each possible hidden face among letters and digits, do the following.
    for hidden in "AEIOUKXZ0123456789":
        # Determine the letter side and the number side of this card and hidden face pair.
        letter = card if card.isalpha() else hidden
        # Determine the number side as whichever face is a digit.
        number = card if card.isdigit() else hidden
        # If the pair is a real letter and number pair with a vowel and an odd number, it breaks the rule.
        if letter.isalpha() and number.isdigit() and is_vowel(letter) and is_odd(number):
            # Record that this card can falsify the rule.
            can_falsify = True
    # Print whether turning this card could ever reveal a violation.
    print("card", card, "can reveal a violation:", can_falsify)


CHAPTER 35. ANALOGICAL AND CAUSAL REASONING (PROCESS)

This chapter is about two of the most powerful forms of human thinking: reasoning by analogy, and reasoning about cause and effect.

Analogy is seeing that one situation is like another and carrying understanding across, which is at the heart of insight, invention, and everyday explanation.

Causal reasoning is working out what makes what happen, which is what lets us predict, control, and intervene in the world rather than just watch it.

Both abilities are things humans do far better than any other animal and, until recently, far better than machines, so they sit close to the core of what makes human cognition special.

In systems terms, the analogy engine is a structure aligner that maps relations between two situations, and the causal engine is a graph learner that infers arrows of influence from patterns of observation and action.

The tag (PROCESS) marks these as real capacities a model of the mind must reproduce.


35.1 Analogical reasoning

Analogical reasoning is understanding something new by comparing it to something you already know.

When a teacher explains electricity as water flowing through pipes, or a scientist pictures the atom as a tiny solar system, they are using analogy to carry structure from a familiar case to an unfamiliar one.

This section explains the leading theory of how analogy works and the practical business of retrieving and using analogies.


35.1.1 Structure-mapping theory

The most influential account of analogy is structure-mapping theory, developed by Dedre Gentner starting in 1983.

Its central claim is that a good analogy is not about surface similarity but about shared relational structure - the pattern of relationships among the parts, rather than the parts themselves.

Consider the analogy between the solar system and the atom.

The planets and the sun do not look at all like electrons and a nucleus; what carries over is the relationship, namely that lighter things revolve around a heavier central thing that attracts them.

Structure-mapping says the mind lines up the two situations so that the system of relations in the familiar case maps onto the new case, and it prefers deep, connected systems of relations over isolated shared features.

Gentner called this preference the systematicity principle: we favour analogies that carry over an interconnected web of relations, because these support rich further inferences.

This is why a good analogy is so useful; once you map the structure, you can make new predictions about the unfamiliar case by reading them off the familiar one.

As a mechanism, the mapper takes two relational descriptions as input, searches for a consistent one-to-one alignment of their objects that preserves relations, scores candidate alignments by systematicity, and outputs both the best mapping and the candidate inferences it licenses.

The theory was made concrete as a working computer program, the Structure-Mapping Engine, built by Gentner with Brian Falkenhainer and Kenneth Forbus in the late 1980s, which is one of the most cited models of analogy ever made.

Its lasting contribution is the clear idea that analogy is fundamentally about aligning relationships, not matching appearances.


35.1.2 Analogical retrieval, transfer, and schema induction

Having a theory of how analogies are mapped raises a practical worry: to use an analogy, you first have to think of it, and this turns out to be the hard part.

Analogical retrieval is the process of calling to mind a relevant past case when you meet a new problem.

The uncomfortable finding, seen in the fortress-and-tumour studies of Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak in the early 1980s, is that people are much better at mapping an analogy once it is pointed out than at retrieving it on their own.

Worse, retrieval tends to be driven by surface similarity - people are reminded of past cases that look alike - even though useful analogies depend on deep structure that surface looks can hide.

This mismatch is important: the very thing that makes an analogy powerful, its deep shared structure, is not the thing that reliably brings it to mind.

In systems terms retrieval and mapping are two stages with different indexes: the retrieval stage queries long-term memory with a cue dominated by surface features and returns candidates in a second or two, while the mapping stage aligns relational structure over several seconds of deliberate comparison, so the pipeline fails most often at its first stage.

Analogical transfer is then the payoff, using the retrieved case to solve the new problem, and it succeeds only when the mapping is sound and the deep structure truly matches.

Schema induction is the happy long-term result of comparing analogous cases.

When you line up two examples that share a deep structure and notice what they have in common, you can abstract a general schema - a stripped-down mental template of the shared pattern that no longer depends on either specific case.

Gick and Holyoak showed that people who compared two analogous stories, rather than reading just one, were far more likely to abstract the common principle and apply it to a new problem.

This gives a concrete teaching lesson: comparing several examples helps people extract the underlying idea, which then transfers more readily than any single example would.


35.2 Causal reasoning and learning

Causal reasoning is figuring out what causes what.

It is one of the mind's most vital jobs, because knowing that A causes B lets you predict B, produce B by bringing about A, or prevent B by blocking A - powers that mere correlation cannot give you.

This section covers how the mind might represent causal structure and how it learns causes from experience.


35.2.1 Causal graphical models

In recent decades, philosophers, computer scientists, and psychologists have adopted a common mathematical language for describing causal knowledge, called causal graphical models, also known as causal Bayes nets.

The idea is to picture the world as a diagram of nodes and arrows, where each node stands for a variable, such as smoking or lung disease, and each arrow points from a cause to its effect.

This simple picture is powerful because it captures not just that things go together but which way the influence flows, and it can represent chains, common causes, and common effects.

A crucial strength of these models is that they distinguish merely watching from actively intervening.

If you only observe that yellowed fingers and lung disease go together, you might wrongly treat one as a cause of the other, when in fact both are effects of a common cause, smoking.

The graphical framework handles this by representing what happens when you reach in and set a variable yourself, which cuts the ordinary incoming arrows and reveals the true causal structure.

In systems terms the causal model is a stored graph data structure: queries about prediction read the graph forwards along the arrows, queries about explanation read it backwards, and queries about intervention first surgically delete the arrows into the manipulated node and then read forwards.

Researchers such as Alison Gopnik, Clark Glymour, and colleagues proposed around 2004 that both children and adults represent causal knowledge in something like this form, and learn it in broadly the way the mathematics prescribes.

The framework has been influential because it gives a precise, testable account of causal thinking and links human reasoning to the same tools now used in statistics and artificial intelligence.


35.2.2 Covariation, mechanism, and intervention

Where does causal knowledge come from in the first place?

Research points to three complementary sources of evidence the mind uses: covariation, mechanism, and intervention.

Covariation means noticing that things vary together - the cause tends to be present when the effect is, and absent when it is not.

This is a natural starting point, and much early psychology, including the work of Harold Kelley in the 1960s and 1970s, treated causal learning as essentially the tracking of such patterns of co-occurrence.

But covariation alone is famously not enough, captured in the maxim that correlation does not imply causation; two things can move together because one causes the other, or because a third thing causes both, or by sheer coincidence.

Mechanism means understanding the hidden process that connects a cause to its effect - not just that flipping the switch turns on the light, but the wiring and current in between.

People lean heavily on mechanism knowledge; we are much more willing to believe a causal claim when we can imagine a plausible process linking the two events.

Intervention means learning by doing rather than merely watching - deliberately changing something and seeing what follows.

Intervention is the most powerful source of causal evidence, because acting on the world yourself rules out the possibility that some hidden third factor is secretly producing the pattern, which is exactly why controlled experiments are the gold standard of science.

As inputs to the causal learner, the three sources differ in cost and quality: covariation arrives free with passive observation over many episodes, mechanism knowledge arrives from stored domain theories, and intervention requires spending an action but returns the least ambiguous evidence per trial.

Even young children learn causes better when they can poke and act on a toy than when they only observe it, showing that this preference for intervention runs deep.


35.2.3 Causal power and the estimation of strength

Beyond learning whether A causes B, people also judge how strongly A causes B, and this turns out to need more than counting co-occurrences.

Patricia Cheng proposed an influential account in 1997 called the power PC theory, where PC stands for probabilistic contrast.

The core problem it solves is this: simply comparing how often the effect occurs with and without the candidate cause can be misleading, because other background causes may already be producing the effect much of the time.

If a garden is already well watered by rain, adding a sprinkler will seem to have little power, not because the sprinkler is weak but because there is little room left for it to make a difference.

Cheng's theory offers a way to estimate a cause's underlying power, meaning its capacity to produce or prevent the effect on its own, by correcting for what the background causes are already doing.

The theory distinguishes generative causes, which bring the effect about, from preventive causes, which stop it, and gives a formula for each.

In systems terms the strength estimator takes two frequencies as input, the effect rate with the candidate cause present and the rate with it absent, and outputs a power estimate by dividing the raw contrast by the headroom the background leaves for a generative cause to act.

The power PC theory has been influential and fits many findings, but it is not the only contender, and it competes with pure covariation accounts and with Bayesian causal models over which best describes human strength judgments.

The debate is unsettled, and the honest summary is that people clearly go beyond raw co-occurrence when judging causal strength, taking account of the background, though researchers still argue about the exact rule they use.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ A target situation description, a set of objects and relations delivered by comprehension and perception.

◦ Stored base cases, relational descriptions of past situations retrieved from long-term memory.

◦ Covariation statistics, event co-occurrence counts accumulated by observation.

◦ Action outcomes, the results of the reasoner's own interventions.

◦ Domain mechanism knowledge, stored theories of processes that could link causes to effects.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ An object-to-object mapping between base and target, consumed by problem solving.

◦ Candidate inferences, predictions carried from the base into the target, consumed by reasoning and imagination.

◦ Induced schemas, abstracted relational templates written into long-term memory.

◦ A causal graph with strength estimates on its arrows, consumed by prediction, planning, and intervention choice.

• STATE.

◦ The current alignment under construction, the partial mapping held in working memory.

◦ The library of relational cases and schemas in long-term memory.

◦ The running causal graph hypothesis and its co-occurrence tallies.

◦ Confidence in each arrow, updated as observations and interventions arrive.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Systematicity weight, the preference for deep interconnected relation systems over isolated matches.

◦ Surface similarity weight in retrieval, the gain on appearance features when memory is queried.

◦ One-to-one constraint strictness, how firmly each base object may map to only one target object.

◦ Background rate estimate, the assumed effect rate from unobserved causes in power judgments.

◦ Intervention preference, the willingness to spend actions to disambiguate structure.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Analogical reminding: candidate cases surface from memory within about 1 to 2 seconds of reading a cue in reminding studies.

◦ Deliberate mapping and comparison: seconds to tens of seconds of controlled alignment work.

◦ Schema induction: emerges across a study session when at least two cases are explicitly compared.

◦ Causal impression from covariation: builds over tens of trials in contingency learning experiments.

◦ Exact time to compute one structure mapping in the head: REFUSED, because mapping latency depends on the size of the relational descriptions and no single supported human value exists.

• MODES.

◦ Retrieval mode, cue-driven search of memory for candidate analogues; triggered automatically by encountering a new problem.

◦ Mapping mode, deliberate structural alignment of a chosen base with the target; triggered by a retrieved or supplied candidate.

◦ Observational causal learning mode, passive accumulation of covariation; the default when action is unavailable.

◦ Interventional mode, active experimentation that cuts incoming arrows; triggered when the reasoner can act and structure is ambiguous.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Retrieval failure, missing a useful analogy because its surface differs from the current problem.

◦ Surface capture, mapping to a case that looks alike but shares no deep structure, yielding false inferences.

◦ Correlation-to-cause error, reading a common-cause pattern as a direct causal link.

◦ Illusory causation, inferring an arrow from coincidence or from a vivid imagined mechanism.

◦ Discounting error, underestimating a real cause because background causes already saturate the effect.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list called base_relations containing relation triples for the solar system, each triple naming a relation, a first object, and a second object.
Create a list called target_relations containing relation triples for the atom.
Create a list called base_objects containing the distinct objects in the base.
Create a list called target_objects containing the distinct objects in the target.
Create a variable called best_score with initial value negative one.
Create a variable called best_mapping with initial value empty.
For each possible one-to-one mapping from base objects to target objects, do the following.
    Set a number variable called score to zero.
    For each triple in base_relations, do the following.
        Translate the triple's objects through the mapping to make a predicted target triple.
        If the predicted target triple is present in target_relations, then add one to score.
    If score is greater than best_score, then set best_score to score and set best_mapping to the current mapping.
Report the best mapping and its score.
For each base relation whose translated triple is absent from the target, report it as a candidate inference about the target.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Load the permutations function to enumerate one-to-one mappings.
from itertools import permutations

# Create the base relations describing the solar system as relation triples.
base_relations = [("attracts", "sun", "planet"),
                  ("revolves_around", "planet", "sun"),
                  ("more_massive_than", "sun", "planet"),
                  ("hotter_than", "sun", "planet")]

# Create the target relations describing the atom as relation triples.
target_relations = [("attracts", "nucleus", "electron"),
                    ("revolves_around", "electron", "nucleus"),
                    ("more_massive_than", "nucleus", "electron")]

# Create the list of distinct base objects.
base_objects = ["sun", "planet"]
# Create the list of distinct target objects.
target_objects = ["nucleus", "electron"]

# Create a variable called best_score with initial value negative one.
best_score = -1
# Create a variable called best_mapping with initial value empty.
best_mapping = None

# For each one-to-one assignment of target objects to base objects, do the following.
for perm in permutations(target_objects):
    # Build the mapping dictionary from base objects to this permutation of target objects.
    mapping = dict(zip(base_objects, perm))
    # Set the structural consistency score to zero for this mapping.
    score = 0
    # For each relation triple in the base, do the following.
    for relation, a, b in base_relations:
        # Translate the triple's objects through the mapping to predict a target triple.
        predicted = (relation, mapping[a], mapping[b])
        # If the predicted triple is present in the target, add one to the score.
        if predicted in target_relations:
            # Add one matched relation to the score.
            score = score + 1
    # If this mapping scores higher than the best so far, remember it.
    if score > best_score:
        # Record the new best score.
        best_score = score
        # Record the new best mapping.
        best_mapping = mapping

# Print the best object mapping and its relational match score.
print("best mapping:", best_mapping, "matched relations:", best_score)

# For each base relation whose translation is absent from the target, propose an inference.
for relation, a, b in base_relations:
    # Translate the triple through the best mapping.
    predicted = (relation, best_mapping[a], best_mapping[b])
    # If the predicted triple is not already known in the target, report it as a candidate inference.
    if predicted not in target_relations:
        # Print the carried-over prediction about the target domain.
        print("candidate inference:", predicted)


CHAPTER 36. JUDGMENT UNDER UNCERTAINTY: HEURISTICS AND BIASES (PROCESS)

This chapter is about how people make judgments when they do not and cannot know for sure - estimating probabilities, guessing quantities, and predicting outcomes.

Its central discovery, from the work of Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman beginning around 1970, is that people rely on a small set of mental shortcuts, called heuristics, which are usually helpful but which lead to predictable, systematic errors, called biases.

This work reshaped psychology and economics and earned Kahneman the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, after Tversky had died in 1996 and so could not share it.

In systems terms, the judgment system answers hard probability queries by substituting cheap proxy computations, such as similarity or ease of recall, and the biases are the signature distortions each proxy introduces.

The tag (PROCESS) marks this as a real feature of human cognition that any faithful model of the mind must capture.


36.1 The heuristics

A heuristic is a rule of thumb - a quick, intuitive shortcut for making a judgment without laborious calculation.

Heuristics are not stupidity; they are efficient tools that usually serve us well and let us act fast in a complicated world.

The catch is that each shortcut has a characteristic way of going wrong, and this section describes the three most famous heuristics and the errors they produce.


36.1.1 Representativeness and its fallacies

The representativeness heuristic is judging how likely something is by how much it resembles a typical example or stereotype of its kind.

If a description sounds like a librarian, you judge the person likely to be a librarian, based on the match to your mental image, while ignoring how many librarians there actually are.

In systems terms the heuristic answers the probability query by routing it to a similarity computation: the input is a description and a category prototype, the output is a resemblance score returned within a second, and the base rate input is simply never read.

This shortcut causes several distinctive errors.

One is neglect of base rates, where people ignore how common something is in the first place.

If there are far more farmers than librarians, a quiet, bookish person is still probably a farmer simply because farmers are so much more numerous, but representativeness tempts people to overlook this.

A second and striking error is the conjunction fallacy, revealed by the famous Linda problem.

People read a description of Linda as a bright, outspoken woman deeply concerned with social justice, then judge it more probable that Linda is a bank teller and a feminist than that she is simply a bank teller.

This cannot be true, because a combination of two things can never be more probable than one of them alone - every feminist bank teller is a bank teller.

About eighty-five percent of people made this error in the original study, because the fuller description resembles their image of Linda even though, by the iron rules of probability, adding a condition can only make something less likely, never more.

A third error is insensitivity to sample size, where people forget that small samples are far more prone to extreme results than large ones.

Together these fallacies show that people often substitute the easy question how similar is this for the hard question how probable is this, which is efficient but can be badly wrong.


36.1.2 Availability

The availability heuristic is judging how likely or how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.

If instances spring readily to memory, you judge the thing frequent; if they are hard to recall, you judge it rare.

This often works, because common things genuinely are easier to remember, but it misleads whenever ease of recall is driven by something other than true frequency.

In systems terms availability substitutes a memory retrieval fluency signal for a frequency count: the input is a category cue, the proxy output is how quickly and plentifully examples arrive within the first second or two of search, and any factor that boosts retrieval, such as vividness, recency, or media exposure, contaminates the estimate.

Vivid, dramatic, or recent events are especially easy to recall, so we overestimate their likelihood.

A classic example is that many people fear dying in a plane crash or a shark attack more than in a car crash or from heart disease, even though the ordinary risks are vastly greater, because the dramatic events get heavy news coverage and stick in memory.

Tversky and Kahneman showed the effect cleanly by asking whether English has more words beginning with the letter K or more words with K in the third position.

Most people say more words begin with K, because such words are easier to bring to mind, when in fact there are more words with K in third position - our search strategy, not the real frequency, drove the answer.

Availability helps explain distorted risk perception, the influence of the media on public fear, and why a single memorable anecdote can outweigh reams of statistics in people's minds.


36.1.3 Anchoring and adjustment

Anchoring and adjustment is a shortcut for estimating an unknown quantity: you start from some initial number, the anchor, and then adjust up or down from it.

The catch is that the adjustment is usually too small, so the final estimate stays pulled toward the starting number, even when that number is arbitrary and irrelevant.

Tversky and Kahneman demonstrated this dramatically by spinning a wheel of fortune that landed on a random number and then asking people to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations.

People who saw a high spin gave much higher estimates than those who saw a low spin, even though everyone could see the number came from a spinning wheel and had nothing to do with the question.

The random anchor still dragged their answers toward it, which shows how powerful and how irrational anchoring can be.

As a mechanism, the estimator initialises its output register with whatever number is available in the input stream and then runs an adjustment loop that terminates as soon as the value feels plausible, so the stopping rule, not the anchor's relevance, determines how far the estimate travels.

Anchoring is remarkably robust and hard to resist; it works even when people are warned about it, even when the anchor is obviously absurd, and even among experts.

It has large practical consequences, shaping how we react to opening offers in a negotiation, initial price tags, first salary figures, and early estimates of any kind.

The practical lesson is that the first number on the table exerts a gravitational pull, so where a discussion starts can matter as much as the facts.


36.2 The biases of confidence and hindsight

Beyond errors in estimating probabilities, people show systematic distortions in how sure they feel and in how they remember what they once expected.

These biases concern our judgment of our own knowledge, which makes them especially important and especially hard to notice from the inside.

This section covers overconfidence and the twin distortions of hindsight and confirmation.


36.2.1 Overconfidence and its calibration

Overconfidence is the tendency to be more certain of our judgments than our actual accuracy warrants.

A useful way to measure this is calibration, which asks whether your confidence matches your hit rate over many judgments.

If you are well calibrated, then of all the times you say you are ninety percent sure, you should be right about ninety percent of the time.

The common finding is that people are overconfident: when they say they are ninety percent sure, they are often right far less often, perhaps seventy or seventy-five percent of the time.

This appears across many settings, from general-knowledge quizzes to professional forecasts, and it tends to be worse on hard questions than easy ones.

In systems terms confidence is a published meta-signal that should track the probability the answer output is correct, and calibration testing compares the signal against the measured hit rate over many trials; the standing finding is a positive offset between the signal and the rate.

There are nuances that keep the picture honest.

Overconfidence can shrink or even reverse for very easy questions, an effect called the hard-easy effect, and how you ask the question changes how much overconfidence appears.

Some researchers, such as Gerd Gigerenzer, have argued that a good deal of apparent overconfidence is an artefact of asking about single tricky items rather than natural frequencies, so the size of the effect is debated.

Still, the broad message stands: people generally hold their beliefs with more confidence than the evidence justifies, which matters wherever confident judgments guide important decisions.


36.2.2 Hindsight and confirmation bias

Two further biases concern how we handle evidence over time.

Hindsight bias is the tendency, once you know how something turned out, to believe you knew it all along.

After an election, a game, or a medical diagnosis, the outcome suddenly feels as though it had been obvious and predictable, even to people who predicted otherwise beforehand.

Baruch Fischhoff demonstrated this in the 1970s by showing that people who were told an outcome then remembered having expected it more strongly than they actually had.

In systems terms hindsight bias is a destructive memory update: learning the outcome overwrites the stored record of the earlier prediction, so the system cannot later read back its own true prior and cannot compute an honest error signal from which to learn.

Hindsight bias is harmful because it makes us think the world is more predictable than it is, it feeds unfair blame of people who could not really have foreseen an outcome, and it stops us learning properly from surprises.

Confirmation bias, met earlier in the chapter on reasoning, is the companion tendency to seek and favour evidence that fits what we already believe while neglecting evidence against it.

Together these two biases distort the whole cycle of belief.

Confirmation bias skews the evidence we gather going forward, and hindsight bias rewrites our memory of what we expected looking back, so that our beliefs can feel far better supported and far more consistent than they really are.


36.3 The interpretation of the biases

Having catalogued the biases, scientists disagree sharply about what they mean.

Do they show that the human mind is fundamentally flawed, or that psychologists have been judging it against an unfair and unrealistic standard?

This section presents the two leading interpretations, which represent one of the genuine live debates in the field.


36.3.1 The heuristics-and-biases reading

The original interpretation, from Tversky, Kahneman, and their followers, is called the heuristics-and-biases programme.

Its message is that human judgment systematically departs from the rules of probability and logic, because we rely on intuitive shortcuts instead of proper calculation.

On this reading, the biases are real flaws - not random slips but predictable, direction-specific errors baked into how intuition works.

Kahneman later folded this into his well-known two-system picture, popularised in his 2011 book, where a fast, intuitive mode of thought, called System One, produces the quick heuristic answers, and a slow, effortful mode, called System Two, can sometimes catch and correct them but often does not bother.

In systems terms this reading holds probability theory fixed as the reference specification and scores the human output against it, predicting that errors persist even with incentives and expertise because the proxy computations themselves are the source.

The practical upshot of this view is somewhat pessimistic about unaided human judgment, and it has fuelled efforts to help people decide better, from statistical training to structured decision procedures.

This reading has been enormously influential across psychology, medicine, law, and economics, where it helped launch the field of behavioural economics.


36.3.2 The rational and ecological reinterpretation

A vigorous opposing camp, led most prominently by Gerd Gigerenzer, argues that calling these shortcuts biases is often unfair.

Their central point is that the standard used to judge people - abstract, textbook probability applied to artificial word problems - is the wrong yardstick for minds that evolved to work in real environments.

Change the format of a problem to match how information naturally arrives, and much of the apparent irrationality shrinks or disappears.

A powerful example is that many people who stumble on probability problems stated in percentages solve the very same problems easily when the numbers are given as natural frequencies, such as saying ten out of every thousand people rather than one percent.

Gigerenzer's positive proposal is that of ecological rationality, the idea that simple heuristics are not lazy approximations but smart tools finely matched to the structure of the environments where they are used.

His fast-and-frugal heuristics research shows that simple rules, using little information, can match or even beat complicated calculations in the messy, uncertain real world, an outcome sometimes called a less-is-more effect.

In systems terms this reading scores the same output against a different specification, expected performance in the natural input distribution, and predicts that reformatting the input to natural frequencies or moving the task into its native environment will largely remove the error, which is a testable difference from the first reading.

On this view a heuristic is rational relative to its environment, and it counts as a bias only when applied in a setting it was not suited to.

The two camps have argued for decades, and the fairest summary is that both have a point.

Human intuition really does produce systematic errors on many tasks, exactly as the heuristics-and-biases programme showed, and yet those same intuitions are often remarkably well adapted to the natural problems of real life, exactly as the ecological view insists.

The disagreement is less about the facts of behaviour, which both sides largely accept, than about which standard of good thinking we should hold people to - and that, fittingly for a chapter on judgment under uncertainty, remains genuinely open.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ A judgment query, the quantity or probability to be estimated, delivered by language comprehension or by an internal goal.

◦ Case descriptions and category prototypes, supplied by semantic memory for similarity computation.

◦ Retrieval fluency signals, the speed and volume with which examples surface from episodic memory.

◦ Candidate anchors, any numbers present in the recent input stream.

◦ Base rate and sample size information, available in the input but frequently unread.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Probability and quantity estimates, consumed by decision making, planning, and communication.

◦ A confidence signal attached to each estimate, consumed by metacognition and by other people.

◦ Risk feelings, affective weightings of possible outcomes, consumed by choice and avoidance behaviour.

◦ Updated memories of past predictions, written back to memory and vulnerable to hindsight rewriting.

• STATE.

◦ The current anchor value held in the estimation register.

◦ The accessible sample of remembered instances feeding availability.

◦ Prototype representations of categories feeding representativeness.

◦ The stored record of prior predictions, which hindsight bias silently overwrites.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Similarity gain, how strongly resemblance drives probability judgments.

◦ Fluency gain, how strongly ease of recall drives frequency judgments.

◦ Adjustment stopping threshold, the plausibility level at which anchoring adjustment halts.

◦ Base rate weight, the read strength on prior frequencies, near zero under pure representativeness.

◦ Confidence offset, the standing gap between stated confidence and hit rate.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Heuristic judgment latency: intuitive estimates arrive within about 1 to 2 seconds, faster than deliberate calculation.

◦ Availability sampling window: the first seconds of memory search dominate frequency impressions.

◦ Anchoring persistence: anchor effects survive across the whole judgment episode and are documented to persist across delays of days in some studies.

◦ Hindsight consolidation: the knew-it-all-along shift is measurable as soon as the outcome is learned and endures thereafter.

◦ Duration of one adjustment step in anchoring: REFUSED, because the literature measures final estimates and not the internal step time, so no supported value exists.

• MODES.

◦ Heuristic mode, fast proxy-based judgment by similarity, fluency, or anchoring; the default under time pressure, load, or low stakes.

◦ Deliberate mode, slower rule-based calculation that can check and correct the heuristic answer; triggered by detected conflict, high stakes, training, or accountability.

◦ Frequency format mode, reasoning over natural counts such as ten out of a thousand; triggered by input formatted as frequencies, and markedly more accurate than percentage mode.

◦ Calibration mode, explicit tracking of confidence against outcomes; engaged only with feedback and deliberate record keeping, as in trained forecasters.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Base rate neglect, ignoring how common categories are when a description resembles a stereotype.

◦ Conjunction fallacy, rating a conjunction as more probable than one of its parts.

◦ Availability distortion, overestimating vivid, recent, or well-publicised risks.

◦ Anchoring capture, estimates dragged toward arbitrary starting numbers.

◦ Overconfidence, stated certainty exceeding measured accuracy, worst on hard items.

◦ Hindsight rewriting, memory of past predictions bent toward known outcomes.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called base_rate with initial value 0.01, the share of people who have the disease.
Create a number variable called hit_rate with initial value 0.9, the chance the test is positive when the disease is present.
Create a number variable called false_alarm_rate with initial value 0.09, the chance the test is positive when the disease is absent.
Set the intuitive answer to hit_rate, because intuition reads the test's accuracy as the probability of disease.
Calculate the probability of a true positive as base_rate multiplied by hit_rate.
Calculate the probability of a false positive as one minus base_rate, multiplied by false_alarm_rate.
Calculate the Bayesian posterior as the true positive probability divided by the sum of the true positive and false positive probabilities.
Report the intuitive answer and the Bayesian answer.
Simulate ten thousand random people, giving each the disease with probability base_rate and a test result according to the rates.
Count the simulated people who test positive, and count those who test positive and truly have the disease.
Report the simulated frequency answer as the second count divided by the first count.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Load the random module for the natural frequency simulation.
import random

# Create the base rate, the share of people who have the disease.
base_rate = 0.01
# Create the hit rate, the chance the test is positive when the disease is present.
hit_rate = 0.9
# Create the false alarm rate, the chance the test is positive when the disease is absent.
false_alarm_rate = 0.09

# Set the intuitive answer to the hit rate, mistaking test accuracy for the posterior.
intuitive_answer = hit_rate

# Calculate the probability of a true positive as base_rate times hit_rate.
true_positive = base_rate * hit_rate
# Calculate the probability of a false positive as the healthy share times the false alarm rate.
false_positive = (1 - base_rate) * false_alarm_rate
# Calculate the Bayesian posterior as true positives over all positives.
bayesian_answer = true_positive / (true_positive + false_positive)

# Print the intuitive answer that neglects the base rate.
print("intuitive answer:", round(intuitive_answer, 3))
# Print the correct Bayesian answer that respects the base rate.
print("Bayesian answer:", round(bayesian_answer, 3))

# Seed the random number generator so the run is repeatable.
random.seed(36)
# Set the count of people who test positive to zero.
positives = 0
# Set the count of people who test positive and truly have the disease to zero.
sick_positives = 0

# Simulate ten thousand random people one at a time.
for person in range(10000):
    # Give this person the disease with probability equal to the base rate.
    sick = random.random() < base_rate
    # If the person is sick, the test is positive with probability hit_rate.
    if sick:
        # Draw the test result using the hit rate.
        positive = random.random() < hit_rate
    # Otherwise the test is positive with probability false_alarm_rate.
    else:
        # Draw the test result using the false alarm rate.
        positive = random.random() < false_alarm_rate
    # If the test came out positive, count this person among the positives.
    if positive:
        # Add one to the count of positive tests.
        positives = positives + 1
        # If the person is also truly sick, count them among the sick positives.
        if sick:
            # Add one to the count of sick people with positive tests.
            sick_positives = sick_positives + 1

# Print the natural frequency answer, sick positives over all positives.
print("simulated frequency answer:", round(sick_positives / positives, 3))

CHAPTER 37. DECISION MAKING AND CHOICE (PROCESS)

This chapter is about how people choose.

Every day you face options, and picking one over the others is an act your mind performs constantly, from what to eat to whether to take a new job.

Decision making is the set of mental processes by which a person weighs possible options and settles on one.

Seen as an engineered system, the decision maker is a component that subscribes to a stream of options and evidence, holds a reference point and a set of learned values as state, and publishes a single committed choice along with a confidence signal.

It matters because good decisions protect our money, our health, and our time, and because the ways our choices go wrong are surprisingly regular and can be studied like any other part of nature.

This chapter first lays out the tidy mathematical rules that say what a perfectly rational chooser should do, then turns to the messier and more accurate accounts of what real people actually do, and finally looks at how choices unfold moment by moment.


37.1 The normative theories

A normative theory is a theory of how something ought to be done, as opposed to a description of how it is actually done.

In the study of choice, the normative theories are the clean rules of ideal rationality: they tell us what a flawless decision maker with unlimited patience and no biases would choose.

They matter because they give us a yardstick.

Without a standard for the best possible choice, we could not even say that a real person had made a mistake.

In systems terms, a normative theory is a reference implementation: an idealised algorithm against which the actual, resource-limited implementation in the head can be benchmarked.


37.1.1 Expected value and expected utility

Imagine a gamble: a coin flip that pays you ten dollars for heads and nothing for tails.

Expected value is the long-run average payoff of a gamble, found by multiplying each possible outcome by its probability and adding the results.

For that coin flip the expected value is one half times ten dollars plus one half times zero, which comes to five dollars.

The idea is centuries old and grew out of letters between mathematicians trying to price bets fairly.

For a long time people assumed a rational person should simply pick whatever choice has the highest expected value.

But that rule quickly runs into trouble.

Consider a famous puzzle known as the Saint Petersburg paradox, described by the mathematician Daniel Bernoulli in 1738.

It describes a game whose expected value in dollars is infinite, yet almost nobody would pay more than a few coins to play it.

Bernoulli's fix was to say that what people really value is not raw money but the personal usefulness or satisfaction that money brings, a quantity he called utility.

Utility is the subjective worth of an outcome to a particular person, as distinct from its objective size in dollars or units.

The key insight is that money has diminishing returns: the first thousand dollars matters far more to a poor person than the thousandth thousand matters to a rich one.
