PART TEN. METACOGNITION, CONSCIOUSNESS, AND AWARENESS

================================================================================

CHAPTER 42. METACOGNITION, CONFIDENCE, AND MONITORING (PROCESS)

This chapter is about thinking about your own thinking.

Metacognition is the mind's ability to watch and judge its own mental states, for example knowing that you know an answer, sensing that you have forgotten a name, or feeling unsure whether you studied enough.

It matters enormously because a mind that can judge its own reliability can decide when to trust itself, when to check again, when to keep studying, and when to ask for help.

As a system, metacognition is a second-order process: its inputs are signals about first-order cognition, and its outputs are confidence estimates and control commands that redirect that cognition.

We will look at how metacognition is structured, at how it applies to memory in particular, at how confidence is measured scientifically, and at how monitoring turns into the control of study and action, including the crucial ability to hold back when unsure.


42.1 The structure of metacognition

This section lays out the basic anatomy of metacognition: the kinds of knowledge and regulation it involves, and the simple two-level picture that organises the whole field.


42.1.1 Metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation

The term metacognition was popularised by the developmental psychologist John Flavell in the 1970s, and it literally means cognition about cognition.

It is standard to split metacognition into two broad parts, and the split is easy to grasp.

The first part is metacognitive knowledge, which is what you know about how minds and memory work, including your own.

Metacognitive knowledge includes beliefs like knowing that you personally remember faces better than names, or that spreading study out over several days beats cramming, or that noisy rooms hurt your concentration.

The second part is metacognitive regulation, which is what you actually do to manage your thinking as it happens.

Metacognitive regulation includes planning how to approach a task, monitoring how well it is going, and adjusting your strategy when it is going badly.

A simple way to hold the two apart is that knowledge is what you believe about thinking, while regulation is the live steering of thinking in the moment.

In systems language, knowledge is long-term stored state that changes slowly over weeks and years, while regulation is a fast online loop operating within a task, taking moment-to-moment monitoring signals as input and producing strategy adjustments as output within seconds.

The two are connected, because accurate knowledge helps you regulate well, but they can also come apart, since someone may know the right strategy in the abstract yet fail to use it under pressure.


42.1.2 The meta-level and object-level framework

The most influential single framework for metacognition was set out by Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens in 1990, and it gives the whole field a clean skeleton.

They proposed that a mind can be divided into two levels.

The object level is the part that does the basic work of perceiving, learning, and remembering, that is, the ordinary cognition.

The meta-level is a part that holds a model of the object level, meaning a rough internal picture of what the object level is doing and how well.

Two channels of information connect the levels, and this is the heart of the idea.

Monitoring is the flow of information upward, from the object level to the meta-level, telling the meta-level how well things are going, for example a feeling that an answer is shaky.

Control is the flow of information downward, from the meta-level to the object level, changing what the object level does, for example a decision to slow down and re-read.

This is exactly the architecture engineers call a supervisory control loop: a plant, meaning the object level, a model-holding supervisor, meaning the meta-level, an upward sensor channel, and a downward command channel.

A powerful insight from this framework is that monitoring and control can dissociate, meaning they do not always work together.

A system might monitor without controlling, receiving the signal that it is unsure but doing nothing about it, or it might control without monitoring, applying a blanket rule without knowing whether it is right.

This two-level picture with upward monitoring and downward control has proven so useful that it is now applied well beyond human memory, including to attempts to give artificial systems the ability to judge their own reliability.


42.2 Metamemory

Metamemory is metacognition aimed specifically at memory, that is, judging what you know, what you have learned, and what you will be able to recall later.

This section covers the main memory judgments people make and the leading account of where those judgments come from.


42.2.1 Judgments of learning and feeling of knowing

Two judgments have been studied more than any others, and both are things you have surely experienced.

A judgment of learning is a prediction, made while or just after studying something, about how likely you are to remember it on a later test.

For instance, after reading a pair of foreign words you might feel confident you will recall them tomorrow, and that feeling is a judgment of learning.

A feeling of knowing is a different judgment, made when you cannot recall something right now, about whether you would recognise the answer or eventually retrieve it.

The classic case is a fact on the tip of your tongue, where you cannot produce the name but feel certain you know it and would spot it in a list.

Researchers care about these judgments because they can be compared against what the person actually remembers later, which lets us measure how accurate a person's self-knowledge really is.

Each judgment is a small predictor module: its input is whatever evidence is available at judgment time, its output is a probability-like rating, and its quality is scored later against the actual test outcome.

One reliable and initially surprising finding concerns timing.

Judgments of learning made after a delay are usually more accurate than those made immediately after studying, a result known as the delayed judgment of learning effect.

The reason is that an immediate judgment can lean on information that is only fleetingly available right after study, which is misleading, whereas a delayed judgment forces you to actually try to retrieve the item, and how that retrieval goes is a much better guide to later memory.

The timescale matters here: the misleading surface information fades within seconds to minutes, so a judgment made minutes or longer after study is forced to sample the durable trace, which is the one that predicts the later test.


42.2.2 The cue-utilisation account of monitoring

A natural but wrong assumption is that when you judge your own memory, you somehow read off the true strength of the memory directly, like checking a fuel gauge.

The cue-utilisation account, developed by Asher Koriat in 1997, argues that this is not how it works, and it is the leading theory of where memory judgments come from.

Koriat's central claim is that people have no direct access to the strength or durability of their memory traces.

Instead, they infer how well they know something by noticing and using various cues, which are indirect clues that happen to be available.

Koriat grouped these cues into three kinds.

Intrinsic cues are features of the material itself, such as how easy or hard a set of words looks to learn.

Extrinsic cues are features of the study situation, such as how many times you have gone over the material or the conditions you studied under.

Mnemonic cues, sometimes called internal cues, are signals from your own mind during the attempt, such as how quickly and fluently an answer comes to you.

In systems terms this makes the monitor an inference engine rather than a sensor: its inputs are cues correlated with memory strength, its output is an estimated strength, and its accuracy is bounded by how well those cues actually correlate with the hidden variable.

Because judgments are built from cues rather than read directly from memory, they can be systematically fooled.

For example, information that feels fluent and easy in the moment can create a false sense of having learned it, which is why students often overestimate how well they know material they have merely re-read.

This account is important because it explains both when self-monitoring is accurate and when it reliably misleads us, and the delayed judgment of learning effect from the previous sub-section fits it neatly, since a delay changes which cues are available to use.


42.3 Confidence and metacognitive sensitivity

Confidence is the feeling of being right, and this section explains how scientists have learned to measure the quality of that feeling rigorously, separating a good self-monitor from a merely confident or merely accurate person.


42.3.1 Type-one and type-two performance

To measure metacognition precisely, researchers separate two layers of performance, and the labels type one and type two are worth learning.

Type-one performance is how well you do the actual task, for example whether you correctly detect a faint signal or answer a question right.

Type-two performance is how well your confidence tracks your type-one performance, that is, whether you feel more confident when you are actually correct and less confident when you are actually wrong.

The key point is that these two can come apart.

A person could be very accurate at the task yet have poor insight, feeling equally confident whether right or wrong, or a person could be less accurate yet have excellent insight, reliably knowing which of their answers to trust.

Good metacognition is precisely good type-two performance: confidence that discriminates your correct responses from your incorrect ones.

In interface terms, the type-one channel outputs a decision, the type-two channel outputs a confidence rating attached to that decision usually within a second or so of it, and the two channels can be scored independently, which is what lets researchers study self-knowledge as its own ability rather than confusing it with plain skill at the task.


42.3.2 Calibration, resolution, and the measurement of insight

Once we treat confidence as measurable, we can ask in what specific ways it can be good or bad, and there are two main qualities to distinguish.

Calibration is whether your confidence matches your actual accuracy on average.

A well-calibrated person who says they are seventy percent sure is right about seventy percent of the time, whereas a poorly calibrated person might be right only fifty percent of the time when they say seventy, which is overconfidence.

Resolution, also called metacognitive sensitivity, is whether your confidence distinguishes your correct answers from your incorrect ones on a case-by-case basis.

Good resolution means your high-confidence answers really are more often correct than your low-confidence ones, so your confidence carries useful information about which specific judgments to trust.

Calibration and resolution are different: you could be perfectly calibrated on average yet have zero resolution if you give the same confidence to everything, so both matter.

As measurements, calibration compares the mean of the confidence output stream to the mean of the accuracy stream, while resolution asks whether the confidence output covaries with accuracy trial by trial, and the code sample at the end of this chapter computes a simple version of each.

A serious measurement problem is that naive measures of resolution get contaminated by two nuisances: how good the person is at the task itself, and their general tendency to be cautious or bold in reporting confidence, which is called response bias.

To solve this, Brian Maniscalco and Hakwan Lau in 2012 introduced a measure called meta-d-prime, built within signal detection theory, which is a mathematical framework for separating true sensitivity from mere bias.

Meta-d-prime estimates how much of the information the person had was actually used by their confidence judgments, and by comparing it to their raw task ability it yields a purer index of metacognitive efficiency that is not fooled by how cautious or how skilled the person is.

The practical upshot for a beginner is that measuring insight well is genuinely hard, and modern methods exist precisely to avoid mistaking a bold guesser, or simply a good performer, for a person with real self-knowledge.


42.4 The control side of metacognition

Monitoring is only half the story; the point of watching your own mind is to do something with what you learn.

This section covers how metacognitive monitoring feeds back into action, from deciding what to study to the deep ability to withhold a response when you are not sure.


42.4.1 The allocation of study and effort

The clearest place to see monitoring turn into control is studying.

When you study, you are constantly making small decisions about where to put your effort, and metacognition is what guides those decisions.

The general finding is that people use their sense of how well they know each item to decide what to work on next, spending more time on material that feels unlearned and less on material that feels mastered.

This links directly back to the Nelson and Narens framework, where monitoring, such as a low judgment of learning for a hard item, drives control, such as choosing to restudy that item.

As a scheduler, the mechanism takes per-item learning estimates as input and outputs a study-time allocation, updating the allocation each time an item is revisited, on a timescale of seconds per decision.

There is an interesting wrinkle, though, because how people allocate effort depends on the situation and on their goals.

When time is short or material is very hard, people sometimes sensibly abandon the hardest items and pour effort into the ones that are still within reach, rather than throwing good time after lost causes.

The broad and practical lesson is that accurate monitoring is valuable mainly because it enables good control, and a student whose sense of their own learning is miscalibrated will misallocate study time even if they work hard.


42.4.2 Metacognition as the mechanism by which a system declines to act

The deepest function of metacognition may be a simple and powerful one: knowing when not to act.

An intelligent system that could not tell its reliable judgments from its unreliable ones would have to treat every hunch as equally trustworthy, which is dangerous.

Metacognition provides the brake, because a confidence signal that is low can be used to withhold a response, to gather more evidence, to defer to someone else, or to say honestly that you do not know.

This is often described in terms of an optional response, where a person or system is allowed to opt out of answering when its own monitoring says it is likely to be wrong, and good metacognition shows up as opting out mostly on the items it would have gotten wrong.

Mechanically, this is a threshold gate on the output channel: the confidence signal is compared to a criterion, and responses below the criterion are routed to withholding, evidence gathering, or deferral instead of action.

The ability to decline is what turns raw competence into trustworthy behaviour, since being right when confident and quiet when unsure is far more useful than being loudly certain all the time.

This point reaches well beyond human psychology and into artificial intelligence, where a growing concern is building systems that can reliably judge and report the limits of their own knowledge rather than answering everything with the same false confidence.

For a mind of any kind, then, metacognition is the faculty that makes self-restraint and honest uncertainty possible, which is why it closes this chapter and opens naturally onto the questions of awareness that follow.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Object-level performance signals, such as retrieval fluency, response speed, and partial recall, from the perception, memory, and decision systems.

◦ Cues about the material and situation, such as apparent difficulty and number of study repetitions, from perception and episodic memory.

◦ Decision evidence traces, meaning the strength of the evidence behind each first-order response, from the decision system.

◦ Task goals and deadlines, from the executive control system.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Confidence ratings and probability-like judgments, consumed by the decision system, by other people, and by the experimenter.

◦ Judgments of learning and feelings of knowing, consumed by the study-allocation controller.

◦ Control commands, such as restudy this item, slow down, gather more evidence, or withhold the response, consumed by the object level.

◦ Opt-out decisions, consumed by the response system as a declined answer or an honest do-not-know.

• STATE.

◦ The meta-level model of the object level, meaning the current estimate of how well each task or item is going.

◦ Stored metacognitive knowledge about one's own strengths, weaknesses, and strategies.

◦ The current confidence criterion for responding versus declining.

◦ A record of recent judgments and outcomes used to recalibrate.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ The confidence criterion, meaning how sure the system must be before acting.

◦ Cue weights, meaning how heavily intrinsic, extrinsic, and mnemonic cues count in a judgment.

◦ Metacognitive efficiency, meaning how much of the available first-order evidence the confidence channel actually uses.

◦ Study-time allocation policy, from spend effort on the hardest items to triage toward the reachable ones.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Confidence report latency, typically well under one second after the first-order decision.

◦ The misleading immediate-judgment window after study, seconds to minutes, which the delayed judgment of learning effect exploits by waiting beyond it.

◦ Study-allocation decisions, made in seconds per item during self-paced learning.

◦ Recalibration of metacognitive knowledge, REFUSED, because the literature reports no single characteristic timescale for how quickly self-knowledge updates from feedback.

• MODES.

◦ Monitoring-dominant mode, where the meta-level passively tracks the object level; the default during fluent performance.

◦ Control-engaged mode, where low confidence or detected trouble triggers restudy, slowing, or strategy change.

◦ Respond mode versus opt-out mode, switched by the confidence criterion: above criterion the system answers, below it the system declines or defers.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Overconfidence, especially from fluency illusions, as when re-read material feels learned but is not.

◦ Underconfidence and needless checking, where a sound object level is not trusted.

◦ Zero resolution, where confidence no longer distinguishes right from wrong answers, making the monitor useless even if calibrated on average.

◦ Monitoring-control dissociation, where the system feels unsure yet acts anyway, or applies blanket control without insight.

◦ Clinical breakdowns of insight, as in anosognosia, the unawareness of one's own deficit.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called total confidence with initial value zero.
Create a number variable called total accuracy with initial value zero.
For each trial in the trial list, add the trial confidence to total confidence and add the trial accuracy to total accuracy.
Calculate the calibration gap as total confidence divided by the trial count, minus total accuracy divided by the trial count.
Create a number variable called concordant with initial value zero.
Create a number variable called comparisons with initial value zero.
For each pair made of one correct trial and one incorrect trial, do the following.
    Add one to comparisons.
    If the correct trial's confidence is greater than the incorrect trial's confidence, add one to concordant.
    If the two confidences are equal, add zero point five to concordant.
Calculate the sensitivity as concordant divided by comparisons.
Return the calibration gap and the sensitivity.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Define a function that scores confidence calibration and metacognitive sensitivity.
def score_metacognition(trials):
    # Calculate the mean confidence across all trials.
    mean_conf = sum(conf for conf, correct in trials) / len(trials)
    # Calculate the mean accuracy across all trials.
    mean_acc = sum(correct for conf, correct in trials) / len(trials)
    # Calculate the calibration gap as mean confidence minus mean accuracy.
    calibration_gap = mean_conf - mean_acc
    # Create a list of the confidences given on correct trials.
    conf_correct = [conf for conf, correct in trials if correct == 1]
    # Create a list of the confidences given on incorrect trials.
    conf_wrong = [conf for conf, correct in trials if correct == 0]
    # Create a number variable called concordant with initial value zero.
    concordant = 0.0
    # Create a number variable called comparisons with initial value zero.
    comparisons = 0.0
    # For each confidence from a correct trial, do the following.
    for c_hit in conf_correct:
        # For each confidence from an incorrect trial, do the following.
        for c_miss in conf_wrong:
            # Add one to the comparison count.
            comparisons = comparisons + 1.0
            # If the correct trial's confidence is higher, count the pair as concordant.
            if c_hit > c_miss:
                # Add one to the concordant count.
                concordant = concordant + 1.0
            # If the two confidences are tied, count the pair as half concordant.
            elif c_hit == c_miss:
                # Add zero point five to the concordant count.
                concordant = concordant + 0.5
    # Calculate the sensitivity as the share of concordant pairs, or zero point five if no pairs exist.
    sensitivity = concordant / comparisons if comparisons > 0 else 0.5
    # Return the calibration gap and the sensitivity.
    return calibration_gap, sensitivity

# Create a small data set of trials as pairs of confidence and correctness.
data = [(0.9, 1), (0.8, 1), (0.7, 1), (0.9, 0), (0.6, 1), (0.4, 0), (0.3, 0), (0.7, 0), (0.8, 1), (0.5, 0)]
# Score the data set.
gap, sens = score_metacognition(data)
# Print the calibration gap, where positive means overconfidence.
print("calibration gap:", round(gap, 3))
# Print the sensitivity, where zero point five means no insight and one means perfect insight.
print("sensitivity:", round(sens, 3))


CHAPTER 43. AUTOMATICITY AND UNCONSCIOUS PROCESSING (PROCESS)

This chapter is about how much of the mind runs by itself, out of sight of awareness.

A great deal of skilled behaviour, from reading a word to riding a bicycle, happens fast, effortlessly, and without conscious guidance, and a great deal of information gets processed without our ever noticing it.

This matters because it shows that consciousness is only the tip of a very large iceberg, and it forces us to ask what awareness actually adds.

In systems terms, the chapter contrasts two processing regimes, a slow serial controlled pipeline and a fast parallel automatic one, and examines what practice does to move a task from the first regime to the second.

We will look at the difference between automatic and controlled processing, at the evidence for genuinely unconscious perception and thought, and at the tricky business of measuring what a person is and is not aware of.


43.1 Automatic and controlled processing

This section draws the basic contrast between mental processes that run on their own and those that need effortful supervision, and describes how the first kind grows out of the second through practice.


43.1.1 The criteria of automaticity

An automatic process is one that runs quickly and by itself, without needing much attention or conscious effort.

A controlled process, by contrast, is slow, effortful, deliberate, and demands the limited resource of attention.

The classic experiments distinguishing the two were done by Walter Schneider and Richard Shiffrin in 1977, and they gave the field a working checklist of what automaticity means.

By their classical account, a process counts as automatic to the degree that it has a cluster of features.

It is fast and does not draw on limited attentional capacity, so it can run even while you are busy with something else.

It runs in parallel, meaning several automatic processes can happen at once without slowing each other much.

It is hard to stop or ignore, so it tends to run whether or not you want it to.

And it can operate without conscious awareness or deliberate intention.

Stated as system properties, an automatic process has a flat load curve, meaning its response time barely grows as items are added, while a controlled process has a rising load curve, gaining time for every extra item it must handle serially.

A famous illustration is skilled reading, since a fluent reader cannot look at a familiar word in their own language and not read it, which is why the meaning of the word interferes when you are asked to name the ink colour instead.

A useful caution from modern work is that these features do not always come as a neat all-or-none package.

A process can be automatic in some respects, such as being fast and effortless, while still being partly controllable, so researchers now often speak of degrees and dimensions of automaticity rather than a hard line.


43.1.2 The development of automaticity with practice

Automaticity is mostly not something we are born with; it is something we build through repetition.

The key finding from Schneider and Shiffrin was that automatic detection develops with consistent practice, meaning that when the same stimulus always calls for the same response, that pairing gradually becomes automatic.

Consistency is the crucial ingredient.

When the mapping from stimulus to response is consistent across many trials, performance speeds up, becomes effortless, and stops draining attention, which is the birth of an automatic process.

When the mapping keeps changing, so that a stimulus is sometimes a target and sometimes not, this automatisation does not happen, and the task stays effortful and controlled no matter how much you practise.

As a mechanism, practice with a consistent mapping gradually compiles a lookup: the input is the stimulus, the output is the response, the per-item serial step is bypassed, and the speedup follows the well-documented power law of practice, with large early gains that shrink over hundreds to thousands of trials.

This explains a familiar arc of learning a skill.

A beginning driver must consciously think about every action, using slow controlled processing, but after enough consistent practice the routine parts become automatic and free up attention for conversation or planning the route.

The general principle is that practice moves a task from the effortful controlled mode into the fast automatic mode, which is enormously useful but also has a cost, since automatic habits can be triggered at the wrong time and are hard to suppress, connecting back to the need for inhibition discussed in the executive function chapter.


43.2 The unconscious

This section takes up the stronger claim that information can be perceived and can influence us even when we are not aware of it at all, and it treats this claim with the care it deserves, because it has a history of overstatement.


43.2.1 Subliminal perception and priming

Subliminal perception means perceiving a stimulus that is too weak, too brief, or too hidden to be consciously seen, yet which still affects the mind.

The main laboratory tool for studying it is priming, which means showing one stimulus and measuring how it changes the response to a later one.

In a typical masked priming experiment, a word is flashed very briefly and then immediately covered by a jumble of symbols called a mask, so that the person reports seeing nothing, yet that hidden word can still speed up the recognition of a related word afterward.

The timing here is tight and worth stating: masked primes are typically shown for only tens of milliseconds, roughly 30 to 50 milliseconds in many studies, and the measured effect is a response speedup of a few tens of milliseconds on the following target.

Work by Stanislas Dehaene and others has shown that such masked words can be processed surprisingly deeply, including at the level of meaning, and not merely as visual shapes.

This is genuinely important evidence that a good deal of processing happens before and without consciousness.

However, this is an area where healthy scepticism is essential, and the science has become more careful over time.

A recurring problem is that experiments meant to hide a stimulus completely often fail to do so, and participants may have had a faint, above-chance awareness that was not properly measured.

Recent meta-analyses of subliminal linguistic priming have found evidence of weak statistical power and of residual awareness in many classic studies, which means some famous subliminal effects are smaller or less certain than they were once claimed to be.

The balanced conclusion is that unconscious processing of simple, well-learned stimuli is real, but that dramatic claims about the unconscious mind absorbing complex hidden messages are not well supported, and measuring true unawareness is the hard part.


43.2.2 Implicit cognition and the dissociations that reveal it

Implicit cognition refers to mental processes that influence our thoughts, feelings, and actions without our being aware of the process or sometimes even of its results.

The main way researchers argue that something is implicit is by finding a dissociation, which means a gap between two measures.

A dissociation occurs when a person shows an effect on one measure, such as behaving as if they learned something, while showing nothing on another measure, such as being unable to report or explain what they learned.

In systems language, a dissociation is evidence that a signal reached one output channel, behaviour, while never reaching another output channel, verbal report, which implies at least two separable pathways carrying the information.

A well-known example comes from amnesia, where patients with severe memory loss can improve on a skill or show priming from earlier exposure while sincerely denying any memory of the training, revealing that the influence is real but the awareness of it is absent.

Similar dissociations appear in healthy people in tasks where they pick up on a hidden regularity and use it to respond faster while being unable to state what the regularity was.

These dissociations are the central evidence that memory and learning are not single conscious things but include processes that operate below awareness.

A fair caution, echoing the previous sub-section, is that a dissociation is only convincing if the awareness measure is sensitive enough, because a weak test of awareness can make ordinary conscious knowledge look unconscious, so the strength of these claims depends heavily on how carefully awareness is assessed.


43.3 The measurement of awareness

Everything in this chapter depends on being able to tell what someone is and is not aware of, and that turns out to be one of the thorniest problems in the field, which this section confronts directly.


43.3.1 Objective and subjective thresholds

To claim that something was processed unconsciously, you must define the line below which a stimulus counts as unseen, and there are two very different ways to draw that line.

An objective threshold is defined by performance: a stimulus is treated as unconscious only if the person cannot do better than chance at any forced choice about it, for example cannot guess above chance whether a word was present.

A subjective threshold is defined by report: a stimulus is treated as unconscious if the person says they did not see it and reports no experience of it, even if their behaviour shows some sensitivity.

These two thresholds usually do not sit in the same place, and the gap between them is scientifically revealing.

People often can make above-chance forced-choice guesses about stimuli they sincerely report not seeing, which means that by the subjective criterion the stimulus is unconscious while by the objective criterion it is not.

In measurement terms, the two thresholds are two different acceptance tests on the same input channel, one reading the behavioural output and one reading the report output, and because the report channel is the stricter bottleneck the subjective threshold sits at a higher stimulus strength than the objective one.

Which threshold you choose changes your conclusions dramatically, because the loose subjective criterion makes unconscious perception look powerful and common, while the strict objective criterion makes it look rarer and weaker.

There is no fully agreed answer about which threshold is correct, and this choice is one of the main reasons that estimates of how much the unconscious can do vary so widely between researchers.


43.3.2 The process-dissociation procedure and the no-report paradigms

Because simple awareness measures are so slippery, researchers have developed cleverer methods to separate conscious from unconscious influences, and two are especially important.

The first is the process-dissociation procedure, introduced by Larry Jacoby in 1991.

Its clever idea is to set conscious and unconscious influences against each other by giving people two kinds of instruction: sometimes to use a memory and sometimes deliberately to avoid using it.

If a memory keeps influencing behaviour even when the person is trying hard not to use it, that influence must be automatic and unconscious rather than deliberately controlled, and by comparing the two conditions the method estimates the size of the conscious and the unconscious contributions separately rather than assuming a task is purely one or the other.

As a measurement design, it treats behaviour as the sum of two signal sources and uses an inclusion condition and an exclusion condition as two equations that let the two source strengths be solved for separately.

The second development is the family of no-report paradigms, which come mostly from consciousness research.

The problem they solve is that asking someone to report what they experienced adds extra mental steps, such as making a decision and pressing a button, and those steps have their own brain activity that can be mistaken for the brain activity of consciousness itself.

No-report paradigms try to infer what a person is experiencing without asking them to report it, for instance by using eye movements or physiological signals that naturally track perception, so that the measured brain activity reflects the experience more purely.

This matters because some brain activity once thought to be the signature of consciousness, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, turned out to shrink when the report requirement was removed, suggesting it reflected the act of reporting rather than the experience.

At the same time, this fix is not perfect, since a completely report-free method makes it harder to be sure what the person actually experienced, so the field is still working out how to have it both ways, which leads naturally into the study of consciousness itself.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Stimulus features, including very brief or masked stimuli, from the sensory systems.

◦ Stimulus-to-response mapping history, meaning how consistently a stimulus has called for the same response, from procedural learning.

◦ Attention allocation, as a limited-capacity resource signal, from the attention system, required by controlled processing and largely bypassed by automatic processing.

◦ Task instructions and intentions, from the executive control system.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Fast automatic responses and priming effects, as behaviour, consumed by the motor system with or without awareness.

◦ Slow controlled responses, as deliberate behaviour, consumed by the motor system under attentional supervision.

◦ Report-channel output, meaning what the person can say they perceived or learned, consumed by experimenters and by the person's own reasoning.

◦ Interference signals, as when an automatic reading response collides with a colour-naming goal, consumed by the conflict monitor of the executive system.

• STATE.

◦ The compiled stimulus-to-response associations built by consistent practice.

◦ The current degree of automatisation of each practised task, from fully controlled to fully automatic.

◦ Residual activation from recent primes, which decays quickly.

◦ Implicitly learned regularities that are not available to report.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Mapping consistency, the key training parameter: consistent mappings automatise, varied mappings do not.

◦ Amount of practice, with speedups following a power law of practice.

◦ Masking strength and prime duration, which set how much unconscious processing can occur.

◦ The awareness criterion in use, objective or subjective, which sets where unconscious begins.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Masked prime presentation, typically tens of milliseconds, roughly 30 to 50 milliseconds in classic designs.

◦ Priming effect sizes on response time, typically a few tens of milliseconds.

◦ Automatisation, built over hundreds to thousands of consistent trials, with power-law diminishing returns.

◦ Decay of masked-prime influence, well under one second in most designs.

◦ The exact lifetime of an implicit learning trace, REFUSED, because reported durations range from minutes to months depending on the task and no single characteristic value is supported.

• MODES.

◦ Controlled serial mode, engaged for novel or inconsistent tasks: slow, effortful, capacity-limited, one item at a time.

◦ Automatic parallel mode, engaged for well-practised consistent tasks: fast, low effort, flat load curve.

◦ The transition trigger is accumulated consistent practice, and the reverse transition, de-automatisation, is triggered by changed mappings, injury, or deliberate retraining, and is slow.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Habit capture, where an automatic routine fires in the wrong context and cannot easily be stopped, as in the ink-colour interference effect.

◦ Loss of flexibility, since compiled routines resist modification when the rules change.

◦ Illusory unconsciousness in research, where insensitive awareness measures make conscious knowledge look unconscious.

◦ Overclaiming, the historical failure mode of the field, in which weak subliminal effects were inflated into dramatic stories about hidden persuasion.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called serial step time with initial value two hundred.
Create a number variable called parallel time with initial value fifty.
Create a number variable called automatisation with initial value zero.
Create a number variable called learning rate with initial value zero point zero two.
For each practice block from one to the block count, do the following.
    Create a number variable called block time with initial value zero.
    For each item in the display set, do the following.
        Calculate the item time as automatisation times parallel time plus one minus automatisation times serial step time.
        Add the item time to block time.
    If the mapping is consistent, increase automatisation by learning rate times one minus automatisation.
    Record the block number and the block time.
Return the recorded block times.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Define a function that simulates the growth of automaticity with practice.
def practice_simulation(blocks, set_size, consistent):
    # Create a number variable called serial_step for the controlled time per item in milliseconds.
    serial_step = 200.0
    # Create a number variable called parallel_time for the automatic time per display in milliseconds.
    parallel_time = 50.0
    # Create a number variable called automatisation with initial value zero.
    automatisation = 0.0
    # Create a number variable called learning_rate with initial value zero point zero two.
    learning_rate = 0.02
    # Create an empty list called history.
    history = []
    # For each practice block, do the following.
    for block in range(1, blocks + 1):
        # Calculate the serial component as the set size times the serial step time.
        serial_cost = set_size * serial_step
        # Calculate the parallel component as a single flat time regardless of set size.
        parallel_cost = parallel_time
        # Blend the two regimes according to the current degree of automatisation.
        block_time = automatisation * parallel_cost + (1.0 - automatisation) * serial_cost
        # Append the block number and the rounded block time to the history.
        history.append((block, round(block_time, 1)))
        # If the stimulus-to-response mapping is consistent, move automatisation toward one.
        if consistent:
            # Increase automatisation by the learning rate times the remaining distance to one.
            automatisation = automatisation + learning_rate * (1.0 - automatisation)
    # Return the history of block times.
    return history

# Simulate one hundred blocks of consistent-mapping practice with four items per display.
consistent_run = practice_simulation(100, 4, True)
# Simulate one hundred blocks of varied-mapping practice with four items per display.
varied_run = practice_simulation(100, 4, False)
# Print the first, middle, and last block times for the consistent condition.
print("consistent:", consistent_run[0], consistent_run[49], consistent_run[99])
# Print the first, middle, and last block times for the varied condition.
print("varied:", varied_run[0], varied_run[49], varied_run[99])


CHAPTER 44. CONSCIOUSNESS: CONCEPTS, MEASURES, AND THEORIES (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about consciousness itself, the fact that there is something it is like to be you, to see red, to feel pain, to have an inner life.

It is placed as context because consciousness is the deepest and least settled topic in the science of mind, where careful researchers still disagree about basic questions, and honesty about that disagreement is part of the lesson.

Consciousness matters here for a very practical reason too: as machines grow more capable, questions about what could be conscious, and how we would ever tell, stop being purely philosophical.

Because this is a context chapter, its systems treatment models the leading functional proposal, the global workspace, rather than claiming to model experience itself.

We will separate the key concepts, survey the main scientific theories, look at how the field tries to test them, including a remarkable experiment where rival camps agreed in advance how to be proven wrong, and consider what consciousness might actually be for.


44.1 The concepts

Before theorising, we need to carve the vague word consciousness into sharper pieces, because much confusion comes from people using the one word for several different things.


44.1.1 Access and phenomenal consciousness

The philosopher Ned Block drew a distinction in the 1990s that has organised much of the field, between access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness.

Access consciousness is information being available to the rest of the mind, meaning it can be used to guide reasoning, speech, memory, and action.

Something is access-conscious if you can report it, think about it, and act on it, so access consciousness is defined by what information does for the wider system.

Phenomenal consciousness is the raw felt quality of experience itself, the what-it-is-likeness, such as the actual redness of red or the actual hurt of pain.

The distinction matters because it is at least conceivable that these two come apart, for instance that there could be felt experience that is not fully available for report, or availability without any accompanying feel.

In systems terms, access consciousness is a specification an engineer could test, namely that a signal is readable by reasoning, language, and memory modules, whereas phenomenal consciousness names a property that no input-output test straightforwardly captures, which is precisely the difficulty.

Some thinkers argue the two always go together in practice, and others insist they are genuinely separate, and this disagreement is not merely verbal, because it shapes what one thinks a theory of consciousness even has to explain.

A useful way for a newcomer to hold it is that access consciousness is about function, what the information can be used for, while phenomenal consciousness is about feeling, what the experience is like from the inside.


44.1.2 The hard problem

The hard problem of consciousness is a phrase coined by the philosopher David Chalmers in 1995, and it names why consciousness is uniquely difficult to explain.

Chalmers separated the easy problems from the hard problem.

The easy problems, which are not really easy but are tractable, are about explaining functions and behaviours, such as how the brain integrates information, focuses attention, controls behaviour, or reports its own states.

The hard problem is the question of why any of that physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all, rather than going on in the dark with no inner feel.

Put simply, even if we fully explained every function the brain performs, it seems we could still ask why all that functioning feels like something, and that leftover question is the hard problem.

In systems terms the split is clean: the easy problems ask for mechanisms with inputs, outputs, and state, exactly the kind of description this book gives everywhere, while the hard problem asks why any such mechanism is accompanied by experience, a question that no interface diagram answers.

This is genuinely contested territory.

Some researchers think the hard problem is a real and possibly permanent limit on scientific explanation, some think it will dissolve as the easy problems are solved, and some think it rests on a confusion, so a beginner should understand it as a live and respectable dispute rather than a settled truth.

The main practical effect of the hard problem is that it divides theories of consciousness into those that try to confront felt experience head-on and those that focus on the functions and set the felt quality aside.


44.1.3 Level against content of consciousness

A third useful distinction separates two different questions that the word consciousness runs together.

The level of consciousness is how conscious a creature is overall, its global state, ranging from full alert wakefulness down through drowsiness, dreaming sleep, dreamless sleep, general anaesthesia, and coma.

The content of consciousness is what a conscious creature is conscious of at a given moment, that is, the particular experiences filling awareness right now, such as this page, a background hum, or a passing thought.

Keeping these apart is important because they can vary somewhat independently and involve different brain mechanisms.

In systems language, level is a global operating mode of the whole machine, set by arousal systems on a timescale of minutes to hours, while content is the moment-to-moment selection of which signals occupy awareness, changing on a timescale of hundreds of milliseconds.

Studying level asks what makes the difference between being awake and being under anaesthesia, which is largely about broad brain states and arousal systems.

Studying content asks why, at a fixed level of wakefulness, you become aware of one thing rather than another, which is the question behind many perception experiments.

Much of the experimental work on consciousness holds the level fixed at ordinary wakefulness and manipulates content, for instance by making a stimulus sometimes seen and sometimes not, in order to isolate what changes in the brain when something enters awareness.


44.2 The theories

This section surveys the leading scientific theories of consciousness, which disagree not only on the answers but on what the central question is, and it presents them plainly without pretending one has won.


44.2.1 Global workspace and global neuronal workspace

Global workspace theory begins with a simple and appealing metaphor.

The mind is pictured as a theatre in which many unconscious processes work in the dark, and consciousness is like a spotlight on a stage that makes selected information available to the whole audience of other processes.

The original version was proposed by Bernard Baars, and the idea is that a piece of information becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely across the mind so that many separate systems can use it at once.

Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux developed a brain-based version called the global neuronal workspace theory.

In their account, information becomes conscious when it is amplified and broadcast across a network of long-range connections, especially involving the prefrontal and parietal regions, in a sudden nonlinear surge they call ignition.

Before ignition, a stimulus can be processed locally and unconsciously, but once it triggers this global broadcast it becomes consciously accessible and reportable.

The mechanism is crisply system-like: many specialised processors compete, coalitions of mutually supporting signals accumulate strength, and when one coalition crosses an ignition threshold, typically around 200 to 300 milliseconds after the stimulus in the supporting experiments, its content is written to a shared workspace readable by all modules, which is the algorithm modelled in this chapter's code sample.

The great strength of this theory is that it directly explains access consciousness and connects neatly to experiments on report, attention, and the sudden all-or-none way stimuli often pop into awareness.

Its main perceived weakness is that critics say it explains the functional access to information but says little about phenomenal feel, so it is often accused of setting the hard problem aside rather than answering it.


44.2.2 Higher-order theories

Higher-order theories start from a different intuition: that a mental state becomes conscious only when the mind represents itself as being in that state.

In plainer words, seeing red is not enough to be conscious of red; there must also be a higher-order representation, a kind of inner awareness that you are seeing red.

The lower-order state is the ordinary perception, and the higher-order state is a representation of that perception, and consciousness on this view lives in the relationship between them.

This is why these are called higher-order theories, because the crucial ingredient is a thought or representation about another mental state, one level up.

Architecturally, this adds a monitoring layer whose input is the first-order state and whose output is a representation of that state, so the theory predicts that consciousness fails whenever the monitoring layer fails, even if the first-order processing is intact, which is a different failure prediction than the workspace account makes.

A strength of this approach is that it takes seriously the introspective sense that being conscious involves a kind of self-awareness, and it fits evidence that the prefrontal cortex, associated with such self-monitoring, is involved in consciousness.

A common objection is that it seems to demand a lot of sophisticated self-representation for what feels like simple sensory experience, and critics ask whether a creature must really represent its own mind in order to simply feel pain.

Higher-order theories also connect closely to the metacognition of the previous chapters, since the higher-order representation is a kind of monitoring of one's own states.


44.2.3 Integrated information theory

Integrated information theory, developed by Giulio Tononi starting around 2004, takes the boldest and most unusual approach, and it is worth explaining slowly.

Rather than starting from the brain, it starts from the felt properties of experience itself and asks what any physical system would need to have those properties.

Its central claim is that consciousness just is integrated information, meaning the extent to which a system's parts form a unified whole that is more than the sum of the parts and cannot be cleanly divided without loss.

It proposes a quantity, written with the Greek letter phi, that is meant to measure how much integrated information a system has, and it holds that the amount of consciousness corresponds to phi.

In systems terms this theory is unusual because it defines consciousness not by inputs and outputs at all but by the internal causal structure of the mechanism, so two systems with identical behaviour could differ in consciousness, a claim the more functional theories reject.

A striking consequence is that consciousness becomes a matter of degree and of a system's causal structure, so that any sufficiently integrated system could have some consciousness, a view with panpsychist leanings that many find either profound or troubling.

The theory tries to face the hard problem directly by tying phenomenal experience to a precise structural property, which its supporters see as its great ambition.

It is also heavily criticised, however.

Some critics argue that phi is effectively impossible to calculate for real brains, that the theory makes few testable predictions, and that its claim about which systems are conscious can seem counterintuitive, and in 2023 a large group of researchers publicly argued that the theory was, in their words, unproven and possibly untestable, a charge its defenders dispute.

For a newcomer, the key point is that integrated information theory is genuinely radical, taken seriously by many, and sharply contested by many others.


44.2.4 Recurrent processing and predictive-self accounts

A further family of theories locates consciousness not in a global broadcast or a higher-order thought but in a particular style of local brain activity.

The recurrent processing theory, associated with Victor Lamme, proposes that consciousness arises when signals do not merely flow forward through the sensory system but loop back, with higher areas sending activity back down to lower ones in sustained back-and-forth exchanges.

The idea is that a fast, purely forward sweep of processing can occur unconsciously, and that it is the recurrent, looping activity that turns processing into experience, even without any global broadcast to the front of the brain.

In systems terms the dividing line is dataflow topology: a purely feedforward pipeline is unconscious no matter how deep, and experience begins when the pipeline acquires feedback connections, with the first forward sweep completing within very roughly 100 to 150 milliseconds and recurrence developing after it.

A related and broader family are the predictive-self accounts, which grow out of the idea that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine constantly generating a model of the world and of the body.

On these views, consciousness is bound up with the brain's best current model, and in particular with its model of itself as an embodied agent, so that the felt self is a kind of controlled construction the brain builds to make sense of its own states.

These accounts are attractive because they connect consciousness to the wider predictive-processing framework used elsewhere in cognitive science, and because they naturally include the body and the emotions in the story.

They remain, like all the theories here, incomplete and debated, and part of their value is in widening the range of serious options beyond the two or three most famous theories.


44.3 The empirical programme

Theories are only science if they can be tested against evidence, and this section describes how researchers hunt for the fingerprints of consciousness in the brain and how they have tried to referee the disputes between theories fairly.


44.3.1 The search for the neural correlates of consciousness

A neural correlate of consciousness is the minimal brain activity that is sufficient for a specific conscious experience.

The research strategy, pioneered in part by Francis Crick and Christof Koch in the 1990s, is to hold everything else fixed and find just the brain events that differ when a person is aware of something versus not aware of it.

A favourite tool is to use a stimulus that stays physically constant but is sometimes seen and sometimes not, such as an image shown so briefly it is caught only on some trials, or rivalrous images that flip in and out of awareness, and then to compare brain activity between the aware and unaware cases.

The goal is to subtract away everything that is the same and leave only the neural signature of the experience itself.

In systems terms this is differential debugging: the experimenter holds the input constant, observes the internal trace on aware and unaware runs, and diffs the traces to isolate the component that co-varies with awareness rather than with the input.

This programme has been productive but also harder than it first looked, and a major complication is exactly the report problem discussed in the previous chapter: some of the brain activity that seemed to mark consciousness turned out to reflect the act of reporting or attending rather than the experience, which is why no-report methods became so important.

As a result, researchers now try hard to distinguish the true correlates of an experience from its mere preconditions, such as attention, and its consequences, such as thinking about it and reporting it, and this refinement is a real advance even though a definitive neural correlate has not been pinned down.


44.3.2 Adversarial collaboration as a method for a contested field

When a field is full of committed rival camps, ordinary studies rarely change anyone's mind, because each side interprets ambiguous results in its own favour.

Adversarial collaboration is a method designed to break that deadlock, and it is a genuinely admirable piece of scientific practice worth understanding.

In an adversarial collaboration, the proponents of competing theories sit down together, in advance, and agree on exactly what experiment to run and, crucially, on what results would count as a point for each theory and what results would embarrass it.

Because the predictions and their interpretation are locked in before any data are collected, in a public preregistration, neither side can move the goalposts afterward.

A large effort of this kind, run by a consortium called Cogitate, pitted global neuronal workspace theory against integrated information theory, with the theories' own leading advocates helping design the test.

Around two hundred and fifty six participants viewed images while their brain activity was recorded with several methods at once, and the results, published in the journal Nature in 2025, were mixed for both theories rather than a clean victory for either.

The findings included evidence that information about what a person was consciously seeing could be decoded from the back of the brain, and a relative lack of the sustained prefrontal ignition that the global workspace theory had predicted, which was awkward for that theory, while integrated information theory was challenged by the absence of the sustained posterior synchronisation it had predicted.

In systems terms the two camps had committed to different observable signatures, a frontal broadcast event for the workspace theory and sustained posterior synchronisation for the integration theory, and the recorded traces matched neither signature cleanly.

Neither theory was confirmed or refuted outright, and that ambiguous outcome is itself instructive, because it shows how genuinely unsettled the science of consciousness remains.

The deeper lesson for a beginner is about method: when a question is hard and opinions are entrenched, agreeing in advance on how you could be proven wrong is one of the most honest things science can do.


44.4 The functions of consciousness

Having asked what consciousness is and how to study it, this final section asks what it is good for, that is, what jobs awareness might do that unconscious processing cannot, while remembering that even this is debated.


44.4.1 Access, flexible control, and integration

The most widely supported view of what consciousness does is that it makes information globally available so the whole mind can use it flexibly.

Unconscious processes, as earlier chapters showed, tend to be specialised, fast, and rigid, each doing its own narrow job, whereas consciousness seems to pool information from many sources into a common form that any system can draw on.

This pooling is thought to support flexible, novel, and deliberate behaviour, the kind that cannot run on a fixed habit, which fits the global workspace idea that broadcasting is the core function.

Consciousness is also linked to integration, the binding together of many separate features, such as a colour, a shape, a sound, and a meaning, into a single unified experience of one object or scene rather than a jumble of disconnected parts.

In systems terms the proposed function is a shared bus: specialised modules that normally cannot read each other's outputs gain a common channel, at the price of a severe bandwidth limit, since the workspace holds roughly one content at a time.

On this account, the value of being conscious of something is that it becomes usable by reasoning, language, memory, and planning together, so awareness is the shared workspace where otherwise isolated processes meet.

An important honesty check remains, though, because so much turns out to be doable unconsciously that some researchers question how much extra work consciousness really performs, and pinning down its unique contribution is still an open problem rather than a solved one.


44.4.2 Volition and the sense of agency

The last topic is the feeling that you are the author of your own actions, which is one of the most personally important aspects of conscious life.

The sense of agency is the experience that you are the one causing your actions, that it is you who decides to raise your hand and you who moves it.

This feeling became scientifically famous through experiments by Benjamin Libet in the 1980s.

Libet asked people to make a simple spontaneous movement whenever they felt like it and to note the moment they were first aware of the urge, while he recorded a slow build-up of brain activity called the readiness potential.

His striking result was that the readiness potential seemed to begin before the reported moment of conscious intention, which many took to mean the brain had already started the action before the person consciously decided, appearing to threaten the idea of conscious free will.

The reported timings are worth stating plainly: in Libet's data the readiness potential began roughly 550 milliseconds before the movement, while the reported conscious urge came only about 200 milliseconds before it, leaving a gap of roughly 350 milliseconds in which the brain seemed already under way.

These experiments provoked decades of argument, and the modern verdict is much more cautious than the original headlines.

Later work questioned what the readiness potential actually is, with some evidence suggesting it may partly reflect ordinary background fluctuations in brain activity rather than a specific decision command, and questioned whether the timing of a fuzzy inner urge can be measured accurately at all.

Some studies also found that the readiness potential appears before arbitrary, unimportant choices but not clearly before deliberate, considered decisions, which weakens the leap from Libet's simple finger movements to meaningful human choice.

The careful conclusion today is that Libet's experiments revealed something real and interesting about the timing of awareness and action, but they did not settle the deep questions of free will, and the confident early claim that they disproved conscious agency has not held up.

It is fitting that this outline of cognition ends here, at the sense of agency, because the feeling of being a self who chooses is where the machinery of the mind and the mystery of the person meet, and it is exactly the frontier where the science of human cognition begins to matter for how we think about minds we might one day build.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Candidate contents, as activated representations from perception, memory, emotion, and inner speech, each carried by a coalition of processors.

◦ Attention signals, which amplify some coalitions and weaken others, from the attention system.

◦ Arousal and neuromodulatory state, which sets the global level of consciousness, from brainstem and thalamic systems.

◦ Predictions and self-model signals, from the predictive machinery, on the predictive-self accounts.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ The broadcast content, meaning the currently conscious representation, readable by reasoning, language, memory, planning, and voluntary action.

◦ Verbal and behavioural reports of experience, consumed by other people and by experimenters.

◦ A sense of agency signal accompanying self-caused actions, consumed by self-monitoring and social cognition.

◦ Global state indicators, such as being awake, dreaming, or anaesthetised, observable in physiology.

• STATE.

◦ The current occupant of the workspace, roughly one integrated content at a time.

◦ The current global level, from alert wakefulness through sleep stages to anaesthesia and coma.

◦ The ongoing self-model, including body and agency representations.

◦ The strengths of the competing coalitions not currently broadcast.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ The ignition threshold that a coalition must cross to achieve global broadcast.

◦ Workspace capacity, severely limited, roughly one content at a time.

◦ Amplification gain from attention on candidate coalitions.

◦ The arousal setting that scales all workspace activity, from full wakefulness to none.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Ignition and reportable access, typically around 200 to 300 milliseconds after stimulus onset in the supporting experiments.

◦ The unconscious feedforward sweep preceding any recurrence, very roughly 100 to 150 milliseconds.

◦ In Libet's paradigm, readiness potential onset roughly 550 milliseconds before movement and the reported conscious urge about 200 milliseconds before it.

◦ Changes of global level, minutes to hours for sleep and anaesthesia transitions.

◦ The duration of a single conscious moment, REFUSED, because proposals range from tens to hundreds of milliseconds and the field has not converged on one value.

• MODES.

◦ Wakeful broadcast mode, where competition and ignition run normally; the default alert state.

◦ Dreaming mode, where internally generated coalitions win access with the senses gated; triggered by rapid eye movement sleep physiology.

◦ Reduced or absent modes, in dreamless sleep, anaesthesia, and coma; triggered by arousal system shutdown or disruption.

◦ Within wakefulness, seen versus unseen processing of a given stimulus, switched by whether its coalition crosses the ignition threshold.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Failures of access, as in masking, inattentional blindness, and the attentional blink of about 200 to 500 milliseconds, where content is processed but never broadcast.

◦ Disorders of consciousness, including the vegetative and minimally conscious states, where level is pathologically reduced.

◦ Neglect and blindsight, where content influences behaviour without entering awareness.

◦ Illusions of agency and alien-limb phenomena, where the authorship signal is attached wrongly or missing.

◦ At the level of theory, the field's own failure mode: mistaking the machinery of reporting for the machinery of experiencing.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary called coalitions mapping each coalition name to its starting activation.
Create a number variable called ignition threshold with initial value one.
Create a variable called broadcast with initial value none.
For each time step from one to the step limit, do the following.
    For each coalition in the dictionary, do the following.
        Increase the coalition's activation by a small self-excitation proportional to its activation.
        Decrease the coalition's activation by a small inhibition proportional to the total activation of the other coalitions.
        Add small random noise to the coalition's activation.
        If the coalition's activation is less than zero, set it to zero.
    Find the coalition with the highest activation.
    If that coalition's activation is greater than the ignition threshold, set broadcast to that coalition's name and stop the loop.
If broadcast is none, report that no content reached awareness.
Otherwise, report that the broadcast content is available to all modules.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Load the random module for noise generation.
import random

# Define a function where competing coalitions race for access to a global workspace.
def workspace_race(coalitions, steps=200):
    # Create a number variable called threshold for ignition with value one.
    threshold = 1.0
    # For each time step up to the step limit, do the following.
    for step in range(1, steps + 1):
        # Calculate the total activation across all coalitions.
        total = sum(coalitions.values())
        # For each coalition name in the dictionary, do the following.
        for name in coalitions:
            # Increase the coalition's activation by ten percent self-excitation.
            gain = 0.10 * coalitions[name]
            # Decrease the coalition's activation by inhibition from its rivals.
            loss = 0.04 * (total - coalitions[name])
            # Add small gaussian noise to the coalition's activation.
            noise = random.gauss(0.0, 0.01)
            # Update the coalition's activation and keep it at zero or above.
            coalitions[name] = max(0.0, coalitions[name] + gain - loss + noise)
        # Find the name of the coalition with the highest activation.
        leader = max(coalitions, key=coalitions.get)
        # If the leader's activation crosses the ignition threshold, broadcast it.
        if coalitions[leader] > threshold:
            # Return the winning content and the time step of ignition.
            return leader, step
    # If no coalition ignited within the step limit, return none.
    return None, steps

# Seed the random generator so the run is repeatable.
random.seed(7)
# Create three competing coalitions with different starting activations.
contenders = {"face_percept": 0.30, "inner_speech": 0.25, "background_hum": 0.20}
# Run the race for access to the workspace.
winner, when = workspace_race(contenders)
# If a coalition ignited, print the broadcast content and its ignition time step.
if winner is not None:
    # Announce the globally broadcast content.
    print("broadcast:", winner, "at step", when)
# Otherwise, print that no content reached awareness.
else:
    # Announce the failure of access.
    print("no content reached awareness")
