Distributed cognition is the view that a cognitive process can be carried by a system made up of several people together with their tools and representations, no one of whom holds the whole process in their own head.

Hutchins showed that navigating the ship is accomplished by a team in which each person handles one part, information passes between them and through instruments, charts, and written records, and the successful navigation is a property of the whole system rather than of any single mind.

The tools themselves, such as the chart and the compass, carry part of the cognitive load, storing and transforming information that would otherwise have to be held in a head.

In systems terms, the ship's navigation team is a pipeline of processors connected by communication channels and shared external memories, and the computation is defined over the whole pipeline, with each hand-off taking seconds and the full fix cycle repeating on the order of minutes.

The phrase in the wild signals the study of thinking as it really happens in the messy world of work, rather than in the tidy isolation of the laboratory.

This view reframes many everyday achievements, from flying an airliner to running a hospital, as feats of distributed rather than individual cognition, and it suggests that designing good tools and good teamwork is a way of designing intelligence itself.


52.3.3 Collective intelligence

This sub-section covers the question of whether groups, as groups, can be more or less intelligent, in a way that parallels individual intelligence.

Collective intelligence refers to the ability of a group to perform well across a wide range of tasks, considered as a property of the group rather than of any single member.

In an influential 2010 study, the researcher Anita Williams Woolley and colleagues found that groups show a measurable general ability factor, sometimes called a c factor, so that a team that does well on one kind of task tends to do well on others, much as an individual's g predicts across tasks.

Strikingly, this collective ability was not well predicted by the average intelligence of the members or by the smartest member.

Instead it was linked to how the group interacted: to members taking turns rather than a few dominating, to the social sensitivity of the members in reading one another, and, in that study, to the proportion of women in the group, which the authors traced largely to higher average social sensitivity.

In systems terms, group intelligence depends less on the power of the individual processors and more on the bandwidth and scheduling of the channels between them: turn-taking is a fair scheduler, and social sensitivity is accurate reading of the other processors' states.

The finding suggests that making a group smart is partly a separate problem from making an individual smart, and that how people communicate and share the floor can matter more than raw individual horsepower.

Like much in this young area the results continue to be tested and refined, but the core idea, that intelligence can be a feature of a collective, fits naturally with the distributed view of mind and closes this survey of human cognition on the theme with which it is most concerned: that human thought is, at bottom, a shared and cumulative achievement.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Demonstrations and teaching: observed procedures, pedagogical signals such as eye contact and special tone, and explicit instruction, from other people.

◦ The inherited repertoire: the tools, techniques, symbols, and language passed down by the previous generation.

◦ The immediate situation: the concrete particulars of the setting, read moment to moment by the sense-act loop.

◦ Messages and readings from teammates and instruments in a distributed system.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Faithful reproductions of procedures, consumed by the next learner and by the ratchet.

◦ Innovations: small improvements added to the repertoire, consumed by the group's shared stock.

◦ External representations: marks on charts, written records, and tool states, consumed by other members of the distributed system and by one's own future self.

◦ Group-level task performance, the c factor's observable output, consumed by whoever the team serves.

• STATE.

◦ The group's accumulated cultural repertoire, held redundantly across many heads and many artefacts.

◦ Each learner's position in the zone of proximal development, the moving boundary between unaided and aided competence.

◦ The stage of internalisation of each regulated skill, from social speech through private speech to inner speech.

◦ The contents of shared external memories: charts, logs, displays, and records.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Transmission fidelity: how exactly a procedure survives one teaching hand-off, the parameter the ratchet depends on.

◦ Innovation rate: how often a generation adds an improvement.

◦ Scaffolding gain: how much support the helper supplies, tuned downward as competence rises.

◦ Communication structure: turn-taking equality and members' social sensitivity, the predictors of the c factor.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ The sense-act loop of situated action runs at the pace of the environment, on the order of hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per cycle.

◦ Hand-offs in a distributed team take seconds, with full task cycles such as a navigational fix on the order of minutes.

◦ Scaffolded learning within the zone of proximal development unfolds over days to months of sessions.

◦ Internalisation of speech into inner speech takes years of early childhood.

◦ The cultural ratchet advances per generation, and gene-culture coevolution such as the spread of adult milk digestion took thousands of years.

◦ The decay rate of a group's unwritten shared knowledge: REFUSED, because it depends on turnover and practice in ways the literature does not reduce to one honest value.

• MODES.

◦ Emulation mode, copying goals only, versus imitation mode, copying full procedures; imitation is triggered in humans by pedagogical cues and social context.

◦ Aided mode inside the zone of proximal development versus independent mode outside it, switched by the withdrawal of scaffolding.

◦ Social speech, private speech, and inner speech as successive operating modes of self-regulation.

◦ Individual computation versus distributed computation, switched by task scale: when the task exceeds one head's capacity, the system must distribute across people and tools.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Ratchet slippage: knowledge lost when transmission fidelity drops, as in small isolated populations losing technologies.

◦ Overimitation of superfluous steps, and cascading copying of errors.

◦ Scaffolding failures: help withdrawn too soon, leaving the learner stranded, or too late, blocking independence.

◦ Distributed breakdowns: miscommunication between members, stale or wrong external records, and single points of failure in the pipeline.

◦ Group pathologies that lower the c factor: domination of the floor by a few members and poor reading of others' states.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called shared memory that both agents can read and write, initially empty.
Create a list variable called clues holding the full set of puzzle clues.
Give the first agent only the first half of the clues.
Give the second agent only the second half of the clues.
For each round, do the following.
    For each agent, do the following.
        For each clue the agent holds, do the following.
            If the clue is not yet in the shared memory, then write the clue to the shared memory.
        Read all clues currently in the shared memory.
        If the clues read from the shared memory cover the full set, then declare the puzzle solved by this agent.
    If the puzzle is solved, then stop the rounds.
Check whether either agent could have covered the full set from its private clues alone.
Report that neither agent alone succeeds and that the pair with the shared memory succeeds.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create the full secret code that the team must reconstruct, as a list of six numbered clues.
full_code = [(i, "clue" + str(i)) for i in range(6)]

# Give agent one only the even-numbered clues, a limited private memory.
agent1_clues = [c for c in full_code if c[0] % 2 == 0]

# Give agent two only the odd-numbered clues, a different limited private memory.
agent2_clues = [c for c in full_code if c[0] % 2 == 1]

# Create the shared external memory, an initially empty whiteboard both agents can use.
whiteboard = []

# Define a function that tests whether a set of clues covers the whole code.
def solved(clues):
    # Return whether the set of clue numbers equals the full required set.
    return set(i for i, _ in clues) == set(i for i, _ in full_code)

# Print whether agent one alone can solve the puzzle from private memory.
print("agent1 alone:", solved(agent1_clues))

# Print whether agent two alone can solve the puzzle from private memory.
print("agent2 alone:", solved(agent2_clues))

# Repeat for up to five rounds of taking turns at the whiteboard.
for rnd in range(5):
    # Let each agent take a turn with its own private clues.
    for name, private in (("agent1", agent1_clues), ("agent2", agent2_clues)):
        # For each clue the agent privately holds, share it if it is new.
        for clue in private:
            # If the clue is not yet on the whiteboard, write it there.
            if clue not in whiteboard:
                # Append the clue to the shared external memory.
                whiteboard.append(clue)
        # Read the whiteboard and check whether the combined record solves the puzzle.
        if solved(whiteboard):
            # Print which agent completed the solution and in which round.
            print(name, "completes the code in round", rnd, "using the whiteboard")
            # Stop the loop over agents because the task is done.
            break
    # If the whiteboard now holds the full code, stop the rounds.
    if solved(whiteboard):
        # Leave the round loop because the distributed system has solved the task.
        break

# Print the final size of the shared memory, the part of the thinking held outside both heads.
print("clues held in shared memory:", len(whiteboard))

PART THIRTEEN. THE COMPUTATIONAL FRAMEWORKS OF MIND

================================================================================

CHAPTER 53. RATIONAL ANALYSIS AND THE BAYESIAN BRAIN (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter is about a big and hopeful idea: that a great deal of what the mind does can be understood as trying to do the smartest possible thing given the situation it is in.

Instead of starting with the wiring of the brain, this way of thinking starts with the problem the mind is trying to solve, and asks what the best solution to that problem would look like.

The word "framework" in the chapter title means a way of thinking and a set of mathematical tools, rather than a single fact or a single experiment.

The particular tools here come from probability, which is the branch of mathematics that deals with uncertainty, with how strongly we should believe things when we cannot be sure.

Seen as an engineered system, this framework is unusual because it IS an algorithm: it specifies inputs, which are evidence from the world, an internal state, which is a set of graded beliefs, and an update rule, which is Bayes' theorem, that maps the old state plus new evidence to a new state.

By the end of the chapter you should understand what "rational analysis" is, what people mean when they call the brain "Bayesian," and why many researchers find this one of the most powerful lenses we have on thinking, while others remain skeptical.


53.1 Rational analysis

Rational analysis is a recipe for building theories of the mind by asking what a well-designed mind ought to do, and then checking whether real people do that.

The key move is to look outward at the world before looking inward at the head, because a mind that works well is a mind that fits the world it lives in.


53.1.1 The rational-analysis method and the role of the environment

Rational analysis is a method introduced by the psychologist John Anderson around 1990, in a book called The Adaptive Character of Thought.

The core claim is simple to state: the mind is adaptive, meaning it has been shaped by evolution and by learning to do a good job in the environment it actually faces.

So if you want to understand why the mind behaves a certain way, you should first understand the problem the environment sets, and then work out what the best behaviour would be.

Anderson laid this out as a series of steps, which are worth walking through slowly because they are the heart of the whole approach, and because they read exactly like a systems engineering loop of specify, model, derive, test, and revise.

First, you state precisely what the mind is trying to achieve, that is, its goal.

Second, you build a careful, formal description of the environment, meaning the structure of the world the mind is adapted to, including which events are common and which are rare.

Third, you make only the smallest necessary assumptions about the mind's internal limits, such as limits on speed or memory, so that the environment does most of the explaining.

Fourth, you work out mathematically what the best possible behaviour would be, given the goal, the environment, and those minimal limits.

Fifth, you compare that ideal behaviour against what real people actually do in experiments.

Sixth, if the prediction is wrong, you go back and revise your description of the goal or the environment, and try again.

The word "optimal" appears a lot in this area, and it simply means the best possible given the circumstances, not perfect in some absolute sense.

A helpful way to see the role of the environment is an example about memory that Anderson made famous.

Your memory seems to make some things easy to recall and other things hard, and at first this can look like a flaw.

But Anderson pointed out that the things you have encountered recently, or encountered often, are exactly the things you are statistically most likely to need again soon.

So a memory system that makes recent and frequent items easiest to retrieve is not being lazy; it is betting sensibly on the future based on the pattern of the past.

The environment, in this example, is the statistics of when information tends to be needed, and the mind's behaviour turns out to match those statistics remarkably well.

In systems terms, the method takes as input a formal model of environmental statistics plus a goal function, produces as output a predicted behaviour curve, and runs on the timescale of theory building rather than of the behaving mind itself.

This is the signature of rational analysis: a puzzling quirk of the mind becomes sensible once you look at the shape of the world the mind is solving for.

It is worth being honest about a limitation that critics have raised.

Because the method lets you revise your description of the environment when a prediction fails, a determined theorist can sometimes make almost any behaviour look "rational" after the fact, which weakens the claim.

The best practitioners guard against this by fixing the environment description in advance using independent data about the world, rather than tuning it to fit the very behaviour they are trying to explain.


53.1.2 Rational models of memory, categorisation, and inference

Anderson did not leave rational analysis as an abstract slogan; he applied it in detail to several specific mental abilities, and this sub-section walks through them.

The first is memory, which we have just met.

The rational model of memory treats remembering as a prediction problem: at each moment the mind estimates the probability that a given piece of information will be needed, and it prioritises retrieval accordingly.

As a system, this memory model subscribes to a history of past uses of each item, publishes a need probability for each item, and its characteristic timescale is the slow power-law decay of that probability over hours, days, and years of disuse.

This single idea reproduces several well-known laws of memory, such as the fact that items seen more recently and more frequently are recalled better, because those really are the items most likely to be relevant, given how information tends to recur in everyday life.

The second application is categorisation, which is the mental act of sorting things into kinds, such as deciding that a new animal is a dog.

The rational model of categorisation treats this as guessing which hidden category best explains the thing in front of you, and using that guess to predict the thing's other, unseen properties.

Rather than storing one fixed definition of "dog," the model builds up clusters from experience and asks which cluster a new item most probably belongs to, which nicely handles the fact that real categories have fuzzy, graded membership.

Its systems reading: inputs are observed features of a new item, state is a growing set of learned clusters with their statistics, and output is a probability for each cluster plus predictions of the item's unseen properties, delivered within the second or so a categorisation judgment takes.

The third application is causal inference, which is working out what causes what, for example learning that a certain plant makes you ill.

The rational model treats this as estimating, from your history of observations, how strongly one thing raises or lowers the probability of another.

Here the input is a running table of co-occurrences between candidate cause and effect, the state is a graded belief about causal strength, and the output is a prediction of the effect given an intervention, updated one observation at a time.

Across all three cases the pattern is identical: take a mental ability, describe the statistical problem the world poses, and show that human behaviour looks like a good statistical solution to that problem.

The lasting influence of this work is that it made "what is the mind optimally solving for" a respectable and productive question, and it fed directly into the broader Bayesian programme that the rest of this chapter describes.


53.2 The Bayesian programme

The Bayesian programme is the larger research movement that grew up around the idea that the mind is, at heart, an engine for reasoning under uncertainty.

Its name comes from Bayes' theorem, a rule from probability theory, and this section explains what that rule is and how it has been used to model thinking.


53.2.1 Bayes as a computational-level theory of induction

To understand this sub-section we first need the word "induction."

Induction means reasoning from limited evidence to a general conclusion, such as seeing a few white swans and forming a belief about swans in general.

Induction is hard because the evidence never fully pins down the answer, so you can only ever hold beliefs with some degree of confidence, never certainty.

This is exactly the kind of problem probability theory was built for, and Bayes' theorem is the specific rule for updating beliefs in the light of evidence.

Named after the Reverend Thomas Bayes, an eighteenth-century English clergyman and mathematician, the theorem tells you how to combine two things.

The first thing is your "prior," which is how strongly you believed each possibility before seeing the new evidence.

The second thing is the "likelihood," which is how well each possibility predicts the evidence you actually observed.

Multiply the prior by the likelihood, tidy up the numbers so they add to one, and you get the "posterior," which is your updated belief after seeing the evidence.

In plain words: sensible belief is a blend of what you expected beforehand and how surprising the new data would be under each explanation.

Read as a system, the update rule takes two input signals, a prior distribution and a likelihood function, holds no extra state beyond the current distribution, and publishes the posterior distribution, which then becomes the prior for the next round, an explicit feedback loop.

Now the phrase "computational-level theory" deserves unpacking, because it is doing careful work.

It refers to a distinction made by the vision scientist David Marr, who said you can describe a mental ability at three levels.

The computational level asks what problem is being solved and what the ideal solution is; the algorithmic level asks what steps and representations are used; and the implementation level asks how the brain physically carries it out.

To call Bayes a computational-level theory is to say it describes the problem of induction and its ideal solution, without yet claiming that neurons literally carry out Bayes' theorem step by step.

This is an important and honest caveat, because it means a Bayesian model can be a good description of what the mind achieves even if the brain reaches that achievement by some other, approximate route.

In systems terms the caveat says: the interface specification is claimed to be right, while the internal implementation is deliberately left open.


53.2.2 Hierarchical Bayesian models and learning to learn

A hierarchical Bayesian model is a Bayesian model with more than one level of belief stacked on top of each other, and this stacking turns out to explain something deep about human learning.

The word "hierarchical" here just means layered, with general beliefs sitting above more specific ones.

Picture a child learning words for kinds of things.

At the bottom level, the child learns specific facts, such as what a particular ball looks like.

At a higher level, the child can learn a general lesson about categories themselves, for example that objects of the same kind tend to share their shape more than their colour or size.

A hierarchical Bayesian model captures both levels at once, and the higher-level lesson then guides all future lower-level learning.

As a system, the lower level subscribes to raw examples and publishes beliefs about specific categories, while the upper level subscribes to those lower-level beliefs and publishes a learned prior back down, a two-way message-passing architecture in which the upper level changes on a slower timescale than the lower.

This gives rise to a striking and well-documented effect called "learning to learn," sometimes called forming an overhypothesis.

Learning to learn means that once you have grasped a general regularity, you can master each new specific case from far less evidence than before.

The child who has learned that "kinds go by shape" can learn a brand new word from a single example, because the higher-level knowledge tells her which features matter.

Researchers such as Joshua Tenenbaum, Charles Kemp, and their colleagues showed that hierarchical Bayesian models reproduce this pattern, and they even predict a surprising detail.

The detail is that the broad, abstract lesson can be learned before all the specific details are filled in, which matches the finding that young children show category biases before they have learned all their categories.

This mattered because a long-standing objection to statistical accounts of the mind was that children learn too fast, from too little data, to be mere statistics-gatherers.

Hierarchical models answer that objection by showing how abstract knowledge, itself learned statistically, can make later learning fast and data-thrifty.


53.2.3 Structured probabilistic knowledge: grammars, graphs, and programs

This sub-section makes a point that is easy to miss but very important: being Bayesian does not force you to think of knowledge as a flat list of probabilities.

The probabilities can be laid over rich, structured representations, and choosing the right structure is often where the real explanatory power lies.

The word "structure" here means the shape or organisation of the knowledge, the way its parts connect.

Three kinds of structure come up again and again in this literature.

The first is a graph, which in this technical sense means a set of nodes connected by links, used to show which things influence which others.

A causal graph, for instance, can represent your belief that clouds cause rain, with an arrow from cloud to rain, and probability theory then tells you how to reason over that graph.

The second is a grammar, which is a set of rules for building complex structures out of simpler parts, borrowed from the study of language.

A probabilistic grammar can capture the idea that thoughts, sentences, or even melodies are built by combining pieces according to rules, with probabilities attached to the choices.

The third and most general is a program, meaning a small piece of a step-by-step procedure that generates data.

In this view a concept can be represented as a little probabilistic program that, when run, produces examples of the concept, and learning the concept means inferring the program.

In systems terms, each structure choice fixes the data format of the hypothesis space over which the Bayesian update runs: the same update rule, different schemas for the state it updates.

The unifying insight, argued by researchers including Tenenbaum, Kemp, Thomas Griffiths, and Noah Goodman, is that human knowledge is both structured and probabilistic at the same time.

Structure captures the compositional, rule-like richness of thought, and probability captures our ability to cope with uncertainty and to learn from noisy, incomplete evidence.

The claim that these two ingredients belong together, rather than being rival visions of the mind, is one of the defining ideas of modern computational cognitive science.


53.3 The domains of Bayesian cognition

Having laid out the machinery, this section shows it at work in three concrete areas of thinking, so that the abstract ideas become tangible.

The pattern in each case is the same: take an everyday human ability, and show that people behave as if they were doing careful probabilistic reasoning.


53.3.1 Concept learning and the size principle

Concept learning means figuring out the meaning of a category, such as what counts as a "dog" or a "prime number," from examples.

A famous puzzle is that a few examples usually leave the answer wildly ambiguous, yet people converge on sensible meanings anyway.

Suppose someone points at a few numbers, say 16, 8, 2, and 64, and calls them all "blickets."

The examples fit many rules: powers of two, even numbers, numbers under a hundred, and so on, so how does a learner pick?

Tenenbaum's Bayesian model of concept learning, from the late 1990s, offered an elegant answer built on something called the size principle.

The size principle says that, all else equal, a narrower, more specific hypothesis should be preferred over a broader one when both fit the examples equally well.

The reasoning is that if the true category were the broad one, say "all even numbers," it would be a strange coincidence for every example you were shown to also happen to be a tidy power of two.

The narrow hypothesis "powers of two" predicts the actual examples much more strongly, so it earns a higher likelihood, and Bayes' theorem then favours it.

The mechanism is beautifully mechanical: if examples are assumed to be drawn at random from the true category, then each example has likelihood one divided by the size of the hypothesis, so a hypothesis containing 10 items assigns each example ten times the probability that a hypothesis containing 100 items does.

Crucially, this preference for the narrow hypothesis grows exponentially stronger with each additional example, because each new example that fits the narrow rule makes the broad rule's "coincidence" even more unlikely.

As a system, the learner subscribes to a stream of positive examples, holds as state a posterior weight over every candidate hypothesis, and publishes a generalisation probability for any queried new item, sharpening after every example.

This is a lovely result because it explains, in exact numbers, the human intuition that a run of suspiciously specific examples points to a specific rule.

It also shows how a Bayesian learner can generalise sensibly from just a handful of positive examples, without ever being told what does not count as a blicket.

The chapter's code sample below implements exactly this learner, with a small hierarchical touch: a prior that itself favours simple rules.


53.3.2 Intuitive physics as probabilistic simulation

Intuitive physics means the rough, automatic sense we all have of how physical objects will behave, such as knowing a leaning tower of blocks is about to topple.

You did not compute any equations to feel that; the understanding was fast, effortless, and approximate.

A leading account, developed by Peter Battaglia, Jessica Hamrick, Kevin Smith, Tomer Ullman, Tenenbaum and colleagues, proposes that the mind contains an "intuitive physics engine."

The comparison is to the physics engines inside video games, which are pieces of software that simulate how objects move, fall, and collide well enough to look right, without being perfectly accurate.

The proposal is that your mind runs a similar internal simulation: it imagines how a scene will unfold and reads off the likely outcome.

The probabilistic part is essential and clever.

Because you are never quite certain of the exact positions, weights, and speeds of things, the mind is thought to run the simulation several times with slightly different guesses about those details.

If most of the imagined runs end with the tower falling, you feel confident it will fall; if the runs disagree, you feel unsure.

The systems reading: input is a noisy percept of the scene, the process draws a handful of samples of the scene's uncertain parameters, runs a short forward simulation on each, and publishes an outcome distribution, all within roughly the first second of looking, since stability judgments are made at a glance.

This single idea accounts for a wide range of findings, including how people judge stability, how they predict where objects will land, and how their confidence tracks the genuine ambiguity of a scene.

It is a strong example of the Bayesian programme, because it treats a fast, intuitive human skill as approximate probabilistic reasoning over an internal model of the world.

It is worth noting that this remains an active research area, and some recent work argues that people also fall back on simpler shortcuts when full simulation would be too costly, which connects to the resource-rational ideas of the next chapter.


53.3.3 Intuitive psychology as inverse planning

Intuitive psychology, often called theory of mind, means our everyday ability to make sense of other people in terms of their beliefs and goals.

When you see someone hurry past the bus stop toward a shop, you effortlessly infer they wanted something from the shop more than they wanted the bus.

The Bayesian account of this ability, developed especially by Chris Baker, Rebecca Saxe, and Tenenbaum, is called inverse planning, and the name captures the idea neatly.

Planning, in this technical sense, means working forward from a goal to the actions that would achieve it: given that I want coffee, I walk to the cafe.

Inverse planning runs that logic backward: given that I saw you walk to the cafe, I infer that you probably wanted coffee.

More precisely, the model assumes that people are roughly rational agents who choose actions that tend to achieve their goals, and then it uses Bayes' theorem to work out which goals and beliefs best explain the actions you observed.

The framework rests on the tools of decision-making under uncertainty, in which an agent with goals picks actions to reach them, and the observer inverts that process to recover the hidden goals.

In systems terms, the observer subscribes to a stream of observed actions, holds a forward model of rational planning as fixed machinery plus a posterior over candidate goals as state, and publishes a running goal estimate that is revised action by action as the other person's path unfolds.

This account is attractive because it explains not just single guesses but the whole graded pattern of our social inferences, including how we revise our guess about someone's goal as their path unfolds.

Recent work has begun to join intuitive psychology and intuitive physics together, so that an observer reasons about what someone wants while also reasoning about the physical world that person is acting in, which is closer to how real social understanding works.


53.4 Bayes at the neural level

So far Bayes has been a description of what the mind achieves, at Marr's computational level.

This section turns to the harder question of how a brain made of neurons could actually carry out anything like probabilistic reasoning.

Two main proposals compete, and they make different bets about what the noisiness of the brain is for.


53.4.1 Probabilistic population codes

To understand this we need the idea of a population code.

A population code means representing something not with a single cell but with the combined pattern of activity across a whole group, or population, of neurons.

For example, the direction of a moving object might be encoded by which cells in a group fire most strongly and how strongly, rather than by any one cell alone.

A probabilistic population code, developed by Wei Ji Ma, Jeff Beck, Peter Latham, Alexandre Pouget and colleagues around 2006, adds a crucial twist.

The twist is that the population does not just signal a single best guess; it automatically represents a whole probability distribution, that is, a spread of how likely each possible value is.

The clever part is that the natural variability of neurons, the fact that they fire a slightly different number of spikes each time, is not treated as a nuisance to be averaged away.

Instead, that variability is exactly what carries the information about uncertainty: broadly speaking, a stronger and crisper burst of population activity signals a more confident, narrower estimate, and a weaker one signals more doubt.

A further attractive feature is that, under this scheme, combining two sources of evidence in the statistically correct way turns out to correspond to simply adding the two populations' activity together, which is something neurons can plausibly do.

The systems reading: the input is a sensory drive, the output at every instant is a full distribution encoded in the population's firing pattern, and the combination operation is a parallel add, running at the timescale of neural integration, tens of milliseconds.

So probabilistic population codes offer a concrete story in which representing and combining uncertainty falls naturally out of ordinary neural machinery.


53.4.2 Sampling against parametric representations of uncertainty

This sub-section lays out the main rival to the population-code story, and the debate between them.

The two proposals differ in what a moment of neural activity is taken to represent.

The population-code view just described is often called parametric, meaning the neural activity at any instant encodes the full probability distribution all at once, spelled out in its shape.

The sampling view, developed by researchers including Jozsef Fiser, Pietro Berkes, Gergo Orban, and Mate Lengyel, proposes something quite different.

On the sampling view, the brain represents a probability distribution not by holding it whole at every instant, but by drawing examples from it one after another over time.

An analogy helps: if you want to describe the range of heights in a city, you could either write down the full curve of how common each height is, which is the parametric way, or you could just call out a series of individual people's heights, which is the sampling way, letting the pattern emerge over the sequence.

On this account the moment-to-moment fluctuation of neural activity is not noise around a fixed answer; it is the brain trying out different possibilities, each fluctuation a fresh sample from its beliefs.

The two views make different systems predictions: the parametric view says uncertainty is available in a single read of the population, so confidence should be usable almost instantly, while the sampling view says uncertainty accumulates over a sequence of samples, so confidence should sharpen with time and judgments made under time pressure should be more variable.

Each view has appeal.

The parametric view explains how the brain can combine and act on uncertainty instantly, while the sampling view explains why neural activity is so variable and why our own judgments seem to fluctuate as if we were drawing from a distribution.

The honest current state of the science is that this is unsettled, and interestingly some recent analyses suggest the two views may not be as opposed as they first seemed, since certain sampling schemes can be read as producing a kind of population code.

For a beginner, the key point to carry away is that there is a genuine, live scientific question here, and researchers have not yet agreed on how, or even whether, the brain literally implements probabilistic reasoning.


53.5 The process-model question

This final section confronts a gap that runs through the whole chapter.

The gap is between saying what the ideal answer is, at the computational level, and saying how a real, limited mind actually reaches an answer in real time, which is the level of process.


53.5.1 Rational process models and sampling algorithms in the mind

A process model is a theory of the actual steps a mind takes, moment by moment, as opposed to just the ideal outcome it approximates.

This matters because exact Bayesian reasoning is usually far too hard to compute in full; the number of possibilities to weigh can be astronomically large.

So if the mind is even roughly Bayesian, it cannot be doing the exact calculation; it must be using some shortcut that lands close enough.

A leading idea is that the mind uses sampling algorithms, which are methods that approximate a probability distribution by drawing a manageable number of examples from it rather than considering every possibility.

Statisticians and computer scientists rely on exactly these methods, under names such as Monte Carlo methods, precisely because they make otherwise impossible probability calculations practical.

The proposal, developed by Griffiths, Tenenbaum, Ed Vul, Goodman and others, is that the mind does something similar, and that this explains features of human thought that look irrational at first.

For instance, our guesses are noticeably variable, we give somewhat different answers to the same question on different occasions, and sampling predicts exactly this kind of scatter.

There is even a striking analysis by Vul, Goodman, Griffiths, and Tenenbaum showing that, when thinking is costly, it can be sensible to base a decision on just one or a very few samples rather than many.

This reframes what looks like sloppiness as a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and effort, and it ties the Bayesian programme directly to the resource-rational ideas of the next chapter.

In systems terms, a rational process model replaces the ideal update rule with an anytime approximation: an algorithm whose answer improves with every sample drawn, and which can be interrupted at any moment to act on the best answer so far.

So rational process models try to keep the successes of the Bayesian computational-level story while facing up to the fact that real minds must approximate, and they propose sampling as the bridge.


53.5.2 The probabilistic language of thought

The probabilistic language of thought is an ambitious attempt to bring together the two big themes we have seen: rich, structured, program-like knowledge, and probabilistic reasoning under uncertainty.

The older phrase "language of thought," from the philosopher Jerry Fodor, is the idea that thinking happens in an internal, language-like system with words and grammar of its own, so that thoughts are built from parts according to rules, much as sentences are.

The probabilistic version, developed by Goodman, Tenenbaum, and colleagues, says that this internal language is one for writing little probabilistic programs.

A probabilistic program, recall, is a short procedure that generates data with some randomness built in, so that running it produces not one fixed output but a range of possible outputs with different likelihoods.

On this view a concept is a program that can generate examples of itself, a belief about the world is a program that generates possible observations, and reasoning is running and inverting these programs.

To make this concrete and testable, researchers built an actual computer programming language for it, called Church, named in honour of the logician Alonzo Church.

Church and its successors let scientists write down a candidate mental model as real code, run it, and compare its behaviour against what people do, which turns philosophical proposals into precise, checkable predictions.

The appeal of the probabilistic language of thought is that it promises the best of both worlds at last: the compositional, unlimited creativity of structured symbolic thought, and the graceful handling of uncertainty that probability provides.

Whether the human mind really works this way is far from settled, and the framework is demanding to test, but it stands as one of the most complete visions on offer for how a single system could be both structured and probabilistic.

Notice how naturally the systems approach fits here: on this account the mind is literally a runtime for probabilistic programs, so describing cognition as software is not a metaphor but the theory itself.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Evidence stream: discrete observations or examples from the environment, such as labelled examples of a concept, sensory measurements, or another agent's observed actions.

◦ Hypothesis space: a structured set of candidate explanations, formatted as rules, causal graphs, grammars, or probabilistic programs, supplied by long-term knowledge.

◦ Prior distribution: a weighting over the hypothesis space, supplied either innately, by earlier learning, or by a higher level of a hierarchical model.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Posterior distribution: an updated weighting over hypotheses, consumed by decision, action, and language systems and fed back as the next round's prior.

◦ Generalisation judgments: the probability that a new item belongs to the learned concept, consumed by categorisation and prediction processes.

◦ Confidence signal: the spread of the posterior, consumed by metacognition and by the stopping rules of the next chapter.

• STATE.

◦ The current posterior over hypotheses, carried forward between observations.

◦ In hierarchical models, one posterior per level, with upper levels acting as learned priors for lower levels.

◦ In sampling process models, the current set of drawn samples standing in for the full distribution.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Hypothesis space size and structure: how many candidate explanations are entertained and in what format.

◦ Prior strength: how much evidence is needed to overturn initial beliefs.

◦ Likelihood model: the assumed process generating examples, for instance random sampling from the true concept, which is what produces the size principle.

◦ Sample count: in process models, how many samples are drawn before acting, often as low as one to a few.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ A single Bayesian belief update in perception operates within the timescale of a perceptual judgment, on the order of a few hundred milliseconds, as in cue-combination experiments.

◦ Hierarchical overhypothesis learning operates over developmental time, from days to years, as in children learning the shape bias during the second year of life.

◦ The number of internal simulation runs or samples behind an intuitive judgment: REFUSED, because the literature infers few samples indirectly and gives no agreed per-sample duration.

◦ The neural implementation timescale under the parametric versus sampling debate: REFUSED, because the two accounts assign different meanings to the same tens-of-milliseconds fluctuations and the question is unsettled.

• MODES.

◦ Exact inference mode: small hypothesis spaces are updated in full, triggered when the space is enumerable, as in simple concept games.

◦ Approximate sampling mode: large spaces are handled by drawing a few samples, triggered when full enumeration is intractable, which is the normal case.

◦ Learning mode against exploitation mode: early evidence reshapes the posterior strongly, while a sharply peaked posterior makes the system behave as if it held a fixed rule, the transition being driven by accumulated evidence.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Wrong priors: with a mistaken prior the update is faithful but the conclusions are wrong, as in stubborn belief perseverance.

◦ Wrong hypothesis space: the true explanation is never considered, so no amount of evidence can find it.

◦ Few-sample noise: decisions based on one or two samples are variable and occasionally wildly off, which reads as probability matching and inconsistent judgment.

◦ Unfalsifiability at the theory level: the rational analyst can redescribe the environment until any behaviour looks optimal, a failure of the method rather than the mind.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called hypotheses containing each candidate rule, its set of members, and its prior probability.
Create a list variable called examples containing the observed positive examples.
For each hypothesis in hypotheses, set its posterior to its prior probability.
For each example in examples,
    For each hypothesis in hypotheses,
        If the example is a member of the hypothesis set,
            Multiply the hypothesis posterior by one divided by the size of the hypothesis set.
        Otherwise,
            Set the hypothesis posterior to zero.
Create a number variable called total with initial value zero.
For each hypothesis in hypotheses, add the hypothesis posterior to total.
For each hypothesis in hypotheses, divide the hypothesis posterior by total.
Create a number variable called generalisation with initial value zero.
For each hypothesis in hypotheses,
    If the query item is a member of the hypothesis set,
        Add the hypothesis posterior to generalisation.
Return generalisation as the probability that the query item belongs to the concept.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a dictionary mapping each hypothesis name to its set of members from one to one hundred.
hypotheses = {
    # Set powers of two to the numbers two, four, eight, up to sixty four.
    "powers of two": {2 ** k for k in range(1, 7)},
    # Set even numbers to every second number from two to one hundred.
    "even numbers": set(range(2, 101, 2)),
    # Set multiples of four to every fourth number from four to one hundred.
    "multiples of four": set(range(4, 101, 4)),
    # Set numbers under fifty to the numbers one to forty nine.
    "numbers under fifty": set(range(1, 50)),
}

# Create a dictionary of priors that favours simpler, broader rules slightly.
priors = {"powers of two": 0.2, "even numbers": 0.4,
          "multiples of four": 0.2, "numbers under fifty": 0.2}

# Define a function that returns the posterior after seeing the examples.
def learn(examples):
    # Create an empty dictionary called posterior.
    posterior = {}
    # For each hypothesis name and member set in the hypotheses dictionary,
    for name, members in hypotheses.items():
        # Set the score to the prior probability of the hypothesis.
        score = priors[name]
        # For each example in the examples list,
        for x in examples:
            # If the example is in the member set, apply the size principle, otherwise set the score to zero.
            score = score * (1.0 / len(members)) if x in members else 0.0
        # Store the score under the hypothesis name.
        posterior[name] = score
    # Set the total to the sum of all scores.
    total = sum(posterior.values())
    # Divide each score by the total so the posterior adds to one.
    return {name: s / total for name, s in posterior.items()}

# Define a function that returns the probability that a query item fits the concept.
def generalise(posterior, query):
    # Add up the posterior of every hypothesis whose member set contains the query.
    return sum(p for name, p in posterior.items() if query in hypotheses[name])

# Set the observed examples to sixteen, eight, two, and sixty four.
examples = [16, 8, 2, 64]
# Learn the posterior from the examples.
post = learn(examples)
# For each hypothesis, print its posterior probability.
for name, p in sorted(post.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
    # Print the hypothesis name and its rounded posterior.
    print(name, round(p, 4))
# Print the generalisation probability for thirty two and for ten.
print("is 32 a blicket:", round(generalise(post, 32), 4))
print("is 10 a blicket:", round(generalise(post, 10), 4))


CHAPTER 54. BOUNDED, RESOURCE-RATIONAL, AND ECOLOGICAL RATIONALITY (FRAMEWORK)

The previous chapter asked what an ideal mind would do.

This chapter asks a more down-to-earth question: what should a mind do when it is not ideal, when its time, memory, and computing power are all sharply limited?

That question turns out to change the picture in deep ways, because once you take limits seriously, behaviour that looked foolish can start to look wise.

This chapter introduces three closely related traditions that each take limits as their starting point: bounded rationality, resource-rational analysis, and ecological rationality.

In systems terms, the previous chapter specified the ideal function to compute; this chapter adds the engineering constraints, a compute budget, a deadline, and a cost per operation, and asks for the best algorithm that fits inside them.

They share a hopeful conviction, that human thinking is much smarter than the long catalogue of human "biases" would suggest, once you judge it by the right standard.


54.1 Bounded rationality

Bounded rationality is the founding idea of this whole family: that real minds are rational within bounds, doing the best they can with the limited resources they have.

It was the great insight of Herbert Simon, an American scientist so wide-ranging that he won both a Nobel Prize in economics and the top award in artificial intelligence.


54.1.1 Satisficing and aspiration levels

Simon coined the word "satisficing," a blend of "satisfy" and "suffice," and it names one of the most useful ideas in the study of decision-making.

Satisficing means choosing the first option that is good enough, rather than searching on and on for the very best option.

The contrast is with "optimising," which means finding the single best possible choice, something that often requires examining every alternative.

Simon argued that optimising is usually impossible in real life, because there are too many options, too little time, and too little information to consider them all.

So instead of maximising, people set what Simon called an "aspiration level," which is a threshold of acceptability, a bar for how good is good enough.

You then search through options one at a time and stop as soon as something clears the bar.

Think of looking for somewhere to eat in an unfamiliar town: you do not survey every restaurant and rank them; you walk until you find one that looks decent enough, and you go in.

As a system, satisficing is a sequential search loop: input is a stream of options with their values, state is the current aspiration level, output is the first option whose value clears the threshold, and the loop terminates in as many steps as it takes to find one, not in as many steps as there are options.

The aspiration level is not fixed forever; it adjusts to experience.

If good options keep turning up easily, you raise your bar, and if everything is disappointing, you lower it, so the standard itself adapts to the environment.

That adjustment is a feedback controller on the threshold parameter, running on a slower timescale than the search itself.

Simon's point was not that people are lazy or stupid, but that satisficing is a genuinely intelligent response to a world too complex to fully compute.

This reframing, that stopping when you have enough can be the smart move, is the seed from which the rest of the chapter grows.


54.1.2 The scissors of mind and environment

Simon offered a memorable image for how thinking works, and it is worth learning because it recurs throughout this field.

He said that rational behaviour is shaped "by a scissors whose two blades are the structure of task environments and the computational capabilities of the actor."

The point of the scissors image is that a single blade cuts nothing.

To understand why someone behaves as they do, you cannot look only at the mind, and you cannot look only at the world; you have to see how the two meet, just as cutting needs both blades pressing together.

The first blade is the mind's limits: how much it can remember, how fast it can compute, how much it can attend to.

The second blade is the structure of the environment: which situations arise often, how regular or predictable the world is, what information is freely available.

A behaviour that seems irrational when you stare only at the mind can turn out to be an excellent fit once you see the shape of the world it evolved and learned to handle.

In systems terms this is a design principle rather than a mechanism: the specification of any cognitive algorithm must include the statistics of its input distribution, because an algorithm is only well designed relative to the inputs it will actually receive.

This is a profound methodological lesson, and it directly connects Simon's bounded rationality to Anderson's rational analysis from the previous chapter, since both insist that you cannot understand the mind without understanding its world.

The scissors image is the shared foundation that the two remaining traditions in this chapter build upon, each emphasising one blade or the way the blades are matched.


54.2 Resource-rational analysis

Resource-rational analysis is a modern, mathematically precise upgrade of Simon's bounded rationality.

Its guiding idea is to treat the mind's limits not as an excuse for failure but as a formal part of the problem to be solved.


54.2.1 The optimal use of limited computation

The central proposal, developed especially by Tom Griffiths, Falk Lieder, and their colleagues in the 2010s, can be stated in one sentence.

Resource-rational analysis says the mind makes the best possible use of its limited computational resources, so it optimises subject to the cost of thinking.

Notice the careful shift from the previous chapter.

Classical rational analysis asked, what is the best answer, and it ignored how hard that answer is to compute.

Resource-rational analysis asks, what is the best answer you can afford, given that thinking itself takes time and effort that are worth something.

Formally, this means the mind is imagined to weigh two things against each other: the quality of the decision it would reach, and the computational cost of the thinking needed to reach it.

The right amount to think is the amount where a little more thinking would no longer be worth its cost.

The systems reading is direct: the objective function being maximised is expected decision value minus computation cost, the input is the current state of deliberation, and the output is a choice between "compute more" and "act now," evaluated afresh at every step of thinking.

This is a powerful reframing because it turns human limits from a problem into part of the solution.

A person who thinks quickly and roughly rather than slowly and exactly is not failing to be rational; they may be being rational about the price of their own thinking.

The approach has been used to re-derive many well-known mental shortcuts as the answers you should give if you correctly account for the cost of computation, which is the theme of the sub-sections that follow.


54.2.2 Rational metareasoning and the value of computation

This sub-section introduces the machinery that lets resource-rational analysis actually work: reasoning about your own reasoning.

The technical term is "metareasoning," where the prefix meta means about itself, so metareasoning means thinking about how to think.

The idea is that a smart but limited agent should not just think about the world; it should also make good decisions about how much thinking to do and which thoughts to have.

To make this precise, researchers use a quantity called the "value of computation."

The value of computation is the expected benefit you would gain from performing a particular mental operation, such as considering one more option or imagining one more outcome, minus the cost of doing it.

If a further step of thinking is likely to improve your decision by more than it costs, it is worth taking; if not, you should stop and act.

Rational metareasoning, then, is the policy of always choosing the mental operation with the highest value of computation, and stopping when no operation is worth its cost.

As a system, the metareasoner sits one level above the reasoner: it subscribes to the reasoner's current estimates and their uncertainty, publishes a control signal that either triggers one more computation or commits to an action, and holds as state the running estimates plus a count of computations spent.

This gives a principled answer to a question that plagues any limited thinker: when should I stop deliberating and just decide?

Lieder and Griffiths used this framework to model how people select among different problem-solving strategies, treating the choice of strategy as itself a rational decision about how to spend limited mental effort.

The beauty of the approach is that it explains the flexible, situation-dependent way people switch between careful thought and quick shortcuts, without having to call either one irrational.

The chapter's code sample below builds exactly this kind of agent: it simulates possible outcomes one at a time and stops the moment another simulation is no longer expected to pay for itself.


54.2.3 Heuristics as resource-rational strategies

A heuristic is a mental shortcut, a simple rule of thumb that gives a good-enough answer quickly instead of a perfect answer slowly.

For decades, many heuristics were viewed mainly as sources of error, the origins of the famous "biases" catalogued in the study of judgment.

Resource-rational analysis offers a strikingly different reading: many heuristics are exactly the strategies a limited mind should use, because they buy most of the benefit of full reasoning at a fraction of the cost.

A clear example is the anchoring effect, the well-documented tendency for people's numerical estimates to be pulled toward whatever number they happened to consider first.

This has long been listed as a bias, an irrational contamination of judgment.

But Lieder, Griffiths and colleagues showed that if you start from an initial guess and then adjust it by a series of small mental steps, each step being costly, then stopping the adjustment early, and therefore staying somewhat anchored, is precisely what you should do to balance accuracy against effort.

On this reading the anchoring bias is not a flaw in the machinery; it is the fingerprint of a mind spending its limited thinking wisely.

In systems terms, anchoring-and-adjustment is an iterative refinement algorithm with an early-exit condition, and the observed bias is simply the residual error left at the optimal exit point.

The general lesson is that before you call a mental shortcut irrational, you should ask what the ideal strategy would be for a thinker who has to pay for every computation, because the shortcut may turn out to be that ideal strategy.

This does not mean every bias is secretly optimal, and researchers are careful not to over-claim, but it does mean that the label "bias" should not be applied before the resource-rational analysis has been done.


54.3 Ecological rationality

Ecological rationality is the third tradition, and it puts the spotlight on the second blade of Simon's scissors: the structure of the environment.

Its central claim is that whether a simple strategy is smart or foolish depends entirely on the world it is used in.


54.3.1 Fast-and-frugal heuristics and the adaptive toolbox

This programme is associated above all with the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute in Berlin.

They describe human thinking in terms of "fast-and-frugal heuristics," and both adjectives matter.

Fast means the rule reaches a decision quickly; frugal means it uses very little information, often ignoring most of what is available.

A famous example is the "take-the-best" heuristic for choosing between two options, such as guessing which of two cities is larger.

Take-the-best looks at the single most useful clue first, for instance whether a city has a major sports team, and if that clue distinguishes the two options, it decides then and there and ignores everything else.

Only if the best clue fails to separate them does it move to the next clue, and so on, but often the very first clue is enough.

As a system, take-the-best is a short program with a fixed cue ordering as its only stored state: input is a pair of options with their cue values, the loop reads cues in order of validity, and the output is a choice emitted at the first discriminating cue, so its running time is measured in cues consulted, typically one to three.

Gigerenzer's group describes the mind as holding an "adaptive toolbox," a collection of many such simple heuristics, each suited to a particular kind of problem.

The image is of a handyman's toolbox with different tools for different jobs, rather than one all-purpose master strategy.

Intelligence, on this view, lies largely in selecting the right simple tool for the situation at hand, and in the fact that each tool is matched to the structure of the environments where it works well.

The word "ecological" in ecological rationality points exactly to this matching: a heuristic is rational not in the abstract but in relation to a particular ecology, a particular kind of world.


54.3.2 Less-is-more effects and the bias-variance trade-off

The most provocative claim of the ecological rationality programme is the "less-is-more" effect, and this sub-section explains both the claim and the deep statistical reason behind it.

A less-is-more effect is a situation where using less information, or a simpler rule, actually produces better decisions than using more information or a more complex rule.

This sounds impossible at first, because surely more information can only help.

Gigerenzer's group documented many cases, across three decades, where simple heuristics that deliberately ignore most of the data match or even beat sophisticated methods that use all of it, especially when predicting new, unseen cases.

The explanation comes from a fundamental principle in statistics and machine learning called the bias-variance trade-off, which is worth understanding because it explains why simplicity can win.

When you use a strategy to predict something, your errors come from two sources.

The first source is bias, meaning the strategy is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it is systematically off.

The second source is variance, meaning the strategy is so flexible that it over-reacts to the particular quirks and noise of the small sample of data it happened to see, so it swings around wildly from one sample to the next.

A very complex strategy has low bias but high variance: it can fit anything, including the noise, so it generalises poorly to new cases.

A very simple heuristic has higher bias but much lower variance: it may miss some subtle structure, but it is not fooled by noise, so it can predict new cases more reliably.

When data are scarce or noisy, which is the normal condition of real life, the simple heuristic's steadiness beats the complex method's flexibility, and less genuinely is more.

In systems terms this is a debate about model capacity: the two sides predict differently how prediction error on new cases should change as training data shrink, with the ecological side predicting that low-capacity heuristics overtake high-capacity models exactly when samples get small, a prediction that has been repeatedly confirmed.

This gives the less-is-more effect a rigorous foundation, and it shows that the ecological rationality programme and modern statistics are pointing at the same truth from two directions.


54.4 Rational inattention and the cost of control

The final section brings the economist's way of thinking to the question of attention and mental effort.

The unifying idea is that paying attention and exerting mental control are themselves costly resources, so they should be spent according to a cost-benefit logic, just like money.


54.4.1 Information-theoretic limits on attention

Rational inattention is a theory that comes originally from economics, developed by the Nobel laureate Christopher Sims around 1998 to 2003.

The starting observation is that people cannot absorb and process all the information around them; there is a hard limit on how much they can take in.

To make this precise, Sims borrowed a measure from information theory, the mathematical study of communication founded by Claude Shannon.

Information theory measures information in units called bits, and it treats any limited processor, including a mind, as a channel that can pass only so many bits per unit of time.

Rational inattention says that, given this channel limit, a person should choose to attend to exactly the information that matters most for their decisions, and remain deliberately ignorant of the rest.

Crucially, being inattentive is not a failure here; it is the optimal allocation of a scarce resource.

If some feature of the world barely affects your welfare, it is rational not to spend precious channel capacity tracking it, even if the information is freely available.

The theory predicts, for example, that people will pay close attention to information when the stakes are high and the situation is uncertain, and will tune it out when it would not change what they do.

The systems reading: the attention allocator subscribes to estimates of stakes and uncertainty for each information source, holds a fixed capacity budget in bits as its central parameter, and publishes an allocation of that budget across sources, re-allocating as stakes change.

This connects the study of attention, which Part Three of this outline treats as a psychological process, to a clean economic principle about spending a limited resource where it does the most good.


54.4.2 Control allocation as an economic problem

This sub-section extends the same economic logic from attention to the broader idea of cognitive control and mental effort.

Cognitive control means the effortful steering of your own thinking, the deliberate work of concentrating, resisting a habit, or holding a goal in mind against distraction.

Everyday experience tells us this kind of control feels effortful and that we are reluctant to sustain it, and the puzzle is why mental effort should feel costly at all when no muscle is being tired.

A leading answer, developed by Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick, Jonathan Cohen and colleagues, is captured in a framework called the expected value of control.

The expected value of control is the net worth of exerting mental control in a given situation, calculated by weighing the benefits that control would bring against the intrinsic cost of the effort it requires.

On this account, your mind is constantly making an implicit economic decision: is it worth the effort to concentrate harder here, or should I coast on an easier, automatic response?

You allocate more control when the payoff justifies it, such as during a demanding, important task, and you withhold it when the reward is not worth the strain.

As a system, the control allocator subscribes to signals of task payoff, error rate, and conflict, publishes a control intensity that gates other processes, and updates that intensity on the timescale of task blocks, seconds to minutes, rather than moment to moment.

Treating effort as a cost that must be justified by expected benefit explains a great deal, including why we procrastinate on tedious tasks, why we tire of concentration, and why we reserve our hardest thinking for what matters most.

This closes the chapter on a satisfying unity: attention, effort, and control are all limited resources, and a great deal of the mind's apparent laziness or bias dissolves once you see it as the sensible husbanding of resources that are genuinely costly to spend.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Decision problem: a set of options with uncertain values, arriving from perception, memory, or imagination.

◦ Resource signals: available time, current fatigue, and competing demands, from interoception and task context.

◦ Stakes signal: how much the outcome matters, from motivational systems.

◦ Environment statistics: how regular, redundant, and noisy the current world is, learned from experience.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Committed choice: the selected option, consumed by the action system.

◦ Stop-thinking signal: the metareasoner's decision to end deliberation, consumed by whatever reasoning process is running.

◦ Strategy selection: which heuristic or careful procedure to run, consumed by downstream reasoning.

◦ Attention and control allocations: how much capacity and effort each task receives, consumed by perception and executive processes.

• STATE.

◦ Current best estimate of each option's value, plus the uncertainty around each estimate.

◦ The running count or cost of computations spent so far in the current deliberation.

◦ The aspiration level, adjusted by recent search experience.

◦ The learned cue ordering and toolbox of heuristics, built up over long experience.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Cost per computation: the price of one more mental step, which sets how early deliberation stops.

◦ Aspiration threshold: the bar for "good enough" in satisficing.

◦ Channel capacity: the bits-per-second limit of rational inattention.

◦ Effort cost weight: how strongly the expected value of control discounts effortful strategies.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ A single deliberation episode in simple choices typically runs from a few hundred milliseconds to a few seconds before the stopping rule fires, as in standard response-time experiments.

◦ Aspiration-level adaptation runs over multiple encounters, minutes to days, as experience recalibrates what counts as good enough.

◦ Vigilant cognitive control degrades measurably within tens of minutes of sustained demand, as in vigilance-decrement studies.

◦ The monetary or utility value of one unit of mental effort: REFUSED, because published estimates vary widely across tasks and no consensus number exists.

◦ The brain's information-channel capacity in bits per second: REFUSED, because estimates range over orders of magnitude depending on the task and the level of description.

• MODES.

◦ Deliberative mode against heuristic mode: high stakes, high uncertainty, and available time trigger careful computation, while low stakes or time pressure trigger a fast-and-frugal tool.

◦ Search mode against commit mode in satisficing: search continues while options fall below the aspiration level and terminates at the first option that clears it.

◦ Exploit mode against re-tune mode: the aspiration level and cue ordering stay fixed while they keep working, and shift when outcomes repeatedly disappoint.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Anchoring: adjustment stops early, leaving estimates pulled toward the starting point, the visible residue of a rational stopping rule.

◦ Mis-set thresholds: an aspiration level too high yields endless search and choice paralysis, while one too low yields premature, poor commitments.

◦ Ecological mismatch: a heuristic tuned to one environment is deployed in another, so a normally smart shortcut produces systematic error.

◦ Control misallocation: effort costs are overweighted, appearing clinically as apathy and avolition, or underweighted, appearing as perseverative overcontrol.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called estimated values with one running estimate per option, each with initial value zero.
Create a list variable called sample counts with one counter per option, each with initial value zero.
Create a number variable called cost per simulation holding the cost of one mental simulation.
Repeat the following loop.
    For each option, calculate the uncertainty of its estimate as one divided by one more than its sample count.
    Calculate the value of computation as the largest uncertainty among the options minus the cost per simulation.
    If the value of computation is less than or equal to zero,
        Exit the loop.
    Select the option with the largest uncertainty.
    Draw one noisy simulated outcome for the selected option.
    Add one to the selected option's sample count.
    Update the selected option's running estimate toward the simulated outcome by one divided by its sample count.
Select the option with the highest running estimate.
Return the selected option as the committed choice.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module for noisy simulated outcomes.
import random

# Set the true, hidden values of three options.
true_values = [0.55, 0.60, 0.40]
# Set the cost of running one more mental simulation.
cost_per_sim = 0.02
# Create a list of running value estimates, one per option, starting at zero.
estimates = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
# Create a list of sample counts, one per option, starting at zero.
counts = [0, 0, 0]

# Define a function that simulates one noisy outcome of choosing an option.
def simulate(option):
    # Return the true value plus zero-mean noise with spread zero point two.
    return true_values[option] + random.gauss(0.0, 0.2)

# Define a function that returns each option's estimate uncertainty.
def uncertainties():
    # Return one divided by one more than the sample count, for each option.
    return [1.0 / (1 + c) for c in counts]

# Repeat the think-or-act loop until thinking stops paying.
while True:
    # Get the current uncertainty of every option.
    unc = uncertainties()
    # Calculate the value of computation as the largest uncertainty minus the cost.
    value_of_computation = max(unc) - cost_per_sim
    # If one more simulation is not worth its cost, stop deliberating.
    if value_of_computation <= 0:
        break
    # Select the most uncertain option to think about next.
    target = unc.index(max(unc))
    # Draw one simulated outcome for that option.
    outcome = simulate(target)
    # Add one to that option's sample count.
    counts[target] += 1
    # Move the running estimate toward the outcome by the learning fraction.
    estimates[target] += (outcome - estimates[target]) / counts[target]

# Select the option with the highest running estimate.
choice = estimates.index(max(estimates))
# Print how many simulations were spent on each option.
print("simulations per option:", counts)
# Print the final estimates rounded to two decimal places.
print("estimates:", [round(e, 2) for e in estimates])
# Print the committed choice.
print("chosen option:", choice)


CHAPTER 55. CONNECTIONISM AND PARALLEL DISTRIBUTED PROCESSING (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter is about a completely different way of picturing the mind from the symbol-and-rule picture that dominated early cognitive science.

Connectionism proposes that thinking arises from the cooperation of very many simple units, loosely inspired by brain cells, none of which understands anything on its own.

The name comes from the word "connection," because in these models the knowledge lives not in the units but in the strengths of the connections between them.

Parallel distributed processing, usually shortened to PDP, is the fuller name for the same movement, and its two key words tell you its character.

"Parallel" means many things happen at once rather than one step at a time, and "distributed" means each piece of knowledge is spread across many units rather than stored in one place, both of which make these systems feel more brain-like than a step-by-step symbolic program.

In systems terms a connectionist model is refreshingly explicit: its state is a vector of unit activations plus a matrix of connection weights, its operating cycle is a parallel weighted sum passed through a squashing function, and its learning rule is a small weight change driven by error, all of which this chapter will make concrete in code.


55.1 The foundations

This section covers the two historical pillars on which connectionism rests: the early, limited networks of the mid-twentieth century, and the breakthrough in the 1980s that overcame their limits.

Understanding this history explains both why connectionism was once written off and why it came roaring back.


55.1.1 The perceptron and its limits

The perceptron was one of the earliest artificial neural networks, built and championed by the psychologist Frank Rosenblatt in the late 1950s.

An artificial neural network is a system of simple connected units that pass signals to one another, very loosely modelled on neurons in the brain.

The perceptron was exciting because it could learn: it adjusted the strengths of its connections in response to examples, gradually getting better at sorting inputs into categories.

Its operating cycle, in systems terms, is a single parallel pass: inputs arrive as a vector, each is multiplied by a weight, the products are summed, and the unit outputs one or zero depending on whether the sum clears a threshold, with learning nudging each weight after every classification error.

For a while this fuelled great optimism that such machines might soon learn to do almost anything.

Then in 1969 two prominent researchers, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert, published a book called Perceptrons that changed the mood entirely.

They proved mathematically that a simple, single-layer perceptron has a fundamental limit: there are easy problems it can never solve, no matter how it is trained.

Their most famous example was a logical operation called exclusive-or, usually written XOR, which is true when exactly one of two inputs is on but false when both or neither are on.

The reason a single-layer perceptron cannot learn XOR is that the pattern cannot be separated by a single straight dividing line, and a single-layer perceptron can only ever draw such a straight boundary.

This result, though narrow, was widely taken as a verdict on the whole approach, and funding and enthusiasm for neural networks collapsed for over a decade, a lull sometimes called an artificial-intelligence winter.

The crucial detail, often lost at the time, is that Minsky and Papert's proof applied strictly to networks with no middle layer, and they only conjectured, without proving, that adding layers would not help.

That conjecture turned out to be wrong, which sets up the breakthrough of the next sub-section.


55.1.2 Distributed representation and backpropagation

The revival of connectionism in the 1980s rested on two ideas working together: distributed representation, and a learning method called backpropagation.
