Distributed representation means encoding each concept as a pattern of activity spread across many units, rather than dedicating one unit to one concept.

Under this scheme the idea of "dog" is not a single cell that lights up; it is a particular pattern across a whole population, and different concepts are different patterns over the same shared units.

This turns out to have lovely consequences: similar concepts naturally have similar patterns, the system degrades gracefully if some units are damaged, and it can generalise to new cases that resemble old ones.

Graceful degradation means performance falls off gently rather than crashing when part of the system is lost, which is strikingly like how real brains tolerate damage.

From a systems standpoint, distribution is a fault-tolerance property of the storage format: because every concept is spread over every weight, deleting any single component removes a little of everything rather than all of something, and the code sample at the end of this chapter demonstrates this directly by damaging a trained network.

The second idea, backpropagation, solved the learning problem that had doomed the perceptron, by making it possible to train networks with one or more middle layers.

A middle layer, usually called a hidden layer, is a layer of units sitting between the input and the output, and such layers let a network draw curved, complex boundaries, which is exactly what solving XOR requires.

Backpropagation, whose name is short for backward propagation of error, is a procedure for adjusting all the connection strengths in a multi-layer network so that its output moves closer to the desired answer.

It works by comparing the network's output to the correct answer, measuring the error, and then passing responsibility for that error backward through the layers, nudging each connection a little in the direction that would reduce the error.

Repeated over many examples, this slowly sculpts the connections until the network performs the task, and it lets the hidden layers discover useful internal features on their own.

The single-layer ancestor of backpropagation is the delta rule: change each weight by the learning rate times the error times the input, which is the rule the code sample below uses, and backpropagation is exactly this rule generalised so the error signal can be passed through hidden layers.

Backpropagation was made famous in 1986 by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams, as part of a landmark two-volume collection titled Parallel Distributed Processing, edited by Rumelhart and James McClelland.

That collection is the founding document of modern connectionism, and the same backpropagation method, scaled up enormously, is what drives today's deep learning systems, a point we return to at the end of the chapter.


55.2 The classic models of cognition

Having the machinery is one thing; showing it explains real human thinking is another.

This section presents the celebrated early connectionist models that took specific mental abilities and reproduced them, often overturning the assumption that the mind must be running explicit rules.


55.2.1 The past-tense debate and rules against networks

The past-tense debate was one of the most heated and illuminating arguments in cognitive science, and it turned on a homely fact about English verbs.

Most English verbs form their past tense by a simple rule, adding "-ed," as in walk to walked, but a stubborn minority are irregular, as in go to went or sing to sang.

The traditional view was that the mind must contain an explicit rule for the regulars plus a memorised list for the irregulars, two separate mechanisms.

In 1986 Rumelhart and McClelland startled the field with a single connectionist network that learned to produce past tenses without any explicit rule at all.

The network simply learned, from many examples, the statistical mapping from a verb's sound to its past-tense sound, and out of that one learned mapping came both regular and irregular forms.

Remarkably, the network even reproduced a famous quirk of children learning English, called over-regularisation, in which children who once correctly said "went" start saying "goed" before eventually recovering.

That a network with no built-in rule could mimic this child-like pattern was a powerful demonstration that rule-like behaviour might emerge from a system that contains no rules.

The linguists Steven Pinker and Alan Prince fired back sharply in 1988, arguing that the network had real flaws and that the evidence still favoured two separate mechanisms, a rule route and a memory route.

This dual-route reply remains influential, and the debate was never decisively settled in either direction.

In systems terms the two sides propose different architectures for the same input-output mapping, and they predict differently: the single-network account predicts graded interference between regulars and irregulars and frequency effects everywhere, while the dual-route account predicts that the rule route should apply uniformly regardless of a regular verb's frequency, and experiments probing these signatures have found support for both, which is why the debate persists.

Its lasting importance is that it crystallised the deepest question dividing the field: is the mind a manipulator of explicit symbolic rules, or a network in which apparently rule-governed behaviour emerges from learned statistics?


55.2.2 Reading and the triangle model

Reading aloud is another everyday skill that became a proving ground for connectionism, because it too mixes regularity with exceptions.

Many English words are pronounced by regular spelling-to-sound patterns, as in "mint" and "hint," but others are irregular exceptions, as in "pint," which breaks the pattern.

The triangle model, developed by Mark Seidenberg and James McClelland in 1989 and later refined by David Plaut and colleagues, is a connectionist account of how we read.

It is called the triangle model because it links three kinds of representation arranged at the corners of a triangle: the written form of a word, its sound, and its meaning.

Between these corners sit layers of hidden units, and the network learns the mappings among print, sound, and meaning from exposure to many words.

As a system, the model subscribes to a spelling pattern at its orthographic corner, publishes a pronunciation at its phonological corner within the several hundred milliseconds a skilled reader needs to begin naming a word, and its state is the single weight matrix that simultaneously encodes the regular patterns and the exceptions.

The important claim is that a single learned network can handle both regular and exception words, and can pronounce novel made-up words too, all without separate rule-based and lookup mechanisms.

This directly challenged the older "dual-route" theory of reading, which held that skilled reading needs two distinct pathways, one applying rules and one looking up exceptions.

The triangle model showed that one connectionist system, sensitive to the statistics of the language, could do the job that two separate mechanisms were thought to require.

As with the past-tense debate, the argument was not fully resolved, and dual-route theorists have their own strong models, but the triangle model established connectionism as a serious contender for explaining a core human skill.


55.2.3 Recurrent networks and the discovery of structure in time

The models discussed so far mostly handle inputs presented all at once, but much of cognition, above all language, unfolds over time, one word after another.

Handling time requires a network that can remember what came before, and that is what a recurrent network provides.

A recurrent network is one whose connections loop back on themselves, so that some of its activity is fed back in as part of the next input, giving it a kind of short-term memory of its own recent states.

In systems terms the recurrence adds a state register: at every step the network's input is the current item concatenated with a copy of its own previous hidden pattern, so the hidden layer becomes a compressed running summary of the sequence so far.

The pioneering example is the simple recurrent network introduced by Jeffrey Elman in a 1990 paper with the evocative title "Finding Structure in Time."

Elman's network was given the humble task of predicting the next item in a sequence, for instance the next word in a stream of text, and learning only from whether its predictions were right.

The results were remarkable, and they are the reason the paper became a classic.

From nothing but the prediction task, the network discovered where word boundaries fall in a continuous stream of letters, because predictability drops at the end of a word.

It also developed internal representations that grouped words into categories such as nouns and verbs, and that respected grammatical relationships like which nouns can go with which verbs, even though no one had labelled any of this.

In other words, structure that linguists describe with explicit rules emerged inside the network purely from the effort of predicting what comes next.

This was a profound demonstration, and its spirit lives on directly in today's large language models, which are, at heart, enormous next-item predictors that discover linguistic structure from raw text.


55.2.4 Semantic cognition as an emergent

Semantic cognition means our organised knowledge of the meanings of things: what a robin is, that it is a bird, that birds can fly, that a robin is more like a canary than like an oak tree.

A natural assumption is that such knowledge is stored as an explicit filing system, a built-in hierarchy of categories with facts attached to each.

James McClelland and Timothy Rogers, building on the PDP tradition, argued instead that this organised knowledge is emergent, meaning it arises on its own from a network learning many small facts, without any hierarchy being built in.

The word "emergent" is key: it means a large-scale order that appears out of the interaction of many simple parts, none of which contains the order itself.

In their model, a network is simply trained on many statements of the form thing-relation-property, such as "robin can fly" and "oak has bark," over and over.

As it learns, the network's internal patterns for different things gradually organise themselves so that similar things come to have similar patterns, producing, without instruction, exactly the groupings and resemblances that our conceptual knowledge shows.

The systems reading: input is a stream of item-relation-property triples, state is the slowly changing weight matrix, and the published output is a property prediction for any queried item, with the hierarchy visible only as the geometry of the hidden patterns, coarse splits forming before fine ones over the course of training.

The model reproduces subtle facts about human semantic knowledge, including the order in which children differentiate concepts, first splitting living from non-living, then finer distinctions, and the specific ways this knowledge breaks down in brain disease.

The broad lesson, running through this whole section, is the connectionist signature claim: rich, structured, rule-like knowledge need not be built in, because it can emerge from a simple system learning the statistics of experience.


55.3 The theory of network dynamics

This section steps back from specific tasks to look at the general mathematical behaviour of these networks, the way their activity flows and settles over time.

Understanding this behaviour reveals why networks are naturally good at certain things, above all memory and the satisfaction of many soft constraints at once.


55.3.1 Attractor networks and content-addressable memory

An attractor network is a network whose pattern of activity, once set going, tends to flow toward and settle into one of a set of stable states, called attractors.

The word "attractor" is apt: like a valley that a rolling ball rolls down into, a stable state pulls nearby patterns of activity toward it until the network comes to rest there.

The great pioneer of this idea was the physicist John Hopfield, whose 1982 network showed how a simple recurrent network could store a set of patterns as its stable resting states.

This gives rise to a powerful and brain-like kind of memory called content-addressable memory.

Content-addressable memory means you retrieve a stored item by supplying part or a rough version of its content, rather than by knowing an address or location where it is filed.

The contrast is with a computer's ordinary memory, where you must know the exact address to get something back.

In an attractor network, if you present a partial or noisy version of a stored pattern, the network's activity flows downhill into the nearest attractor and completes the pattern, filling in the missing parts.

As a system, retrieval is a settling loop: input is a corrupted pattern loaded as the initial state, each cycle updates units in parallel from their weighted neighbours, and the output is the stable pattern reached after a modest number of cycles, so retrieval time is measured in update cycles rather than in search steps.

This is exactly what human memory feels like: a snatch of a tune, a whiff of a smell, or half a face is often enough to bring the whole memory flooding back.

Attractor dynamics also explain the graceful degradation mentioned earlier, since the memory is spread across the whole network and a partial injury only blurs the valleys rather than deleting particular files.

So a very simple mechanism, activity settling into valleys, captures several of the most human features of memory at once.


55.3.2 Energy landscapes and constraint satisfaction

This sub-section gives the deeper mathematical picture behind attractor networks, and it centres on a beautiful idea borrowed from physics called an energy landscape.

Hopfield showed that you can attach a single number to every possible state of the network, which he called its energy, by analogy with physical systems that settle into low-energy states.

You can then picture all the network's possible states as a landscape of hills and valleys, where height corresponds to energy, and the stable attractor states are the bottoms of the valleys.

The key mathematical fact is that, as the network updates its units, its energy can only stay the same or go down, so the activity always rolls downhill and eventually comes to rest in a valley.

This gives a vivid and exact way to understand what the network is doing: it is always seeking a low point in its energy landscape.

In systems terms the energy function is a global progress guarantee: it proves the settling loop terminates, because a quantity bounded below strictly decreases until no update changes anything.

The same picture explains why these networks are natural constraint-satisfaction machines.

Constraint satisfaction means finding a solution that respects as many as possible of a set of competing requirements that cannot all be perfectly met at once.

In the network, each connection acts as a soft constraint: a positive connection says two units "want" to agree, a negative one says they "want" to differ, and no single arrangement can satisfy every such pull.

Rolling downhill in the energy landscape is precisely the process of finding the state that best balances all these competing pulls at the same time, in parallel.

This matters for cognition because so much of thinking, from understanding an ambiguous sentence to interpreting a dim scene to solving a puzzle, involves juggling many soft, partial constraints together rather than following one rigid rule.

The energy-landscape view thus gives connectionism a principled account of how a mind might settle, quickly and in parallel, on the interpretation that best fits everything it knows.


55.4 Deep learning as a cognitive model

The final section brings the story up to the present, where the connectionist ideas of the 1980s have grown, through vastly bigger networks and data, into the deep learning systems that now dominate artificial intelligence.

The question this section asks is not whether these systems are useful, but what, if anything, they teach us about the human mind.


55.4.1 Deep networks as models of perception and language

Deep learning refers to neural networks with many layers stacked one above another, the word "deep" simply meaning many-layered, trained on very large amounts of data with the descendants of backpropagation.

These are the direct heirs of the 1980s connectionist networks, differing mainly in scale, in the amount of data and computing power poured into them.

A genuinely surprising scientific finding is that these engineering systems, built to perform tasks rather than to mimic biology, turn out to be among the best available predictors of activity in the brain.

In vision, deep networks trained to recognise objects develop internal layers whose responses closely match, layer by layer, the responses recorded from the primate visual system along its object-recognition pathway.

That an artificial network optimised only to label images should end up resembling the brain's own visual stages is a striking convergence, and it suggests that both may be finding similar solutions to the same problem.

A parallel story holds in language, where large networks trained simply to predict upcoming words have been found to predict aspects of human brain activity during reading and listening better than earlier, hand-built theories did.

In systems terms these comparisons treat the network and the brain as two implementations of the same interface, and test the match stage by stage: present the same input to both, record the internal signals of both, and measure how well one predicts the other.

These results have made deep networks a serious tool in the science of the mind, not just in engineering, because they give researchers working models that can be probed, compared to brains, and tested against behaviour.

At the same time, sober voices caution that matching brain activity is not the same as explaining it, since a deep network is itself so complex that it can be as hard to understand as the brain it models.

So deep learning has become both a promising model of perception and language and a fresh puzzle in its own right, and the field is still working out how much genuine understanding it delivers.


55.4.2 The nativism and emergentism debate reopened

The rise of deep learning has breathed new life into one of the oldest arguments about the mind, the debate between nativism and emergentism.

Nativism is the view that much of the mind's structure is innate, built in from birth, so that a child comes equipped with prior knowledge, for instance about grammar or about objects, that makes learning possible.

Emergentism is the opposing view that such structure is not built in but emerges from general-purpose learning applied to rich experience, so that what looks innate is really the product of learning.

This argument is ancient, but modern deep networks have given it a sharp new test bed.

The reason is that a large network typically starts with very little built-in knowledge and learns almost everything from data, so it is a working example of the emergentist bet.

When such a system, after training on enough text, produces fluent and largely grammatical language, emergentists point to it as evidence that powerful structure can indeed be learned from experience alone, without innate grammar of the kind nativists proposed.

Nativists reply that today's networks learn from astronomically more data than any child ever hears, and often still make errors no child would make, so the comparison does not settle the question of what human children need.

They also note that the network's architecture is itself a kind of built-in prior, so no learning is ever truly from a blank slate, which complicates the whole debate.

In systems terms the two sides predict differently what happens when you shrink the training data toward a child's real diet: nativists predict a learner without built-in structure should fail to reach child-level grammar at child-scale data, while emergentists predict that better learning algorithms plus richer, more child-like input can close the gap, and running exactly this experiment is now an active research programme.

The honest state of the field is that this remains genuinely open, and thoughtful researchers on both sides agree the interesting question is no longer "innate or learned" but "what minimum of built-in structure lets the rest be learned."

For a beginner, the lesson to carry from this final sub-section is that connectionism, born as one framework among several decades ago, now sits at the very centre of the biggest questions in both cognitive science and artificial intelligence, and that the argument it reignited about what the mind must be given versus what it can learn is far from over.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Input pattern: a vector of activation values representing a stimulus, arriving from perceptual encoding or from another network's output.

◦ Teaching signal: the desired output pattern during learning, supplied by the environment, a caregiver, or the next item in a sequence for prediction learning.

◦ Recurrent feedback: in recurrent and attractor variants, a copy of the network's own previous activation state.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Output pattern: a vector of activations representing a classification, a pronunciation, a prediction, or a completed memory, consumed by action systems or by downstream networks.

◦ Error signal: the difference between output and teaching signal, consumed internally by the learning rule.

◦ Hidden representation: the internal pattern over hidden units, readable by other processes and, in research, by scientists probing what the network has learned.

• STATE.

◦ The activation vector: the current pattern across all units, the fast-changing working state.

◦ The weight matrix: the connection strengths, the slow-changing store where all learned knowledge lives.

◦ In recurrent networks, the context copy of the previous hidden state, providing short-term memory of the sequence.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Learning rate: how large a step each weight takes toward reducing error.

◦ Network size and depth: numbers of units and layers, which set representational capacity.

◦ Activation function and threshold: the squashing rule turning a unit's summed input into its output.

◦ Training exposure: the number of example presentations, which determines where the network sits between novice and expert performance.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ One unit update in the brain's implementation is bounded by the neuronal membrane time constant, roughly 10 to 20 milliseconds, so a settling episode of a few dozen cycles fits within a few hundred milliseconds, matching recognition times.

◦ Weight change is slow relative to activation flow: human skill learning of the kind these networks model unfolds over hours to years of practice.

◦ The number of settling cycles for a given attractor retrieval: REFUSED, because it depends on network size, noise, and cue quality, and no single literature value exists.

◦ The wall-clock time per training epoch: REFUSED, because it is a property of the simulating hardware, not of the cognitive model.

• MODES.

◦ Performance mode against learning mode: forward activation flow runs at every use, while weight updating engages only when a teaching or error signal is present.

◦ Feedforward mode against settling mode: layered networks map input to output in one pass, while recurrent and attractor networks iterate until stable, the architecture determining the mode.

◦ Intact mode against degraded mode: with damage, the network does not switch algorithms but slides gracefully into a noisier version of the same computation.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Graceful degradation under damage: lesioning units or weights blurs all knowledge a little rather than deleting single items, matching patterns seen in brain injury and dementia.

◦ Over-regularisation during learning: statistically dominant patterns temporarily capture exceptional cases, as in children saying goed.

◦ Catastrophic interference: rapid training on new material can overwrite old knowledge, a known weakness that motivated complementary learning accounts.

◦ Spurious attractors: settling networks can rest in blend states that correspond to no stored memory, producing confident but false completions.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called weights holding one small random number for each connection from each input unit to each output unit.
Create a number variable called learning rate with initial value zero point two.
Repeat the following for each training pass.
    For each training pattern with its input list and its target list,
        For each output unit,
            Create a number variable called activation with initial value zero.
            For each input unit, calculate the product of the input value and its weight to this output unit, and add the result to activation.
            Pass activation through the squashing function to get the output value.
            Calculate the error as the target value minus the output value.
            For each input unit, multiply the learning rate by the error and by the input value, and add the result to the connecting weight.
To test graceful degradation, set a fraction of the weights to zero.
For each training pattern, compute the output values again with the damaged weights.
Report that the outputs are degraded but still close to the targets.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for the squashing function and the random module for weights and damage.
import math, random

# Define the squashing function that maps any sum to a value between zero and one.
def squash(x):
    # Return one divided by one plus the exponential of negative x.
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x))

# Create four training patterns mapping distributed animal features to two category units.
# Each input is four features; each target is bird-likeness and fish-likeness.
patterns = [([1, 1, 0, 0], [1, 0]),   # robin: wings and feathers make a bird.
            ([1, 0, 1, 0], [1, 0]),   # sparrow: wings and small body make a bird.
            ([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1]),   # minnow: small body and fins make a fish.
            ([0, 1, 0, 1], [0, 1])]   # trout: feature mix that makes a fish.

# Create a weight matrix of small random numbers, one row per output unit.
weights = [[random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) for _ in range(4)] for _ in range(2)]
# Set the learning rate to zero point five.
rate = 0.5

# Define a function that computes both output values for an input pattern.
def forward(inputs):
    # For each output unit, squash the weighted sum of the inputs.
    return [squash(sum(w * i for w, i in zip(row, inputs))) for row in weights]

# Repeat the training loop for two hundred passes through the patterns.
for _ in range(200):
    # For each input pattern and its target pattern,
    for inputs, targets in patterns:
        # Compute the current outputs.
        outputs = forward(inputs)
        # For each output unit, apply the delta rule to its incoming weights.
        for j in range(2):
            # Calculate the error as the target minus the output.
            error = targets[j] - outputs[j]
            # For each input unit, nudge the weight by rate times error times input.
            for i in range(4):
                weights[j][i] += rate * error * inputs[i]

# Print the trained outputs for every pattern.
print("trained:", [[round(o, 2) for o in forward(p)] for p, t in patterns])

# Damage the network by zeroing one randomly chosen weight per output unit.
for j in range(2):
    # Set one incoming weight of this output unit to zero.
    weights[j][random.randrange(4)] = 0.0

# Print the outputs after damage to show graceful degradation.
print("damaged:", [[round(o, 2) for o in forward(p)] for p, t in patterns])

CHAPTER 56. DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS AND FOUR-E COGNITION (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter is about a family of ideas that quietly challenges the most common picture of the mind.

The common picture says the mind is like a computer inside the head: it takes in information, runs steps on it, and spits out behaviour.

The ideas in this chapter say that this picture leaves out too much.

They say the mind is better understood as something that unfolds continuously in time, like a river flowing, and that it is not trapped inside the skull but reaches out into the body and the surrounding world.

The phrase four-E cognition, usually written 4E cognition, is a shorthand for four related claims, each starting with the letter E: that cognition is embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended.

We will unpack each of those words slowly, because none of them means what it might seem to at first glance.

The label framework in the heading means this chapter offers a way of thinking and a set of tools, rather than a single finding, and it gives the earlier chapters on perception, memory, and thought a different lens to be seen through.

In systems terms, the chapter proposes a change of unit: instead of a boxed processor with an input port and an output port, the unit of analysis becomes a closed loop of brain, body, and environment, exchanging continuous signals with no clean start or finish line.

Why should a beginner care?

Because if these thinkers are even partly right, then building a mind - which is konnectome's goal - may require more than a very clever program; it may require a body and a world for that program to live in.


56.1 The dynamical systems approach

This section introduces a mathematical way of describing things that change over time, and the claim that the mind is one of those things.

A dynamical system, in plain terms, is anything whose current state depends on its past state and keeps evolving moment by moment: a swinging pendulum, the weather, a population of rabbits, or, on this view, a thinking brain.

The dynamical approach borrows the mathematics that physicists and engineers already use for such systems and asks whether the same mathematics can describe cognition.

As a system specification, a dynamical model needs only three things: a state vector that summarises the present, a differential equation or update rule that maps the present state to its rate of change, and a set of parameters that shape the flow.

The point of the section is to show what changes when you stop asking what steps the mind computes and start asking how the mind flows.


56.1.1 State space, attractors, and coupling

Let us define three tools that this approach uses constantly, because they carry the whole idea.

The first is state space.

A state is just a complete snapshot of a system at one instant: for a pendulum it is its position and its speed right now.

State space is the imaginary space of every possible snapshot the system could ever be in, so that each point in that space is one possible complete condition of the system.

As the system changes over time, the point that represents it traces a path through this space, and that path is a compact picture of the system's whole history and future.

The second tool is the attractor.

An attractor is a region of state space that the system tends to fall into and settle around, the way a marble rolls to the bottom of a bowl no matter where in the bowl you release it.

Some attractors are single resting points, like the marble coming to rest; some are repeating loops, like a heartbeat that keeps returning to the same rhythm; and some are stranger, wandering patterns that never exactly repeat yet stay within bounds.

In cognitive terms, a stable habit, a settled decision, or a locked-in perception can be pictured as the system falling into an attractor.

The third tool is coupling.

Two systems are coupled when the state of each continuously feeds into and shapes the state of the other, so that neither can be understood alone.

The classic everyday image is two people walking side by side who fall into the same stride without trying: each person's steps nudge the other's until the two bodies form a single, larger rhythmic system.

The dynamical claim is that brain, body, and environment are coupled in exactly this way, so the real unit of cognition is the whole coupled loop, not the brain by itself.

This matters because coupling can produce coordinated, intelligent-looking behaviour without any inner plan directing it, simply from the back-and-forth between parts.

Read as a mechanism, the coupled loop takes as input the continuous state of each partner, produces as output a coordinated joint trajectory, and settles on the timescale of the movement itself - fractions of a second to a few seconds - with the attractor landscape as its only stored program.

The best-studied laboratory case is rhythmic finger coordination, captured by the Haken-Kelso-Bunz (HKB) model of 1985, in which two fingers moving together have exactly two stable attractors, in-phase and anti-phase, and the anti-phase pattern abruptly collapses into the in-phase one when the movement is driven faster - and the code sample at the end of this chapter shows the in-phase attractor capturing two mismatched oscillators in miniature.


56.1.2 The dynamical hypothesis and its evidence

The dynamical hypothesis is a bold, named claim, and it is worth stating carefully because it is often exaggerated.

It was set out most sharply by the philosopher Tim van Gelder in an article titled The Dynamical Hypothesis in Cognitive Science, published in the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 1998.

Van Gelder proposed that cognitive systems are dynamical systems and are best understood with the mathematics of change over time, rather than as digital computers manipulating symbols.

In its strongest form the hypothesis says the mind has no inner symbols and no stored rules at all, only continuously changing quantities, which is a genuinely radical suggestion.

In systems terms the two sides predict different observables: a symbolic account predicts discrete state transitions with rule-shaped error patterns, while the dynamical account predicts smooth trajectories, gradual drifts, hysteresis - a system's tendency to stay in its current pattern beyond the point where it first became unstable - and abrupt phase transitions when a control parameter crosses a threshold.

The most influential body of evidence comes from developmental psychology, in the work of Esther Thelen and Linda Smith, whose 1994 book A Dynamic Systems Approach to the Development of Cognition and Action is the landmark text.

Thelen and Smith studied how babies learn to reach and to walk and famously re-examined a puzzle known as the A-not-B error.

In that puzzle an infant who has repeatedly found a toy hidden at location A will often keep reaching to A even after watching the toy be hidden at a new location B, and the traditional reading blamed an immature concept of hidden objects.

Thelen and Smith argued instead that the error falls out of the dynamics of the reach itself - the built-up habit of moving toward A, the memory in the muscles, the delay before acting - so that small changes to the body and the situation make the error come and go, which is what their experiments found.

Their slogan was that development has, in their words, no structures and no rules, only patterns that self-organise out of the coupling of a growing body with a rich world.

It is fair to a beginner to add the honest caveat that most researchers today accept the dynamical approach as a valuable description and a source of real insight, especially for skilled movement and development, while doubting the strongest claim that representations can be dispensed with entirely.

The dynamicist Randall Beer and the critic Chris Eliasmith have both argued, from opposite sides, that the deepest question is not whether the mind changes over time - everyone agrees it does - but whether describing that change requires us to keep talking about internal representations, and that question remains open.


56.2 Embodied cognition

This section turns to the first of the four Es, the claim that thought is shaped, through and through, by the fact that we have bodies.

Embodied cognition is the idea that the details of our physical form - our hands, our upright posture, our senses, our capacity to move - are not merely tools the mind uses but are woven into the very content and style of our thinking.

As a systems claim, embodiment says the body is not a peripheral device on the far side of a clean interface; it is part of the processor, so the format of thought inherits the format of sensing and moving.

The section explains two of the most concrete lines of evidence for that idea, one from language and one from the way we understand meaning.


56.2.1 Conceptual metaphor and sensorimotor grounding

Start with a plain observation about everyday speech.

We say a warm smile, a close friend, a high price, a heavy heart, and a bright idea, borrowing words from the world of touch, space, weight, and light to talk about feelings and thoughts that have no temperature, distance, or brightness of their own.

The linguist George Lakoff and the philosopher Mark Johnson, in their 1980 book Metaphors We Live By, argued that this is not a decoration on top of thought but a window into how thought is built.

Their claim, known as conceptual metaphor theory, is that we understand abstract ideas - affection, importance, morality, time - by mapping them onto concrete bodily experiences such as warmth, size, cleanliness, and movement through space.

The term sensorimotor grounding names the underlying proposal: that abstract concepts are anchored in, and partly made of, the brain's records of sensing and moving.

Sensory here means to do with the senses, and motor means to do with movement, so a sensorimotor grounding is a footing in perception and action.

Seen as a mechanism, the metaphor system takes an abstract target concept as input, retrieves a stored mapping to a concrete bodily source domain, and outputs an interpretation coloured by that source, all within the few hundred milliseconds of normal word understanding.

For example, the idea that affection is warmth is thought to grow from a baby's earliest experience of being held close by a warm caregiver, so the concept of a loving relationship keeps a thread back to bodily heat.

There is suggestive experimental support: studies have reported that briefly holding a warm drink can make people judge a stranger as more generous and caring, though it is honest to say that several such bodily-priming effects have been hard to reproduce reliably, and the field now treats the flashier findings with caution.

The careful version of the claim, which most researchers accept, is the weaker and better-supported one: that understanding words about actions and objects tends to engage the brain's sensory and motor systems, so meaning is at least partly re-enacted in the body rather than handled as pure abstract code.


56.2.2 Simulation semantics

Simulation semantics is a specific and testable version of the embodiment idea, focused on how we grasp the meaning of words and sentences.

Semantics is simply the study of meaning, so simulation semantics is the theory that we get at meaning by simulation.

To simulate here means to partly re-run, in the brain, the perception or action that a word refers to, as a kind of inner rehearsal.

The proposal, developed by researchers such as Lawrence Barsalou and Benjamin Bergen, is that when you understand the sentence the pilot grasped the lever, your brain faintly reactivates the visual and motor patterns of seeing a lever and closing a hand around it, and that this partial re-enactment is what understanding consists of.

As a process, the simulator subscribes to a stream of words, publishes a partial sensorimotor re-enactment as its output, and runs fast enough to keep pace with speech, which arrives at roughly two to three words per second.

Barsalou's broader framework, called perceptual symbol systems and set out in an influential 1999 paper, holds that concepts are not abstract symbols stripped of all sensory character but are compressed records of perception and action that can be replayed.

One striking piece of supporting evidence is the action-sentence compatibility effect reported by Arthur Glenberg and Michael Kaschak in 2002: people are faster to judge a sentence sensible when the hand movement the response requires matches the direction of the action described, as if reading about handing something toward yourself had already primed the inward motion.

Neuroimaging adds that reading action words like kick, pick, and lick activates regions of the motor strip near the parts that control the foot, hand, and mouth respectively, which fits the simulation story.

The honest boundary of the theory is the hardest case: it is much clearer how you would simulate kicking than how you would simulate justice, democracy, or the number seven, and critics press exactly there, so how far simulation reaches into fully abstract thought is still debated.


56.3 Embedded and extended cognition

This section covers the middle two Es, which are about the world beyond the body.

Embedded cognition is the modest claim that thinking is deeply dependent on the surrounding environment and offloads work onto it.

Extended cognition is the bolder claim that parts of the environment can literally become parts of the thinking mind.

In engineering language, embedded cognition says the mind uses external storage and external computation heavily; extended cognition says those external resources are inside the system boundary, not outside it.

The section walks from the modest claim to the bold one and shows where the argument gets contentious.


56.3.1 The extended-mind thesis and the parity principle

The extended-mind thesis is one of the most provocative ideas in modern philosophy of mind, and it was launched by a single short paper.

The philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers published The Extended Mind in the journal Analysis in 1998, and it has shaped the debate ever since.

Their claim is that the mind does not stop at the skin.

When a notebook, a smartphone, or a sketch on paper plays the same functional role that a piece of memory or reasoning would play if it happened inside the head, then, they argue, that external object is a genuine part of the cognitive process, not merely a helpful accessory.

Their argument rests on a rule of thumb they call the parity principle, which can be stated in plain words as follows.

If a part of the world does a job that we would happily call thinking had it gone on inside the head, then we should call it thinking wherever it happens, because it would be arbitrary prejudice to count location alone as decisive.

Their famous illustration is a thought experiment about two people, Inga and Otto.

Inga hears of an exhibition, recalls from her biological memory that the museum is on a certain street, and walks there.

Otto has a memory impairment from Alzheimer's disease and instead keeps a notebook in which he has reliably written the museum's address; he consults it and walks there.

Clark and Chalmers argue that Otto's notebook plays exactly the role Inga's memory plays - it stores a standing belief he can look up and act on - so the notebook deserves to be counted as part of Otto's memory and mind.

Stated as a systems test, parity is an interface test: if an external store offers the same read access, reliability, and automatic trust as biological memory, then from the point of view of the running cognitive process the two are the same component, differing only in access latency - seconds for the notebook versus well under a second for biological recall.

The main objection, raised by the philosophers Fred Adams and Kenneth Aizawa, is called the coupling-constitution fallacy: the worry that just because something is tightly linked to your thinking, it does not follow that the thing is a part of your thinking, any more than a fuel line is a part of the engine's combustion.

Beginners should know this remains a live philosophical dispute rather than a settled result, but even critics grant its practical lesson, that human cognition leans heavily on external props.


56.3.2 Scaffolding and cognitive niche construction

These two terms name the practical, less controversial heart of the embedded and extended story, and they are easy to grasp with examples.

Scaffolding, a term drawn from the developmental psychologist Lev Vygotsky and the builder's platform he had in mind, means the temporary external support that lets a person accomplish something they could not yet manage alone.

A child learning arithmetic counts on fingers, then on a number line drawn on paper, then in the head, so the external aids scaffold the skill until the inner skill can stand without them.

Adults scaffold constantly too: we make grocery lists so we need not hold items in memory, we arrange the ingredients on the counter in the order a recipe needs, and we use calendars, calculators, and search engines to carry loads our unaided brains would struggle with.

In systems terms, scaffolding is load balancing: working memory, which holds only about four chunks at once, offloads state to an external medium with effectively unlimited capacity, at the price of slower access through the eyes and hands.

Cognitive niche construction is the broader and more striking idea, borrowed from biology where niche construction means an animal reshaping its environment - as a beaver builds a dam - so that the changed environment then shapes the animal in turn.

Applied to cognition, it means humans continually rebuild their surroundings into thinking-friendly forms: we invent writing, numerals, maps, diagrams, road signs, and filing systems, and these external structures then do a large share of the cognitive work and pass down through culture to the next generation.

The philosopher Andy Clark captures the moral by calling humans natural-born cyborgs, meaning we are the animals whose special trick is to fuse our brains with tools and symbols we ourselves have made.

For konnectome the lesson is concrete rather than mystical: a great deal of human intelligence is stored not in the individual head but in the shared, engineered world, so a fair comparison between human and machine intelligence has to take that external scaffolding into account.


56.4 Enactivism and ecological psychology

This section covers the last E, the enacted mind, together with an older cousin called ecological psychology.

Enactivism is the view that a mind is not a thing that passively receives a picture of the world but an activity that brings a world into being through living and doing.

Ecological psychology is the related tradition, founded earlier, that stresses how much useful information is already out there in the environment for an active creature to pick up.

Both traditions push against the idea that perceiving is building an inner copy of the world, and the section explains their three central ideas.

In systems terms both traditions shrink the internal state the perceiver must maintain and enlarge the role of the sensor-actuator loop: less stored model, more live sampling.


56.4.1 Autopoiesis and the enactive approach

To understand enactivism you have to start with a strange word that comes from biology.

Autopoiesis, coined by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela in the 1970s, literally means self-producing, and it names the defining trick of a living cell: it is a system that continuously makes and repairs the very components and boundary that keep it in existence.

A cell builds the membrane that holds it together, and that membrane in turn lets the cell keep building itself, so life is a self-sustaining loop rather than a fixed structure.

The enactive approach, launched by Varela together with the philosopher Evan Thompson and the psychologist Eleanor Rosch in their 1991 book The Embodied Mind, extends this biological insight into a theory of cognition.

Their core claim is that cognition is not the representation of a pre-given outside world by a pre-given inside mind, but rather the bringing forth, or enacting, of a meaningful world through the ongoing activity of a living body.

The technical word for how a creature actively assigns meaning to its surroundings is sense-making, and the idea is that things in the environment become significant - food, threat, shelter - only in relation to a living system's need to keep itself going.

A simple illustration: a lump of sugar is not intrinsically good; it becomes good only from the standpoint of a bacterium that must feed to survive, so the meaning is created in the encounter, not read off the world.

Read as a specification, sense-making takes the organism's viability needs and the current environmental encounter as inputs, and outputs a valence - an assignment of good, bad, or neutral - that exists nowhere in the world alone and nowhere in the organism alone, only in their meeting.

This tradition also brings consciousness and the felt, first-person quality of experience back to the centre of cognitive science, which mainstream information-processing accounts had tended to set aside, and that is one reason it has attracted renewed attention.


56.4.2 Sensorimotor contingency

Sensorimotor contingency theory is a sharper, more concrete member of the enactive family, aimed specifically at explaining perception.

A contingency is just a lawful if-then dependency, a reliable pattern of the form if I do this, then that will follow.

A sensorimotor contingency, then, is the reliable rule that links a movement to the change it produces in what you sense.

The theory was set out by the psychologists Kevin O'Regan and Alva Noe in an influential 2001 paper, and its central claim is surprising: seeing is not the brain building a picture, but the brain's practical mastery of these movement-to-sensation rules.

To perceive a bottle as round is, on this view, to implicitly know how the image on your eye would shift as you turned it, and to perceive something as red is to know how that surface would respond to changing light.

As a mechanism, the perceiver's state is a learned table of movement-to-sensation laws; its input is the current sensory change paired with the movement that caused it; its output is the recognition of what kind of thing is out there; and its sampling loop runs at the pace of eye movements, roughly three to four fixations per second.

The theory explains a puzzle that troubles picture-in-the-head accounts, the puzzle of why the world looks rich and detailed even though the eye takes in sharp detail only at its centre: it looks detailed because you can, at any instant, flick your eyes to sample any part, so the detail is available on demand from the world rather than stored all at once inside.

This dovetails with striking findings on change blindness, where people fail to notice large changes to a scene when the change is masked by a flicker or an eye movement, which suggests we hold far less of the world in our heads than it feels like we do.

The provocative slogan associated with this view is that the world serves as its own best model, meaning that instead of maintaining a full inner replica, the brain leaves the information out in the world and goes back to look whenever it needs it.


56.4.3 Affordances and direct perception

Affordance and direct perception are the two flagship ideas of ecological psychology, founded by the American psychologist James J. Gibson across works culminating in his 1979 book The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception.

An affordance is what the environment offers an animal for action: a chair affords sitting, a handle affords grasping, a gap affords passing through, and a ledge affords stepping up.

Gibson's key point is that we perceive the world in terms of these action possibilities directly, so that we see a doorway as walk-through-able rather than first seeing a bare shape and only later reasoning out what we could do with it.

Crucially an affordance is relational: a step affords climbing only relative to the length of your own legs, so the very same stair is climbable for an adult and a barrier for a toddler, which means affordances are defined jointly by the world and the body that meets it.

In systems terms, affordance perception is a function of two inputs - the structured light from the scene and the perceiver's own body dimensions and action capacities - and its output is not a description but a menu of currently possible actions, refreshed continuously as the animal moves.

Direct perception is Gibson's bolder companion claim, that the information needed to perceive the world accurately is already present in the structured light reaching the eyes, so perceiving does not require the brain to add hidden inferences or fill in missing pieces.

Gibson pointed, for instance, to optic flow - the way the whole visual scene streams outward around a point as you move forward - which specifies your heading and speed directly and reliably, giving the moving animal usable information for free.

This puts Gibson in sharp, deliberate opposition to the constructivist tradition of Hermann von Helmholtz, treated earlier in this outline, which holds that perception is a form of unconscious inference that must guess at a world the senses underdetermine.

In systems terms the two sides predict differently: Gibson predicts that enriching the stimulus removes the need for internal assumptions, so a fully structured natural scene should never mislead a moving observer, while the constructivist predicts that even rich scenes are interpreted through prior assumptions, so illusions should persist wherever the priors and the world disagree.

The honest state of the debate is that each side captures real cases: Gibson is compelling for an animal freely moving through a well-lit natural world flooded with information, while the constructivists are compelling for the impoverished, ambiguous, or illusory displays that fill the psychology laboratory, and much modern work tries to reconcile the two rather than crown a winner.


56.5 Chapter systems treatment

The process modelled here is coordination by coupling: two or more rhythmic components, none of them in charge, settling into a shared pattern purely through mutual influence, as captured in miniature by the Haken-Kelso-Bunz (HKB) model of bimanual coordination.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ The continuous state of each coupled component, formatted as a phase angle per oscillator, sourced from proprioception - the body's sense of its own limb positions - and from vision or hearing of the partner's movement.

◦ A control parameter such as movement frequency or task demand, sourced from voluntary intention or the pace of the environment.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A relative phase signal, the difference between the component phases, formatted as an angle where zero means in-phase and one hundred eighty degrees means anti-phase, consumed by the motor system as the current coordination pattern.

◦ A stability signal, the moment-to-moment variability of relative phase, consumed by the system itself as an early warning that the current pattern is about to break.

• STATE.

◦ The current phase of each oscillator and nothing more; the coordination pattern itself is not stored anywhere but re-created continuously by the coupling.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Coupling strength, which sets how hard each component pulls on the other.

◦ The ratio of the two coupling terms in the HKB potential, which determines whether the anti-phase attractor exists at all.

◦ Movement frequency, the control parameter whose increase destroys the anti-phase attractor.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Relaxation into the in-phase attractor after a perturbation takes on the order of a few movement cycles, which at ordinary movement rates is roughly one to a few seconds.

◦ In Kelso's finger experiments the anti-phase pattern loses stability and switches to in-phase as pacing rises through roughly two to three cycles per second.

◦ A single characteristic time for cognition-wide dynamics: REFUSED, because the dynamical approach explicitly denies that one timescale governs all cognitive processes.

• MODES.

◦ In-phase mode, both components moving together, stable at all achievable frequencies.

◦ Anti-phase mode, components alternating, stable only at low frequencies; the transition to in-phase is triggered when rising frequency flattens the anti-phase basin until noise carries the system out of it.

◦ Uncoupled mode, each component free-running at its own frequency, entered when coupling strength falls near zero, for example when partners stop attending to each other.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Unwanted entrainment, as when a speaker cannot help falling into an audience's clapping rhythm.

◦ Hysteresis errors, in which the system clings to an old pattern past the point where it stopped being appropriate, as in the infant A-not-B reach toward the old hiding place.

◦ Loss of flexibility in disorders of coordination, where attractors are too deep to escape, and pathological instability, where they are too shallow to hold, as studied in movement disorders.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called phase one with initial value zero.
Create a number variable called phase two with initial value two point eight.
Create a number variable called own frequency one with initial value one point zero.
Create a number variable called own frequency two with initial value one point one.
Create a number variable called coupling strength with initial value zero point eight.
Create a number variable called time step with initial value zero point zero one.
For each step from one to two thousand, do the following.
    Calculate the relative phase as phase one minus phase two.
    Calculate the pull on oscillator one as the negative of coupling strength times the sine of the relative phase.
    Calculate the pull on oscillator two as coupling strength times the sine of the relative phase.
    Add own frequency one plus the pull on oscillator one, times the time step, to phase one.
    Add own frequency two plus the pull on oscillator two, times the time step, to phase two.
    If the step is a multiple of four hundred, print the relative phase reduced to the range from negative pi to pi.
Print the final relative phase, which has settled near zero, the in-phase attractor.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for the sine function and pi.
import math

# Create a number variable called phase_one with initial value zero.
phase_one = 0.0
# Create a number variable called phase_two with initial value two point eight.
phase_two = 2.8
# Create a number variable called own_frequency_one with initial value one point zero.
own_frequency_one = 1.0
# Create a number variable called own_frequency_two with initial value one point one.
own_frequency_two = 1.1
# Create a number variable called coupling_strength with initial value zero point eight.
coupling_strength = 0.8
# Create a number variable called time_step with initial value zero point zero one.
time_step = 0.01

# Define a function that reduces an angle to the range from negative pi to pi.
def wrap(angle):
    # Return the angle shifted by pi, taken modulo two pi, then shifted back by pi.
    return (angle + math.pi) % (2 * math.pi) - math.pi

# For each step from one to two thousand, do the following.
for step in range(1, 2001):
    # Calculate the relative phase as phase_one minus phase_two.
    relative_phase = phase_one - phase_two
    # Calculate the pull on oscillator one as the negative of coupling_strength times the sine of the relative phase.
    pull_one = -coupling_strength * math.sin(relative_phase)
    # Calculate the pull on oscillator two as coupling_strength times the sine of the relative phase.
    pull_two = coupling_strength * math.sin(relative_phase)
    # Add own_frequency_one plus pull_one, times the time_step, to phase_one.
    phase_one = phase_one + (own_frequency_one + pull_one) * time_step
    # Add own_frequency_two plus pull_two, times the time_step, to phase_two.
    phase_two = phase_two + (own_frequency_two + pull_two) * time_step
    # If the step is a multiple of four hundred, print the wrapped relative phase.
    if step % 400 == 0:
        # Print the step number and the wrapped relative phase rounded to three decimals.
        print("step", step, "relative phase", round(wrap(relative_phase), 3))

# Print the final relative phase, which has settled near zero, the in-phase attractor.
print("settled relative phase:", round(wrap(phase_one - phase_two), 3))


CHAPTER 57. PREDICTIVE PROCESSING, ACTIVE INFERENCE, AND THE FREE ENERGY PRINCIPLE (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter presents one of the most ambitious and talked-about ideas in the recent science of mind, a single principle that some researchers hope can explain perception, action, learning, attention, and even emotion all at once.

The core intuition is simple to state: the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine that is always guessing what its senses will report next, and everything it does is in the service of making better guesses.

In systems terms the whole chapter describes one control loop: a generative model - an internal machine that can produce predicted sensory data from hypotheses about the world - runs forward, a comparator subtracts prediction from input, and the residual error drives every update in the system.

We will build this up in three stages of increasing ambition.

The first stage, predictive coding, is a well-supported account of how the brain might perceive by predicting.

The second stage, the free energy principle, is a grand and controversial attempt to derive that account from a single mathematical rule about how any self-preserving thing must behave.

The third stage, active inference, extends the rule from perceiving the world to acting in it.

A beginner should hold on to one honest warning throughout: the further we go up this ladder, the more mathematically imposing and the more disputed the claims become, so admiration and skepticism are both appropriate.


57.1 Predictive coding

This section explains the most concrete and best-evidenced idea in the chapter, a theory about the mechanics of perception.

Predictive coding proposes that instead of passively passing sensory signals up from the eyes and ears to the brain, the brain is constantly sending predictions down and only passing up the parts it got wrong.

As an engineering scheme this is a compression strategy: transmitting only the residual error uses far less bandwidth than transmitting the whole signal, which is exactly why the same trick is used in video compression.

The section describes how that would work as a layered system and traces the idea back through a long history so the reader sees it is not a passing fashion.


57.1.1 Hierarchical prediction and error minimisation

Let us define the machinery piece by piece, because the whole theory is really just this one loop repeated.

A hierarchy here means a stack of processing levels, with lower levels close to the raw senses - the parts of the brain that first receive signals from the eyes - and higher levels handling more abstract, general descriptions such as objects, causes, and contexts.

The central proposal is that each higher level is continuously trying to predict what the level just below it is doing, and it sends that prediction downward.

The lower level compares the prediction it receives against what it is actually registering, and it computes the difference between the two.

That difference is called prediction error, and it is simply the mismatch between what was expected and what arrived.

The key move is that the brain sends only this prediction error back up the hierarchy, not the whole signal, because whatever the higher level already predicted correctly carries no news and can be left unsaid.

The higher levels then adjust their picture of the world to reduce the error next time, and the whole system keeps looping until the errors settle down to a minimum, at which point the brain's guess and the world are in agreement and you have a stable perception.

To minimise error is thus the single job of the system, and perception, on this account, is the brain's best current hypothesis about the hidden causes out in the world that are producing the sensory signals.

Read as an interface, each level subscribes to two signals - the prediction descending from above and the error ascending from below - and publishes two signals, its own prediction downward and its own residual error upward, with the loop iterating on the timescale of tens to a few hundred milliseconds within a single act of perception.

The influential computational demonstration of this scheme was given by Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard in a 1999 paper in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

They showed that a network built this way, with error-signalling units and prediction-sending units, could reproduce puzzling features of real visual neurons, such as why a neuron that fires for a short line can go quiet when the line is extended - a phenomenon called end-stopping - which falls out naturally if that neuron is reporting prediction error rather than raw stimulus.

An everyday way to feel the idea: you stop hearing the steady hum of a refrigerator because your brain predicts it perfectly, so it generates no error and drops out of awareness, and the moment it switches off the change is a large prediction error that you notice at once.


57.1.2 The Helmholtzian analysis-by-synthesis lineage

This sub-section places predictive coding in a long tradition so the reader sees its deep roots.

The German physicist and physiologist Hermann von Helmholtz proposed in the 1860s that perception is a process of unconscious inference, meaning the brain unconsciously reasons from ambiguous sensory clues to its best guess about the hidden outside cause.

Helmholtz's insight was that the senses alone never fully fix what is out there - the same patch of light on the eye could come from countless different scenes - so the brain must add assumptions to settle on one interpretation, and it does this so fast and so automatically that we never notice the guessing.

Analysis by synthesis is the name later given to the strategy this implies, and the phrase is worth unpacking.

Analysis means breaking an incoming signal down to figure out what produced it, and synthesis means generating or constructing a candidate signal from a hypothesis about its cause.

Analysis by synthesis, then, is the trick of understanding an input by trying to build it: the brain guesses at a cause, synthesises the sensory pattern that cause would produce, compares that to the real input, and revises the guess until the built pattern matches, which is exactly the predictive-coding loop described above.

The term was introduced in the 1950s and 1960s in speech research, and the psychologist Ulric Neisser gave it prominence in his founding 1967 textbook Cognitive Psychology, so the idea had been circulating for decades before the modern mathematical versions arrived.

Because this sub-section describes a lineage rather than a mechanism, the systems reading is a prediction contrast: a pure feed-forward account predicts that perception should be no slower or richer when input is degraded, while any analysis-by-synthesis account predicts that degraded input forces extra generate-and-compare cycles, visible as slower recognition and stronger influence of expectations.

The lineage matters because it shows predictive coding is the latest expression of a very old and durable intuition, that to perceive is to construct, going back at least to Helmholtz and arguably to much older philosophy about how the mind meets the world.


57.2 The free energy principle

This section climbs to the most ambitious and most contested idea in the chapter.

The free energy principle, associated above all with the neuroscientist Karl Friston, tries to show that predictive processing is not just one clever strategy the brain happens to use, but something that any system which manages to keep existing must be doing.

It is a beautiful and sweeping claim, and it is also famously hard to follow and hotly argued over, so the section aims to give the honest gist without pretending it is simple or settled.


57.2.1 Variational free energy as a bound on surprise

We need to define three ideas gently: surprise, free energy, and the bound between them.

Surprise, in this technical sense, does not mean the feeling of being startled; it is a mathematical measure of how unexpected a sensory state is, given the brain's model of the world, where states the model deems very unlikely count as high surprise.

The principle starts from a biological observation dressed in mathematics: a living thing survives only by staying within a narrow range of states - a body temperature near thirty-seven degrees, oxygen in the blood, and so on - and being knocked far outside that range is, from the model's point of view, a highly surprising and usually fatal condition.

So a system that persists must, in effect, keep its sensory states unsurprising, which means it must minimise surprise over the long run.

The snag is that a brain cannot actually compute surprise directly, because doing so would require knowing the probability of its sensations averaged over every possible way the world could be, which is impossible to work out.

This is where variational free energy comes in: it is a quantity the brain can compute from what it has, and it is mathematically guaranteed to always be greater than or equal to the true surprise, so it sits above surprise like a ceiling.

The word variational is borrowed from a branch of mathematics for finding the best approximation, and the word free energy is borrowed by analogy from physics; a beginner can safely treat the whole term as a name for a computable stand-in for surprise.

Because free energy is an upper bound on surprise - a ceiling - pushing the ceiling down forces the surprise underneath it down too, so a system that keeps minimising free energy is thereby keeping its surprise low without ever having to measure surprise directly.

As a computation, the free-energy calculator takes the current sensory input and the system's current approximate belief as inputs, and outputs a single scalar cost that the rest of the system treats as the quantity to drive downhill.

The pleasing payoff is that minimising variational free energy turns out to be mathematically the same as minimising prediction error, which ties this grand principle back to the concrete predictive-coding machinery of the previous section.


57.2.2 Markov blankets and self-organisation

To make the principle apply to any self-preserving thing and not just to brains, Friston reaches for a concept called the Markov blanket.

Named after the mathematician Andrey Markov, a Markov blanket is a statistical boundary that separates the inside of a system from the outside, defined so that the two only ever influence each other through the boundary itself and never directly.

In plainer words, it is the set of variables that stands between a thing and its environment, like a skin or a cell membrane, such that the inside can only sense the outside and act on the outside through that intervening layer.

The blanket has two working parts: sensory states, through which the world affects the system, and active states, through which the system affects the world, and together they wrap the internal states off from the external ones.

For an engineer this is simply an interface specification: the blanket is the complete list of input channels and output channels, and the claim is that everything cognitive happens in the traffic across that interface.

Self-organisation is the term for how order and structure can arise and maintain themselves in a system without any outside designer arranging them, purely from the local interactions of the parts, the way a whirlpool organises itself in draining water.

Friston's grand argument is that any system that manages to hold itself together against the universe's relentless tendency toward disorder - any system with a Markov blanket that persists over time - will look, from the outside, exactly as if it were minimising the free energy of its sensory states, and therefore as if it were modelling and predicting its world.

On this reading, prediction is not a special talent of clever brains but the signature of existence itself for anything that stays distinct from its surroundings, from a single cell to a person.

It is fair to tell a beginner that this is the most disputed step in the whole chapter: admirers find it a breathtaking unification, while critics, including sympathetic ones, argue that the Markov-blanket formalism is applied loosely and that the leap from a mathematical description to a claim about what systems are really doing is not fully earned.


57.2.3 The unification claim across brain theories

This sub-section explains why the free energy principle has generated so much excitement despite its difficulty.

The unification claim is the promise that a single principle - minimise free energy - can be shown to contain, as special cases, many of the separate theories that different fields had developed on their own.

Friston and colleagues argue, for instance, that predictive coding is what free-energy minimisation looks like for perception, that the reinforcement-learning theories of reward described earlier in this outline are what it looks like for action, that the efficient-coding ideas from sensory neuroscience fall out of it, and that even the exploratory drive of curiosity can be derived from it.

The appeal is the appeal of physics envy in the best sense: just as physicists prize a single equation that explains many separate phenomena, a single principle that knits together perception, action, learning, and attention would be a major theoretical achievement.

Because this sub-section describes a debate rather than a mechanism, the systems contrast is this: if the unification is real, then the parameters of the separate theories should turn out to be constrained by one another rather than freely tunable, whereas if the principle is merely a flexible language, each re-description will add free parameters and forbid nothing.

The counter-view, pressed by careful commentators, is that a principle general enough to cover everything risks explaining nothing in particular, because it may be too flexible to rule any specific observation out, and a theory that no possible finding could contradict is more a framework or a language than a testable claim.

The current honest verdict, which a beginner deserves, is mixed: the free energy principle is widely regarded as mathematically elegant and genuinely generative of new experiments and models, while its status as a true law of mind and life rather than a very general modelling stance remains unsettled and actively debated.


57.3 Active inference

This section extends the predictive story from perceiving to doing, which is where it becomes a full theory of behaviour rather than only of perception.

Active inference is the idea that action, just like perception, is in the business of minimising prediction error, but it does so from the other end.

Where perception changes your model to fit the world, action changes the world to fit your model, and the section unpacks how that reversal works and what it explains.

In control-engineering terms, perception is state estimation and action is feedback control, and active inference claims both are performed by one and the same error-cancelling machinery.


57.3.1 Action as the fulfilment of prediction

Here is the pivotal and slightly dizzying idea, stated plainly first.

In ordinary thinking, we predict what will happen and then act separately for our own reasons; in active inference, acting simply is making a prediction come true.

The proposal is that when you decide to reach for a cup, your brain issues a confident prediction that your hand is already at the cup, which creates a large prediction error because your hand is in fact still on the table.

There are two ways to wipe out that error: change the prediction to match reality, or change reality to match the prediction, and active inference says the motor system takes the second route by moving the hand until the sensed position finally matches the predicted position, at which point the error vanishes.

Movement, on this view, is the body cancelling its own prediction errors by making the predicted state actually happen, and this is called the fulfilment of prediction.

The signals that drive the muscles are recast as predictions about the sensations the body expects to feel when the movement is complete, and the spinal reflexes act to close the gap - a proposal sometimes described as motor control by active inference rather than by classical motor commands.

As a mechanism, the motor loop takes a proprioceptive prediction as its input, publishes muscle activity as its output, holds the target prediction as its only state, and closes its error at the speed of spinal reflex arcs, tens of milliseconds, far faster than deliberate correction.

This tidy scheme raises an obvious worry that the theory must answer: if a strong enough prediction can move your arm, why do wishful expectations not move it constantly, and the answer offered is a mechanism called precision control, treated below and in the earlier perception chapters, which decides how much weight a given prediction or error is allowed to have.

The elegance a beginner can appreciate is the symmetry: perception and action become two sides of one coin, both merely different ways of reducing the mismatch between what the brain expects and what its senses report.


57.3.2 Expected free energy as the sum of epistemic and pragmatic value

To choose among possible actions, and especially to plan ahead, active inference introduces a forward-looking quantity, and it splits neatly into two motivations everyone can recognise.

Expected free energy is the free energy a system anticipates it would incur in the future if it followed a particular course of action, so where ordinary free energy scores the present, expected free energy scores imagined futures, letting the system compare plans before committing.

The system is said to prefer the course of action with the lowest expected free energy, and the mathematics shows that this quantity breaks into two parts that pull the agent in two familiar directions.

The first part is pragmatic value, which is the drive to reach outcomes you prefer - to get food when hungry, warmth when cold, the goal you actually want - and it is the exploiting, goal-seeking side of behaviour.

The second part is epistemic value, from a Greek root meaning to do with knowledge, and it is the drive to reduce your uncertainty - to gather information, to resolve ambiguity, to find out - and it is the exploring, curious side of behaviour.
