The lovely result is that a single formula yields both the urge to get what you want and the urge to learn what you do not know, so curiosity is not bolted on as an extra but drops out of the same principle as goal-seeking.

As a computation, the planner takes as inputs the current belief state, a menu of candidate actions, and a table of preferred outcomes; for each action it simulates the expected observations, scores them for preference satisfaction and for expected information gain, and publishes the action with the best combined score - which is exactly what the code sample at the end of this chapter does in a two-room world.

This gives a principled account of the exploration-exploitation trade-off discussed in the learning chapters, the everyday dilemma of whether to return to the restaurant you know is good or to try the new one you know nothing about, and here that trade-off is simply the balancing of pragmatic against epistemic value.

For a field trying to build agents that both pursue goals and explore sensibly, this unified treatment of wanting and wondering is one of active inference's most attractive offerings.


57.3.3 Interoceptive inference and the emotional self

This sub-section extends the predictive framework inward, to the body's own internal states, and reaches a striking claim about feelings.

Interoception is the perception of the internal condition of your own body: your heartbeat, your breathing, your gut, your temperature, your sense of hunger or fullness.

Interoceptive inference is the proposal that the brain perceives these inner signals in exactly the same predict-and-correct way it perceives the outside world, by generating predictions about the state of the body and updating them against the actual signals coming from within.

The neuroscientist Anil Seth, building on work with Hugo Critchley, argued in influential papers around 2013 that emotions are the brain's best guesses about the causes of its own bodily sensations, so a racing heart and tight chest get interpreted, in context, as fear or excitement depending on what the brain predicts is going on.

On this view an emotion is not a raw readout of the body but an inference about the body, which is why the same physical arousal can be felt as different emotions in different situations - a point that connects to older two-factor theories of emotion covered elsewhere in this outline.

As a mechanism, the interoceptive loop subscribes to slow visceral signals - heart rate, breathing, gut state, operating over seconds to minutes rather than milliseconds - combines them with contextual predictions, and publishes a felt emotional state that the rest of cognition consumes as a summary of how the body is doing.

Seth memorably describes both ordinary perception and emotional feeling as a controlled hallucination, meaning the felt world and the felt self are always the brain's constructed best guess, reined in and corrected by sensory signals but built from the inside out.

This framework has become clinically interesting because it offers a way to understand disorders of the sense of self and of bodily feeling - such as anxiety, depression, and dissociation - as disturbances in interoceptive prediction, though this is a young research area and the clinical picture is still being worked out and should be described with care.

The larger significance for a beginner is that predictive processing here reaches all the way to the emotional and embodied self, suggesting that who you feel yourself to be is, on this theory, another model the brain is continually inferring.


57.4 The philosophy and the disputes

This section steps back from the machinery to weigh what it all means and where thoughtful people disagree.

Having laid out predictive coding, the free energy principle, and active inference, we now ask the harder questions: what picture of the mind does this paint, what obvious objection does it face, and how does it sit alongside the four-E ideas of the previous chapter?

The section is deliberately even-handed, because this is a frontier where the honest answer is often that the matter is not resolved.


57.4.1 The prediction-machine reading of mind

This sub-section states the sweeping philosophical picture that the framework invites, and names its most articulate champion.

The prediction-machine reading of mind, argued at length by the philosopher Andy Clark in his 2016 book Surfing Uncertainty and in a much-cited 2013 article, holds that the brain is, at bottom, an organ for prediction, and that this one idea reorganises how we should think about perception, action, imagination, and understanding.

On this reading the boundary between perceiving and imagining softens, because both are the brain running its internal model, the difference being only whether sensory prediction errors are currently reining the model in.

It also reframes attention, which becomes the brain turning up the volume on the prediction errors it judges reliable and turning down the ones it judges noisy, a process called precision weighting that we met in the perception chapters.

In systems terms precision weighting is gain control: each error channel carries a multiplier, attention sets the multiplier, and the same architecture explains focused perception, imagination with the input gain near zero, and dreaming with the gain fully closed.

Clark's careful version resists the wildest conclusions and tries to marry the prediction-machine idea to the embodied and extended views of the previous chapter, insisting that a predicting brain is still a brain in a body in a world, not a solitary calculator.

The reading is attractive because it is unifying and concrete, and it is worth flagging that even its friends treat it as a promising organising vision rather than a finished proof, since much of the neural evidence is consistent with predictive processing without uniquely requiring it.


57.4.2 The dark-room problem and its answers

This sub-section presents the single most famous objection to the framework, because facing it teaches the theory better than any praise could.

The dark-room problem is a sharp thought experiment aimed at the claim that the brain acts to minimise surprise.

The objection runs like this: if all you must do to keep your sensations unsurprising is to find a silent, dark, unchanging room and stay there forever, then a creature obeying the free energy principle should crawl into such a room and never leave, since a dark room is maximally predictable.

Since real animals plainly do not do this - they seek stimulation, novelty, food, mates, and change - the objection charges that the principle predicts the opposite of how living things actually behave.

The standard answer has two parts, and both are worth understanding.

First, an animal's predictions are not blank; they are set by its nature and its needs, so a creature genuinely expects to eat, to move, to see daylight, and to encounter its own kind, which means a dark empty room is in fact wildly surprising and unwelcome relative to what the creature's model expects of a life worth living.

Second, the epistemic-value term from active inference, described above, positively rewards reducing uncertainty, so a well-built agent is driven to explore and gather information rather than to stagnate, and boredom in the dark room is exactly the pull of unresolved uncertainty demanding to be reduced.

Defenders therefore argue the dark room only looks tempting if you forget that surprise is measured against the organism's own expectations, which are already those of an active, embodied, needful creature.

In systems terms the dispute is about where the preference table lives: the objection assumes an agent whose preferred-outcome distribution is flat, and the defence answers that no viable agent ships with a flat preference table, because the table is part of the organism's design.

Critics reply that this rescue works only by quietly loading the answer into the creature's built-in expectations, which raises the further question of where those expectations come from, so the exchange is a good example of how the framework's disputes tend to run: each patch invites a deeper question, and the debate continues.


57.4.3 The tension and reconciliation with four-E cognition

This closing sub-section asks how the prediction framework relates to the embodied and enactive ideas of the last chapter, and the relationship is genuinely complicated.

At first glance the two look opposed.

Predictive processing seems to put a rich internal model at the very centre of the mind, with the brain building and updating an inner representation of the world, whereas four-E cognition, especially in its enactive and ecological forms, was suspicious of inner models and wanted to relocate cognition into the body and the world.

So there is a real tension between a picture of the mind as an inner prediction engine and a picture of the mind as world-involving activity that travels light on internal representation.

Yet many thinkers, Andy Clark foremost among them, argue the two can be reconciled, and the bridge is action.

Because active inference makes the body's movements and the sampling of the world part of the very process of minimising error, the predicting brain is not a sealed calculator but a system that constantly reaches out, moves, and manipulates the environment to keep its predictions on track, which is exactly the embodied, world-engaged picture the four-E camp wanted.

A helpful middle position holds that the amount of internal modelling is a dial rather than a fixed setting: some tasks lean on rich inner prediction while others lean on cheap, direct exploitation of information in the world, and the same predictive machinery can slide between the two depending on what is efficient.

In systems terms the two camps predict differently: a heavy-model account predicts that cutting the agent off from the world mid-task should barely disturb short-term performance, because the model carries on, while a light-model account predicts immediate degradation, because the world was doing the storage.

The most radical enactivists remain unconvinced and still object to any essential role for internal representation, so a beginner should understand this as an ongoing negotiation rather than a completed peace treaty.

The productive upshot for konnectome is that these are not simply rival teams to pick between; they are increasingly seen as complementary constraints on any complete theory of mind, which is precisely the stance this outline takes toward competing frameworks throughout.


57.5 Chapter systems treatment

The process modelled here is active inference in miniature: an agent in a two-room world that chooses among actions by scoring each one's expected free energy, so that looking before leaping emerges from the same rule as leaping.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Sensory observations, formatted as discrete outcomes such as a cue light or the presence of food, sourced from the environment through the sensory states of the Markov blanket.

◦ A preference distribution over outcomes, formatted as prior probabilities that encode what the agent wants to sense, sourced from the agent's design or biology.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A posterior belief over hidden world states, formatted as a probability distribution, consumed by the planner.

◦ A selected action, formatted as a discrete command through the active states of the blanket, consumed by the environment.

• STATE.

◦ The current belief distribution over hidden states, and the generative model itself: the likelihood mapping from hidden states to observations and the preference table over outcomes.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Cue reliability, the probability that the informative observation is truthful.

◦ Preference strength, how sharply the agent favours its desired outcome.

◦ The relative weighting of epistemic and pragmatic value, which tunes curiosity against greed.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ A perceptual belief update in cortical hierarchies is reflected in mismatch responses - such as the mismatch negativity, an automatic brain response to unexpected sounds - peaking roughly 100 to 250 milliseconds after the surprising event.

◦ Spinal reflex arcs that cancel proprioceptive prediction error act within tens of milliseconds.

◦ Interoceptive states evolve over seconds to minutes, the timescale of heartbeat, breathing, and visceral change.

◦ A single time constant for free-energy minimisation as such: REFUSED, because the principle is claimed to hold at every timescale from reflex to evolution, so no one value is defensible.

• MODES.

◦ Perceptual mode, updating beliefs to fit sensations, engaged when sensory precision is high and action is withheld.

◦ Active mode, changing the world to fit predictions, engaged when the agent commits to a plan and proprioceptive predictions are given high precision.

◦ Exploratory mode, dominated by epistemic value when uncertainty is high, switching to exploitative mode, dominated by pragmatic value, once uncertainty is resolved - the switch is automatic because information gain shrinks as beliefs sharpen.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Hallucination and delusion, modelled as prediction gain set too high relative to sensory evidence, so the model overrides the world.

◦ Anxiety and panic, modelled as miscalibrated interoceptive predictions that read ordinary bodily signals as alarming.

◦ Pathological inaction or compulsive checking, modelled as preference and precision settings that make every option's expected free energy nearly equal or make uncertainty never feel resolved.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called belief that food is in room one, with initial value zero point five.
Create a number variable called cue reliability with initial value zero point nine.
Create a list called actions containing check the cue, enter room one, and enter room two.
Define a function that returns the entropy of a belief, as the negative sum over both options of probability times the logarithm of probability.
For each decision round, do the following.
    For each action in the actions list, do the following.
        If the action is check the cue, set its pragmatic value to a small negative checking cost, and set its epistemic value to the current entropy minus the expected entropy after seeing the cue.
        If the action is enter a room, set its epistemic value to zero, and set its pragmatic value to the believed probability that the food is in that room, times the preference strength.
        Calculate the action score as the pragmatic value plus the epistemic value.
    Choose the action with the highest score.
    If the chosen action is check the cue, sample a cue observation from the world, and update the belief with Bayes rule using the cue reliability.
    Otherwise, enter the chosen room, report whether the food was found, and stop.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for logarithms and the random module for sampling.
import math, random

# Create a variable holding the true food room, sampled at random from room one and room two.
true_food_room = random.choice([1, 2])
# Create a number variable called belief_room_one with initial value zero point five.
belief_room_one = 0.5
# Create a number variable called cue_reliability with initial value zero point nine.
cue_reliability = 0.9
# Create a number variable called preference_strength with initial value two point zero.
preference_strength = 2.0

# Define a function that returns the entropy of a two-option belief.
def entropy(p):
    # If the belief is certain either way, return zero.
    if p <= 0.0 or p >= 1.0:
        return 0.0
    # Return the negative sum of probability times log probability for both options.
    return -(p * math.log(p) + (1 - p) * math.log(1 - p))

# Define a function that returns the belief after a cue observation, by Bayes rule.
def updated_belief(p, cue_says_one):
    # Set the likelihood of this cue if food is in room one, from the cue reliability.
    like_one = cue_reliability if cue_says_one else 1 - cue_reliability
    # Set the likelihood of this cue if food is in room two, from the cue reliability.
    like_two = 1 - cue_reliability if cue_says_one else cue_reliability
    # Return the normalised posterior probability that food is in room one.
    return (p * like_one) / (p * like_one + (1 - p) * like_two)

# For each decision round from one to five, do the following.
for decision_round in range(1, 6):
    # Calculate the probability that the cue would say room one, under the current belief.
    prob_cue_one = belief_room_one * cue_reliability + (1 - belief_room_one) * (1 - cue_reliability)
    # Calculate the expected entropy after checking the cue, averaged over both cue outcomes.
    expected_entropy = prob_cue_one * entropy(updated_belief(belief_room_one, True)) + (1 - prob_cue_one) * entropy(updated_belief(belief_room_one, False))
    # Set the score of checking as the expected entropy reduction minus a small checking cost.
    score_check = entropy(belief_room_one) - expected_entropy - 0.05
    # Set the score of entering room one as the believed chance of food there times the preference strength.
    score_room_one = belief_room_one * preference_strength - preference_strength
    # Set the score of entering room two as the believed chance of food there times the preference strength.
    score_room_two = (1 - belief_room_one) * preference_strength - preference_strength
    # Collect the three scores in a dictionary keyed by action name.
    scores = {"check": score_check, "enter room 1": score_room_one, "enter room 2": score_room_two}
    # Choose the action with the highest score.
    action = max(scores, key=scores.get)
    # Print the round, the belief, and the chosen action.
    print("round", decision_round, "belief food in room 1 =", round(belief_room_one, 3), "->", action)
    # If the chosen action is to check the cue, observe and update the belief.
    if action == "check":
        # Sample whether the cue truthfully points at the food room, using the cue reliability.
        truthful = random.random() < cue_reliability
        # Set the cue reading to point at room one when truth and the food location agree.
        cue_says_one = (true_food_room == 1) == truthful
        # Update the belief with Bayes rule using the cue reading.
        belief_room_one = updated_belief(belief_room_one, cue_says_one)
    # Otherwise, enter the chosen room, report the result, and stop.
    else:
        # Set the chosen room number from the action name.
        chosen_room = 1 if action == "enter room 1" else 2
        # Print whether the agent found the food, and leave the loop.
        print("entered room", chosen_room, "- food found:", chosen_room == true_food_room)
        break

CHAPTER 58. REPRESENTATION, SYMBOLS, AND THE ARCHITECTURE OF THOUGHT (FRAMEWORK)

This chapter takes up the oldest and deepest quarrel in the science of mind, the quarrel over what a thought is made of.

One camp says thoughts are built like sentences, out of discrete symbols combined by rules, so that having a mind is a bit like having an inner language.

Another camp says thoughts are patterns of activity spread across a web of simple units, with no inner sentences at all, so that meaning is a matter of pattern rather than of language.

In systems terms the quarrel is about the data format of cognition: discrete structured records processed by rule application, or continuous distributed vectors processed by pattern transformation.

This is not a dry technicality; it decides what kind of thing we should try to build if we want to build a mind, and it has run for forty years without a clean winner.

The chapter also confronts two problems that have haunted every attempt to make representation work - how symbols get their meaning, and how a mind decides what is relevant - and it closes with the question of whether the mind is one general-purpose machine or a bundle of specialised ones.

The tag framework signals that this chapter supplies the conceptual tools and debates that the theories of whole minds, coming later in the outline, will draw upon.


58.1 The language of thought

This section lays out the most influential version of the symbols-and-rules picture.

The language of thought hypothesis holds that thinking literally happens in a kind of mental language, with its own words and its own grammar, distinct from any spoken language like English.

The section explains what that language is supposed to be and why its defenders think it is forced on us by the very shape of human thought.


58.1.1 Mentalese and the representational theory of mind

Let us define the central proposal and the philosopher behind it.

The language of thought hypothesis was put forward most forcefully by the philosopher Jerry Fodor, especially in his 1975 book The Language of Thought, and it is one of the most important ideas in modern philosophy of mind.

Fodor's claim is that there is an inner symbolic system, often nicknamed Mentalese, in which our thinking is actually carried out, so that when you believe it is raining there is, somewhere in your cognitive machinery, a symbolic structure that means it is raining, put together from more basic symbols according to rules.

Mentalese is not English or any other public language; it is supposed to be the underlying code that all human thought runs in, which is why speakers of different languages can nonetheless share the same thoughts.

This sits inside a broader view called the representational theory of mind, which needs unpacking in two halves.

A representation is anything that stands for something else - a word, a picture, a symbol - and the representational theory of mind says the mind works by storing and manipulating internal representations that stand for things and situations in the world.

The theory adds a crucial second half about what beliefs and desires really are: to believe that it is raining is to have a particular mental representation, meaning it is raining, held in a particular functional role, the belief role, while to want it to stop raining is to have a related representation held in the desire role.

Thinking, on this account, is computation over these symbols: the mind transforms one symbolic structure into another according to rules, much as a computer transforms strings of code, which is why this view is the philosophical backbone of the classical, symbol-processing approach to artificial intelligence.

As a system specification, Mentalese defines a storage format of typed, composable records; an instruction set of rule applications over those records, with each rule application taking on the order of tens of milliseconds if the production-cycle estimates from the architecture chapters carry over; and two registers, belief and desire, distinguished not by content but by the functional role the record is held in.

The great appeal of the view is that it neatly explains how thoughts can be about things and how reasoning can be truth-preserving, and the great burden it carries, addressed later in this chapter, is explaining how those inner symbols come to mean anything at all.


58.1.2 Productivity, systematicity, and compositionality

This sub-section gives the three properties of thought that defenders treat as the decisive evidence for a language-like inner code, and they are best learned through examples.

Productivity is the fact that you can understand and produce an effectively unlimited number of new thoughts you have never met before.

No one had ever considered the sentence a purple giraffe is reading Tuesday to the moon before you read it just now, yet you grasped it instantly, and this endless novelty from finite means cries out for explanation.

Systematicity is the fact that the ability to think certain thoughts comes bundled with the ability to think related ones, in a non-accidental pattern.

Anyone who can think John loves Mary can also think Mary loves John; you never meet a mind that can think the first but is constitutionally unable to think the second, and this reliable bundling looks like no coincidence.

Compositionality is the underlying explanation the language-of-thought camp offers for both: it is the principle that the meaning of a complex thought is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are put together.

Because John, loves, and Mary are reusable parts with stable meanings, and because there are rules for combining them, you automatically get both the endless novelty of productivity and the reliable bundling of systematicity, all from a small stock of symbols and a grammar for arranging them.

In systems terms these three properties are an engineering constraint on any candidate architecture: the representation format must support unbounded composition from a finite part inventory, guaranteed recombination of any parts once learned, and meaning that is a deterministic function of parts plus structure.

The argument, then, is an inference to the best explanation: the easiest way to explain why thought is productive, systematic, and compositional is to suppose that thoughts really do have parts and structure, that is, that there really is a language of thought.

This is a genuinely powerful argument, and it sets the challenge that the rival camp, connectionism, has spent decades trying to answer, which is the subject of the next section.


58.2 The classical and connectionist debate

This section stages the central confrontation of the chapter.

On one side stands the classical view just described, that the mind is a symbol-manipulating system with a language-like structure.

On the other stands connectionism, the view that the mind is a neural network of simple interconnected units whose knowledge lives in the strengths of their connections rather than in stored symbols.

The section follows the argument through its famous opening challenge, the replies it provoked, and its surprising return in the age of modern artificial intelligence.


58.2.1 The systematicity challenge

This sub-section states the objection that has organised the whole debate since the late 1980s.

In 1988 Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn published a long and forceful article, Connectionism and Cognitive Architecture: A Critical Analysis, which threw down a challenge that connectionists have been answering ever since.

Their argument, boiled down, was this: thought is systematic, as the previous section explained, and the classical view explains that systematicity naturally, because a symbol structure literally contains reusable parts that can be recombined.

A connectionist network, they charged, has no such built-in parts; it is a soup of activation across units, and nothing in its basic design guarantees that a network able to represent John loves Mary must also be able to represent Mary loves John.

Therefore, they concluded, insofar as connectionist networks do manage to be systematic, they must be doing so by secretly implementing a classical symbol system underneath, in which case connectionism is not a rival theory of the mind's architecture but merely a story about how the brain's hardware might run the real, symbolic software.

The force of the challenge is that it does not deny neural networks can be built or can learn; it denies that they explain the structured character of thought without smuggling in the very symbols they claimed to replace.

As a systems contrast, the two sides make different guarantees: the classical architecture guarantees recombination by construction, at the cost of needing a separate story about learning, while the connectionist architecture guarantees learning by construction, at the cost of needing a separate story about recombination.

This put the burden squarely on connectionists to show either that their networks can be genuinely systematic on their own terms, or that human thought is less rigidly systematic than Fodor and Pylyshyn assumed, and both replies were duly attempted.


58.2.2 The connectionist replies and tensor-product binding

This sub-section covers the most important technical answer to the challenge.

The central difficulty for a neural network is called the binding problem for representation: how can a network keep track of which role each thing plays, so that John-as-lover and Mary-as-loved do not smear together into a mere set containing John and Mary with no who-did-what-to-whom?

The most influential answer came from Paul Smolensky, who proposed a mathematical technique called tensor-product binding in work through the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The idea, in plain terms, is to represent each element of a thought as a pattern of activity for its content - a pattern for John, a pattern for Mary - and to separately represent each structural slot as another pattern - a pattern for the lover role, a pattern for the loved role.

Binding a filler to a role is then done by a specific mathematical combination, the tensor product, which fuses the John pattern with the lover-role pattern into a single composite pattern that keeps the two locked together, so the network can tell John-as-lover from John-as-loved.

By adding up such role-filler bindings, a network can encode a whole structured thought as one big activity pattern, and crucially it can later pull the pieces back out, which shows a network can carry genuine structure without a classical list of symbols.

As a mechanism, the binder takes role vectors and filler vectors as inputs, publishes one superimposed composite pattern as output, holds nothing between operations but the fixed role and filler vocabularies, and decomposes on demand by projecting the composite back through a chosen role vector - exactly the operation the code sample at the end of this chapter performs.

Smolensky offered this as proof that connectionism could answer the systematicity challenge on its own ground, honouring structure while remaining a network rather than a symbol processor.

Fodor and his collaborator Brian McLaughlin replied in 1990 that the trick did not fully work, arguing that tensor-product representations have their constituents only in a weak sense - the parts can be extracted by computation but are not literally present and causally active in the way classical symbols are - so the deep explanatory advantage of the classical view survived.

The exchange never reached a knock-out on either side, and it left the field with a sophisticated toolkit for building structure into networks and a lingering philosophical disagreement about whether that structure is the real thing or a clever imitation.


58.2.3 The modern reprise: systematic generalisation in neural networks

This sub-section brings the decades-old debate right up to the present, because it has been reborn inside modern artificial intelligence.

The old philosophical question turned into a concrete engineering test the moment powerful neural networks began doing impressive things, because one could now simply measure whether they generalise systematically.

Systematic generalisation means handling new combinations of familiar parts: if a system has learned the word jump and has learned to do things twice, it should be able to jump twice the first time it is asked, without special training on that exact combination.

In 2018 the researchers Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni built a clean test of this, a task called SCAN in which a network learns to turn simple commands into sequences of actions, and they arranged it so the test demanded new combinations of words the network had only seen separately.

Their result was a sharp rediscovery of Fodor and Pylyshyn's point: standard sequence-learning networks did nearly perfectly when the test items resembled the training items, but failed badly when success required recombining known parts in genuinely new ways, which is exactly the systematicity that classical symbols deliver for free.

This shows the forty-year-old debate was not idle philosophy; the same crack reopened in the most advanced learning systems of the day.

The story does not end in defeat for networks, however.

In 2023 Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni reported in the journal Nature that a network trained with a technique called meta-learning - roughly, training the network on a stream of little learning problems so that it learns how to recombine parts in general, rather than memorising any one mapping - could reach human-level systematic generalisation on these tasks.

In systems terms the finding relocates compositionality from the architecture to the training regime: recombination becomes a learned mode of operation, switched on by the right distribution of training problems, rather than a wired-in property of the data format.

The careful lesson for a beginner is balanced: systematic, compositional generalisation does not come automatically to neural networks and remains a real weakness of many of them, yet it is not proven impossible either, and it appears to be something a network can be taught to do rather than something it must have wired in from the start.

That balance is why the classical-versus-connectionist question is best regarded not as won by either side but as reshaped, with modern work trying to get the structure-respecting strengths of symbols and the learning strengths of networks in one system, which is a central ambition for projects like konnectome.


58.3 The hard problems of representation

This section confronts two deep difficulties that any theory of internal representation must eventually face, whichever side of the previous debate it favours.

The first is how a symbol inside a head, or a pattern inside a network, comes to be about anything in the world at all.

The second is how a mind manages to focus on what matters and ignore the endless things that do not, in a world where almost anything could in principle be relevant.

Both problems are famous for being easy to state and stubbornly hard to solve.


58.3.1 The symbol grounding problem restated

This sub-section revisits, in the setting of this chapter, a problem introduced earlier in the outline, because it strikes right at the language-of-thought view.

The symbol grounding problem, named and sharpened by the cognitive scientist Stevan Harnad in a 1990 paper, asks how the symbols inside a mind or a computer come to have meaning rather than being empty tokens.

Harnad's vivid way of posing it was to imagine trying to learn a first language purely from a dictionary written in that same unknown language: every word is defined only by other words you also do not know, so you spin forever among meaningless symbols and never touch anything real.

A pure symbol system, like the classical language of thought or a traditional artificial-intelligence program, seems to face just this predicament, because its symbols are defined only by their relations to other symbols and rules, with no anchor to the world outside the system.

Harnad's proposed cure was grounding through the senses and the body: at least some symbols must be tied directly to the system's own perception and action - the symbol for red hooked to the actual detection of red things, the symbol for grasp hooked to actual grasping - so that meaning can climb up from that sensory footing rather than floating free.

In systems terms grounding is an interface requirement: a representation system needs at least some channels whose values are set by transducers - devices that convert physical energy into signals - rather than by other representations, so that the reference of the base vocabulary is fixed outside the loop of symbols defining symbols.

This connects the whole debate of this chapter back to the embodied and enactive ideas of Chapter 56, because grounding is essentially the demand that symbols be rooted in a body's real dealings with a real world.

The problem has taken on fresh urgency with today's large language models, which learn from vast amounts of text and can be seen as a modern version of the dictionary-go-round, learning words only from other words, and researchers now actively debate how much such systems really understand and whether adding images, sound, and action - so-called multimodal grounding - genuinely solves the problem or only softens it, a question that is very much open.


58.3.2 The frame problem and the problem of relevance

This sub-section explains a difficulty that many regard as the single hardest obstacle for building a general mind.

The frame problem began as a narrow technical puzzle in artificial intelligence, first named by John McCarthy and Patrick Hayes in 1969, about how a reasoning program should keep track of what stays the same when an action happens.

If a robot moves a cup, it should update the cup's location but somehow know, without checking every fact it holds, that moving the cup did not change the colour of the walls, the day of the week, or the price of tea, and stating all the things that do not change turns out to be maddeningly hard.

Philosophers, above all Jerry Fodor and Daniel Dennett, broadened this into a far deeper worry usually called the problem of relevance.

The problem of relevance is this: in any real situation, an unbounded number of facts might conceivably bear on what to do, and there is no obvious way for a mind to zero in on the few that actually matter without somehow already reviewing the countless ones that do not.

When you plan a trip you effortlessly ignore that you own an umbrella of a certain colour and that Rome was founded long ago, yet in some odd circumstance either fact could be the crucial one, so relevance cannot simply be fixed in advance by a rule.

Fodor argued this makes central cognition - the open-ended, bring-anything-to-bear part of thinking, as opposed to walled-off perception - especially resistant to explanation, and he expressed his pessimism in a wry law that the more global and free-ranging a cognitive process is, the less anyone understands it.

The reason this cuts against the classical symbol picture is that a system of symbols and rules seems to have no efficient way to survey its whole store of knowledge for relevance without grinding to a halt, whereas humans do it in an instant and usually without effort.

In systems terms the problem is a scaling failure: exhaustive relevance checking costs time proportional to the size of the knowledge store, which for a lifetime of knowledge is intractable, yet human retrieval of the relevant fact typically completes within about a second, so whatever mechanism the brain uses, it is not exhaustive search.

A fair statement for a beginner is that the frame and relevance problems remain genuinely unsolved in the general case; they are a large part of why common sense has proven so much harder to build than narrow expertise, and they set a real bar that any candidate architecture of mind, konnectome included, has to face honestly.


58.4 Modularity

This section addresses the final structural question of the chapter, whether the mind is one thing or many.

Modularity is the idea that the mind is made up of separate, specialised subsystems - modules - each dedicated to a particular job, rather than being one flexible general-purpose processor.

The section contrasts a limited version of this idea with a far more sweeping one, and then returns to the relevance problem to explain why the disagreement matters.


58.4.1 Fodorian and massive modularity

This sub-section lays out the two main versions of the modularity idea and who argued for each.

The influential starting point is Jerry Fodor's 1983 book The Modularity of Mind, which proposed what is now called Fodorian modularity.

Fodor argued that the input systems of the mind - perception and language, the parts that take in sensory signals and decode speech - are modules, and he gave a list of properties that make something a module.

The key properties are that a module is domain-specific, meaning it handles only one narrow kind of information such as vision or grammar; that it is mandatory, meaning it runs automatically whether you want it to or not; that it is fast; and above all that it is informationally encapsulated, meaning it does its work using only its own limited store of information and cannot consult everything else the mind knows.

In systems terms a Fodorian module is a sealed service: a fixed input format, a fixed output format, a private database, no read access to the rest of the system, and a fast, mandatory execution path - and encapsulation is precisely what buys the speed, because a process that consults nothing beyond its own store has nothing to wait for.

The classic evidence for encapsulation is a visual illusion that persists even after you learn it is an illusion: the two lines in the Muller-Lyer figure keep looking unequal in length no matter how firmly you know they are equal, because your visual module cannot be talked out of its output by your beliefs.

Crucially, Fodor held that only the input systems are modular, and that central cognition - reasoning, believing, deciding - is precisely not modular but open and unencapsulated, which is why, on his view, it falls prey to the relevance problem and resists scientific understanding.

The rival and much bolder view, called massive modularity, was developed by evolutionary psychologists such as Leda Cosmides and John Tooby and defended philosophically by Peter Carruthers in his 2006 book The Architecture of the Mind.

Massive modularity claims that the whole mind, all the way up through reasoning and decision, is composed of many special-purpose modules, each shaped by evolution to solve a specific recurring problem faced by our ancestors, such as detecting cheaters in social exchange, choosing mates, or avoiding contamination.

On this view there is no single general-purpose thinker at the centre; what feels like general intelligence is the combined output of a large committee of specialised devices, and the appeal of the theory is that it explains how a mind could be built up by natural selection acting on one problem at a time.

The two views frame a real spectrum, from a mostly general mind with a few modular senses to a mind that is modular through and through, and where the truth lies is still debated.


58.4.2 The problem of central, isotropic cognition

This closing sub-section explains the sticking point that keeps the modularity debate alive, and it ties the whole chapter together.

The word isotropic is borrowed from physics, where it means the same in every direction, and Fodor used it to describe a troubling feature of central thinking: in principle, any piece of knowledge you have can be brought to bear on any problem, so information flows in from every direction with no fixed walls.

Central cognition is also what Fodor called Quinean, after the philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine, meaning that whether you should believe something can depend on your entire web of beliefs at once, the way a scientist judging a new theory may have to weigh it against everything else science holds.

These two features - isotropic and Quinean - are exactly what makes central cognition powerful and flexible, and exactly what makes the relevance problem of the previous section so severe, because a system open to everything has no easy way to avoid considering everything.

In systems terms the two camps predict differently: massive modularity predicts that central reasoning should show domain-specific speedups, domain-specific failures, and dissociations where one reasoning domain breaks while others survive, while the general-engine view predicts broadly correlated performance across domains and a single bottleneck that any hard problem competes for.

Fodor's pointed conclusion was that modularity works as an account of the mind's edges, the input systems, precisely because those systems are walled off and limited, but that the same trick cannot be extended to the open, isotropic centre, and that is why he thought the hardest part of the mind was also the least understood.

This is where the massive-modularity camp pushes back hardest, insisting that even the centre is really a collection of specialised modules and that the appearance of open, anything-goes reasoning is a kind of illusion produced by many narrow devices working together, though critics doubt a pile of specialists can ever capture the genuine flexibility of human thought.

The reason a beginner should care, and the reason this makes a fitting close to the chapter, is that the whole matter bears directly on how one would build a mind: a designer who believes in massive modularity will assemble many special-purpose components, while a designer who believes central cognition is genuinely general and isotropic will search for one flexible reasoning engine and must then confront the still-unsolved relevance problem head-on.

That unresolved choice - many specialised machines or one general one, and how either could tame relevance - is one of the central open questions this outline carries forward into its later treatment of complete cognitive architectures, and it is one of the deepest questions facing any project, konnectome among them, that hopes to build a mind rather than merely a clever tool.


58.5 Chapter systems treatment

The process modelled here is structured representation by role-filler binding: composing the thought John loves Mary from vector parts, superimposing the bindings into one pattern, and decomposing that pattern to recover who did what to whom.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Filler vectors, formatted as fixed-length lists of numbers standing for the content elements such as John and Mary, sourced from the system's learned vocabulary.

◦ Role vectors, formatted as fixed-length lists of numbers standing for the structural slots such as lover and loved, sourced from the system's structural vocabulary.

◦ A query role, formatted as a role vector, sourced from whatever process wants to read a slot of the composed thought.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A composite thought pattern, formatted as a matrix that is the sum of the role-filler tensor products, consumed by memory and by downstream inference.

◦ A decoded filler, formatted as the vocabulary item whose vector best matches the unbinding result, consumed by whatever process asked the query.

• STATE.

◦ The fixed role and filler vocabularies, and the current composite pattern; nothing else persists between bind and unbind operations.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Vector dimensionality, which sets capacity: more dimensions allow more near-orthogonal roles and fillers before crosstalk corrupts decoding.

◦ The number of bindings superimposed in one composite, which trades expressiveness against interference.

◦ The similarity threshold below which a decoded filler is rejected as noise.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ If binding is carried out by the rule-firing machinery of a production system, one composition or decomposition step costs on the order of one production cycle, about 50 milliseconds.

◦ Human comprehension of a simple subject-verb-object sentence, the behavioural envelope for composing such a structure, completes within roughly one to two seconds at normal speech rates.

◦ A neural time constant for tensor-product binding specifically: REFUSED, because tensor-product binding is a mathematical proposal whose neural implementation and timing have not been established.

• MODES.

◦ Composition mode, building the composite from role-filler pairs, triggered by the arrival of a structured input to encode.

◦ Decomposition mode, projecting the composite through a query role to recover a filler, triggered by a downstream request to read a slot.

◦ Superposition mode, holding several bindings in one pattern, entered whenever more than one pair is bound and exited when the pattern is cleared.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Crosstalk: with too many bindings or insufficiently distinct vectors, unbinding returns a blend, so John-as-lover bleeds into Mary-as-loved - the vector version of a binding error.

◦ Illusory conjunctions, in which features or fillers from different objects are recombined wrongly, as reported in divided-attention experiments.

◦ Loss of systematicity: a network that never acquires clean role vectors can store familiar combinations yet fail on novel recombinations, which is exactly the failure the SCAN experiments measured.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list called vocabulary that maps each name, John and Mary and Kim, to a four-number filler vector.
Create a list called roles that maps the lover role and the loved role each to a four-number vector, chosen at right angles to each other.
Define a function called bind that takes a filler vector and a role vector and returns their outer product as a four-by-four matrix.
Define a function called unbind that takes a composite matrix and a role vector and returns the vector produced by multiplying the matrix by the role vector.
Define a function called nearest that takes a vector and returns the vocabulary name whose vector has the highest dot product with it.
Create a matrix called thought filled with zeros.
Add the binding of the John vector with the lover role to the thought matrix.
Add the binding of the Mary vector with the loved role to the thought matrix.
Print the name nearest to the result of unbinding the thought with the lover role.
Print the name nearest to the result of unbinding the thought with the loved role.
Create a second thought matrix by binding Mary as lover and John as loved.
Print the decoded slots of the second thought, showing that the same parts in swapped roles yield the reversed sentence.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a dictionary called vocabulary mapping each name to a four-number filler vector.
vocabulary = {"John": [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0], "Mary": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0], "Kim": [1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]}
# Create a dictionary called roles mapping each role to a vector, with the two roles at right angles.
roles = {"lover": [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "loved": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]}

# Define a function called bind that returns the outer product of a filler and a role.
def bind(filler, role):
    # Return the matrix whose entry at row i and column j is filler i times role j.
    return [[f * r for r in role] for f in filler]

# Define a function called add_into that adds one matrix into another, entry by entry.
def add_into(target, matrix):
    # For each row index and column index, add the matrix entry to the target entry.
    for i in range(len(target)):
        for j in range(len(target[i])):
            target[i][j] = target[i][j] + matrix[i][j]

# Define a function called unbind that multiplies a composite matrix by a role vector.
def unbind(composite, role):
    # Return the vector whose entry i is the dot product of row i with the role vector.
    return [sum(row[j] * role[j] for j in range(len(role))) for row in composite]

# Define a function called nearest that returns the vocabulary name best matching a vector.
def nearest(vector):
    # Return the name whose filler vector has the highest dot product with the vector.
    return max(vocabulary, key=lambda name: sum(a * b for a, b in zip(vocabulary[name], vector)))

# Define a function called compose that builds a thought matrix from a lover and a loved.
def compose(lover_name, loved_name):
    # Create a four-by-four matrix called thought filled with zeros.
    thought = [[0.0] * 4 for _ in range(4)]
    # Add the binding of the lover filler with the lover role into the thought.
    add_into(thought, bind(vocabulary[lover_name], roles["lover"]))
    # Add the binding of the loved filler with the loved role into the thought.
    add_into(thought, bind(vocabulary[loved_name], roles["loved"]))
    # Return the composed thought matrix.
    return thought

# Compose the thought John loves Mary as one superimposed pattern.
thought_one = compose("John", "Mary")
# Print the filler decoded from the lover slot and from the loved slot of the first thought.
print("thought one:", nearest(unbind(thought_one, roles["lover"])), "loves", nearest(unbind(thought_one, roles["loved"])))
# Compose the reversed thought Mary loves John from the same parts in swapped roles.
thought_two = compose("Mary", "John")
# Print the decoded slots of the second thought, showing the reversed sentence.
print("thought two:", nearest(unbind(thought_two, roles["lover"])), "loves", nearest(unbind(thought_two, roles["loved"])))

PART FOURTEEN. COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURES: UNIFIED THEORIES OF MIND

================================================================================

CHAPTER 59. WHAT A COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE IS (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter introduces one of the biggest ideas in the science of the mind: the notion of a cognitive architecture.

A cognitive architecture is a proposed blueprint of the fixed machinery of thinking, the part of the mind that stays the same no matter what task you happen to be doing.

Read as an engineered system, an architecture is a specification: it names the memories (the state), the processors that read and write them, the communication channels between them, the tunable parameters, and the clock rate at which the whole assembly runs.

The idea matters because most research studies one small ability at a time, like memory for a list of words or the speed of noticing a light, while a cognitive architecture tries to say how all of those abilities fit together inside a single working mind.

In this chapter we will build up the concept slowly, meet the argument that the mind needs one unified theory rather than a hundred separate ones, list the jobs any mind has to do, and then survey the main families of architectures that researchers have built.


59.1 The concept

This section explains what people mean by the word architecture when they are talking about the mind, and why that word was borrowed from building design and computer engineering.

The short version is that an architecture is the stable framework, and knowledge is the changing content that gets poured into it.


59.1.1 The fixed architecture against the variable knowledge that runs on it

The central idea here is a split between two things: a fixed part that does not change from moment to moment, and a variable part that does.

Think of a modern computer.

The hardware and the operating system are fixed for the whole time you own the machine.

The documents, photos, and programs you load onto it change all the time.

A cognitive architecture is meant to be like the fixed part: the built-in structure and processes of the mind that stay constant across every task, every day, and every topic.

The variable part is your knowledge, meaning the specific facts, skills, and memories you happen to have picked up.

Here technical jargon is worth pausing on: by knowledge, architecture researchers mean any content the mind holds and uses, from a fact like Paris is in France to a skill like how to tie a shoelace.

The claim is that the same fixed machinery lets one person become a chef and another become a violinist, because the machinery is identical but the knowledge loaded onto it differs.

An everyday way to picture it is a kitchen.

The stove, oven, sink, and counters are the fixed architecture.

The ingredients and recipes are the variable knowledge.

You can cook thousands of different meals without ever changing the kitchen, and that is exactly the sort of stability an architecture is supposed to have.

In systems terms, the architecture is the processor design and instruction set, while knowledge is the program and the data: the input to the pair is the task environment, the output is behaviour, and the architecture's own state changes only on the slow timescale of development, while knowledge changes on the fast timescale of learning, minutes to years.

Researchers care about this split because if you can pin down the fixed part, you have found something deep and general about how minds work, rather than just a fact about one particular skill.


59.1.2 The distinction from a single-task model

This sub-section contrasts an architecture with something narrower called a single-task model.

A single-task model is a small theory or computer program built to explain just one behaviour, such as how quickly people read a word, or how they decide whether two shapes are the same.

Single-task models are extremely common in psychology, and they are useful, because focusing on one thing lets you be precise about it.

The weakness is that a mind is not a stack of unrelated gadgets.

The same person who reads words also remembers faces, plans a route home, and feels frustrated in traffic, and all of that happens inside one head using overlapping machinery.

A cognitive architecture is deliberately the opposite of a single-task model: it is meant to run many different tasks using one shared set of parts, so that reading, remembering, and planning all draw on the same memory and the same decision process.

An analogy is the difference between a single kitchen gadget and a whole kitchen.

An egg slicer does exactly one job.

A kitchen can produce breakfast, a birthday cake, and a soup, because its parts combine flexibly.

In systems language, a single-task model is a dedicated circuit with one input format and one output format, while an architecture is a general-purpose platform whose interfaces must accept any task the environment can pose, which is a far stronger requirement on the design.

The test of an architecture, then, is breadth: can this one framework, without being rebuilt, take on a task its designers did not have in mind when they made it.

That breadth is hard to achieve, which is why architectures are ambitious and why relatively few of them exist compared with the huge number of single-task models.


59.1.3 Where an architecture sits among Marr's levels

To place architectures precisely, it helps to use a famous three-way distinction from the vision scientist David Marr, published in his 1982 book Vision.

Marr argued that any information-processing system, including the brain, can and should be described at three separate levels of analysis, and that confusing the levels causes muddled thinking.

The first level is the computational level, which asks what problem is being solved and why: for vision, the goal of recovering the shapes of objects from patterns of light.

The second level is the algorithmic level, which asks what procedure and what representations are used to solve that problem: the specific step-by-step recipe and the form the information takes.

Here representation is jargon meaning a way of standing in for information, such as a list of numbers, a picture, or a symbol.

The third level is the implementation level, which asks how the procedure is physically carried out: in the brain, that means neurons and their connections; in a computer, transistors.

A cognitive architecture lives mainly at Marr's middle level, the algorithmic one, because it specifies the representations the mind uses and the processes that operate on them.

Some architectures reach downward toward the implementation level by trying to match brain regions or by using simulated neurons, and some reach upward by taking seriously what problems the mind evolved to solve.

In systems terms the three levels are the requirements document, the software design, and the hardware, and an architecture is the software design: it fixes data structures and control flow while leaving the physical substrate open.

The useful takeaway for a beginner is that an architecture is not mainly a theory of neurons and not mainly a theory of life goals; it is a theory of the mental machinery in between, the format of thoughts and the operations that shuffle them around.


59.2 Unified theories of cognition

This section introduces the dream that motivated the whole field: the idea that psychology should aim for one grand theory that ties everything together.

The person most associated with this dream is Allen Newell, an American scientist who helped found both artificial intelligence and cognitive psychology.


59.2.1 Newell's argument that cognition needs one theory, not many

In 1990 Allen Newell published a book called Unified Theories of Cognition, based on lectures he had given, and in it he made a pointed complaint about his own field.

His complaint was that psychology had become a heap of small, disconnected findings, each explained by its own little model, with nothing to hold them together.

Newell argued that this was a scientific dead end, because you can always invent a fresh mini-theory for each new experiment, and doing so never forces your ideas to be consistent with each other.

His proposal was that researchers should try to build a single unified theory of cognition, one framework required to account for memory, perception, language, problem solving, and the rest all at once.

The discipline of a unified theory is that every piece has to work with every other piece, so a choice you make to explain memory constrains what you are allowed to say about attention.

This is a debate about method rather than a mechanism, and the two sides predict different things in systems terms: the unified camp predicts that one fixed set of modules and parameters can fit data across many tasks without retuning, while the many-models camp predicts that each task will keep demanding its own free parameters and that forcing one platform will degrade the fits.

Newell did not claim to have finished such a theory; he offered his own architecture, called Soar, as a candidate and an example of the effort, not as the final answer.

It is fair to note that not everyone agreed then or agrees now.

Many psychologists still find focused single-task models more productive, and some doubt that one theory can or should cover everything.

But Newell's challenge reshaped the field, and the very existence of cognitive architectures is largely his legacy.


59.2.2 The functional criteria a mind must satisfy

Newell did not just say build one theory; he tried to say what such a theory would have to explain, by listing the functions a real mind must perform.

The word functional here means defined by what it does rather than what it is made of, so a functional criterion is a job the mind must accomplish, regardless of whether neurons or silicon do it.

Newell offered lists of requirements that a human cognitive architecture would have to satisfy in order to count as genuinely mind-like.

These included things like behaving flexibly as a function of the environment, showing adaptive and goal-directed behaviour, operating in real time, using vast amounts of knowledge, using natural language, and learning from experience.

Read as engineering, this is a requirements specification: real-time operation is a latency budget of a few hundred milliseconds per decision, vast knowledge is a storage and retrieval requirement, and flexibility is a demand that the input interface accept arbitrary task descriptions.

The point of such a list is to raise the bar: a toy model that does one clever trick but cannot learn, cannot use language, and cannot act in real time has not really explained a mind.

By writing the requirements down, Newell turned a vague ambition into a checklist that any proposed architecture could be measured against.

This checklist idea is important because it gives the field a shared standard, so that different research groups building different architectures can at least ask the same questions about each one.


59.2.3 The Newell test as a multi-criterion evaluation

The checklist idea was later sharpened into something now called the Newell Test, in an influential 2003 article by John Anderson and Christian Lebiere in the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

Anderson and Lebiere took Newell's overlapping lists and distilled them into twelve criteria for judging a theory of cognition.

Their twelve were, in plain words: behaving flexibly, adapting behaviour to reach goals, operating in real time, holding up under real-world complexity, using a vast store of knowledge, integrating diverse knowledge, using natural language, learning from the environment, showing development from infancy to adulthood, arising through evolution, and being realizable in the brain, together with dynamic responsiveness to changing situations.

The word multi-criterion simply means judged by many standards at once rather than a single score.

Their key argument was that no theory should be praised or dismissed on one dimension alone; instead each theory should be graded on every criterion, and its pattern of strengths and weaknesses laid bare.

To demonstrate, they graded two rivals: classical connectionism, meaning neural-network style models, and their own architecture ACT-R.

They concluded that connectionism scored well on learning and development but poorly on handling symbols and structured knowledge, while ACT-R scored well precisely because it combined a symbolic level with a sub-symbolic one.

In systems terms the Newell Test is a benchmark suite: instead of one score on one workload, a candidate architecture is run against twelve workloads, and its acceptance report is the full grade sheet.

Whether or not you accept their verdicts, the deeper lesson is the method: honest evaluation means showing where your favourite theory is weak, not just where it shines.


59.3 The functional requirements of any mind

This section walks through the jobs a mind has to do, grouped into a few clusters, so that a beginner can see the full scope of what an architecture must deliver.

Think of it as a job description for a mind, written before we look at any particular candidate for the post.


59.3.1 Memory, learning, perception, and action

At the most basic level, a mind must take in information, hold onto information, improve with experience, and do something in the world.

Perception is the intake: turning raw signals from the eyes, ears, skin, and other senses into usable information about what is out there.

Memory is the holding: keeping information available over time, from a few seconds of holding a phone number in mind up to a lifetime of remembering your childhood home.

Architects usually distinguish a short-term or working memory, which holds a small amount of information you are actively using right now, roughly four chunks for a few seconds unless refreshed, from long-term memory, which stores knowledge more or less permanently.

Learning is the improving: changing the mind's knowledge or skills as a result of experience, so that next time you do better or faster.

Action is the output: moving muscles, speaking, or otherwise affecting the environment based on what you have perceived and decided.

As a system, perception is the input driver running on a timescale of tens to hundreds of milliseconds, working memory is the fast volatile store, long-term memory is the slow persistent store, learning is the background write process, and action is the output driver, and every architecture must implement all five interfaces.

An everyday illustration ties them together: you hear a kettle whistle (perception), recall that this means the water is boiling (memory), get quicker at responding to that sound over the years (learning), and reach out to switch it off (action).


59.3.2 Decision, goal management, and attention under bounded resources

Beyond the basics, a mind must choose what to do, keep track of what it is trying to achieve, and focus its limited capacity wisely.

Decision means selecting one option out of several, such as which route to take or which word to say next.

Goal management means holding and organizing the things you are trying to accomplish, including breaking a big goal like cook dinner into smaller sub-goals like boil the pasta and heat the sauce.

Attention means directing limited processing capacity toward some information and away from the rest, because a mind cannot fully process everything at once.

The crucial phrase is bounded resources, which is jargon for the plain fact that a real mind has limits: limited time, limited memory, limited attention, and limited energy.

This idea is often called bounded rationality, a term from the economist and cognitive scientist Herbert Simon, meaning that people make reasonable decisions within their limits rather than perfect decisions with unlimited thinking.

In systems terms these three are a scheduler: goals form a priority stack, attention is the allocation of a narrow processing channel, and decision is the arbitration step that commits the channel to one option per cycle, on a characteristic timescale of a few hundred milliseconds per deliberate choice.

An architecture that assumed infinite memory or instant, cost-free thinking would be unrealistic, so a good architecture must show how a limited system still manages to act sensibly.

For example, when you walk into a crowded party looking for a friend, you cannot inspect every face at once; attention lets you scan a few at a time, and goal management keeps you searching until you succeed or give up.


59.3.3 Metacognition, motivation, and emotion

The most advanced requirements concern a mind thinking about itself, wanting things, and feeling things.

Metacognition means cognition about cognition, that is, the mind monitoring and controlling its own thinking, such as noticing that you do not understand a sentence and choosing to reread it.

Motivation means the forces that energize and direct behaviour, the reasons a system does anything at all, from hunger to curiosity to the wish to finish a job.

Emotion means states like fear, joy, or frustration that colour thinking, shape priorities, and prepare the body and mind to respond.

For a long time these were treated as outside the core of cognition, sometimes dismissed as messy extras, but most researchers now agree that a complete theory of mind must include them.

The reason is that motivation decides which goals get pursued, emotion rapidly flags what matters and adjusts behaviour, and metacognition lets the system correct and manage itself.

In systems terms, motivation supplies the reward signal that sets goal priorities, emotion is a fast global broadcast that re-tunes parameters like thresholds and gains within seconds, and metacognition is a monitoring loop that reads the system's own performance signals and issues control commands back to it.

It is honest to say this cluster is where architectures are weakest and where researchers most disagree, because feelings and self-awareness are genuinely hard to pin down and measure.

Some architectures, which we will meet later, make motivation and emotion central, while others leave them mostly untouched, and there is no settled consensus yet on the right approach.


59.4 The taxonomy of architectures

A taxonomy is a way of sorting things into groups, the way biologists sort living things into families.

This section gives the standard sorting of cognitive architectures into a few broad families, so you have a map before we tour individual examples.


59.4.1 The symbolic, the emergent, and the hybrid

The most common taxonomy splits architectures into three families based on how they represent and process information: symbolic, emergent, and hybrid.

Symbolic architectures represent knowledge using discrete symbols and explicit rules, much like sentences and if-then instructions, so that a thought is built out of nameable parts you could in principle read off.

An everyday image is a filing cabinet full of written rules and labelled cards; thinking is manipulating those cards according to the rules.

Emergent architectures, also called connectionist or neural, represent knowledge in the pattern of activity and connection strengths across many simple units loosely inspired by neurons, so that a thought is a spread of activity rather than a single symbol.

Here emergent means that intelligent behaviour arises from the interaction of many small, unintelligent parts, none of which contains the whole idea by itself, the way a wave emerges from many water molecules.

Hybrid architectures deliberately combine both styles, using symbols and rules for some jobs and neural-style distributed processing for others, on the bet that the mind itself uses both.

In systems terms the split is a choice of data format and processor: symbolic systems use structured records processed by a matcher, emergent systems use numeric vectors processed by weighted sums, and hybrids define a translation interface between the two formats.

Each family has real strengths and real weaknesses: symbolic systems handle structured reasoning and language cleanly but can be brittle and hard to make learn; emergent systems learn gracefully and tolerate noise but struggle with precise rules and structured symbols; hybrids try to get the best of both, at the cost of greater complexity.

There is no universal agreement on which family is correct, and the three-way split is a useful map rather than a proven fact about the brain.


59.4.2 The forty-year survey and the landscape of the field

To see the whole landscape at once, it helps to look at a large survey published by Iuliia Kotseruba and John Tsotsos, which reviewed roughly forty years of cognitive-architecture research.

Their paper, whose final version appeared in 2020 in the journal Artificial Intelligence Review, examined a curated set of 84 architectures, of which they counted 49 as still actively developed at the time.

They noted that the true number of architectures ever proposed runs into the hundreds, so even a big survey covers only part of a sprawling field.

They organized the field using the same symbolic, emergent, and hybrid families described above, and they compared architectures on core abilities such as perception, attention, action selection, memory, learning, and reasoning.

They also surveyed practical uses, reviewing hundreds of real projects in which architectures had been applied to things like robotics, human-computer interaction, and games.

This sub-section is a piece of history rather than a mechanism, and in systems terms its lesson is a comparison of interface coverage: the survey graded each architecture on which of the standard subsystems it actually implements, and found that no single design yet implements them all well.

Two honest lessons come out of such a survey.

First, the field is large, lively, and fragmented, with many architectures pursuing different bets rather than converging on one winner.

Second, most architectures remain research tools rather than finished theories of the mind, and no single architecture yet meets all of Newell's criteria, so the grand unified theory Newell called for is still a work in progress.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Sensory input from the task environment, arriving as continuous perceptual signals that the architecture's perception subsystem converts into internal representations.

◦ Task instructions and goals, arriving as structured descriptions that are loaded into the goal store.

◦ Reward and feedback signals from the environment, arriving as scalar outcomes that drive the learning subsystem.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Motor commands and speech, sent to the body's effectors, which are the muscles and organs that act on the world.

◦ Behavioural predictions such as reaction times and error rates, consumed by experimenters comparing the architecture against human data.

• STATE.

◦ Working memory holding the current goal, the current situation, and a handful of active items.

◦ Long-term memory holding the accumulated knowledge, both facts and skills.

◦ The fixed architectural structure itself, which by definition does not change with the task.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Working memory capacity, decay rates, learning rates, decision thresholds, and the duration of one processing cycle; each concrete architecture fixes its own values.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ One elementary cognitive cycle: about 50 milliseconds, the grain adopted by the major production-system architectures.

◦ Deliberate decision or simple reaction: roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds.

◦ Working memory span: about four chunks held over seconds.

◦ Knowledge growth: minutes to years, the timescale of learning rather than of the fixed architecture.

• MODES.

◦ Routine mode, in which stored knowledge directly drives behaviour, switching to deliberative mode when stored knowledge is insufficient and the system must search, plan, or subgoal; the trigger is the failure of a direct match between situation and knowledge.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Overload when task demands exceed working memory capacity, producing forgetting of goals and steps; brittleness when knowledge does not cover the situation; and for the science itself, the failure mode is fragmentation, a heap of single-task models with no unifying account.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called long_term_memory that holds knowledge items.
Create a list variable called working_memory with no items.
Create a text variable called goal with initial value the current task goal.
While the goal is not achieved, repeat the following cycle.
    Read the current input from the environment and add it to working_memory.
    Find every knowledge item in long_term_memory whose condition matches working_memory.
    If at least one item matches, do the following.
        Select the best matching item.
        Apply the selected item's action to working_memory and to the environment.
        Remove the matched condition from working_memory, since it was consumed.
    Otherwise, do the following.
        Create a new sub-goal to resolve the missing knowledge.
        Set goal to the new sub-goal.
    Remove from working_memory any item older than the capacity allows.
    Advance the simulated clock by one cycle of 50 milliseconds.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a list variable called long_term_memory holding condition and action pairs.
long_term_memory = [
    # Add a rule: if the kettle whistles, switch it off.
    ("kettle whistles", "switch off kettle"),
    # Add a rule: if the kettle is off, pour the water.
    ("kettle off", "pour water"),
    # Add a rule: if the water is poured, the goal is done.
    ("water poured", "done"),
]

# Create a list variable called percepts holding the stream of inputs.
percepts = ["kettle whistles", "kettle off", "water poured"]

# Create a list variable called working_memory with no items.
working_memory = []

# Create a number variable called clock_ms with initial value zero.
clock_ms = 0

# Create a number variable called capacity with value four chunks.
capacity = 4

# For each percept in the stream, run one architectural cycle.
for percept in percepts:
    # Add the percept to working_memory.
    working_memory.append(percept)
    # Keep only the most recent items up to the capacity.
    working_memory = working_memory[-capacity:]
    # Create a variable called chosen with no value yet.
    chosen = None
    # For each condition and action pair in long_term_memory, test for a match.
    for condition, action in long_term_memory:
        # If the condition is present in working_memory, select this pair.
        if condition in working_memory:
            # Set chosen to the action and stop searching.
            chosen = action
            break
    # Advance the clock by one 50 millisecond cycle.
    clock_ms = clock_ms + 50
    # If a rule was chosen, act; otherwise report an impasse.
    if chosen:
