Second, it is meant to be written both by human designers, who script parts of the system's thinking, and by the system's own learning algorithms, so the boundary between the program and the knowledge it works on is deliberately blurred.

Hyperon keeps the AtomSpace idea from Classic, so knowledge still lives in a large graph of atoms, but MeTTa provides a more uniform way to express both the knowledge and the operations that transform it.

From a systems standpoint the change is that code and data now live in the same store and share the same format, so the system's own programs become inputs and outputs of its learning processes, which removes a boundary most software keeps fixed and makes self-modification a first-class operation.

Because Hyperon is recent and still being built, its promise should be read as a direction of travel rather than a demonstrated general intelligence, and its claims remain to be proven in practice.


62.5 The motivational architectures

This section covers hybrids whose special contribution is to put wanting and feeling at the centre, on the view that a mind without drives and emotions is not a full mind but only a calculator.

These architectures ask where goals come from in the first place, and how emotion shapes and steers thinking rather than merely decorating it.


62.5.1 MicroPsi and the Psi theory of motivation and emotion

MicroPsi is an architecture built by Joscha Bach, and it is a computer implementation of the Psi theory, a theory of mind proposed by the psychologist Dietrich Dorner.

The distinctive feature of the Psi theory is that it starts not from reasoning but from needs, treating an agent as a creature driven by a set of underlying demands that it must keep satisfied.

The theory builds up its picture of motivation and emotion through a chain of concepts, and it helps to walk the chain in order.

A demand is a basic need that can fall out of balance, such as a need for energy, for water, for safety, or for social bonding.

An urge is the signal that arises when a demand is unmet, a felt pressure pushing the agent to do something about it.

A motive is an urge that has become attached to a particular goal, so that the general pressure of hunger becomes the specific aim of getting to the kitchen.

On top of these, the theory adds cognitive modulators, which are global settings that adjust how the whole mind operates, for example how fast it acts, how widely it pays attention, and how deeply it thinks.

In this account, emotion is not a separate add-on but emerges from the particular configuration of these modulators together with the state of the urges, so a feeling is, in effect, a whole-system mode of operating.

The systems reading is a layered control loop: each demand is a regulated variable with a set point, the urge is the error signal proportional to the deviation, the motive is the error signal bound to a goal that action selection can pursue, and the modulators are global gain settings, so an emotion is a point in the modulator parameter space rather than a module of its own.

The everyday intuition is that when you are anxious you act faster, scan more widely, and think less deeply, and the Psi theory treats exactly that kind of shift as what an emotion is.

MicroPsi matters because it offers a concrete, runnable proposal for how motivation and emotion could be woven into the machinery of cognition from the ground up, rather than treated as afterthoughts.


62.5.2 DUAL and AMBR and emergent macro-behaviour from micro-agents

DUAL is a hybrid architecture developed by Boicho Kokinov and his team at the New Bulgarian University, and it takes a strikingly different approach to being hybrid.

Most hybrids are hybrid at the large scale, meaning they have a separate symbolic module bolted next to a separate connectionist module.

DUAL is instead hybrid at the small scale, because it is made of a great many tiny agents, sometimes called daemons, and each single agent is itself both symbolic and connectionist at once.

Each little agent carries a scrap of symbolic content, such as a small frame of structured knowledge, and at the same time carries connectionist properties, such as an activation level that says how active it currently is and weighted links that spread activation to its neighbours.

The important consequence is that the intelligent behaviour of the whole system is not written down anywhere in advance, but emerges from the swarming interaction of these many small hybrid agents forming and dissolving temporary coalitions.

Emergence here means that large, organised behaviour arises out of the local interactions of many simple parts, without any single part being in charge, rather as the coordinated turns of a flock of birds arise from each bird reacting only to its neighbours.

As a system, each micro-agent's inputs are the activation arriving over its weighted links, its output is its own activation and its symbolic content when active enough to compute, its speed of processing scales with its activation, and there is no central controller, so the global state is simply the current pattern of active coalitions.

Built on top of DUAL is a model called AMBR, which stands for Associative Memory-Based Reasoning, and it is a model of how people make analogies.

An analogy is seeing that one situation is structured like another, as when you understand electricity by likening it to water flowing in pipes.

AMBR treats analogy-making not as a single neat procedure but as the emergent result of several overlapping processes running together, including perceiving the situation, retrieving related memories, mapping one situation onto another, and learning from the result.

The lesson of DUAL and AMBR for this chapter is that hybridity can be pushed all the way down to the level of individual agents, and that some of the mind's most creative feats, such as analogy, may be emergent crowd behaviour rather than the output of any one dedicated part.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Environment state observations, delivered each cycle as a feature vector or symbol structure from the perception front end.

◦ Reward and outcome feedback, a scalar success or failure signal from the environment or an internal evaluator, consumed by the implicit learning channel.

◦ Drive and demand levels, scalar need signals from the motivational subsystem that set which goals action selection pursues.

◦ Instructed knowledge, explicit rules or facts supplied by a teacher or programmer for top-down flow.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Selected actions, discrete commands per decision cycle, consumed by the motor or environment interface.

◦ Extracted explicit rules, if-then structures written to the symbolic store and available for report, teaching, and inspection.

◦ Broadcast content, in workspace-style hybrids such as LIDA, the winning coalition published to all modules at once.

◦ Control adjustments, metacognitive settings such as the explicit-versus-implicit mixing weight, consumed by the processing subsystems.

• STATE.

◦ Connection weights of the implicit network, the slowly changing statistical skill store.

◦ The explicit rule and fact base, including per-rule success statistics used to decide generalisation and deletion.

◦ Current activations, the working pattern in the network, the workspace, or the agent population, refreshed every cycle.

◦ Drive levels and modulator settings, the motivational and emotional configuration of the whole system.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Learning rate of the implicit channel, controlling how fast weights move per outcome.

◦ Rule extraction threshold, the success statistic a state-action pair must cross before an explicit rule is created.

◦ Explicit-versus-implicit mixing weight, the arbitration gain between the two channels.

◦ Exploration rate, the probability of trying a non-preferred action to gather new experience.

◦ Attention and priority budgets, in NARS-style and workspace-style systems, the fraction of processing given to each competing item.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ One decision or cognitive cycle: several cycles per second in LIDA's proposal, in the region of a few hundred milliseconds per beat, consistent with the production-rule cycle of about 50 milliseconds for a single rule firing in production-system relatives.

◦ Implicit skill learning: REFUSED as a single number, because trial-and-error weight learning spans minutes to years depending on task and practice schedule.

◦ Rule extraction: REFUSED, because the literature ties it to accumulated success counts rather than to a clock time.

◦ Modulator and emotion shifts in Psi-style systems: REFUSED, because published implementations treat these as parameterised rather than empirically fixed.

• MODES.

◦ Implicit-dominant mode, where behaviour is driven mainly by the network, triggered by novelty of the domain, time pressure, or absence of applicable rules.

◦ Explicit-dominant mode, where behaviour is driven mainly by rules, triggered by available matching rules, instruction, or metacognitive demand for care.

◦ Bottom-up learning mode, where success statistics are converted into new rules, triggered by the extraction threshold being crossed.

◦ Top-down learning mode, where taught rules are compiled into implicit skill through practice, triggered by repeated successful rule use.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Implicit-explicit dissociation errors, where the system does the right thing but reports the wrong rule, or recites the right rule but acts against it.

◦ Premature or overgeneral rule extraction, crystallising a spurious regularity from a lucky streak, the machine analogue of superstition.

◦ Arbitration failure, weighting the wrong channel for the situation, as when deliberate rule-following disrupts a fluent skill, the choking-under-pressure pattern.

◦ Blackboard contention in shared-store designs, where multiple processes overwrite or starve one another on the common memory.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary called weights that maps each state and action pair to a number with initial value zero.
Create a dictionary called counts that maps each state and action pair to a success count and a trial count, both starting at zero.
Create an empty list called rules.
Create a number variable called extraction threshold with initial value 0.7.
Create a number variable called minimum trials with initial value 10.
For each episode in the training run, repeat the following.
    Observe the current state from the environment.
    Search the rules list for a rule whose condition matches the current state.
    If a matching rule is found, set the chosen action to the action named by that rule.
    Otherwise, with a small exploration probability choose a random action, and otherwise choose the action whose weight for the current state is largest.
    Perform the chosen action and receive an outcome signal of success or failure from the environment.
    If the outcome is success, increase the weight for the current state and chosen action by the learning rate times the difference between one and that weight.
    If the outcome is failure, decrease the weight for the current state and chosen action by the learning rate times that weight.
    Increase the trial count for the current state and chosen action by one.
    If the outcome is success, increase the success count for the current state and chosen action by one.
    Calculate the confidence as the success count divided by the trial count for the current state and chosen action.
    If the trial count is at least the minimum trials and the confidence is greater than the extraction threshold and no matching rule already exists, create a rule stating that in this state one should take this action, and append it to the rules list.
Report the final rules list as the explicit knowledge extracted from the implicit skill.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module for exploration and for the simulated environment.
import random

# Create a dictionary called weights that maps each state and action pair to a number with initial value zero.
weights = {}
# Create a dictionary called counts that maps each state and action pair to a success and trial count pair.
counts = {}
# Create an empty list called rules.
rules = []
# Create the parameter variables for learning rate, extraction threshold, minimum trials, and exploration.
learning_rate, threshold, min_trials, explore = 0.2, 0.7, 10, 0.1
# Create the list of possible states and the list of possible actions.
states, actions = ["wet_road", "dry_road"], ["slow_down", "speed_up"]

# Define a function that returns success or failure for a state and action, as the environment.
def environment(state, action):
    # If the road is wet, slowing down usually succeeds and speeding up usually fails.
    if state == "wet_road":
        # Return success with probability 0.9 for slowing down and 0.2 for speeding up.
        return random.random() < (0.9 if action == "slow_down" else 0.2)
    # Otherwise, on a dry road, speeding up usually succeeds.
    return random.random() < (0.85 if action == "speed_up" else 0.4)

# For each episode number from zero up to but not including two thousand, repeat the trial loop.
for episode in range(2000):
    # Observe the current state by sampling one state at random.
    state = random.choice(states)
    # Search the rules list for a rule whose condition matches the current state.
    match = next((r for r in rules if r[0] == state), None)
    # If a matching rule is found, set the chosen action to the action named by that rule.
    if match:
        action = match[1]
    # Otherwise, with the exploration probability choose a random action, else the highest-weight action.
    else:
        action = random.choice(actions) if random.random() < explore else max(
            actions, key=lambda a: weights.get((state, a), 0.0))
    # Perform the chosen action and receive a success or failure outcome from the environment.
    success = environment(state, action)
    # Look up the current weight for the state and action pair, defaulting to zero.
    w = weights.get((state, action), 0.0)
    # Move the weight toward one on success and toward zero on failure, scaled by the learning rate.
    weights[(state, action)] = w + learning_rate * ((1.0 - w) if success else (0.0 - w))
    # Look up the success and trial counts for the state and action pair, defaulting to zero and zero.
    s, t = counts.get((state, action), (0, 0))
    # Increase the trial count by one, and the success count by one only on success.
    s, t = s + (1 if success else 0), t + 1
    # Store the updated counts back into the counts dictionary.
    counts[(state, action)] = (s, t)
    # Calculate the confidence as the success count divided by the trial count.
    confidence = s / t
    # If enough trials have occurred and confidence exceeds the threshold and no rule exists, extract a rule.
    if t >= min_trials and confidence > threshold and match is None:
        # Append the new explicit rule for this state and action to the rules list.
        rules.append((state, action))

# For each extracted rule, print it in readable if-then form with its confidence.
for state, action in rules:
    # Print the rule condition, the rule action, and the observed confidence.
    s, t = counts[(state, action)]
    print("IF", state, "THEN", action, "confidence", round(s / t, 2))


CHAPTER 63. THE COMMON MODEL OF COGNITION AND GLOBAL THEORIES (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter steps back from individual architectures to ask a bigger question, which is whether the many competing designs have started to agree with one another about what a mind must contain.

The surprising answer explored here is that, after decades of separate work, several leading architectures converged on a shared skeleton, and researchers wrote that shared skeleton down and called it the Common Model of Cognition.

The chapter also introduces the broad theories, especially about attention and consciousness, that keep reappearing inside these architectures and that inform their design.


63.1 The Common Model of Cognition

This section presents the Common Model of Cognition, which is not itself a working program but a written statement of the points on which the major architectures now agree.

It matters because a genuine consensus, hard-won from independent efforts, is one of the strongest kinds of evidence a young science can offer about which of its ideas are likely to be right.


63.1.1 The origin and the naming as the standard model of the mind

The Common Model of Cognition was introduced in 2017 by three senior architecture researchers, John Laird, Christian Lebiere, and Paul Rosenbloom.

They first named it the Standard Model of the Mind, borrowing the phrase deliberately from physics, where the Standard Model is the agreed-upon core theory of fundamental particles that a whole community shares.

The borrowing carried a clear message, namely that the study of mind might be mature enough to have its own agreed core, a set of commitments that most serious researchers would sign.

The name was later softened to the Common Model of Cognition, partly to avoid overstating how settled things are and to make clear the model is a developing consensus rather than a finished law.

The consensus was distilled chiefly from three long-running architectures that had been built largely independently, namely Soar, ACT-R, and Sigma, all of which are covered elsewhere in this outline.

It is important to be honest about what the model is not, because its own authors stress that it is abstract, deliberately incomplete, and not something you can run as a program.

In systems language, the Common Model is a reference architecture rather than an implementation: it specifies the required components and the data paths between them, and it deliberately leaves the internal algorithms of each component unspecified, which is exactly the level at which the community could agree.

It includes only what the community can actually agree is necessary for a humanlike mind, and it leaves the many still-disputed matters out on purpose, which is precisely what makes the agreement meaningful.


63.1.2 The consensus modules: perception, motor, working memory, declarative and procedural memory

The Common Model says that a humanlike mind is organised into a small number of major components, and the agreement on this short list is the model's central content.

There are five components in the standard statement, and each one is easy to describe in everyday terms.

Perception is the component that turns incoming signals from the senses into usable internal information, the mind's way of taking in the world.

The motor component, sometimes called action, is the component that turns the mind's decisions into movements and outputs, the mind's way of acting on the world.

Working memory is a central holding area where information from all the other components comes together and is worked on, rather like a workbench or a whiteboard where the current problem is laid out.

Declarative memory is the long-term store of facts and events, the knowledge that something is the case, such as that Paris is a city or that you ate breakfast this morning.

Procedural memory is the long-term store of skills and rules for acting, the knowledge of how to do things, and in the Common Model it is specifically a production system, meaning a store of if-then rules called productions that fire when their conditions are met.

The arrangement is that working memory sits in the middle as the shared workspace, the perception and motor components connect it to the outside world, and the two long-term memories feed knowledge into it and receive new knowledge from it.

The data-flow reading is a hub-and-spoke bus: working memory is the hub through which all traffic passes, perception writes to it, motor reads from it, declarative memory answers retrieval requests posted on it, and procedural memory watches it and fires the matching production, with working memory limited to about four chunks at a time and a production cycle of about 50 milliseconds setting the clock.

The everyday picture is a workshop, with a central bench, a door for materials coming in and finished goods going out, a filing cabinet of facts, and a rack of tools-and-techniques, all serving work done on the bench.


63.1.3 The consensus commitments: symbolic-plus-subsymbolic, pervasive learning, bounded rationality

Beyond the list of parts, the Common Model also agrees on several deeper commitments about how those parts work, and these commitments are where the real theoretical bite lies.

The first commitment is that the mind is both symbolic and subsymbolic at the same time, which is the hybrid stance made into a shared principle.

This means each piece of knowledge has a symbolic side, a clear structured content, and a subsymbolic side, a set of numerical quantities such as how active, how useful, or how reliable it is, and both sides matter for how the mind behaves.

The second commitment is pervasive learning, meaning that the mind is not a fixed device that merely applies knowledge but is constantly changing, with learning happening throughout the system as a normal part of ordinary processing rather than in a separate training phase.

The third commitment is bounded rationality, a term from the economist and cognitive scientist Herbert Simon, which means that the mind tries to act sensibly but always within hard limits on its time, memory, and computing power.

Bounded rationality is the honest middle path between two extremes, rejecting both the fantasy of a perfect flawless reasoner and the caricature of a purely irrational one, and instead describing a mind that does the best it reasonably can with what it has.

In systems terms the three commitments translate directly: every stored item carries both a structure and a set of numeric metadata, every module runs its own online learning rule as a side effect of normal operation, and the whole machine is specified under hard resource budgets rather than as an idealised optimiser.

Taken together these three commitments say that the agreed mind is a hybrid, ever-learning, resource-limited system, and that is a substantive picture that rules out many simpler proposals.


63.1.4 The extensions under discussion: metacognition, emotion, and the two systems

The Common Model is a living document, and there is active discussion about what should be added to it as the consensus grows, which this sub-section surveys.

One proposed extension is metacognition, the mind's monitoring and control of its own thinking, on the view that a full mind must be able to notice when it is uncertain, when it is stuck, and when it should change strategy.

Recent published proposals have argued in detail for adding a metacognitive layer to the model, though it is not yet part of the settled core, so this remains a matter under discussion rather than an agreed addition.

A second proposed extension is emotion, on the view, shared with motivational architectures like MicroPsi, that feelings are not decorative but genuinely shape attention, memory, and decision, and that leaving them out leaves the model incomplete.

Here too there are worked-out proposals for how emotion might be folded into the Common Model, and here too the matter is still open rather than resolved.

A third topic under discussion is the relationship to the famous two-systems idea, the distinction between fast automatic intuition and slow deliberate reasoning, and researchers have written about how that popular distinction maps onto the Common Model's machinery.

Because these are debates rather than mechanisms, it helps to state what each side predicts in systems terms: adding metacognition predicts a measurable monitoring signal and strategy switches the base model cannot produce, adding emotion predicts global parameter shifts that change speed and breadth of processing under load, and the two-systems mapping predicts that fast responses bypass the slow retrieval path while deliberate ones occupy working memory for many cycles.

The healthy way to read all of this is that the core of the model is stable and agreed, while a well-defined frontier of proposed extensions is being debated openly, which is exactly how a maturing science should look.


63.2 The global theories that inform architectures

This section turns from the engineering consensus to the broad psychological theories that keep showing up inside architectures, especially theories about how a mind brings its scattered parts together into one coherent stream.

These are theories rather than blueprints, but they supply the guiding pictures that architects reach for when they decide how the parts of a mind should be organised.


63.2.1 Global workspace theory and the theatre metaphor

Global Workspace Theory is a theory of how a mind with many parallel specialist processes manages to have a single, unified stream of awareness and coordinated action, and it was proposed by the psychologist Bernard Baars.

Its guiding picture is the theatre of the mind, and the metaphor is worth laying out because so many architectures, LIDA above all, are built on it.

In the metaphor the mind is a theatre full of specialised processors working in parallel in the dark, each an expert at some narrow job, and most of them unconscious most of the time.

There is a stage, which stands for working memory, a limited space where only a little can be present at once.

There is a spotlight, which stands for attention, picking out one small portion of what is on the stage.

Whatever the spotlight illuminates is then broadcast to the whole audience of specialist processors, and that global broadcast, that making-available-to-everyone, is what the theory identifies with conscious awareness.

The point of the metaphor is functional, explaining why consciousness might exist at all, namely that a global broadcast lets many separate expert systems share the same important information and coordinate their work around it.

As a system, the theory specifies a many-producers, one-channel, many-consumers topology: parallel modules publish candidate content, a competition selects one item at a time for the limited-capacity channel, and the selected item is broadcast to every module, so consciousness is identified with the transmission on the shared bus rather than with any single module.

This theory is attractive to architecture builders precisely because it is about integration, the problem of getting many separate parts to act as one, which is the core problem any whole-mind design must solve.


63.2.2 The global neuronal workspace and ignition

The Global Neuronal Workspace is the version of the theory that ties the theatre metaphor down to actual brain machinery, and it was developed mainly by the neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene together with Jean-Pierre Changeux and Lionel Naccache.

Where Baars gave a functional metaphor, Dehaene and colleagues proposed a physical implementation, saying that the workspace is realised by a particular kind of neuron, those with long-range connections that reach across distant regions of the brain, concentrated in the frontal and parietal cortex.

The most striking prediction of this version is a phenomenon called ignition, and the idea is vivid enough to picture directly.

Ignition is a sudden, large, brain-wide surge of coordinated neural activity that occurs when a stimulus crosses from being processed unconsciously to being consciously perceived, rather like a fire that smoulders quietly and then all at once flares up and spreads.

Below the threshold, a stimulus is handled locally and quietly by a few regions and never reaches awareness, but once it crosses the threshold the long-range network ignites and the information is broadcast widely, and that is the moment of conscious access.

In systems terms ignition is a nonlinear threshold on a recurrent network: input strength below threshold decays locally, input strength above threshold triggers self-sustaining positive feedback across the long-range loops, and the reported signature is a late, widespread wave of activity beginning roughly 300 milliseconds after the stimulus, which distinguishes seen from unseen trials.

This gives the theory testable teeth, because ignition should be visible in brain recordings as a specific late, widespread pattern of activity that distinguishes stimuli people report seeing from those they do not.

The Global Neuronal Workspace is influential precisely because it converts a philosophical metaphor into concrete, measurable claims about timing and brain circuits, though, as later chapters discuss, it remains one contested theory of consciousness among several.


63.2.3 The society of mind

The Society of Mind is a theory put forward by Marvin Minsky, one of the founders of artificial intelligence, and it offers a very different guiding picture from the single theatre.

Its central image is that the mind is not one unified thing at all but a society, a large collection of many small, simple, mindless parts that Minsky called agents.

Each agent on its own is stupid, able to do only some tiny job, and none of them is intelligent, yet the claim is that intelligence emerges from the way huge numbers of these simple agents are organised and interact.

The everyday parallel is a large human organisation, in which no single clerk understands or controls the whole enterprise, yet the coordinated activity of many limited individuals produces sophisticated collective behaviour.

Minsky's picture deliberately has no single boss and no central stage, which contrasts sharply with the spotlight-and-broadcast picture of global workspace theory, and this contrast frames a real and ongoing debate.

That debate is between centralised pictures of the mind, in which one shared workspace ties everything together, and distributed pictures, in which order emerges from many local interactions with no centre, and different architectures lean different ways.

The two sides predict differently in systems terms: a workspace design predicts a single measurable bottleneck, serial conscious access, and a global broadcast signature, while a society design predicts no privileged channel, graceful degradation when any part fails, and coordination visible only as patterns across many local links.

The Society of Mind matters here because it is the intellectual ancestor of the micro-agent architectures such as DUAL, and because it keeps the field honest about the possibility that unity of mind might be an appearance produced by a crowd rather than the work of any central part.


63.3 The convergence narrative

This section examines the story that ties the chapter together, namely that independent lines of work have been drifting toward a common picture of the mind, and asks carefully what that drift does and does not prove.

It is a section about how to interpret agreement, which is a subtle matter, because agreement can be a sign of truth or merely a sign of shared habits.


63.3.1 How independent architectures converged on a shared structure

The convergence narrative is the observation that architectures built by different teams, for different reasons, over several decades, gradually came to look alike in their basic structure.

Soar, ACT-R, and Sigma did not set out to agree, and they differ greatly in their inner workings, yet all three ended up with a central working memory, separate stores for facts and for skills, a rule-based procedural component, and links to perception and action.

The Common Model of Cognition is simply the written record of that convergence, the shared skeleton read off from the systems that grew toward it.

The reason this is impressive is that convergence from independent starting points is a familiar signature of getting something right, in the same way that different explorers drawing similar maps of a coastline suggests the coastline is really shaped that way.

Part of the explanation is that all these architectures were held to the same demanding standard, having to account for a wide range of the same human experimental data, and being forced to fit the same reality tends to push different designs toward the same answers.

In systems language, the shared constraint set acted like a shared specification: any design required to reproduce human reaction times, error patterns, and learning curves under bounded resources keeps rediscovering the same bus-and-stores topology, which is evidence that the topology is forced by the data rather than by taste.

So the convergence is not a coincidence of fashion but at least partly a response to shared constraints from human behaviour, which strengthens the case that the shared structure reflects something real.


63.3.2 What the convergence does and does not establish

It would be easy to overread the convergence, so this final sub-section is a careful weighing of what it is and is not good evidence for.

What the convergence does establish is that the shared skeleton is a strong, well-tested engineering consensus, a design that many independent groups found they needed in order to cover a broad range of human performance, which is genuine and hard-won.

What the convergence does not establish is that this skeleton is the final or the only possible truth about the mind, because several qualifications must be kept firmly in view.

First, the converging architectures were not wholly independent, since their builders read one another's work, shared a research culture, and inherited common assumptions, so some of the agreement may reflect shared intellectual ancestry rather than shared discovery of fact.

Second, the Common Model is admittedly incomplete, leaving out contested but possibly essential matters such as emotion, consciousness, and much of learning, so agreement on a partial skeleton is not agreement on a whole mind.

Third, the whole family shares a broadly symbolic-plus-subsymbolic, production-system style, and rival traditions, such as the purely dynamical, embodied, and enactive approaches, would draw the map quite differently, so the consensus is a consensus within one school more than across all of them.

Put in systems terms, the rival traditions predict a different architecture altogether: a dynamical or enactive account predicts continuous coupled variables with no discrete working memory buffer and no production cycle, so the debate is empirically live and the two families predict different fine-grained timing signatures.

The balanced conclusion is that the convergence is real and valuable and is probably the safest ground the field currently has to build on, while remaining a working consensus open to revision rather than a proven and complete account of the mind.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Sensory signals from the environment, raw or feature-coded input consumed by the perception component.

◦ Task goals and instructions, structures placed into working memory by perception or by prior cycles.

◦ Retrieval results, declarative chunks returned by long-term memory in answer to posted requests.

◦ Outcome feedback, reward and error signals consumed by the pervasive learning mechanisms in every component.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Motor commands, discrete actions issued by the motor component to the body or environment.

◦ Working memory updates, the changed contents of the central buffer, visible to all components on the hub.

◦ New long-term knowledge, freshly stored declarative chunks and newly compiled or tuned productions.

◦ In workspace theories, a global broadcast, the selected conscious content published to all specialist processors.

• STATE.

◦ Working memory contents, the current small set of active chunks on the central bus.

◦ Declarative memory, the fact store with per-chunk activation and reliability values.

◦ Procedural memory, the production store with per-rule utility values.

◦ Perceptual and motor buffers, the in-flight input interpretations and pending actions.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Working memory capacity, about four chunks in the human case.

◦ Production cycle time, the clock period of the procedural matcher.

◦ Retrieval threshold and noise, controlling which declarative chunks can be recalled and how reliably.

◦ Learning rates for utility tuning, chunk strengthening, and compilation.

◦ In workspace variants, the ignition threshold, the input strength needed to trigger global broadcast.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Production cycle: about 50 milliseconds per rule firing, the consensus figure inherited from ACT-R and Soar.

◦ Working memory span: about four chunks, a capacity rather than a duration, held only while actively maintained.

◦ Conscious access in the Global Neuronal Workspace: ignition beginning roughly 300 milliseconds after stimulus onset, the late widespread signature separating seen from unseen.

◦ Declarative retrieval latency: REFUSED as a single value, because it varies with chunk activation from tens of milliseconds to failure, and the model makes it a function, not a constant.

• MODES.

◦ Reactive mode, where a single production fires directly off the current situation, triggered by a confident match and no impasse.

◦ Deliberative mode, where many cycles chain through working memory to search and plan, triggered by an impasse or novel goal.

◦ Learning-in-passing mode, always on under the pervasive-learning commitment, with every cycle nudging utilities and activations.

◦ Below-threshold versus ignited processing in workspace variants, switched by stimulus strength and attention crossing the ignition threshold.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Working memory overflow, losing task-relevant chunks when more than the capacity is needed, producing slips and place-losing errors.

◦ Retrieval failure and misretrieval, blocked or wrong facts when activations mislead, the tip-of-the-tongue pattern.

◦ Bottleneck congestion, degraded dual-task performance when two demanding streams contend for the serial cycle.

◦ Overreading the consensus, a failure of the field rather than the machine, mistaking a within-school agreement for a proven law.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list called working memory that is empty and has a capacity of four chunks.
Create a dictionary called declarative memory mapping fact names to fact values.
Create a list called procedural memory holding production rules, each with a condition, an action, and a utility number.
Repeat the following decision cycle until the goal in working memory is marked complete.
    Ask the perception component for the current observation and form it into a chunk.
    Add the observation chunk to working memory.
    If working memory holds more chunks than its capacity, remove the oldest chunks until it fits.
    Find every production rule whose condition matches some chunk in working memory.
    If no rule matches, post a retrieval request naming the most recent chunk to declarative memory.
        If declarative memory holds a matching fact, add that fact to working memory as a new chunk.
        Otherwise, mark the goal as failed and stop the cycle.
    Otherwise, select the matching rule with the highest utility.
    If the selected rule's action is a motor action, send the action to the motor component and record the outcome.
    Otherwise, apply the rule's action to working memory by adding or changing chunks.
    Adjust the selected rule's utility upward if the outcome was good and downward if it was bad.
Report the contents of working memory as the result of the run.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a list called working memory that starts empty, with a capacity of four chunks.
working_memory, CAPACITY = [], 4
# Create a dictionary called declarative memory mapping fact names to fact values.
declarative = {"paris": "city", "goal_answer": "city"}
# Create a list of production rules, each holding a condition word, an action, and a utility number.
procedural = [
    # Rule one: if a question chunk is present, request a retrieval of its topic.
    ["question", "retrieve", 0.6],
    # Rule two: if a fact chunk is present, answer using the fact.
    ["fact", "answer", 0.8],
]

# Define a function that sends an answer to the motor component by printing it.
def motor(text):
    # Print the answer text as the outward action.
    print("MOTOR OUTPUT:", text)

# Place the perceived question about paris into working memory as the starting chunk.
working_memory.append(("question", "paris"))
# Repeat the decision cycle up to ten times, each cycle standing for about fifty milliseconds.
for cycle in range(10):
    # If working memory holds more chunks than its capacity, remove the oldest chunks until it fits.
    while len(working_memory) > CAPACITY:
        working_memory.pop(0)
    # Find every rule whose condition word matches the type of some chunk in working memory.
    matches = [r for r in procedural if any(c[0] == r[0] for c in working_memory)]
    # If no rule matches, stop the cycle because the system has reached an impasse.
    if not matches:
        break
    # Select the matching rule with the highest utility number.
    rule = max(matches, key=lambda r: r[2])
    # If the selected action is a retrieval, ask declarative memory for the topic of the question chunk.
    if rule[1] == "retrieve":
        # Find the question chunk and look up its topic in declarative memory.
        topic = next(c[1] for c in working_memory if c[0] == "question")
        # If declarative memory holds the fact, add it to working memory as a fact chunk.
        if topic in declarative:
            working_memory.append(("fact", topic, declarative[topic]))
        # Increase the rule's utility slightly because the retrieval succeeded.
        rule[2] = rule[2] + 0.05
    # Otherwise, if the selected action is answering, send the fact to the motor component and finish.
    elif rule[1] == "answer":
        # Find the fact chunk in working memory.
        fact = next(c for c in working_memory if c[0] == "fact")
        # Send the assembled answer sentence to the motor component.
        motor(fact[1] + " is a " + fact[2])
        # Increase the rule's utility slightly because the goal was achieved, then stop.
        rule[2] = rule[2] + 0.05
        break


CHAPTER 64. CROSS-CUTTING MECHANISMS, EVALUATION, AND APPLICATIONS (ARCHITECTURE)

This chapter looks across the whole family of architectures rather than at any single one, and it does three things in turn.

First it identifies the recurring mechanisms that show up, in one form or another, in nearly every architecture, so that you can see the common toolkit beneath the different names.

Then it asks the hard question of how anyone can tell whether an architecture is any good, which is the problem of evaluation.

Finally it surveys what these architectures are actually used for in the world, which is the test of whether all this theory earns its keep.


64.1 The shared mechanisms

This section pulls out the handful of jobs that every whole-mind design has to solve, and shows the range of ways the field has solved each one, so the reader can recognise the same underlying function wearing different costumes.


64.1.1 The memory systems across architectures

Almost every cognitive architecture divides its memory into several distinct stores rather than using one undifferentiated pool, and the pattern of division is remarkably consistent.

The most common split is between a short-term working memory, the small active workspace holding what the system is dealing with right now, and one or more long-term memories that hold knowledge lastingly.

The long-term side is itself usually split again, mirroring a distinction from human psychology, between declarative memory for facts and events and procedural memory for skills and rules.

For example ACT-R, whose name stands for Adaptive Control of Thought - Rational, keeps declarative chunks of fact separate from procedural production rules, Soar keeps several long-term memories including one for facts and one for procedures, and the Common Model enshrines exactly this factual-versus-skill division as part of its agreed core.

The systems reading is that the stores differ on every engineering axis at once: working memory is small, fast, and volatile, declarative memory is large, slower, and content-addressed by cue similarity, and procedural memory is write-slow but execute-fast, matched against the current state on every cycle.

The reason this division recurs is that the two kinds of knowledge behave differently, since a fact can be learned in one exposure and stated at once, whereas a skill is built up gradually through practice and is hard to put into words, and a single store cannot do justice to both.

Recognising this shared pattern is useful because it lets you see past surface differences in naming and notice that most architectures are making the same basic bet about how memory should be carved up.


64.1.2 The learning mechanisms: chunking, reinforcement, instance-based, and evolutionary

Architectures also share a small toolkit of learning mechanisms, and it helps to name the main four plainly, since almost every system uses some combination of them.

Chunking is learning by bundling several small steps that were just worked out into a single larger unit that can be used directly next time, so that a solution painfully assembled once becomes a ready-made shortcut later, and it is central to Soar.

Reinforcement learning is learning from the consequences of actions, gradually raising the tendency to take actions that led to reward and lowering the tendency to take actions that led to disappointment, the same trial-and-error principle that trains animals with treats.

Instance-based learning is learning by simply storing individual experienced episodes and then handling new situations by recalling and reusing the most similar past instances, so that knowing comes from remembering particular cases rather than from distilling general rules.

Evolutionary learning is learning by keeping a population of candidate solutions, letting the better ones survive and combine and mutate over many generations, and thereby discovering good structures through a designed imitation of natural selection.

As systems, the four differ in their inputs and timescales: chunking consumes a trace of a just-solved problem and writes one new rule immediately, reinforcement consumes a scalar reward and nudges numeric preferences over many trials, instance-based learning consumes whole episodes and pays its cost at recall time, and evolutionary learning consumes fitness scores over a population and operates on the slowest timescale of all, many generations.

Most architectures mix several of these, for example using reinforcement to tune which rules to prefer while using chunking to build new rules, and seeing them as a shared toolkit makes the differences between architectures easier to grasp as different recipes drawn from common ingredients.


64.1.3 Perception, action, and the grounding of symbols

Every architecture must connect to the world at both ends, taking information in through perception and pushing behaviour out through action, and how well they do this varies a great deal.

Perception is the front end that converts raw sensory signals into the internal items the rest of the system can reason with, and action is the back end that converts internal decisions into movements and outputs.

Historically many architectures treated these ends lightly, feeding in already-tidied symbolic descriptions and reading out abstract actions, because their designers were mainly interested in the reasoning in the middle.

That shortcut runs straight into the symbol grounding problem, which is the difficulty that a symbol inside a system means nothing on its own unless it is somehow connected to real perception and action in the world, just as a word in a dictionary defined only by other words never touches reality.

An architecture whose symbols are handed to it by a programmer has, in a sense, borrowed its meaning from the programmer, whereas an architecture that builds its symbols out of its own sensing and acting has a better claim to genuinely grounded knowledge.

In systems terms grounding is a question about where the transduction boundary sits: an ungrounded design takes clean symbols as its input format and emits abstract action labels, while a grounded design takes raw sensor streams as input, emits actuator commands as output, and must learn the mapping between the two in between, which is a far harder interface contract.

This is one of the main pressures pushing the field toward robotics and toward richer perception, because putting an architecture in a body that must sense and act for itself forces its symbols to be earned rather than given.

The honest state of affairs is that grounding remains only partly solved, and how thoroughly an architecture grounds its symbols is one of the clearest ways its maturity can be judged.


64.1.4 Attention, the central bottleneck, and resource allocation

Because no architecture has unlimited computing power, every one must have some way of deciding what to work on and what to ignore, and this is the function of attention within an architecture.

Attention in this setting means the mechanism that selects, from far more information and far more possible actions than the system could ever handle at once, the small portion it will actually process now.

Closely related is the idea of a central bottleneck, a narrow point through which only one, or very few, streams of processing can pass at a time, which forces the system to serialise, meaning to handle certain things one after another rather than all together.

This mirrors a well-documented human limit, since people are strikingly bad at doing two demanding thinking tasks at the very same instant, and architectures reproduce that limit through their own bottlenecks.

Global Workspace based systems such as LIDA embody the bottleneck as the competition for the single spotlight, so that only the winning content is broadcast, while production-system architectures embody it in the limited working memory and the choosing of a single action each cycle.

As a system, attention is a scheduler over a fixed budget: its inputs are the salience and priority values attached to competing items, its output is an admission decision per cycle, and its characteristic timescale is the decision cycle itself, so the cost of the bottleneck shows up as queuing delay whenever demand exceeds the single-channel capacity.

More broadly this is a problem of resource allocation, meaning the wise spending of a fixed budget of attention and computation, and how gracefully an architecture spends that budget is a large part of how humanlike its behaviour looks.


64.1.5 Metacognition, emotion, and motivation as modules

The final shared theme is that the more ambitious architectures include machinery for the mind watching, wanting, and feeling, not just the mind reasoning, and treat these as first-class parts rather than extras.

Metacognition, as a module, is the part that monitors the rest of the system and adjusts it, noticing for instance that the current approach is failing and that a different strategy is needed, and CLARION's metacognitive subsystem is a clear example.

Motivation, as a module, is the part that generates goals and drives in the first place, answering why the system does anything, and MicroPsi's demands and urges are a worked-out example of building motivation in from the ground.

Emotion, as a module or as an emergent state, is treated as a set of whole-system adjustments that change how the mind operates under different conditions, for example acting faster and attending more narrowly under threat, again as in MicroPsi's modulators.

Seen together the three form a supervisory control layer: motivation supplies the reference goals, emotion supplies global gain scheduling that retunes speed and breadth of processing, and metacognition supplies the feedback loop that monitors performance and switches strategies, all operating on a slower timescale than the basic decision cycle they govern.

The reason these appear is a shared recognition that a purely cold reasoning engine leaves out much of what actually drives and shapes human thought, and that a genuinely humanlike mind must want things, feel things, and govern itself.

At the same time these are the least settled parts of the field, which is exactly why, as the previous chapter noted, metacognition and emotion are proposed extensions to the Common Model still under debate rather than agreed core.


64.2 Evaluation

This section faces the awkward central question of the whole enterprise, which is how anyone can actually tell whether one architecture is better than another, or whether any of them is any good at all.

Evaluation is genuinely hard here, and being honest about that difficulty is more useful than pretending there is a clean scoreboard.


64.2.1 The fitting of human data across tasks

The main and most respected way an architecture earns credibility is by fitting human data, meaning by producing behaviour that matches, in detail, what real people do in real experiments.

Fitting the data means more than getting the right answer, since it means reproducing the fine grain of human performance, such as how long people take, which errors they make, and how they speed up with practice, across many different tasks.

The strongest form of this test is breadth, because a good architecture should account for many different phenomena, from memory to attention to problem solving, using the same fixed machinery rather than a fresh special model for each task.

ACT-R is often praised on exactly this ground, having been used to model an enormous range of laboratory tasks while keeping its core mechanisms and even many of its numerical settings the same, which is a serious achievement.

In systems terms an evaluation run is a pipeline: the inputs are the model, a task set, and the human reference data, the procedure holds core parameters fixed across tasks, the outputs are error scores per task such as mean squared difference on reaction times and error rates, and the summary statistic is fit averaged across tasks penalised by the number of free parameters.

The everyday standard being applied is that a theory that can bend to fit anything explains nothing, so the value lies in fitting a lot of independent data with a small, fixed set of assumptions.

Still, fitting human data has a well-known weakness, namely that a flexible model with enough adjustable numbers can sometimes match results without capturing the real mechanism, so careful evaluators also ask whether the fits generalise to new situations the model was not tuned on.


64.2.2 The problem of a unified benchmark across architectures

A benchmark is a shared, standardised test that lets you compare different systems fairly by running them all on the very same challenge, and the central difficulty of this section is that cognitive architectures have no good one.

In some fields benchmarks are everything, since machine-learning systems, for instance, compete on identical datasets so that progress can be measured cleanly, but architectures have resisted this kind of common yardstick.

There are several honest reasons for the lack, and it is worth naming them so the absence does not look like mere negligence.

Different architectures were built for different purposes and emphasise different capacities, so a single test would inevitably favour whatever it happened to measure and unfairly penalise systems designed for other things.

The architectures also differ in how much of the surrounding scaffolding, such as perception and the specific task knowledge, is hand-built versus learned, which makes it hard to know whether a good result reflects the architecture or the cleverness of the person who set it up.

There is also no agreement on what the single most important thing to measure even is, since breadth, human likeness, learning ability, and practical usefulness can all reasonably be prized, and they pull in different directions.

Stated as an interface problem, a fair benchmark would need a common input format every architecture can consume, a common output format every architecture can produce, and a declared budget for hand-built task knowledge, and no such shared interface contract currently exists, which is why the comparisons stay apples to oranges.

The consequence is that the field evaluates largely case by case, architecture by architecture and task by task, and the absence of a shared benchmark is widely recognised as a real weakness that makes progress harder to measure and claims harder to compare.


64.3 Applications

This section leaves theory behind and asks what cognitive architectures are actually good for in practice, because a design for a mind, however elegant, ultimately has to prove itself by doing useful work.

The applications fall into a few broad areas, and together they show that these architectures are not only philosophical exercises but working tools.


64.3.1 Human-behaviour and performance modelling

The first and most established application is using an architecture as a stand-in for a human being, in order to predict how real people will behave and perform.

The idea is that if an architecture genuinely captures how a mind works, you can put it in the place of a person doing a task and read off, in advance, how long the person will take, where they will make mistakes, and how a change to the task will help or hurt.

A major use is in the design of equipment and interfaces, where a modelled operator can be run through a proposed cockpit layout or software screen so that designers can find slow steps and likely errors before any real person is exposed to them.

This matters because testing designs on modelled minds is far faster, cheaper, and safer than running large studies with people at every step, especially in high-stakes settings such as aviation and driving.

Architectures such as ACT-R, and specialised systems like EPIC, whose name stands for Executive Process Interactive Control and which focuses on the fine timing of perception and movement, have been used exactly this way to predict human performance in demanding tasks.

As a system, the modelled operator is a simulator with the task interface as input, predicted keystroke-level timings and error locations as output, and a characteristic resolution of tens of milliseconds, which is what makes it useful for spotting bottlenecks in second-scale interactions.

The value of these predictions rests entirely on the architecture being an accurate model of the mind, which is why this application and the evaluation questions of the previous section are two sides of the same coin.


64.3.2 Intelligent tutoring systems

A second and notably successful application is the intelligent tutoring system, which is a computer teacher that adapts to each individual student, and it is arguably the field's clearest real-world win.

The most famous example is the Cognitive Tutor, a family of tutoring programs for subjects such as high-school mathematics, built by Carnegie Learning on the foundation of John Anderson's ACT-R theory.

The core trick is that the tutor contains a cognitive model of how a skilled student solves the problems, and it uses this model in two connected ways.

The first is model tracing, meaning the tutor follows along with each step the student takes and compares it against the steps its inner model would take, so it can recognise at once when a student goes wrong and offer help right there.

The second is knowledge tracing, meaning the tutor keeps a running estimate, for each separate skill, of the probability that this particular student has now mastered it, updating that estimate every time the student gets a relevant problem right or wrong.

In systems terms the tutor is an observer-controller pair: model tracing is the observer, taking the student's step stream as input and emitting a match-or-mismatch signal per step, and knowledge tracing is the state estimator, holding one mastery probability per skill and updating it on every observed outcome, with problem selection as the control output that steers practice toward low-mastery skills.

Using these estimates the tutor gives each student more practice on exactly the skills they have not yet mastered and less on the ones they have, which personalises the teaching in a way a single human teacher with thirty pupils cannot easily match.

Controlled studies of these tutors in real schools have reported meaningful learning gains over traditional classroom instruction, which makes intelligent tutoring one of the strongest pieces of evidence that architecture research can pay off in practice, though, as with all education research, exact effects vary with how and where the tutors are used.


64.3.3 Human-robot interaction and cognitive robotics

A third application places a cognitive architecture inside a robot, so that the robot's behaviour is driven by a model of a mind rather than by narrow special-purpose programming, and this area is called cognitive robotics.

The appeal is that a robot working alongside people in an unpredictable world needs many of the same capacities a mind needs, such as perceiving its surroundings, remembering, setting goals, planning, and adapting, which is exactly what an architecture is supposed to provide in an integrated way.

Human-robot interaction adds a further demand, namely that the robot should understand and cooperate with people, which calls for capacities such as taking turns, following shared attention, and forming some model of what its human partner knows and wants.

Putting an architecture in a robot also confronts it directly with the grounding problem discussed earlier, because a physical robot cannot be handed clean symbols by a programmer but must build its understanding out of its own noisy sensors and imperfect actuators.

The systems demand is real-time closure of the loop: sensor input arrives continuously, actuator commands must go out fast enough to keep the body safe, and any architecture whose decision cycle cannot keep pace with the world's own timescale fails in a way no offline simulation would reveal.

For this reason cognitive robotics is not only an application but also a demanding test bed, since a body in the real world exposes any gaps in an architecture's perception, action, and real-time coping that a tidy simulation would hide.

Architectures including Soar, ACT-R, and ICARUS, the last of which was designed with physical agents in mind, have been used to control robots, though robust, general, humanlike robot behaviour remains an unsolved and actively pursued goal rather than an accomplished fact.


64.3.4 Autonomous agents and synthetic characters

The fourth application uses architectures to drive software agents and characters that act on their own inside virtual worlds rather than in physical robots.

An autonomous agent here means a piece of software that pursues its own goals over time without step-by-step human control, for example a simulated soldier in a military training exercise or a non-player character in a game or simulation.

A synthetic character means such an agent designed specifically to seem like a believable person or creature, with apparent goals, memories, and emotions, so that people interacting with it find it convincing and lifelike.

Cognitive architectures are attractive for this because they can give a character genuine internal structure, so that its behaviour arises from remembering, wanting, and deciding rather than from a shallow script, which tends to make the character more flexible and more believable.

The motivational and emotional architectures are especially relevant here, since a character that has something like drives and feelings, as in the Psi-theory tradition, can react to events with a plausible inner life rather than a fixed set of canned responses.

In systems terms the character is the same architecture with a cheaper interface: its perception input is the game state rather than raw sensors and its motor output is a game command rather than a joint torque, which is why virtual worlds serve as an affordable middle step between pure simulation and full robotics.

A long-standing large-scale use is in training simulations, where architecture-driven agents play the roles of teammates, opponents, and bystanders so that human trainees can practise in realistic populated scenarios.

Across all four applications the common thread is the same, namely that whenever a task needs a whole coordinated mind rather than one narrow skill, an integrated cognitive architecture is a natural tool, and how well it performs in these roles is, in the end, the most demanding test of whether the theories in this part of the outline are on the right track.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Candidate model, an architecture with a fixed core parameter set, supplied by the modeller to the evaluation harness.

◦ Task battery, a set of task definitions each with stimuli and scoring procedure, drawn from the experimental literature.

◦ Human reference data, per-task behavioural measures such as mean reaction times, error rates, and learning curves.

◦ Application demands, in deployment, the sensor streams, student steps, or game states of the target setting.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Per-task fit scores, numeric discrepancy measures between model behaviour and human data, consumed by the modeller and reviewers.

◦ A breadth summary, the count of tasks fit acceptably under one fixed parameter set, the field's main credibility currency.

◦ Predicted human performance, timings and error locations, consumed by interface designers and tutors.

◦ Diagnosed weaknesses, the tasks and mechanisms where fits fail, feeding the next design revision.

• STATE.

◦ The frozen core parameter vector, held constant across all tasks in a breadth evaluation.

◦ Per-task knowledge scaffolding, the hand-built task rules and representations, which must be declared because they confound comparison.

◦ Accumulated fit records across tasks, the running scoreboard of the evaluation.

◦ In tutoring deployments, per-student mastery estimates, one probability per skill.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Number of free parameters permitted, the flexibility budget that fit scores must be penalised against.

◦ Fit criterion, the discrepancy measure chosen, such as squared error on reaction times or correlation on error patterns.

◦ Generalisation split, the division between tasks used for tuning and tasks held out for testing.

◦ Scaffolding budget, how much hand-built task knowledge each contestant is allowed.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Model-predicted behaviour is scored at the resolution of the human data, commonly tens of milliseconds for reaction times, anchored by the roughly 50 millisecond production cycle.

◦ Skill mastery in tutoring: REFUSED as a constant, because knowledge-tracing updates are per-opportunity and mastery time varies by skill and student.

◦ Robot control loop deadlines: REFUSED, because required rates depend on the platform and task, from milliseconds for balance to seconds for dialogue.

• MODES.

◦ Tuning mode, where parameters may move to fit the training tasks, entered when a new model or task is introduced.

◦ Frozen evaluation mode, where all parameters are locked and held-out tasks are run, entered when credibility is being claimed.

◦ Deployment mode, where the architecture serves as operator model, tutor, robot controller, or character, entered when fits are judged good enough to use.

◦ Diagnosis mode, where failures are traced to mechanisms, entered whenever a fit or a deployment falls short.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Overfitting, matching data through parameter flexibility rather than mechanism, exposed when held-out tasks fail.

◦ Scaffolding illusion, results that reflect the modeller's hand-built task knowledge rather than the architecture, the confound a missing benchmark cannot control.

◦ Benchmark bias, any single shared test unfairly favouring the capacities it happens to measure.

◦ Deployment mismatch, a model accurate in the laboratory failing in the field, as when a tutor mis-estimates mastery or a robot controller misses real-time deadlines.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list called task battery holding several tasks, each with a name, a difficulty number, and the human mean response time for that task.
Create a dictionary called model parameters holding a base time number and a time per difficulty step number.
Create an empty list called fit records.
For each task in the task battery, do the following.
    Calculate the model predicted time as the base time plus the time per difficulty step times the task difficulty.
    Calculate the error as the model predicted time minus the human mean time for the task.
    Calculate the squared error as the error times the error.
    Append the task name, the predicted time, the human time, and the squared error to the fit records.
Calculate the mean squared error as the sum of the squared errors divided by the number of tasks.
Calculate the root mean squared error as the square root of the mean squared error.
Count how many tasks have a prediction within ten percent of the human time, and call this the breadth count.
Print each fit record showing the task name, the predicted time, and the human time.
Print the root mean squared error and the breadth count as the overall evaluation of the model.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the math module for the square root function.
import math

# Create a list called task battery holding tasks, each with a name, a difficulty, and a human mean time in milliseconds.
task_battery = [
    # Each task gives its name, its difficulty in steps, and the observed human mean response time.
    ("simple_reaction", 1, 250.0),
    ("choice_reaction", 3, 420.0),
    ("mental_arithmetic", 8, 730.0),
    ("memory_scanning", 5, 520.0),
    ("problem_solving", 12, 950.0),
]
# Create a dictionary called model parameters holding a base time and a time per difficulty step.
params = {"base": 180.0, "per_step": 55.0}
# Create an empty list called fit records.
fit_records = []

# For each task in the task battery, compute the model prediction and its error.
for name, difficulty, human_time in task_battery:
    # Calculate the model predicted time as the base time plus the per-step time times the difficulty.
    predicted = params["base"] + params["per_step"] * difficulty
    # Calculate the error as the predicted time minus the human mean time.
    error = predicted - human_time
    # Calculate the squared error as the error times the error.
    squared_error = error * error
    # Append the task name, the predicted time, the human time, and the squared error to the fit records.
    fit_records.append((name, predicted, human_time, squared_error))

# Calculate the mean squared error as the sum of squared errors divided by the number of tasks.
mse = sum(rec[3] for rec in fit_records) / len(fit_records)
# Calculate the root mean squared error as the square root of the mean squared error.
rmse = math.sqrt(mse)
# Count how many tasks have a prediction within ten percent of the human time, as the breadth count.
breadth = sum(1 for rec in fit_records if abs(rec[1] - rec[2]) <= 0.1 * rec[2])

# For each fit record, print the task name, the predicted time, and the human time.
for name, predicted, human_time, squared_error in fit_records:
    # Print the comparison line for this task, rounding times to whole milliseconds.
    print(name, "predicted", round(predicted), "ms, human", round(human_time), "ms")
# Print the root mean squared error as the overall fit measure.
print("Root mean squared error:", round(rmse, 1), "ms")
# Print the breadth count as the number of tasks fit within ten percent under one fixed parameter set.
print("Tasks fit within ten percent:", breadth, "of", len(task_battery))

PART FIFTEEN. THE FRONTIER AND THE BRIDGE TO ARTIFICIAL GENERAL INTELLIGENCE

================================================================================

CHAPTER 65. PROGRAM INDUCTION AND THE PROBABILISTIC LANGUAGE OF THOUGHT (FRONTIER)

This chapter is about one of the boldest ideas at the meeting point of the science of mind and the science of machines.

The idea is that a concept in your head - what a dog is, what the number seven is, how a handwritten letter is drawn - might be stored not as a picture or a list of features, but as a little program, a recipe of steps for producing or recognising examples of the thing.

If that is true, then learning is a kind of programming, the mind writing short programs to explain what it sees, and a machine that learned the way we do would have to write such programs too.

Read as an engineered system, a program-induction learner takes observed examples as input, searches a space of candidate programs as its core operation, holds a growing library of reusable program parts as its state, and outputs the shortest program that explains the data well.

The word "frontier" in the chapter tag is honest: these are live research bets, not settled textbook facts, and this chapter tells you where the excitement is and where the doubts are.

We will meet three linked ideas: concepts as programs, a "probabilistic language of thought" in which those programs are written, and a broader agenda for building machines that learn and think the way people do.


65.1 Concepts as programs

This section introduces the central image of the whole chapter, so it is worth slowing down over.

A program, in plain terms, is a set of instructions that a machine can follow step by step to produce a result, the way a recipe produces a cake.

The claim here is that many human concepts behave like programs: compact, made of reusable parts, and able to generate endless new examples from a few simple rules.

The word "probabilistic" will keep appearing, and it just means "involving chance and degrees of belief" rather than fixed certainty, because the mind is rarely sure and must weigh possibilities.

In systems terms, a concept-as-program is a generative module: its input is a request to produce or evaluate an example, its output is either a generated instance or a probability score for an observed instance, and its stored form is the program text itself, which is far more compact than a table of remembered examples.


65.1.1 Bayesian program learning

Bayesian program learning is a specific, celebrated proposal that a concept is a probabilistic program, a recipe with some randomness built in, that can generate the examples we see.

The name honours Thomas Bayes, an eighteenth-century clergyman whose rule for updating beliefs in the light of evidence is the mathematical backbone of the approach, so "Bayesian" here means "reasoning about probabilities by combining what you expected beforehand with what you observe".

The landmark study was published in the journal Science in 2015 by Brenden Lake, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, and Joshua Tenenbaum, under the title "Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction".

Their test bed was handwriting.

They built a data set called Omniglot, which contains 1,623 different handwritten characters drawn from 50 different alphabets around the world, with each character produced by 20 different people.

The word "Omniglot" simply blends "omni", meaning all, with "glot", meaning tongue or language, so it is meant to be a collection of all the world's scripts.

The hard test they set is called one-shot learning, which means learning a brand new concept from a single example, something young children do easily and most machines of the time did badly.

Show a person one example of an unfamiliar letter and they can recognise other people's versions of it, draw new versions themselves, and even invent plausible new letters in the same style.

Their model captured this by treating each character as a program that builds the letter out of pen strokes, where each stroke is itself made of smaller sub-strokes, and the strokes are joined at relations like "start where the last stroke ended".

As a system, the learner subscribes to a single image of a new character, searches for the stroke program most likely to have drawn it, and publishes that program as the learned concept, which can then be run forwards to draw new examples or run backwards to classify other images.

Three ideas did the heavy lifting, and they are worth naming because they recur across the chapter.

The first is compositionality, which means building complex things by combining a small set of simpler parts, the way sentences are built from words.

The second is causality, which here means that the program mimics the real physical process that produced the data, in this case the actual motions of a pen, rather than just the finished ink.

The third is learning to learn, which means that experience with earlier concepts, such as earlier alphabets, tunes the system so that each new concept is easier to acquire.

The result was striking: the model learned new characters from one example about as accurately as human adults, and in "visual Turing test" style judging, people could not reliably tell the model's drawings from human ones.

A Turing test, named after the mathematician Alan Turing, is any test in which a judge tries to tell machine output from human output, and failing to tell them apart is taken as a mark of humanlike performance.

It is important to be even-handed about what this did and did not show.

It showed that a structured, program-like model with very little data could match humans on a task where large pattern-learning networks of the day needed far more examples.

It did not show that the brain literally stores letters as this exact kind of program, and it was limited to a fairly clean, well-defined domain.

The authors themselves followed up in 2019 with an "Omniglot challenge" progress report, honestly concluding that even several years later, machines were still not learning these concepts in a fully humanlike way, so the problem remains open.


65.1.2 Library learning and wake-sleep program synthesis

If concepts are programs, a natural next question is where the reusable parts, the building blocks, come from.

This sub-section is about a system that tries to grow its own toolbox of parts while it learns, rather than being handed the parts in advance.

The system is called DreamCoder, described by Kevin Ellis and colleagues, including Joshua Tenenbaum and Armando Solar-Lezama, in work published around 2020 and 2021.

Program synthesis, the phrase in the heading, means getting a computer to write programs by itself to solve tasks, given only examples of what the answer should look like.

Library learning means that as the system solves many small problems, it notices chunks of code that keep proving useful and files them away as new named building blocks, exactly as a human programmer factors out a helper routine to reuse later.

Over time the library deepens, so that early crude solutions become the raw material from which higher-level concepts are composed, and later problems that once looked hard become easy because the right building block already exists.

The learning method is called wake-sleep, a two-phase cycle inspired by an older idea in machine learning and loosely evocative of the roles of waking and sleeping in the brain.
