In the "wake" phase the system is awake and working, searching for programs that solve the current tasks using the library it has so far, guided by a neural network that has learned to guess promising solutions.

In the "sleep" phase the system steps back from the data, reviews the programs it found, distils out common patterns into new library concepts, and even dreams up practice problems for itself to train its guessing network.

A neural network, for readers meeting the term, is a computing system loosely inspired by brain cells, made of many simple units whose connection strengths are adjusted by experience so the whole learns from examples.

In systems terms this is a two-mode controller: the wake mode consumes tasks and the current library and produces solved programs, the sleep mode consumes those programs and produces an enriched library and a better search heuristic, and the alternation between modes is scheduled by the training loop rather than by the data.

DreamCoder was shown to work across eight varied domains, from making lists and sorting to drawing pictures and rediscovering simple laws of physics, learning concepts a human would recognise, such as the idea of a vector or of sorting.

The reason this matters for a science of mind is that it is a working demonstration of a system that bootstraps, meaning it lifts itself up by its own effort, building richer and richer concepts out of poorer ones, which is one candidate story for how human conceptual knowledge grows over a lifetime.

The honest caveat is that these systems still work best in tidy, formal domains and are far from the open, messy richness of everyday human concepts, so the demonstration is a proof of principle rather than a finished model of the mind.


65.2 The probabilistic language of thought

This section names the medium in which all these little programs are supposed to be written.

The phrase "language of thought" is old and comes from the philosopher Jerry Fodor, who argued in the 1970s that thinking happens in an internal, language-like code, sometimes nicknamed "mentalese", with its own words and grammar.

The newer twist, "probabilistic", adds chance and uncertainty to that code, so that thoughts are not rigid logical statements but recipes that can express "probably", "usually", and "it depends".

The proposal is that this probabilistic code is general purpose, one shared format in which the mind can frame perception, physical intuition, and reasoning about other people alike.

In systems terms the claim is architectural: instead of many special-purpose formats, one intermediate representation carries every kind of thought, the way a single machine code underlies many different applications on one computer.


65.2.1 The probabilistic-programming substrates

A substrate is the underlying material or foundation on which something is built, so a "probabilistic-programming substrate" is the concrete computer language in which these thought-programs can actually be written and run.

The key tool is a class of computer languages called probabilistic programming languages, which let you write down a model of how some part of the world randomly generates data, and then automatically run the model backwards to infer likely causes from observed effects.

The founding example in this line of cognitive science is a language called Church, introduced in 2008 by Noah Goodman, Vikash Mansinghka, Daniel Roy, Keith Bonawitz, and Joshua Tenenbaum, and named in honour of the logician Alonzo Church.

Church was built on top of a well-known style of programming from the Lisp and Scheme tradition, extended so that any part of a program can make a random choice, which lets a short program stand for a rich space of possible worlds.

The theoretical claim attached to these tools is the probabilistic language of thought hypothesis, put forward by Goodman, Tenenbaum, and Tobias Gerstenberg, that concepts are functions in such a probabilistic mental code and that thinking is running and conditioning these programs.

To "condition" a program means to fix some facts as observed and ask the program what else is then likely, which is how a single generative recipe can answer endless different questions.

As a system, a probabilistic program has two directions of data flow: forwards, it takes random choices as input and publishes simulated data, and backwards, it takes observed data as input and publishes a probability distribution over the hidden choices that could have produced it.

Researchers have used this framework to model a wide sweep of human inferences, including judgments that draw on seeing, on imagining how physical objects will move, and on reasoning about what other people want and believe.

The appeal is unification: instead of a separate special-purpose theory for each mental task, one flexible language expresses a world model, and the same inference machinery answers many questions about it.

The open worry, which fair-minded advocates acknowledge, is that running such programs exactly is often far too slow to be plausible for a real brain, which pushes the field toward approximate short-cuts, a theme we return to in the chapter on rational process models.


65.2.2 Rational meaning construction and the translation from language

This sub-section connects the probabilistic language of thought to ordinary human language, which is a natural bridge to the large-language-model chapters that follow.

The guiding study is a 2023 paper by Lionel Wong, Gabriel Grand, and colleagues, with Joshua Tenenbaum and Noah Goodman among the authors, titled "From Word Models to World Models".

Its subtitle spells out the plan: "Translating from Natural Language to the Probabilistic Language of Thought".

The proposal is called rational meaning construction, and the everyday version of the idea is this: understanding a sentence means turning its words into a small runnable model of the situation, which you can then think with.

Their design uses a modern large language model, a system trained on huge amounts of text to predict words, but only as a translator.

The large language model reads an English sentence and converts it into code in a probabilistic programming language, and then a separate, trustworthy reasoning engine actually runs that code to draw conclusions.

The word "rational" here signals that the final answers come from principled probability calculations, not from the language model's raw guesswork, which the authors argue makes the reasoning more reliable and more humanlike.

They connect the translator to purpose-built modules, such as a physics simulator for reasoning about how objects move and a planner for reasoning about goals, so that language can tap into these specialised thinking tools.

In systems terms this is a pipeline architecture: the input is a natural-language sentence, the first stage publishes program code, the second stage runs the code and publishes probabilistic conclusions, and the interface between the stages is the probabilistic language of thought itself.

The larger significance is a division of labour that many researchers find attractive: use text-trained networks for their fluency with words, but hand the heavy reasoning to explicit, checkable world models.

This is one of the most active current attempts to marry the strengths of the two traditions, and it is early work, so its promise is real but not yet proven at scale.


65.3 The integrative agenda

This final section steps back from particular systems to the overall research programme they belong to.

An agenda, in plain terms, is a to-do list, and "integrative" means it tries to bring many pieces together into one coherent effort.

The agenda asks a simple, ambitious question: what would it actually take to build a machine that learns and thinks the way a person does.


65.3.1 The core ingredients of humanlike learning and thought

The reference point here is an influential and much-debated 2017 article by Brenden Lake, Tomer Ullman, Joshua Tenenbaum, and Samuel Gershman, titled "Building machines that learn and think like people", published with open commentary in the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

The article argues that human intelligence rests on a few core ingredients that most machine-learning systems of the time lacked, and it lays them out as a checklist.

The first ingredient is developmental start-up software, meaning the knowledge babies seem to bring to the world very early, in particular an intuitive physics for how objects move and an intuitive psychology for reading goals and beliefs in other agents.

Intuitive physics means a rough, fast, built-in sense of how the physical world behaves, such as expecting an unsupported object to fall.

Intuitive psychology means an equally quick sense that other creatures act to reach goals given their beliefs, which is what lets a baby be surprised by a person who takes the long way around when a short path is open.

The second ingredient is learning as rapid model-building rather than slow pattern-matching, the idea that people build a small explanatory model from a handful of examples instead of needing thousands.

The third ingredient is compositionality and learning to learn together, so that new knowledge is assembled from reusable parts and each thing learned makes the next thing faster to learn.

The fourth ingredient concerns thinking fast, the ability to run these rich models quickly using clever approximations rather than exhaustive calculation.

In systems terms the two sides of this debate make different predictions: the ingredients camp predicts that a system without built-in structure will need vastly more data and will fail on novel recombinations, while the learning-first camp predicts that enough data and scale will let the structure emerge inside the network on its own.

The article was pointed in its critique of pure deep-learning systems, and it drew vigorous replies from researchers who felt it underrated how much structure networks can learn on their own, so it should be read as one influential side of a genuine and continuing debate.

That debate has only sharpened since 2017 as large networks have grown far more capable, and reasonable experts still disagree about how many of these ingredients a system must be given versus how many it can learn.


65.3.2 Building machines that learn and think like people, and with people

The heading deliberately echoes the 2017 title but adds two crucial words, "with people", pointing to a newer turn in the programme.

The reference is a 2024 article in Nature Human Behaviour by Katherine Collins, Ilia Sucholutsky, Joshua Tenenbaum, Thomas Griffiths, and many colleagues, titled "Building machines that learn and think with people".

Its central shift is from machines as tools we use to machines as thought partners, systems that collaborate in reasoning rather than just answering.

A thought partner, in their sense, is a system you think alongside, one that is insightful, reliable, and trustworthy enough to genuinely help you reason, plan, and decide.

The proposed way to build such partners keeps the Bayesian spirit of the earlier work: the machine should actively build and reason over a model of the world and a model of the particular human it is helping.

Modelling the human matters because a good partner tracks what you already know, what you are trying to do, and where you are likely to go wrong, so it can offer the right help at the right moment.

In systems terms a thought partner subscribes to two streams, the state of the shared task and the state of the human, and publishes assistance that is conditioned on both, which is a strictly richer interface than a question-in, answer-out tool.

This reframes the goal of the whole frontier: not only to reproduce a single mind in a machine, but to design machines that fit into and strengthen the thinking of the people and groups who use them.

It is an aspiration and a design philosophy as much as a finished result, and the authors present it as a direction of travel rather than a solved problem.

For a project like konnectome, which aims at general and beyond-human machine intelligence, this "with people" framing is important because it treats humanlike cognition not as an end in itself but as the ground for a genuine partnership between human and artificial minds.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Observed examples of a concept, such as images of a character or terms of a number sequence, in whatever raw format the domain provides.

◦ A library of primitive operations and previously learned program parts, supplied by earlier learning.

◦ A prior over programs, usually favouring shorter programs, which encodes the expectation that the world is simply structured.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ The best program found, a compact generative recipe for the concept, consumed by later recognition, generation, and reasoning processes.

◦ A posterior probability, meaning an updated degree of belief, for each candidate program given the data, consumed by decision processes that must weigh alternatives.

◦ New library entries, reusable program fragments distilled from solutions, consumed by future learning episodes.

• STATE.

◦ The current library of concepts and parts, which grows across episodes.

◦ The set of candidate programs under consideration during a search, with their scores.

◦ Learned search guidance, such as a trained recognition network that proposes promising programs first.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ The trade-off weight between fitting the data well and keeping the program short, the heart of the Bayesian scoring rule.

◦ The maximum program length or search depth the learner will consider.

◦ The size of the primitive vocabulary, which fixes the expressive power of the language of thought.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ One-shot concept learning in humans: a single exposure of a few seconds suffices for a new handwritten character, as the Omniglot studies showed.

◦ Machine search time per concept: REFUSED, because it depends entirely on hardware, program space, and implementation, and no canonical value exists in the literature.

◦ Library growth in DreamCoder-style systems: unfolds over many wake-sleep cycles, typically hours to days of computation in published runs, but REFUSED as a general constant because it is implementation bound.

• MODES.

◦ Wake mode, searching for programs that explain current data using the existing library, triggered by the arrival of new tasks.

◦ Sleep abstraction mode, compressing found solutions into new library concepts, triggered by the end of a wake phase.

◦ Sleep dreaming mode, generating practice problems from the learner's own programs to train its search heuristic, alternating with abstraction on a schedule.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Search failure, where the true program exists in the space but is never found because the space is astronomically large.

◦ Mis-specified primitives, where the concept cannot be expressed at all because the language of thought lacks the needed parts.

◦ Overfitting to noise, where an over-long program memorises accidents of the examples instead of the rule, the machine analogue of superstition.

◦ Exact inference being intractably slow, forcing approximations that can settle on plausible but wrong programs.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a list variable called observed sequence containing the example numbers to be explained.
Create a list variable called program space containing every candidate program, where each candidate pairs a starting value with a step rule and a step amount.
Create a variable called best program with initial value nothing.
Create a number variable called best score with initial value negative infinity.
For each candidate in program space, perform the following steps.
    Create a list variable called generated containing the candidate starting value.
    For each position from one up to one less than the length of the observed sequence, apply the candidate step rule and step amount to the last element of generated, and append the result to generated.
    Create a number variable called fit score with initial value zero.
    For each position in the observed sequence, if the generated value at that position equals the observed value at that position, add one to fit score.
    Calculate the description length of the candidate as the number of symbols needed to write it down.
    Calculate the total score as fit score multiplied by ten minus the description length.
    If the total score is greater than best score, set best score to the total score and set best program to the candidate.
Return best program as the learned concept and use it to predict the next number in the sequence.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the itertools module for building the space of candidate programs.
import itertools

# Create a list variable called observed containing the example numbers to be explained.
observed = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]

# Define a function called run_program that takes a start value, a rule name, an amount, and a length.
def run_program(start, rule, amount, length):
    # Create a list variable called seq containing the start value.
    seq = [start]
    # For each step from one up to one less than length, perform the following steps.
    for _ in range(length - 1):
        # If the rule is add, append the last value plus the amount to seq.
        if rule == "add":
            seq.append(seq[-1] + amount)
        # Otherwise, if the rule is multiply, append the last value times the amount to seq.
        elif rule == "mul":
            seq.append(seq[-1] * amount)
        # Otherwise, the rule is square, so append the last value times itself.
        else:
            seq.append(seq[-1] * seq[-1])
    # Return the generated sequence.
    return seq

# Create a variable called best holding no program yet, and a score variable at negative infinity.
best, best_score = None, float("-inf")

# For each combination of start value, rule, and amount, evaluate the candidate program.
for start, rule, amount in itertools.product(range(1, 11), ["add", "mul", "square"], range(1, 11)):
    # Generate the candidate sequence with the same length as the observed sequence.
    generated = run_program(start, rule, amount, len(observed))
    # Count how many positions of the generated sequence match the observed sequence.
    fit = sum(1 for g, o in zip(generated, observed) if g == o)
    # Set the description length to two symbols, or three if the rule needs an amount.
    length_cost = 2 if rule == "square" else 3
    # Calculate the total score as ten times the fit minus the description length.
    score = 10 * fit - length_cost
    # If this score beats the best score, remember this candidate and its score.
    if score > best_score:
        best, best_score = (start, rule, amount), score

# Unpack the best program into its start value, rule, and amount.
start, rule, amount = best
# Print the shortest program that explains the observed sequence.
print("Best program: start at", start, "then repeatedly", rule, amount)
# Print the prediction for the next number by running the program one step longer.
print("Predicted next number:", run_program(start, rule, amount, len(observed) + 1)[-1])


CHAPTER 66. LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS AND FOUNDATION MODELS AS COGNITION (FRONTIER)

This chapter is about the technology that has reshaped both artificial intelligence and the public conversation about minds: the large language model.

A large language model (LLM) is a computer system trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next word in a sequence, and by learning to do that extremely well it becomes able to write, answer questions, translate, and much more.

The word "foundation model" is a broader term for any such large system trained on broad data that can then be adapted to many tasks, so language models are one kind of foundation model, and there are others trained on images, sound, and mixtures of these.

Read as an engineered system, a language model subscribes to a sequence of tokens, meaning word pieces, holds its knowledge in billions of fixed connection strengths plus a temporary context window, and publishes a probability for every possible next token, over and over, one token at a time.

The frontier question, and the reason this belongs in a book about cognition, is whether these systems merely mimic the surface of thought or whether they can teach us something real about how thinking works, in machines and perhaps in us.

This chapter treats these systems even-handedly, both as remarkable engineering and as objects of genuine scientific dispute, because the honest state of the field in 2026 is that experts strongly disagree.


66.1 The capacities of large language models

This section surveys what these systems can actually do, focusing on two abilities that surprised even their builders.

The point is to describe the phenomena carefully before we argue about what they mean, because much of the disagreement in the field is really about interpretation rather than facts.


66.1.1 Emergent abilities and in-context learning

Two words in this heading need plain definitions before anything else.

An emergent ability is a skill that small models do not have and large models do, appearing, or seeming to appear, rather suddenly once a model passes some size.

In-context learning is the striking ability of these models to pick up a new task from a few examples placed in the prompt, the text you give them, without any change to the model's internal settings.

To see in-context learning, imagine typing a few pairs of a word and its opposite and then a new word, and the model continues the pattern and supplies the opposite, having been taught the task purely by the examples in front of it.

This is remarkable because ordinary machine learning changes a system by adjusting its internal connections through training, whereas here the model adapts on the fly, from the prompt alone, with its internals frozen.

In systems terms, in-context learning means the system has two memories on two timescales: slow weights, changed only by training over weeks, and a fast context window, changed within a single response taking seconds, and the new task lives entirely in the fast one.

The claim of sudden "emergence" was popularised around 2022, when researchers reported that certain abilities, such as doing multi-step arithmetic, seemed to switch on abruptly as models grew.

That claim was then seriously challenged.

In 2023 Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda, and Sanmi Koyejo published a widely discussed paper titled "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?".

Their argument is subtle and worth stating fairly: they showed that the appearance of a sudden jump often comes from the yardstick being used, not from the model itself.

If you score a task in an all-or-nothing way, where only a completely correct answer counts, then smooth underlying improvement can look like a sudden leap, whereas a more forgiving score reveals steady, gradual gains.

The debate is not fully closed, because other researchers maintain that some abilities do show genuinely sharp transitions, and the current careful position is that at least some reported "emergence" is an artefact of measurement while some may be real.

For a student, the useful lesson is broader than language models: how you choose to measure a skill can change whether it looks like a smooth climb or a sudden cliff, and this matters throughout the science of the mind.


66.1.2 Chain-of-thought as a reasoning proxy

This sub-section is about a simple trick that makes these models much better at hard problems, and about the argument over what the trick really reveals.

Chain-of-thought means prompting the model to write out its intermediate steps, its "thinking", before giving a final answer, rather than jumping straight to the answer.

The founding demonstration was a 2022 paper by Jason Wei and colleagues showing that when large models are asked to reason step by step, their accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and logic problems improves substantially.

In systems terms, chain-of-thought turns the model's own output stream into a scratch memory: intermediate results are written into the context window and read back on later steps, which extends the effective depth of computation beyond a single forward pass.

A proxy, the word in the heading, means a stand-in, something you observe in place of the thing you actually care about, so "reasoning proxy" asks whether the written-out steps stand in faithfully for the model's real reasoning.

That is exactly where the controversy lies.

The original paper suggested the written steps offer "an interpretable window into the behaviour of the model", a phrase later authors have pushed back on hard.

In 2023 Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, and Samuel Bowman published "Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think", showing that a model's stated reasoning can be unfaithful, meaning the words it writes are not the true cause of its answer.

Their experiments showed that you can quietly bias a model toward a particular answer and it will then invent a plausible-sounding chain of steps that never mentions the real reason, much as a person can confabulate a tidy justification for a gut feeling.

To confabulate means to produce a confident explanation that feels true to the speaker but does not reflect the actual cause of the behaviour.

So the fair summary is a double one: chain-of-thought genuinely improves performance and is practically valuable, yet the visible steps cannot be trusted as an honest transcript of the model's inner workings.

This distinction, between output that helps and output that faithfully explains, echoes a very old theme in psychology, that people too are often poor and unreliable reporters of why they did what they did.


66.2 Large language models as objects of psychology

This section describes a genuinely new scientific move: studying these machines the way psychologists study people.

The motivation is that these systems are too large and too tangled to understand by reading their code, so researchers instead run experiments on them, giving them tasks and observing their behaviour.

This turns the language model into something like a participant in a study, which raises both opportunities and pitfalls that we take in turn.


66.2.1 Machine psychology and the probing of reasoning, theory of mind, and bias

Machine psychology is the young field that applies the methods of experimental psychology to artificial systems, probing their reasoning, their apparent understanding of other minds, and their biases.

The founding move is associated with Marcel Binz and Eric Schulz, who in work published around 2023 treated the model GPT-3 as a subject in classic psychology experiments, testing its decision-making, its search for information, and its reasoning about causes.

To "probe" a system, in this context, means to design a careful task that isolates one ability so you can see whether the system has it.

In systems terms, probing treats the model as a black box: the experimenter controls the input channel, the prompt, observes the output channel, the generated text, and infers what internal processing must lie between, exactly the inferential position psychology has always been in with respect to the brain.

Theory of mind, one target of this probing, is the everyday ability to attribute mental states such as beliefs and desires to others, and in particular to understand that someone can hold a belief that is false.

Researchers have run the standard false-belief tests on language models, and results are genuinely mixed and hotly argued.

Some studies, including a 2024 paper in Nature Human Behaviour testing several models, reported that the strongest models match or approach adult human performance on batteries of theory-of-mind tasks.

Other researchers, notably Tomer Ullman, showed that tiny, meaning-preserving tweaks to the classic tasks can make the same models fail, which suggests they may be leaning on surface patterns from training text rather than genuinely modelling minds.

On bias, the same methods reveal that models reproduce many human cognitive biases, the systematic errors of judgment catalogued elsewhere in this outline, because those patterns are woven through the human text they learned from.

The deepest caution in this whole enterprise is the risk of over-reading: a system can pass a test built to detect an ability in humans without possessing the underlying ability, because it may have found a shortcut that the test was never designed to rule out.

This is why careful machine psychologists insist on varied, adversarial tests, ones deliberately designed to defeat shortcuts, before crediting a model with a genuine competence.


66.2.2 In-context learning as approximate Bayesian inference

This sub-section offers one leading theory for how the in-context learning of the previous section might actually work.

The theory says that when a model adapts to examples in its prompt, it is behaving as if it were doing Bayesian inference, the principled updating of beliefs from evidence introduced in the previous chapter.

The key reference is a 2022 paper by Sang Michael Xie, Aditi Raghunathan, Percy Liang, and Tengyu Ma, titled "An Explanation of In-Context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference".

Their proposal, in plain words, is that during its original training on mountains of text the model implicitly learns about many hidden topics or tasks that generate coherent passages.

When you then show it a few examples, it quietly infers which of those hidden tasks you have in mind and continues accordingly, which is exactly the shape of Bayesian reasoning: use the evidence to figure out the most likely underlying cause.

The word "implicit" matters, because nobody built this reasoning in by hand; the claim is that it falls out naturally from the pressure to predict text well.

In systems terms the two rival accounts predict different things: the Bayesian account predicts that the model's behaviour should track the posterior probability of the candidate task, while the rival fast-internal-learning account predicts that behaviour should track the dynamics of a gradient-like update running inside the network's layers.

If this view is right, it is a beautiful bridge, because it connects a surprising behaviour of engineered systems to the same Bayesian framework that cognitive scientists use to describe human learning.

It should be held with appropriate caution, since it is a theoretical account supported by idealised mathematical settings and specific experiments, and other explanations, including the idea that the model is running a fast internal learning process of a different kind, remain in serious contention.

The mere existence of this debate is itself the interesting fact for a student: a genuinely new phenomenon has appeared, and the field is actively arguing over its mechanism using tools borrowed from the study of the human mind.


66.3 The debates

This section gathers the largest and most consequential disagreements about what these systems are.

These are not narrow technical quarrels; they touch old philosophical questions about meaning, understanding, and the nature of thought.

The right stance for a newcomer is to understand each side's strongest form, because each side has a real point and neither has won outright.


66.3.1 Distributional meaning against grounding

This debate is about whether a system trained only on text can ever really understand what words mean.

The word "distributional" refers to a theory of meaning captured by the slogan that you shall know a word by the company it keeps, meaning that a word's sense can be read off from the patterns of other words it appears alongside.

Language models are the purest embodiment of this idea, since they learn meaning, in whatever sense they do, entirely from statistical patterns of word co-occurrence in text.

"Grounding" is the opposing emphasis, the view that real meaning requires connection to things outside language, to sensations, actions, and the world that words are about.

In systems terms the dispute is about the input interface: the distributional side says a text-only input channel carries enough signal to recover meaning, while the grounding side says meaning requires additional input channels, senses and actions, that close a loop with the world.

The sharpest statement of the grounding worry came in a 2020 paper by Emily Bender and Alexander Koller, with a memorable thought experiment about an octopus.

Imagine two people on separate islands sending messages through an undersea cable, and a hyper-intelligent octopus tapping the cable and learning to imitate the messages perfectly, without ever seeing the islands.

Bender and Koller argue that such an octopus, and by analogy a text-only model, could reproduce fluent conversation yet would be lost the moment real-world reference mattered, because it learned only the form of language, never its link to the world.

The counter-argument, made by defenders of distributional meaning, is twofold: that patterns of use may carry more genuine meaning than the octopus story allows, and that modern systems increasingly are grounded, being trained on images and actions as well as text.

There is no consensus verdict, and the honest position is that this is partly an empirical question about what systems can do and partly a philosophical question about what we should call "meaning" in the first place.


66.3.2 The stochastic-parrot critique and the systematicity gap

This sub-section covers two of the most cited criticisms of large language models, which share a family resemblance.

The phrase "stochastic parrot" comes from a 2021 paper led by Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, and a co-author writing under the name Shmargaret Shmitchell.

"Stochastic" means governed by chance, and a parrot repeats without understanding, so a stochastic parrot is a system that stitches together plausible sequences of words based on statistical likelihood but without any grasp of their meaning.

The critique is partly about understanding and partly a warning about real-world harms, including the way such systems can launder biased and false text from their training data into confident-sounding output.

The "systematicity gap" is a more technical concern with a long pedigree in cognitive science.

Systematicity, an idea pressed by the philosophers Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn in 1988, is the observation that a mind able to understand "the cat chased the dog" can automatically understand "the dog chased the cat", because genuine thought recombines parts in a rule-governed way.

The worry is that neural networks may handle familiar combinations well yet stumble on novel recombinations that a truly systematic reasoner would take in stride, revealing that they generalise by similarity rather than by rule.

In systems terms the two sides predict differently on held-out recombinations: a rule-based system should generalise perfectly to any novel combination of known parts, while a similarity-based system should degrade in proportion to distance from its training experience.

This debate has been reopened rather than settled by recent models, and the evidence is genuinely mixed.

On one hand, work such as a 2023 Nature paper by Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni showed that with the right training regime networks can be pushed to strong systematic generalisation, narrowing the gap.

On the other hand, careful tests keep finding cases where large models fail on simple variations that a systematic reasoner should handle, so the gap is smaller than critics once claimed but has not clearly closed.


66.3.3 Competence against performance in models

This final sub-section imports an old and clarifying distinction from linguistics to make sense of the whole quarrel.

The distinction between competence and performance comes from the linguist Noam Chomsky, who separated what a system knows in principle, its competence, from how it behaves on a given occasion, its performance.

Your own performance departs from your competence all the time: you know English grammar, yet you make slips, lose your train of thought, and misspeak when tired.

Applied to language models, the question becomes whether their failures reveal a genuine lack of underlying ability, a competence limit, or merely a bad day at execution, a performance limit that better prompting or a larger model might fix.

In systems terms the distinction separates the stored function from the run-time conditions: competence lives in the trained weights, while performance also depends on the prompt, the sampling temperature, and the luck of the random draw, so the two sides are arguing about which layer of the system a given failure lives in.

This framing helps because much of the argument between enthusiasts and critics is really a disagreement about which kind of failure they are looking at.

An enthusiast sees a model flub a reasoning problem and calls it a performance slip, curable with a better prompt or more scale.

A critic sees the same flub and calls it a competence gap, a sign that the required ability was never really there.

The value of the distinction is not that it settles the fight, but that it names the crux clearly and warns against two opposite mistakes.

One mistake is to over-credit the system, reading a lucky success as deep competence when it may be shallow pattern-matching.

The other mistake is to over-dismiss it, reading a slip as proof of incapacity when a genuine underlying ability may simply have misfired.

Holding both errors in view at once is the mature stance this fast-moving field demands, and it is the same even-handed discipline that good cognitive science has always required of itself.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ A sequence of tokens, meaning word pieces encoded as numbers, arriving through the prompt or context window.

◦ During training only, a vast corpus of text, and for multimodal foundation models also images, audio, and other data streams.

◦ Sampling settings from the caller, such as temperature, which controls how randomly the next token is drawn.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A probability distribution over the entire token vocabulary for the next position, consumed by a sampling step.

◦ The sampled token stream, consumed by the human reader, by downstream programs, or fed back into the model's own context as chain-of-thought scratch material.

• STATE.

◦ Slow state: billions of trained connection weights, frozen at inference time.

◦ Fast state: the current context window, the running record of prompt plus generated tokens, which is the only memory that changes during a conversation.

◦ Internal per-step activations, recomputed for each forward pass and not retained afterwards.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Model size in number of weights, from millions to over a trillion in current systems.

◦ Context window length in tokens, from a few thousand to over a million tokens in 2025 to 2026 systems.

◦ Sampling temperature and related decoding settings, which trade diversity against reliability.

◦ Training compute and data volume, the levers of the scaling debate.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Per-token generation: on the order of tens of milliseconds per token on modern serving hardware, though the exact figure varies widely with model and hardware.

◦ In-context adaptation: within a single prompt, effectively seconds, because no weight change is involved.

◦ Weight learning: training runs take weeks to months of computation for frontier models.

◦ A constant for "how long the model thinks per decision" in a humanlike sense: REFUSED, because a forward pass is a fixed pipeline and does not map onto human deliberation timescales in any literature-supported way.

• MODES.

◦ Training mode, where weights change under next-token prediction pressure, versus inference mode, where weights are frozen; the switch is an engineering decision, not something the model does.

◦ Direct answering versus chain-of-thought answering, switched by prompting or by post-training that encourages step-by-step output.

◦ Greedy decoding versus sampled decoding, switched by the temperature setting, trading determinism against creativity.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Hallucination, meaning fluent, confident output that is factually false, the signature failure of next-token prediction unmoored from the world.

◦ Unfaithful explanation, where the stated reasoning is not the true cause of the answer.

◦ Bias reproduction, where prejudices in the training text reappear in output.

◦ Brittleness to rephrasing, where a meaning-preserving change in the prompt flips the answer, and loss of information in long contexts.

◦ Systematicity failures on novel recombinations of familiar parts.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary variable called counts that maps each word to a dictionary of following words and their frequencies.
Split the training text into a list of words.
For each adjacent pair of words in the list, add one to the count of the second word under the entry for the first word in counts.
Create a text variable called current word with initial value equal to a chosen starting word.
Create a list variable called generated containing the current word.
Repeat the following steps twelve times.
    Look up the dictionary of followers for the current word in counts.
    If there are no recorded followers, stop the loop.
    Choose the next word at random from the followers, weighting each follower by its frequency.
    Append the next word to generated.
    Set the current word to the next word.
Join the generated list into a sentence and return it.
Note that the model chooses each word only from the single previous word, so it produces locally fluent text while having no memory of the sentence's beginning, which displays both the power and the limit of next-word prediction.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module to sample the next word by weighted chance.
import random

# Create a text variable called corpus holding a tiny training text.
corpus = ("the cat sat on the mat and the cat saw the dog and "
          "the dog sat on the mat and the cat ran from the dog")

# Split the corpus into a list of words.
words = corpus.split()

# Create a dictionary called counts mapping each word to its followers and their frequencies.
counts = {}
# For each adjacent pair of words, count the second word as a follower of the first.
for first, second in zip(words, words[1:]):
    # Get or create the follower dictionary for the first word, then add one for the second word.
    counts.setdefault(first, {})
    # Add one to the frequency of the second word under the first word.
    counts[first][second] = counts[first].get(second, 0) + 1

# Define a function called generate that takes a starting word and a length.
def generate(start, length):
    # Create a variable called current holding the starting word.
    current = start
    # Create a list called out containing the starting word.
    out = [current]
    # Repeat the generation step until the requested length is reached.
    for _ in range(length - 1):
        # If the current word was never seen with a follower, stop early.
        if current not in counts:
            break
        # Read the follower words and their frequencies for the current word.
        followers = list(counts[current].keys())
        weights = list(counts[current].values())
        # Choose the next word at random, weighted by how often it followed in training.
        current = random.choices(followers, weights=weights)[0]
        # Append the chosen word to the output list.
        out.append(current)
    # Join the output words into one sentence and return it.
    return " ".join(out)

# Print a generated sentence, which is locally fluent because each step is a learned prediction.
print("Generated:", generate("the", 12))
# Print the model's whole knowledge about the word cat, to show it is only next-word statistics.
print("What the model knows after the word cat:", counts["cat"])
# Print the limit: the model cannot know whether the sentence began with cat or dog,
# because its only state is the single previous word.
print("Limit: no memory beyond one word, so long-range meaning is impossible.")


CHAPTER 67. WORLD MODELS, MODEL-BASED AGENTS, AND NEUROAI (FRONTIER)

This chapter turns from systems that traffic in words to systems that try to understand and act in a world.

Its unifying idea is the world model, an internal picture of how the environment works that an agent can use to imagine the future and plan before acting.

The chapter also introduces NeuroAI, a research movement that deliberately braids together neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using each to inform and test the other.

Read as an engineered system, a model-based agent runs two coupled loops: an outer loop that acts in the real environment and collects experience, and an inner loop that trains a predictive model on that experience and rehearses candidate futures inside it before committing to a real action.

The reason this is frontier material is that world models and NeuroAI sit at the crossroads where the deepest ambitions of machine intelligence meet the oldest questions about how brains build minds, and the field is moving quickly.

For konnectome, which reaches toward general and beyond-human intelligence grounded in how real brains work, this chapter is close to the heart of the whole enterprise.


67.1 World models

This section explains what a world model is and why an agent that has one can be smarter and more efficient than one that does not.

A world model is an internal, predictive model of an environment, a compact "if I do this, that will probably happen" simulator that an agent carries inside itself.

The everyday analogy is the mental rehearsal you do before a tricky conversation or a parking manoeuvre, imagining outcomes and choosing among them without paying the real-world cost of trying each one.

In systems terms a world model is a function from a state and an action to a predicted next state and reward, learned from experience, and its value is that queries to it are cheap while queries to the real world are expensive and sometimes dangerous.


67.1.1 Learned world models and latent imagination

The key advance in this sub-section is that an agent can learn its world model from raw experience and then do its planning inside that learned model, in imagination, rather than by acting in the real world.

The foundational demonstration is the 2018 paper simply titled "World Models" by David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber.

Their agent first learns to compress what it sees, the flood of pixels from a game, into a small summary, and then learns a second component that predicts how that summary will change over time.

The small summary is called a latent representation, where "latent" means hidden or underlying, so a latent representation is a compact code capturing the essence of a scene while throwing away irrelevant detail.

Because the model can predict how this compact code evolves, the agent can generate imagined experience, a "dream" of the game, and practise entirely inside that dream, which is far faster and cheaper than acting in the real environment.

This is the meaning of latent imagination: planning and learning by rolling the world model forward in the compressed latent space, not by taking real actions.

The idea was carried much further by a line of systems called Dreamer, developed by Danijar Hafner and colleagues from around 2019 onward through several versions.

The Dreamer agents learn a world model from experience and then learn how to behave purely from trajectories imagined inside that model, using a scheme in which one part proposes actions and another judges their value.

Later versions became strong enough that a single Dreamer system could master a wide range of very different control tasks, and by the DreamerV3 stage it could even accomplish hard, long-horizon goals such as gathering resources in an open-ended block-building game from scratch, without task-specific tuning.

That line of work reached a landmark in 2025, when the DreamerV3 results were published in the journal Nature, reporting mastery of over one hundred and fifty tasks with one configuration and the first collection of diamonds in the game Minecraft by an agent learning entirely from its own experience, without human demonstration data.

In systems terms the agent has three learned components: an encoder that compresses observations into latent state, a dynamics model that predicts the next latent state and reward given an action, and a behaviour module trained on imagined rollouts, with real experience arriving on the slow outer loop and imagined experience generated thousands of times faster on the inner loop.

The broad lesson, which resonates with the memory chapters of this outline, is that imagination and prediction are not decorative extras but powerful engines of efficient learning, in machines as, arguably, in us.


67.1.2 Model-based planning in artificial agents

This sub-section names the general approach behind those systems and connects it to a distinction from the learning chapters.

Model-based planning means choosing actions by using a model of the world to simulate and evaluate possible futures before committing to a move.

It contrasts with model-free approaches, which learn good actions directly by trial and error without ever building an explicit model, gradually strengthening whatever worked in the past.

The trade-off between them is the same one that appears in the study of human and animal learning: model-based planning is flexible and adapts fast to change, but is slow and effortful, while model-free habit is fast and cheap, but rigid when the world shifts.

In systems terms the two controllers differ in state and cost: the model-based controller stores a transition model and pays computation at decision time to search it, while the model-free controller stores only cached action values and pays almost nothing at decision time, which is why agents and animals alike arbitrate between them based on how much the extra accuracy is worth.

A vivid success of model-based planning combined with learning is the family of game-playing systems from the group behind AlphaGo, culminating in a system called MuZero.

MuZero, described by Julian Schrittwieser and colleagues in 2020, is notable because it was not told the rules of the games it played, yet it learned its own internal model of the consequences of moves and used that model to plan by searching ahead through imagined continuations.

Searching ahead means considering sequences of possible moves and counter-moves, building a tree of futures, and picking the action that leads to the best evaluated outcomes.

The significance for a science of mind is that these systems make concrete a very old idea about thinking, that to deliberate is to search a space of imagined possibilities, an idea that runs from the problem-solving research of the mid-twentieth century straight through to today's agents.

At the same time, honest practitioners note that learning an accurate enough world model in rich, open environments remains hard, and errors in the model can mislead the planner, so model-based methods are powerful but not a solved problem.


67.2 NeuroAI

This section introduces a movement that treats brains and artificial networks as two examples of intelligent systems worth comparing directly.

NeuroAI is the study at the boundary of neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using brain science to inspire better machines and using machines as testable models of the brain.

The two-way traffic is the point: ideas flow from brains to machines and back, and a model earns its keep partly by predicting real neural data.


67.2.1 Goal-driven deep networks as models of sensory cortex

This sub-section describes one of the clearest scientific successes at the neuroscience-and-AI boundary.

The finding is that when you train a deep neural network to succeed at a natural task, such as recognising objects, its internal activity comes to resemble the activity of real brain regions that do the same job, even though you never told it to imitate the brain.

The word "goal-driven" captures why: the network was optimised only to achieve a goal, good object recognition, and brain-like representations emerged as a by-product of doing the task well.

The influential statement of this approach is a 2016 Nature Neuroscience article by Daniel Yamins and James DiCarlo, "Using goal-driven deep learning models to understand sensory cortex".

Their work focused on the ventral stream, the pathway of brain areas along the lower part of the primate visual system that turns raw light into recognition of objects and faces.

The ventral stream, in plain terms, is the brain's "what is it" pathway for vision, a hierarchy of stages that progressively transform an image into a form in which object identity is easy to read out.

In systems terms the comparison is stage to stage: both systems take an image as input and publish an object identity as output over roughly 100 to 200 milliseconds in the primate brain, and the finding is that the intermediate representations line up layer by layer even though only the goal was shared.

Yamins, DiCarlo, and colleagues found that networks trained to categorise objects developed layers whose responses closely matched the responses of neurons in the corresponding stages of the monkey ventral stream, well enough to predict neural activity to previously unseen images.

This mattered because it offered, for the first time, quantitative and predictive models of a large piece of cortex, moving beyond hand-built theories to systems that could be tested neuron by neuron.

It should be read with care, and its own proponents have said so: matching neural responses does not prove the brain computes in exactly the same way, and later work has found important places where the networks and the brain diverge, which is itself scientifically useful because the mismatches point to what is still missing.


67.2.2 The representational alignment of artificial and biological systems

This sub-section is about the general project of measuring, and where possible increasing, how similar the internal representations of two systems are.

A representation, in this setting, is the pattern of internal activity a system uses to stand for something, so two systems are "aligned" to the degree that they organise their internal patterns in the same way.

Representational alignment is the research programme of comparing these internal patterns across systems, for example between a deep network and a human brain, or between a network and human behaviour.

A 2023 collaborative paper, "Getting aligned on representational alignment", by Ilia Sucholutsky, Thomas Griffiths, and a large group of authors, drew together researchers from machine learning, neuroscience, and cognitive science who had been asking this same question with different vocabularies.

To make such comparisons, scientists use mathematical tools that ask whether things treated as similar by one system are treated as similar by the other, so alignment is about matching the geometry of similarities rather than matching activity unit for unit.

A widely used method in this family is representational similarity analysis, which compares systems by the pattern of what they find alike and unalike rather than by any direct wiring correspondence.

In systems terms an alignment measurement takes two systems' internal activity patterns over a shared set of stimuli as input and publishes a single similarity score as output, and the choice of measuring tool is itself a parameter that can change the verdict.

The practical payoff runs in two directions.

In one direction, alignment is a measuring stick for the brain-likeness of a machine, letting us rank models by how well their internal structure matches neural or behavioural data.

In the other direction, some evidence suggests that machines whose representations are more aligned with human ones learn more robustly and generalise better, hinting that human-like structure is not just pleasing but useful.

The field is careful to note that alignment is a matter of degree and of chosen measure, and that different measuring tools can disagree, so claims of alignment must always specify how it was assessed.


67.2.3 The NeuroAI programme and the embodied Turing test

This sub-section presents an ambitious manifesto for the whole NeuroAI movement and a provocative new benchmark it proposes.

The reference is a 2023 Nature Communications paper, "Catalyzing next-generation Artificial Intelligence through NeuroAI", led by Anthony Zador with a long list of prominent neuroscientists and AI researchers.

Its core argument is that the surest route to more general artificial intelligence is to study and borrow from the brains of animals, which solve problems of perceiving and acting in the world with a competence machines have not matched.

To sharpen this, the authors propose the embodied Turing test, a redefinition of the classic imitation game around animal abilities rather than human conversation.

"Embodied" means having a body and acting in a physical or realistic world, so an embodied Turing test asks whether an artificial agent can interact with the sensorimotor world as skilfully as a real animal.

In systems terms this changes the benchmark interface: instead of a text channel in and a text channel out, the test wires the candidate system to a body with sensors and actuators in a closed loop with a physical or simulated world, and scores it against an animal on the same loop.

The deep point behind this is a reordering of priorities.

The authors argue that the capacities we find most impressive, playing board games and producing fluent language, are recent and narrow, whereas the capacities shared by all animals, moving, foraging, avoiding danger, and adapting to a changing world, are the products of hundreds of millions of years of evolution and are precisely where machines remain weak.

Passing embodied Turing tests, one animal skill at a time, is offered as a concrete roadmap for the next generation of artificial intelligence.

This is a research agenda and a rallying call rather than a settled result, and not everyone in AI agrees that animal-inspired embodiment is the fastest path, so it should be understood as one influential and well-argued position in an open strategic debate.


67.3 The paths to general intelligence

This final section confronts the biggest open question the whole outline has been circling: how, if at all, do we get to genuinely general machine intelligence.

General intelligence here means the flexible, wide-ranging competence to learn and solve problems across many domains, of the kind humans display and current systems, for all their power, still lack.

The section lays out the two leading families of answers side by side, because the honest truth is that the field is genuinely divided and the question is unresolved.


67.3.1 The scaling hypothesis against the missing ingredients

This is the central strategic argument in artificial intelligence today, and it deserves to be stated fairly from both sides.

The scaling hypothesis is the claim that we largely already have the right methods, and that continuing to make models bigger, with more data and more computing power, will carry us most of the way to general intelligence.

Its intellectual backdrop is an essay called "The Bitter Lesson" by Richard Sutton, which observed that across the history of AI, general methods that ride increases in computation have repeatedly beaten cleverly hand-crafted knowledge.

The opposing view holds that scaling alone will hit a ceiling, and that some ingredients are simply missing from current systems, no matter how large they grow.

Candidates for the missing ingredients recur throughout this outline: grounding in a real world, causal understanding, systematic and compositional reasoning, and the ability to keep learning from experience after training ends.

In systems terms the two camps make different predictions about the input pipeline: the scaling camp predicts that more of the same input, text and compute, keeps improving the system, while the ingredients camp predicts diminishing returns until new channels and mechanisms, such as continual experiential learning, are added.

Strikingly, in 2025 Richard Sutton himself argued that today's large language models are not really following his bitter lesson at all, because they learn from a fixed store of human-written text rather than from their own ongoing experience, and he called for architectures that learn continually from interaction, a stance he and colleagues have framed as an "era of experience".

This is a notable development precisely because it comes from the person most associated with the scaling-and-computation view, and it shows that even the leading voices are actively revising their positions.

The fair summary for a newcomer is that no one knows, that both camps have serious arguments and serious scientists, and that the outcome will be settled by evidence over the coming years rather than by argument now.

A project like konnectome sits squarely inside this debate, and the value of the whole cognition outline is precisely that it lays out, ingredient by ingredient, what a mind seems to require, so that the missing-ingredients case can be judged on its merits.


67.3.2 Open-endedness, curiosity, and intrinsic motivation

This closing sub-section describes a third path, one less about size and more about the character of learning itself.

Open-endedness is the property of a process that keeps generating new and increasingly complex challenges and solutions indefinitely, never settling into a final answer.

The inspiration is the grandest open-ended process we know, biological evolution, and human culture, which have gone on producing novelty for a very long time without a fixed goal or a stopping point.

Curiosity and intrinsic motivation are the engine proposed to drive such open-ended learning inside an artificial agent.

Intrinsic motivation means being driven to act by internal rewards, such as novelty, surprise, or the satisfaction of learning, rather than only by external rewards handed out for a specific task.

An intrinsically curious agent seeks out situations it does not yet understand and experiments with them, generating its own goals and thereby teaching itself an ever-widening range of skills, much as a playing child does.

In systems terms an intrinsically motivated agent replaces the external reward input with an internally computed one, typically the prediction error of its own world model, so the agent is literally rewarded for finding places where its model is wrong and fixing them.

Researchers including Kenneth Stanley and Jeff Clune have argued that open-endedness may be an essential and undervalued ingredient for reaching very general, even superhuman, intelligence, and in 2024 groups proposed systems that pursue novelty guided by a model of what humans would find interesting.

There is also a caution voiced within this same community, that truly open-ended, self-directed systems raise real safety questions, since an agent that sets its own ever-changing goals is by design harder to predict and to steer.

The honest closing note for the whole frontier is that these paths, scaling, supplying the missing ingredients, and open-ended intrinsically motivated learning, are not mutually exclusive, and the eventual route to general intelligence may well braid them together.

That uncertainty is not a failure of the field but the ordinary condition of a live science at its edge, and it is exactly the terrain on which a project like konnectome must make its own careful, evidence-guided bets.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Observations from the environment, such as pixels or sensor readings, arriving each time step of the outer acting loop.

◦ Rewards from the environment, or internally computed intrinsic rewards such as prediction error.

◦ The agent's own actions, fed back as inputs to the world model so it can learn action consequences.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Actions to the environment, chosen after imagined rehearsal, consumed by the world itself.

◦ Predicted next states and rewards, consumed internally by the planner and the behaviour learner.

◦ Imagined trajectories, whole sequences of dreamed experience, consumed as training data by the policy.

• STATE.

◦ The learned world model itself, the transition and reward predictions accumulated from experience.

◦ The current latent state, the compressed summary of the situation right now.

◦ A replay buffer of past real experience, and the current policy and value estimates.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ The imagination horizon, how many steps ahead the agent rolls the model before trusting it no further.

◦ The learning rates of the model and the behaviour, and the balance of real to imagined training data.

◦ The exploration rate, how often the agent tries something other than its current best guess.

◦ The intrinsic reward weight, when curiosity is used, controlling how strongly model error attracts the agent.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Real environment steps: set by the environment, from milliseconds in simulation to seconds in robotics, so no single constant exists.

◦ Imagined steps: thousands of times faster than real steps, since they are only computations inside the model; the exact ratio is hardware bound, so a universal number is REFUSED.

◦ DreamerV3 learning to find diamonds in Minecraft: on the order of days of continuous play experience in the published 2025 Nature work.

◦ Human model-based deliberation per decision: roughly hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, consistent with the deliberation findings in the learning chapters.

• MODES.

◦ Acting mode, taking real actions and collecting experience, alternating on a schedule with dreaming mode, training the behaviour on imagined rollouts.

◦ Model-based control versus model-free habit, arbitrated by how much extra reward the costly model search is expected to buy, the same trade-off documented in animals.

◦ Exploration versus exploitation, switched by the exploration rate and, in curious agents, by where the model's prediction error is largest.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Model error compounding: small prediction errors grow over long imagined rollouts, so the planner confidently chooses actions that work only in the dream, the machine analogue of a delusion.

◦ Model exploitation: the behaviour learner finds flaws in the world model and optimises for imaginary rewards the real world never pays.

◦ Stale models: when the world changes, plans built on the old model fail until the model is retrained, mirroring habit-like rigidity.

◦ Curiosity traps: an intrinsically motivated agent can fixate on irreducibly unpredictable noise, such as a screen of static, because its prediction error never falls.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a dictionary variable called model that maps each pair of a state and an action to a recorded next state.
Create a variable called goal holding the target state of the grid.
Repeat the following exploration steps many times.
    Choose a random action from the four moves up, down, left, and right.
    Take the action in the real grid and observe the next state.
    Store the observed next state in model under the current state and action.
    Set the current state to the next state.
Reset the agent to the start state.
Repeat the following planning and acting steps until the goal is reached.
    For each of the four possible actions, perform the following imagined rollout.
        Set an imagined state to the current real state.
        Apply the action inside the model to get the imagined next state.
        From the imagined next state, repeatedly apply the model action that moves closest to the goal, for up to ten imagined steps, counting the steps taken.
        Record the number of imagined steps needed to reach the goal, or a large penalty if the goal was not reached in imagination.
    Choose the action whose imagined rollout reached the goal in the fewest steps.
    Take that single chosen action in the real grid.
Report that the agent planned in imagination and acted in the world.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Import the random module for exploratory action choice.
import random

# Create number variables for the grid size, the start state, and the goal state.
SIZE, START, GOAL = 5, (0, 0), (4, 4)
# Create a dictionary mapping each action name to its movement on the grid.
MOVES = {"up": (0, -1), "down": (0, 1), "left": (-1, 0), "right": (1, 0)}

# Define a function called step that applies an action to a state in the real grid.
def step(state, action):
    # Add the movement to the state and clamp both coordinates inside the grid.
    dx, dy = MOVES[action]
    # Return the clamped next state as the real environment's response.
    return (min(SIZE - 1, max(0, state[0] + dx)), min(SIZE - 1, max(0, state[1] + dy)))

# Create an empty dictionary called model to hold the learned world model.
model = {}
# Create a variable called state holding the start state for exploration.
state = START
# Repeat two thousand exploration steps to learn the world model from experience.
for _ in range(2000):
    # Choose a random action to explore the grid.
    action = random.choice(list(MOVES))
    # Take the action in the real grid and observe the next state.
    nxt = step(state, action)
    # Store the observed transition in the world model.
    model[(state, action)] = nxt
    # Move the agent to the observed next state.
    state = nxt

# Define a function called imagine that rolls the model forward greedily toward the goal.
def imagine(start_state, first_action, horizon=10):
    # Apply the first action inside the model, not the real world.
    s = model.get((start_state, first_action), start_state)
    # For each imagined step up to the horizon, move greedily closer to the goal.
    for t in range(horizon):
        # If the imagined state is the goal, return the number of imagined steps used.
        if s == GOAL:
            return t + 1
        # Choose the modelled action whose imagined result is closest to the goal.
        s = min((model.get((s, a), s) for a in MOVES),
                key=lambda p: abs(p[0] - GOAL[0]) + abs(p[1] - GOAL[1]))
    # Return a large penalty because the goal was not reached in imagination.
    return 999

# Reset the agent to the start state for the acting phase.
state, path = START, [START]
# Repeat planning in imagination and acting in the world until the goal is reached.
while state != GOAL:
    # Choose the real action whose imagined rollout reaches the goal soonest.
    action = min(MOVES, key=lambda a: imagine(state, a))
    # Take the single chosen action in the real grid.
    state = step(state, action)
    # Append the new state to the recorded path.
    path.append(state)

# Print the path, showing the agent planned inside its learned model before each real step.
print("Planned-in-imagination path:", path)

CHAPTER 68. NEURO-SYMBOLIC INTEGRATION AND LANGUAGE AGENTS AS ARCHITECTURES (FRONTIER)

This chapter is about a marriage of two very different ways of building a thinking machine, and about a surprising new kind of machine that has quietly become a working model of a whole mind.

The first way of building is the neural network, a system that learns patterns from mountains of examples but struggles to follow strict rules.

The second way is the symbolic system, a system that follows strict rules and logic but cannot easily learn from raw experience.

For decades these two camps argued with each other, and this chapter tells the story of how researchers began to stitch them together into single systems, a project called neuro-symbolic integration.

It then turns to language agents, which are programs built around a large language model (a computer program trained to predict and produce text, of the kind behind modern chatbots), and shows that these agents have accidentally rebuilt many of the ideas that the classical study of the mind spent fifty years working out.

Read as engineering, the two camps are two subsystems with complementary interfaces: the network consumes raw high-dimensional sensory data and publishes fuzzy pattern judgements, while the symbolic engine consumes clean discrete tokens and publishes traceable chains of inference, and the integration problem is literally the problem of designing the adapter between those two data formats.

The word frontier in the tag means we are now at the unfinished edge of the field, where the science of human thinking meets the engineering of artificial thinking, and where konnectome itself lives.


68.1 Neuro-symbolic integration

This section explains what it means to fuse a pattern-learning network with a rule-following logic engine, and why anyone would want to.

The short answer is that human minds seem to do both at once, effortlessly, and no single technique has managed to copy that on its own.


68.1.1 The combination of pattern learning with symbolic reasoning

A neural network is a web of simple artificial units, loosely inspired by brain cells, that adjusts itself by looking at many examples until it can recognise patterns, such as telling a cat from a dog in a photograph.

Its great strength is learning from messy, real-world data without being told the rules in advance.

Its great weakness is that it does not really reason in steps, it cannot easily explain why it decided something, and it can be fooled or can make confident mistakes on cases unlike its training.

A symbolic system, by contrast, works with symbols and explicit rules, in the way that ordinary arithmetic or formal logic works, chaining statements like all birds have feathers and a robin is a bird to conclude a robin has feathers.

Its strength is exactly where the network is weak: it reasons in clear steps, it handles rules and structure, and its conclusions can be traced and checked.

Its weakness is exactly where the network is strong: it is brittle, it needs its knowledge hand-built by people, and it cannot learn a concept just by being shown examples of it.

Neuro-symbolic integration is the research programme that tries to get the strengths of both in one system, so that the machine can both learn from data and reason with rules.

A recent systematic survey of the field, screening 178 papers published between 2020 and late 2025, sorts the approaches into a few broad recipes.

One recipe is neural helping symbolic, where a network reads raw input, such as an image, and turns it into clean symbols that a logic engine can then reason over.

A second recipe is symbolic helping neural, where rules or a knowledge base guide or constrain what the network learns, so it does not have to discover everything from scratch.

A third recipe is a genuinely hybrid architecture, where the two kinds of processing are woven together and pass information back and forth.

Named examples that beginners may encounter include Logic Tensor Networks, which let logical statements be trained by the same gradient methods that train networks, and Neural Theorem Provers, which learn to carry out proof-like reasoning.

In systems terms, each recipe fixes a different direction of data flow: the first pipes network outputs into the reasoner's input format, the second pipes rule constraints into the network's training signal, and the third builds a bidirectional bus between them, with the conversion between continuous activations and discrete symbols as the hard interface in every case.

The honest state of the field is that this remains a hard and unsolved problem: grounding abstract symbols in real sensory data, and getting robust reasoning that generalises to new situations, are still open challenges rather than finished achievements.


68.1.2 The two systems realised as a fast network and a deliberate symbolic layer

There is a tempting and widely drawn parallel between neuro-symbolic design and a famous idea from the psychology of human thinking, the idea of two systems of thought.

In that psychological picture, associated above all with Daniel Kahneman, System One is fast, automatic, intuitive, and effortless, the sort of thinking that lets you read a word or sense a mood instantly, while System Two is slow, deliberate, effortful, and rule-following, the sort of thinking you use to work out a long multiplication.

Many neuro-symbolic researchers map the neural network onto System One and the symbolic reasoner onto System Two.

The neural part gives the machine fast, intuitive pattern recognition, and the symbolic part gives it slow, careful, step-by-step reasoning that it can fall back on when intuition is not enough.

This is an appealing story and a useful design heuristic, because it suggests building a fast learned component and a deliberate reasoning component and letting them cooperate.

As a debate rather than a mechanism, the two sides make different systems predictions: a literal two-systems design predicts two separable modules with distinct latencies and a switch between them, while the critics predict one graded machinery whose speed and effort vary continuously, with no clean mode boundary to be found.

It is worth stating plainly that the two-systems picture in psychology is itself contested, and many researchers now think the neat split into two systems is an oversimplification rather than a proven fact of the brain.

So the fast-network-plus-deliberate-symbol-layer design should be read as an engineering inspiration drawn from a popular theory, not as a literal blueprint copied from a settled account of the human mind.

Even so, the intuition that a mind needs both a quick pattern-matcher and a slower rule-checker keeps reappearing, and that recurrence is itself a clue that the field is circling something real.


68.2 Language agents as de facto architectures

This section makes a claim that would have surprised researchers twenty years ago: that a practical tool built by engineers, the language agent, has turned out to be a working proposal for the architecture of a whole mind.

The phrase de facto means in fact, whether or not anyone planned it that way, and the point is that language agents became cognitive architectures by accident, through solving practical problems, rather than by design.


68.2.1 The cognitive-architecture reading of language agents

A cognitive architecture, defined earlier in this outline, is a proposal for the fixed machinery a whole mind needs, the permanent structures inside which particular knowledge and skills are the changing content.

A language agent is a system that wraps a large language model inside extra machinery so that it can do more than answer a single question: it can remember, plan over many steps, use tools, and act in an environment.

In 2023, a group of researchers at Princeton, Theodore Sumers, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, and Thomas Griffiths, published a framework called Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents, abbreviated CoALA.
