Their central move was to stop treating the language model as a lone genius that thinks by itself, and to treat it instead as one component sitting inside a larger cognitive system with memory, actions, and a decision loop.

Read this way, a language agent is not just a clever text predictor bolted to some code, it is a candidate answer to the old question of how the parts of a mind fit together.

As a system, the agent subscribes to observations from its environment and to its own stored memories, publishes external actions and new memory entries, and holds as state a working context plus its long-term stores, with the language model serving as the general-purpose processor that every step calls.

That is why this chapter calls language agents de facto architectures: without setting out to solve the grand problem of the unified mind, engineers built systems whose shape strongly resembles the classical proposals for that very problem.

The importance of the CoALA paper is that it gives a common vocabulary for describing these agents in the same terms the science of mind has long used, so that the two conversations, the engineering one and the psychological one, can finally hear each other.


68.2.2 Modular memory, internal and external actions, and the decision cycle

The CoALA framework organises a language agent along three simple dimensions, and each one echoes a long tradition in the study of the human mind.

The first dimension is memory, which CoALA divides into a short-term working memory that holds what the agent is currently thinking about, and several long-term memories, namely episodic memory for records of past experiences, semantic memory for general facts about the world, and procedural memory for learned skills and the agent's own code.

A beginner should notice that these are almost exactly the memory distinctions that psychologists drew from studying human patients decades ago, which is a striking case of the engineering rediscovering the science.

The second dimension is the action space, which CoALA splits into internal actions and external actions.

Internal actions happen inside the agent's own head, so to speak, and include reasoning (thinking a step through), retrieval (pulling a relevant memory into working memory), and learning (writing something new into long-term memory).

External actions reach out into the world, and are called grounding, meaning the agent does something with a tool, a website, a robot body, or another program, and takes in the result.

The third dimension is the decision cycle, a repeating loop in which the agent uses the language model to plan what to do next, chooses an action, executes it, observes what happened, and then goes round again.

This loop, plan then act then observe then repeat, is the same basic rhythm that the oldest cognitive architectures used, where it was often called a recognise-act cycle, so once again the new system has reinvented an old shape.

In systems language, working memory is the small mutable buffer written and read on every cycle, the three long-term stores are append-mostly databases reached only through retrieval and learning actions, and the decision cycle is the clock that serialises everything, so the whole agent is a single loop over a shared workspace.

The overall picture is a mind-like machine: a small workspace of current thoughts, several kinds of long-term store, a set of moves it can make inside itself and out in the world, and a steady beat of decision that ties them together.


68.2.3 The re-invention of architecture ideas in memory-augmented and tool-using agents

Beyond the tidy CoALA summary, the everyday practice of building language agents keeps stumbling onto ideas that the classical architecture tradition worked out long ago.

Consider memory-augmented agents, which are language agents given an external store, often a searchable database of past text, so they are not limited to what fits in the model's short attention span at any moment.

This is, in plain terms, a rediscovery of the distinction between a small fast working memory and a large slow long-term memory, and of the need for a retrieval step that fetches the right item at the right time, all of which are cornerstones of the human memory literature.

Consider tool-using agents, which can call a calculator, run code, search the web, or query a database instead of trying to do everything inside the network.

This mirrors the old insight that a mind offloads work onto the world and onto external aids, and that reliable reasoning often means handing a subtask to a dedicated, rule-following module rather than trusting intuition.

Consider agents that keep a scratchpad of intermediate reasoning, or that critique and revise their own drafts.

These echo the classical idea of a controlled, deliberate layer that monitors and corrects a faster, automatic one, and the idea that thought proceeds by setting subgoals and checking progress against them.

The lesson for a beginner is not that the engineers copied the psychologists, because mostly they did not, but that when you build something that has to act sensibly over time in a complicated world, you are pushed toward the same handful of solutions.

That convergence is quietly encouraging for the whole enterprise, because it suggests these architectural ideas are not arbitrary academic inventions but something closer to necessary features of any competent mind, natural or artificial.


68.3 The convergence of the classical and the modern

This section looks at the meeting point from the other direction, asking what happens when the old, carefully hand-built cognitive architectures are joined to the new language models, and what each side still lacks.


68.3.1 Classical architectures augmented with language models

The classical cognitive architectures are systems such as Soar and ACT-R, decades-long research projects that model the human mind as a set of production rules, meaning if-then rules of the form if the situation looks like this, then do that, running over structured memories.

Their strength is disciplined, transparent, human-like reasoning and learning, tested against real experimental data on how people solve problems and make errors.

Their long-standing weakness is that a person has to hand-build most of their knowledge, rule by rule, which is slow and brittle and cannot easily cover the open-ended messiness of ordinary language and common sense.

Large language models have exactly the opposite profile, carrying vast amounts of loose world knowledge and fluent language but lacking reliable step-by-step discipline and stable memory.

So a natural experiment, actively pursued around 2024, is to bolt the two together.

In some work, the language model acts as a friendly front end that helps a person write and debug ACT-R or Soar models in plain English, turning natural-language descriptions into the formal rules the architecture needs.

In other work, the language model supplies the broad world knowledge and quick guesses, while the classical architecture supplies the structured memory, the goal management, and the verifiable reasoning, so that each covers the other's gap.

The systems reading of these hybrids is a division of latency and reliability: the classical architecture runs a fast, checkable inner loop of production cycles, on the order of 50 milliseconds per cycle in ACT-R's human-calibrated timing, while the language model is called as a slower, fallible oracle whose answers must be validated before they enter the structured store.

The general direction, stated by several researchers, is that the most capable agents are likely to combine all three traditions at once, symbolic reasoning, machine learning, and large language models, rather than betting everything on any single one.

This is still early and experimental work, and no one should claim it is a finished recipe, but it is the clearest practical form the neuro-symbolic dream has yet taken.


68.3.2 What each tradition still owes the other

It helps to end the chapter by being honest about the debts, because each tradition can do something the other cannot, and neither is complete.

The classical symbolic architectures owe the modern networks a solution to learning and grounding.

They have never been good at learning their knowledge from raw perception, at soaking up the sprawling common sense that language models absorb from text, or at coping gracefully with noisy, unexpected input, and the network tradition is exactly where those abilities live.

The modern language models and networks owe the classical architectures a solution to structure, reliability, and control.

They are prone to inventing false information, they have no stable long-term memory of their own, their reasoning can wander or contradict itself, and they cannot by themselves guarantee that a chain of steps is valid, all of which the symbolic tradition was built to handle.

Neither side, on its own, yet gives us a system that both learns richly from the world and reasons dependably about it, which is precisely what a human mind manages to do.

That mutual debt is the real content of the frontier: the interesting question is no longer which tradition wins, but how to build the single system that pays both debts at once.

For konnectome, the practical reading is that these traditions should be treated as complementary constraints on one design rather than as rival creeds, a theme the final chapter returns to.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Environment observations, arriving as text or structured tool output from the world the agent acts in.

◦ A task or goal statement, as text, from the user or a supervising process.

◦ Retrieved memory items, as text records, pulled from the episodic, semantic, and procedural stores on request.

◦ Language-model completions, as text, returned whenever any step queries the model.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ External grounding actions, as tool calls or messages, consumed by the environment.

◦ New memory entries, as text records, consumed by the long-term stores through learning actions.

◦ Intermediate reasoning, as scratchpad text, consumed by the agent's own next cycle.

◦ A final answer or completed task result, as text, consumed by the user.

• STATE.

◦ Working memory: the current context of goal, recent observations, retrieved items, and reasoning so far.

◦ Episodic memory: a growing log of past experiences.

◦ Semantic memory: stored general facts.

◦ Procedural memory: stored skills, prompts, and the agent's own code.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Context capacity: how much text the working memory and model context can hold per cycle.

◦ Retrieval count: how many memory items are fetched per retrieval action.

◦ Reasoning depth: how many internal actions are allowed before an external action is forced.

◦ Learning threshold: how notable an outcome must be before it is written to long-term memory.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Classical production-rule cycle: about 50 milliseconds per rule firing in human-calibrated architectures such as ACT-R.

◦ Language-agent decision cycle: REFUSED, because wall-clock latency depends on the model and hardware deployed, not on any property of the architecture.

◦ Long-term store persistence: effectively unbounded, since entries persist until deleted.

• MODES.

◦ Internal mode: the cycle chooses reasoning, retrieval, or learning actions that change only the agent's own state; entered when the current context is judged insufficient to act.

◦ External mode: the cycle chooses a grounding action that changes the world; entered when the plan names a concrete step whose preconditions are met.

◦ The planner's evaluation of the working-memory context is the switch between the two modes on every cycle.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Hallucination, where the language model asserts false information that then contaminates memory and later reasoning.

◦ Context overflow, where working memory exceeds capacity and early goals or observations are silently dropped.

◦ Retrieval failure, where the relevant memory exists but is not fetched, so the agent repeats old mistakes.

◦ Looping, where the decision cycle keeps choosing internal actions and never grounds, the engineering cousin of rumination.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a text variable called goal holding the task given by the user.
Create an empty list variable called working memory.
Create an empty list variable called episodic memory.
Create a list variable called semantic memory holding known facts.
Add the goal to working memory.
Repeat until the goal is marked done or the cycle limit is reached.
    Ask the planner to read working memory and propose the next action and its argument.
    If the proposed action is retrieve, then.
        For each record in semantic memory and episodic memory, check whether it mentions the argument.
        Add each matching record to working memory.
    If the proposed action is reason, then.
        Create a new thought from the argument and add it to working memory.
    If the proposed action is learn, then.
        Add the argument as a new record to episodic memory.
    If the proposed action is act, then.
        Send the argument to the environment and receive an observation.
        Add the observation to working memory.
    If the proposed action is finish, then.
        Mark the goal as done and report the argument as the answer.
    If working memory holds more items than its capacity, remove the oldest item after the goal.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a text variable called GOAL holding the task given by the user.
GOAL = "find the boiling point of water at sea level"
# Create a list variable called semantic_memory holding known facts.
semantic_memory = ["water boils at 100 C at sea level", "ice melts at 0 C"]
# Create an empty list variable called episodic_memory.
episodic_memory = []
# Create a list variable called working_memory starting with the goal.
working_memory = ["GOAL: " + GOAL]
# Create a number variable called CAPACITY with value six.
CAPACITY = 6

# Define a planner that reads working memory and proposes the next action.
def planner(wm):
    # If any line in working memory is a retrieved fact about boiling, finish with it.
    for line in wm:
        # If the line is a fact mentioning the word boils, return finish with that line.
        if line.startswith("FACT:") and "boils" in line:
            return ("finish", line)
    # If no fact has been retrieved yet, return retrieve with the keyword boils.
    if not any(line.startswith("FACT:") for line in wm):
        return ("retrieve", "boils")
    # Otherwise return reason with a note that more thought is needed.
    return ("reason", "no fact found, think again")

# Repeat the decision cycle at most ten times.
for cycle in range(10):
    # Ask the planner for the next action and its argument.
    action, arg = planner(working_memory)
    # Print the cycle number, the chosen action, and the argument.
    print("cycle", cycle, "action", action, "arg", arg)
    # If the action is retrieve, search both long-term stores for the keyword.
    if action == "retrieve":
        # For each record in the two stores, add matches to working memory as facts.
        for record in semantic_memory + episodic_memory:
            # If the record mentions the keyword, add it to working memory.
            if arg in record:
                working_memory.append("FACT: " + record)
    # If the action is reason, add the new thought to working memory.
    elif action == "reason":
        working_memory.append("THOUGHT: " + arg)
    # If the action is finish, write the episode to episodic memory and stop.
    elif action == "finish":
        # Add a record of this solved task to episodic memory.
        episodic_memory.append("solved: " + GOAL + " -> " + arg)
        # Print the final answer and leave the loop.
        print("answer:", arg)
        break
    # If working memory exceeds capacity, drop the oldest item after the goal.
    if len(working_memory) > CAPACITY:
        working_memory.pop(1)


CHAPTER 69. COMPUTATIONAL PSYCHIATRY AND THE BREAKDOWN OF COGNITION (CONTEXT)

This chapter is about what we can learn from minds that are suffering, and about a young field that tries to describe mental illness in the precise language of mathematics and computation.

That field is called computational psychiatry.

Its guiding idea is simple and humane: if we have good computational models of how a healthy mind acquires, weighs, and acts on information, then a mental disorder can often be understood as one of those models running with a particular setting pushed too high or too low.

In systems language, a disorder is read not as a different machine but as the same machine with a parameter out of its healthy range, which is why every model in this chapter has knobs, and every clinical story names the knob.

Two payoffs follow.

First, we may get better, more mechanistic descriptions of conditions such as depression, psychosis, and addiction, described not just by lists of symptoms but by the specific information-processing step that has gone awry.

Second, and this is the reason the chapter belongs in a book about the intact mind, watching cognition break down in specific ways is one of the most powerful ways to discover how it was built in the first place.

The tag context signals that this chapter situates the science rather than adding a new mechanism, and it should be read with care and respect, because it concerns real human suffering, not abstractions.


69.1 The programme

This section introduces computational psychiatry as a research programme: what it is trying to do, and the two broad styles in which it does it.


69.1.1 Theory-driven against data-driven computational psychiatry

Computational psychiatry, as set out in influential reviews by researchers including Peter Dayan, Read Montague, Quentin Huys, and Klaas Stephan, comes in two broad flavours that answer two different questions.

The theory-driven flavour starts from a mechanistic model of how some cognitive process is supposed to work, such as how a healthy person learns from rewards, and then asks which knob in that model must be turned to reproduce a patient's behaviour.

Its aim is to explain, to say in mechanical terms what has changed inside the process, and its great advantage is that it points at a cause you could in principle target with a treatment.

The data-driven flavour starts from the opposite end, feeding large amounts of measurement, such as brain scans, questionnaires, or task performance, into machine-learning methods that look for patterns, groupings, or predictions.

Its aim is not primarily to explain the mechanism but to classify, to forecast who will respond to which treatment, or to sort patients into meaningful subgroups, and it is deliberately agnostic about the underlying cause.

In systems terms the two flavours differ in their interfaces: the theory-driven pipeline takes behaviour as input and publishes fitted model parameters, while the data-driven pipeline takes any measurements as input and publishes labels and forecasts, and only the first claims to expose the machinery inside.

The two flavours are complementary rather than opposed: the data-driven approach can reveal structure that no one predicted, while the theory-driven approach can explain why that structure exists.

A recurring hope in the field, stated by its founders, is to eventually join them, using large-scale data to test and refine mechanistic theories, though this remains more an aspiration than an accomplishment.

A beginner should hold on to a note of caution that the field itself voices: computational psychiatry is young, many of its findings are still small or not yet firmly replicated, and it has so far changed very few actual clinical decisions.


69.1.2 Computational phenotyping and the dimensional framing

A phenotype, in ordinary biology, is a set of observable characteristics of an organism, such as height or eye colour.

A computational phenotype is the same idea moved into the mind: it is a description of a person in terms of the settings, or parameters, of a computational model of their cognition, such as how quickly they learn from bad outcomes or how much they weigh a risk.

The promise of computational phenotyping is a more precise and individual portrait of a patient than a diagnostic label alone can give, because two people with the same diagnosis may have very different underlying parameter settings, and hence may need different help.

This connects to a broader shift called the dimensional framing of mental illness.

Traditional psychiatry has mostly used categories, placing a person either inside or outside a diagnosis such as major depression.

The dimensional view, promoted for example by the Research Domain Criteria initiative of the United States National Institute of Mental Health, instead treats mental difficulty as lying along continuous dimensions of function, such as the capacity for reward learning or for cognitive control, on which everyone falls somewhere and on which disorders are extremes rather than separate kinds.

Computational phenotyping fits this dimensional view naturally, because a model parameter is a number on a continuum, not a yes-or-no label.

The systems reading is direct: a phenotyping pipeline subscribes to a person's trial-by-trial task behaviour, fits a generative model to it over a session of minutes to an hour, and publishes a small vector of parameter estimates that other processes, clinical or scientific, can consume.

The appeal is a psychiatry organised around measurable mechanisms shared across diagnoses, so that, for instance, an over-reliance on habit could be recognised and measured whether it shows up in addiction, in obsessive-compulsive disorder, or in an eating disorder.

The honest caveat, again, is that this is a research vision in progress, and the field is still working out which parameters are stable, meaningful, and clinically useful.


69.2 The modelling frameworks applied to disorder

This section shows the programme in action, taking three of the modelling frameworks that earlier parts of this outline described for the healthy mind and watching what happens when a parameter is pushed out of its normal range.


69.2.1 Reinforcement-learning models of anhedonia and addiction

Reinforcement learning is the framework, described earlier in this outline, in which an agent learns the value of actions by trial and error, guided by the gap between what it expected and what it got, a gap called the reward prediction error.

A useful distinction within it is between model-free control, which is fast, habitual, and cares only about what has been rewarding before, and model-based control, which is slower, goal-directed, and reasons about consequences using an internal map of the world.

Anhedonia is the reduced ability to feel pleasure or to be motivated by reward, and it is a core symptom of depression.

Computational work on anhedonia asks which part of the reward machinery has changed, and a meta-analysis of these models found that depression and anhedonia tend to alter reward sensitivity, meaning how much a reward is valued in the first place, more than they alter the learning rate, meaning how fast a person updates from new outcomes.

Stated as a mechanism, the learner takes in chosen actions and delivered rewards, holds a table of action values as state, and updates each value by the learning rate times the prediction error, where the reward is first scaled by the sensitivity parameter, so lowering that one gain shrinks every prediction error and flattens the whole learned landscape of value.

There is also accumulating evidence that depression is marked by an imbalance in which patients lean less on effortful model-based, goal-directed control and more on model-free habit, though this is a tendency across studies rather than a universal law.

Addiction has been modelled in a related but distinct way.

An influential model proposed that addictive drugs hijack the same dopamine-based prediction-error signal that normally drives healthy learning, artificially inflating it so that drug-related actions keep being valued more and more, in a way that ordinary rewards cannot correct.

More broadly, an over-reliance on model-free, habitual control has been suggested as a common thread running through addiction and several other disorders of self-control, which is exactly the kind of shared, dimensional mechanism the previous section described.

These models are valuable precisely because they are specific: they do not just say a patient is less motivated, they point at a candidate step, such as reward sensitivity or the balance of habit against planning, that could be measured and perhaps treated.


69.2.2 Predictive-coding models of psychosis and of autistic perception

Predictive coding, described earlier in this outline, is the theory that the brain is constantly predicting its own incoming sensations and passing forward only the prediction error, the part it got wrong.

A crucial quantity in this theory is precision, which means the confidence, or reliability weight, the brain assigns to a signal, deciding how much to trust incoming sensory evidence against its own prior expectations.

In systems terms, precision is a gain parameter on the error channel: the perceptual update takes in a prior expectation and a sensory sample, and moves belief toward the sample in proportion to the relative precision of sense against prior, so one ratio decides who wins every disagreement between expectation and evidence.

Psychosis, the family of experiences that includes hallucinations, perceiving things that are not there, and delusions, holding fixed false beliefs, has been modelled as a disturbance of this precision balance.

In one influential formulation, people with schizophrenia hold priors and higher-level beliefs too rigidly, or fail to properly dampen down sensory signals, so that prediction errors are treated as more meaningful than they should be, and the mind builds unusual explanations, that is delusions, to account for them.

Autism, a developmental condition involving differences in social interaction and often an unusual sensitivity to sensory detail, has been given a related but distinct account called the aberrant precision account, associated with work by Rebecca Lawson, Karl Friston, and colleagues, and by Sander Van de Cruys and colleagues.

On this view, the autistic brain assigns unusually high precision to incoming sensory signals, so that small, ordinarily ignorable details are treated as highly informative, which could help explain both an acute eye for detail and the discomfort of a world that keeps generating surprising errors.

A beginner should notice the shared shape: in both psychosis and autism the story is about the same knob, the relative trust placed in sensory evidence against prior expectation, being set differently, which is a beautiful illustration of how one healthy mechanism can, mis-set in different directions, produce very different conditions.

It should be said plainly that these are theories under active debate, supported by suggestive evidence rather than proven beyond dispute, and that real conditions are far more complex than any single knob.


69.2.3 Evidence-accumulation models of decision abnormality

Evidence-accumulation models, described earlier in this outline under names such as the drift-diffusion model, picture a simple decision as the gradual piling up of noisy evidence toward one of two thresholds, with a choice made when the pile crosses a threshold.

Such a model has a few interpretable parts: the drift rate, meaning how fast and cleanly evidence accumulates, which reflects the quality of processing, and the threshold or boundary, meaning how much evidence is demanded before committing, which reflects caution against haste.

As a system, the accumulator subscribes to a noisy momentary evidence stream, holds a single running total as state, and publishes a choice and a response time when the total crosses either boundary, with simple perceptual decisions of this kind typically resolving within a few hundred milliseconds to about a second or two.

The power of these models in psychiatry is that they can separate a slow or error-prone decision into its causes: is the person gathering evidence poorly, a low drift rate, or are they being unusually cautious or unusually hasty, a shifted threshold, or are they simply slow to start and finish for reasons outside the decision itself.

Applied to disorder, this lets researchers ask precise questions, such as whether people in certain states gather less evidence before deciding, sometimes described as jumping to conclusions, a pattern that has been studied in relation to delusional thinking.

The same tools can be pointed at conditions where decisions are slowed, testing whether the slowing comes from more cautious thresholds or from degraded evidence, which matters because the two imply different underlying problems and different remedies.

The general contribution of evidence-accumulation models is that they turn a vague clinical observation, that someone decides oddly, into a set of separable, measurable quantities, each of which is a candidate for the actual site of the difficulty.

As with the other frameworks, these are research tools whose clinical use is still being established, not settled diagnostic instruments.


69.3 What breakdown teaches about the intact mind

This section steps back to draw the lesson that justifies placing a chapter on illness inside a book about the healthy mind: broken cognition is a window onto working cognition.


69.3.1 Failure as a probe of mechanism

There is a long tradition in the science of mind of learning how a system works by studying what happens when a part of it fails, because a failure isolates a component in a way that smooth normal function never reveals.

The classic version of this is neuropsychology, where studying patients who lost one specific ability after brain damage, while keeping others intact, helped prove that memory, language, and perception rely on separable machinery.

Computational psychiatry extends the same logic from damaged brains to mis-tuned processes, and its distinctive move is that it can name the broken part in the vocabulary of a model.

When a reinforcement-learning model shows that reward sensitivity is what changes in anhedonia, it is not only describing a symptom, it is also confirming that reward sensitivity is a real, separable component of the healthy learning system, one that can vary on its own.

When a precision-weighting model captures both psychosis and autism by moving a single trust parameter in opposite directions, it lends weight to the idea that precision weighting is a genuine, adjustable dial in the normal brain, and not just a theorist's convenience.

In this way each disorder, understood mechanistically, doubles as a natural experiment on the intact mind, telling us which parts can come apart from which, and therefore which parts were truly separate to begin with.

This is the deep reason the chapter sits where it does: the catalogue of the healthy mind, built up across this whole outline, gains extra confidence every time a specific breakdown lands exactly on one of its proposed parts.


69.3.2 The translation to biomarker and treatment

The final hope of computational psychiatry is practical: to turn these models into things that help patients, which the field summarises as the path from computation to clinic.

One target is the biomarker, meaning a measurable signal that reliably tracks a condition, its severity, or its likely course.

A computational parameter, such as a person's fitted reward sensitivity or evidence threshold, is a candidate mechanistic biomarker, one that would report not merely that something is wrong but which mechanism is wrong, which is far more useful for choosing treatment.

A second target is treatment selection and personalisation, the idea that knowing a patient's computational phenotype could help predict which therapy or medication will suit them, sparing the current slow process of trial and error.

A third, more distant target is the design of new treatments aimed squarely at a specific inferential or learning abnormality identified by a model, rather than at symptoms in general.

Beginners deserve a clear-eyed summary of where this stands: the promise is real and the logic is sound, but as the field's own leaders stress, very few computational measures have yet crossed into routine clinical use, and much careful validation remains to be done.

The right attitude is therefore hopeful patience: computational psychiatry has already sharpened how we describe mental illness and has repeatedly confirmed the parts of the healthy mind, and its clinical harvest, if it comes, will come gradually and only after rigorous testing.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Trial-by-trial behaviour, as sequences of choices, response times, and outcomes, from experimental tasks.

◦ Delivered rewards and sensory stimuli, as the environment's feedback stream to the modelled learner.

◦ Optional physiological and imaging measurements, as numeric arrays, for the data-driven flavour.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Fitted parameter estimates, as a small numeric vector per person, consumed by researchers and, one day, clinicians.

◦ Simulated behaviour from the fitted model, as choice and timing sequences, consumed by model-checking procedures.

◦ Candidate biomarkers and predicted treatment responses, as scores, consumed by clinical decision processes.

• STATE.

◦ The modelled learner's internal state: learned action values, current beliefs and their precisions, or a running evidence total, depending on the framework.

◦ The fitting procedure's state: the current best parameter estimates and their uncertainty.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Reward sensitivity: the gain applied to a received reward before learning, lowered in models of anhedonia.

◦ Learning rate: the fraction of each prediction error applied to the stored value.

◦ Precision ratio: the trust placed in sensory evidence relative to prior expectation, mis-set in models of psychosis and of autistic perception.

◦ Drift rate and decision threshold: the quality of evidence and the caution demanded, in evidence-accumulation models.

◦ The balance weight between model-based and model-free control.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Phasic dopamine prediction-error signals: onset within roughly 100 milliseconds of an unexpected outcome, as recorded in animal studies.

◦ Simple two-choice decisions modelled by drift diffusion: typically a few hundred milliseconds to about one or two seconds.

◦ Value learning across a task: tens to hundreds of trials, spanning minutes to an hour of testing.

◦ Clinical course of the disorders themselves: REFUSED, because onset and remission vary from weeks to decades across people and conditions, and no single honest constant exists.

• MODES.

◦ Theory-driven mode: fit a mechanistic model and publish parameters; chosen when the question is what has changed inside the process.

◦ Data-driven mode: mine measurements for patterns and publish predictions; chosen when the question is who belongs together or who will respond to what.

◦ Within the modelled learner, model-based against model-free control, switched by the estimated reliability and the cost of planning.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ In the modelled processes: lowered reward sensitivity as anhedonia, inflated prediction error as addiction, mis-weighted precision as psychosis or autistic perceptual difference, and shifted thresholds as jumping to conclusions.

◦ In the programme itself: unidentifiable models where different parameter settings fit equally well, small unreplicated samples, and parameters that fail to stay stable across sessions.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a number variable called learning rate with value zero point three.
Create a list variable called true rewards holding the average payoff of each of two actions.
Define a procedure called run agent that takes a number called reward sensitivity.
    Create a list variable called values holding one zero for each action.
    Repeat for two hundred trials.
        Calculate the probability of the first action from the difference of the two values using a soft choice rule.
        Choose the first action with that probability, otherwise choose the second.
        Draw the reward for the chosen action from its true payoff plus noise.
        Calculate the felt reward as the product of the reward and the reward sensitivity.
        Calculate the prediction error as the felt reward minus the value of the chosen action.
        Add the product of the learning rate and the prediction error to the value of the chosen action.
        Count the trial if the chosen action was the better one.
    Report the final values and the fraction of trials on which the better action was chosen.
Run the agent with reward sensitivity one to model a healthy learner.
Run the agent with reward sensitivity zero point two to model an anhedonic learner.
Compare the two reports: the anhedonic learner shows a flattened value landscape and weaker pursuit of the better option.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Load the math module for the soft choice rule and the random module for noise.
import math
import random
# Create a number variable called LEARNING_RATE with value zero point three.
LEARNING_RATE = 0.3
# Create a list variable called TRUE_REWARDS holding the average payoff of each action.
TRUE_REWARDS = [1.0, 0.2]

# Define a procedure called run_agent that takes a number called reward_sensitivity.
def run_agent(reward_sensitivity, trials=200):
    # Create a list variable called values holding one zero for each action.
    values = [0.0, 0.0]
    # Create a number variable called good_choices with initial value zero.
    good_choices = 0
    # Repeat for the requested number of trials.
    for t in range(trials):
        # Calculate the probability of the first action from the value difference.
        p_first = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-3.0 * (values[0] - values[1])))
        # Choose the first action with that probability, otherwise the second.
        action = 0 if random.random() < p_first else 1
        # Draw the reward as the true payoff plus a little noise.
        reward = TRUE_REWARDS[action] + random.gauss(0, 0.1)
        # Calculate the felt reward as the product of reward and reward sensitivity.
        felt = reward * reward_sensitivity
        # Calculate the prediction error as the felt reward minus the stored value.
        error = felt - values[action]
        # Add the product of the learning rate and the error to the stored value.
        values[action] = values[action] + LEARNING_RATE * error
        # Count the trial if the better action was chosen.
        if action == 0:
            good_choices = good_choices + 1
    # Report the final values and the fraction of better choices.
    return values, good_choices / trials

# Seed the random generator so the demonstration is repeatable.
random.seed(1)
# Run the agent with sensitivity one to model a healthy learner.
healthy_values, healthy_rate = run_agent(1.0)
# Run the agent with sensitivity zero point two to model an anhedonic learner.
anhedonic_values, anhedonic_rate = run_agent(0.2)
# Print the healthy learner's values and choice rate.
print("healthy   values", [round(v, 2) for v in healthy_values], "good choice rate", round(healthy_rate, 2))
# Print the anhedonic learner's values and choice rate.
print("anhedonic values", [round(v, 2) for v in anhedonic_values], "good choice rate", round(anhedonic_rate, 2))


CHAPTER 70. THE INTEGRATION PROBLEM: TOWARD A WHOLE-MIND ACCOUNT FOR KONNECTOME (CONTEXT)

This is the closing chapter, and its job is different from all the others.

Every chapter before this one took a single faculty or framework and laid it out on its own, as if it could be studied in isolation: perception here, memory there, attention, language, reasoning, emotion, each in its own room.

But a real mind is not a set of separate rooms.

It is one thing, doing everything at once, so that a single ordinary moment, catching a friend's eye across a noisy room and knowing at a glance that something is wrong, weaves together perception, attention, memory, emotion, social understanding, and the readiness to act, all in the same breath.

The problem of explaining how the separate pieces become one working mind is called the integration problem, and it is the deepest unsolved problem in the whole science.

In the systems vocabulary this book has built, every chapter so far specified a module: its inputs, its outputs, its state, its parameters, its characteristic times, and its ways of failing.

The integration problem is the question of the missing top-level program, the one that wires those interfaces together, schedules the modules against one another, and makes a single coherent agent out of the catalogue.

This chapter does three things: it shows how the faculties are known to hand off to one another, it lays out the great integrative problems that no one has yet solved, and it reads the whole field back for konnectome, saying plainly what is safe to build on and what must be left to the judgement of whoever does the building.

It is written as a synthesis, a drawing-together, and it aims to leave a beginner not with a tidy finished picture but with an honest map of what is settled, what is contested, and what is still open.


70.1 The composition of the faculties

This section is about composition, meaning how the separate capacities combine and pass work to one another, and about two ideas that have been proposed as the glue that might hold the whole thing together.


70.1.1 How attention gates encoding, how working memory buffers thought, how control coordinates goals

The first thing to see is that the faculties in this outline are not independent, they are wired into one another in a rough division of labour, and a few examples make the pattern vivid.

Attention gates encoding, meaning that what you pay attention to is largely what gets written into memory, and what you ignore mostly does not, so attention acts as a doorway deciding which experiences even get the chance to be remembered.

In interface terms, attention subscribes to the full perceptual stream and publishes a selected subset, and memory encoding subscribes to that subset, so the memory store never sees what the gate discarded.

This is why the failures of attention described earlier, such as not noticing an obvious event because you were focused elsewhere, lead directly to failures of memory: you cannot later recall what never got through the door.

Working memory buffers thought, meaning that the small, temporary workspace of the mind holds the handful of items you are currently juggling, and provides the stage on which reasoning, language understanding, and planning actually happen.

Its systems role is a shared buffer of about four chunks that every deliberate process reads from and writes to, which is why its capacity limit propagates outward as a limit on everything built above it.

Without that buffer there would be nowhere for the intermediate steps of a thought to sit while the next step is computed, which is why limits on working memory ripple out into limits on reasoning and comprehension.

Cognitive control coordinates goals, meaning that a supervisory set of processes keeps the mind pointed at what it is trying to achieve, holds off distractions and habits, switches between tasks, and settles conflicts when two responses compete.

Control is what lets a goal formed now, such as an intention to keep quiet about a surprise, actually govern behaviour minutes later against the pull of habit.

Read as a system, control subscribes to the current goal and to conflict signals from the rest of the machinery, and publishes bias signals that raise or lower the gain on competing processes, operating over seconds to minutes as goals are held and pursued.

Put together, a simple portrait emerges: attention selects, working memory holds, control steers, memory stores and supplies, and perception feeds the whole with a model of the world, each faculty handing its product to the next.

The integration problem is that describing these hand-offs in words, as just done, is not the same as explaining how the machinery actually accomplishes them, and it is that mechanical how that remains open.


70.1.2 Prediction and recurrence as candidate unifiers

Faced with a mind full of separate faculties, theorists have long hoped for a single principle underneath them all, a common currency in which every faculty trades, and two candidates recur across this outline.

The first candidate is prediction.

A large family of theories, running through Bayesian perception, predictive coding, reinforcement learning, and active inference, proposes that the mind is fundamentally a prediction machine, always generating expectations and learning from the errors in them.

The attraction of prediction as a unifier is that it seems to appear everywhere: perception can be cast as predicting sensory input, action as fulfilling predictions about the body, learning as reducing prediction error, and even emotion as prediction about the internal state of the body.

If all the faculties are really running the same predictive loop over different content, then their integration would be less mysterious, because they would already be speaking one language.

In systems terms, prediction proposes a universal message format: every module publishes expectations and subscribes to errors, so integration reduces to routing one type of signal.

The second candidate is recurrence, meaning the pervasive looping of information, where the output of a process is fed back as input, around and around, rather than passing through once in a straight line.

The brain is massively recurrent, full of connections that run backward and sideways as well as forward, and many theorists suspect that this looping is how separate regions come to constrain one another and settle into a single coherent interpretation.

Recurrence offers a mechanism by which distant, specialised parts can talk until they agree, which is exactly what integration requires.

Where prediction proposes a shared format, recurrence proposes a shared dynamics: modules iterate against one another until they relax into a mutually consistent state, so integration is the settling itself.

These two ideas, prediction and recurrence, are the most promising candidate unifiers the field has, and they may well be two sides of one coin, since a predictive brain needs loops to compare predictions with reality.

Honesty requires the caveat that neither is a proven grand unifier, that each has vocal critics, and that showing a principle can be stretched to cover every faculty is not the same as showing it is the true engine of any of them.


70.2 The unsolved integrative problems

This section names the specific hard problems that stand between the field and a real whole-mind account.

These are not gaps that a little more data will fill, they are conceptual knots that have resisted decades of effort, and a beginner should meet them not as failures but as the honest frontier.


70.2.1 The binding problem across perception and symbol

The binding problem is the puzzle of how a mind combines separately processed features into a single unified thing.

In perception, the brain processes an object's colour, shape, motion, and location in different places, yet you experience one red ball moving left, not four loose facts, and no one fully understands how the brain stitches those features to the same object, which is the classic binding problem.

There is a second, deeper version of the problem that reaches into thought itself, the binding of symbols, sometimes called the variable-binding problem.

To think that John loves Mary, and to keep it distinct from the thought that Mary loves John, a mind must bind the role of lover to John and the role of loved to Mary, and hold those bindings together without confusing which filler goes in which slot.

Symbolic systems handle this easily, because keeping track of what fills which role is exactly what symbols are for, but they struggle to learn and to ground those symbols.

Neural networks learn and ground beautifully but have long struggled to keep such bindings crisp and to combine known parts in new arrangements without muddling them, a difficulty at the heart of the old symbolic-versus-connectionist debate.

In systems terms the two sides predict differently: a symbolic account predicts errorless role bookkeeping but hand-built content, while a purely connectionist account predicts graceful learning with occasional binding slips, and human performance shows both signatures, which is why neither account closes the case.

The binding problem therefore sits right on the seam this whole outline keeps returning to, the seam between pattern and structure, and solving integration means solving binding at both the perceptual and the symbolic level at once.


70.2.2 The frame and relevance problem

The frame problem, which began as a technical headache in artificial intelligence and grew into a deep puzzle about the mind, is the problem of relevance: how does a mind know, out of everything it knows, which few things actually matter right now.

When something changes in the world, almost everything else stays the same, and a mind must update the handful of beliefs that the change affects without laboriously checking every belief it holds, yet how it homes in on just the relevant ones, quickly and without exhaustive search, is deeply unclear.

Stated as the relevance problem, it is the challenge of explaining how a process that could in principle draw on knowledge from any domain manages to bring the right knowledge to bear without first sifting through all of it.

This is easy for people and startlingly hard to formalise, and it has been called one of the reasons that building broadly intelligent machines is so difficult.

One intriguing proposal, associated with Murray Shanahan and Bernard Baars, connects the relevance problem to consciousness by way of global workspace theory, the idea that the mind has a limited central workspace onto which one interpretation at a time is broadcast to all the specialised processes at once.

On this view, a workspace that lets many parallel processes compete to contribute, while broadcasting the current winner to everything, might be nature's way of managing relevance without an impossible exhaustive search.

As a system design, this replaces exhaustive search with parallel competition plus broadcast: every module bids on the workspace at once, the winner is published to all, and relevance emerges from the bidding rather than from any central index of what matters.

Whether or not that particular proposal is right, the frame and relevance problem remains a genuine open obstacle, and any whole-mind account has to say how the mind finds the needle without searching the whole haystack.


70.2.3 Central against distributed control and the homunculus regress

A mind that pursues goals, resists distraction, and switches tasks seems to need something that is in charge, and that raises one of the oldest traps in the science of mind.

The trap is the homunculus, Latin for little person, the temptation to explain the mind's control by positing an inner controller that watches the mental screen and pulls the levers.

The trouble is that this explains nothing, because the inner controller would itself need an inner controller to run it, and so on forever, a bottomless regress that just relocates the mystery rather than solving it.

So the field faces a genuine dilemma about the nature of control.

One option is central control, a dedicated executive system, often associated with the front of the brain, that really does coordinate the rest, and the risk here is smuggling the homunculus back in unless the executive is itself explained in mechanical, non-intelligent terms.

The other option is distributed control, the idea that there is no single boss at all, and that orderly goal-directed behaviour emerges from many simple parts interacting and competing, the way a flock of birds wheels as one with no lead bird in command.

Distributed control avoids the regress but owes an account of how genuinely coordinated, flexible, unified behaviour arises from the scramble, which is not easy to give.

In systems terms the two designs predict differently: a central executive predicts a bottleneck whose damage or overload degrades every controlled task at once, while pure distribution predicts no single point of failure but also makes globally consistent, novel plans harder to explain.

The honest position is that this is unresolved, that the truth is probably some disciplined mixture in which control is real but implemented by mindless mechanisms, and that avoiding the homunculus while still explaining coordination is one of the central demands on any whole-mind architecture.


70.2.4 Access, report, and the place of consciousness in a control architecture

The last of the great problems is where consciousness fits into an account of the mind as an information-processing control system.

It helps to separate two senses of the word, following a distinction drawn by the philosopher Ned Block.

Access consciousness refers to information being available to the rest of the mind, poised for use in reasoning, decision, and above all report, meaning your ability to say what you are experiencing.

Phenomenal consciousness refers to there being something it is like to have the experience, the felt redness of red, the ache of an ache, the inner feel of it from the inside.

The science has made real progress on access consciousness, because it can be probed by asking what information a person can report and act on, and theories such as global workspace theory give a plausible mechanical story: information becomes access-conscious when it is broadcast widely across the mind's workspace.

In systems terms, access consciousness names a routing property, that a signal has been published on the global bus and is readable by every module, and studies of the brain's ignition response suggest this broadcast is established around 300 milliseconds after a stimulus, the timescale of the well-studied P3b brain wave.

In a control architecture this has a natural role, because the globally shared, reportable information is exactly what flexible, deliberate control needs to work with, so access consciousness looks like it could be a genuine functional part of the machine.

Phenomenal consciousness is another matter, and it is the site of what David Chalmers named the hard problem, the question of why any physical processing should be accompanied by felt experience at all, rather than going on in the dark.

This remains genuinely unsolved and genuinely contested, with serious thinkers disagreeing about whether it is a problem awaiting a scientific answer, a confusion that will dissolve, or something outside the reach of the current approach entirely.

For a builder of minds the practical stance is to take on the functional, reportable, access side of consciousness as an engineering target, since that part connects to control and behaviour, while treating the hard problem of felt experience with humility as a question the field has not resolved and may not resolve soon.


70.3 The reading of the field for konnectome

This final section turns the whole outline into guidance.

It does not crown a winner, because, as the very first pages warned, the honest state of the science is that several frameworks each explain part of the mind and none explains all of it.

Instead it reads each framework as a constraint on any adequate design, points to where the frameworks agree, and hands forward the questions that belong to the architect and not to a survey.


70.3.1 What each framework contributes as a constraint rather than a creed

The organising choice of this outline, and of konnectome, is to treat the great frameworks not as rival religions to pledge allegiance to, but as constraints, meaning conditions that any true account of the mind will have to satisfy.

A creed asks you to believe one framework and reject the others; a constraint simply records something the mind demonstrably does, which your design had better be able to do too.

Read this way, the symbolic tradition contributes the constraint that a mind can handle structure, rules, and composition, combining known parts into endlessly new arrangements, and that any architecture lacking this will fail at language and reasoning.

The connectionist tradition contributes the constraint that a mind learns rich knowledge from raw, noisy experience and degrades gracefully rather than shattering, and that any architecture lacking this will be brittle and hand-fed.

The Bayesian and probabilistic tradition contributes the constraint that a mind copes with uncertainty by weighing evidence against prior expectation in a broadly sensible, sometimes near-optimal way, and that any architecture ignoring uncertainty will misjudge a probabilistic world.

The reinforcement-learning tradition contributes the constraint that a mind learns what to do from the consequences of acting, guided by prediction errors, and balances habit against goal-directed planning.

The dynamical and embodied tradition contributes the constraint that a mind is a body acting in and coupled to an environment over continuous time, not a disembodied calculator, and that much of intelligence lives in that coupling.

The predictive-processing tradition contributes the constraint that a mind is forever anticipating its own input and learning from the misses, tying perception, action, and learning into one loop.

For an engineer, each constraint is a requirement in a specification: a capability the finished system must expose at its interfaces, testable in principle, regardless of which internal mechanism supplies it.

Held together, these are not a contradiction to be resolved by picking one, they are a specification to be met by a design broad enough to honour all of them, and that is exactly how konnectome is meant to read them.


70.3.2 Where the frameworks agree, and why the agreement is the safest ground to build on

When frameworks that start from utterly different assumptions nonetheless arrive at the same conclusion, that convergence is the strongest evidence the field has, because it is unlikely to be an artefact of any one framework's biases.

So the safest ground to build on is the set of points where the traditions agree despite themselves, and several such points recur across this whole outline.

They agree that the mind runs internal models of the world, representations it uses to perceive, predict, remember, and plan, even though they describe those models in different vocabularies.

They agree that prediction is central, that a mind is forever comparing what it expected with what it got and learning from the difference, a theme shared by Bayesian perception, predictive coding, and reinforcement learning alike.

They agree that the mind has to manage limited resources, that attention, working memory, and control exist precisely because a mind cannot do everything at once and must choose what to process and hold and pursue.

They agree that there are two broad modes of operation, one fast, automatic, and pattern-based, the other slow, effortful, and structured, however much they quarrel over the exact nature of the split.

They agree that learning operates at many timescales at once, from a moment's adjustment to a lifetime's expertise, and that memory is reconstructive and predictive rather than a passive recording.

These agreements are not glamorous and they are not complete, but they are load-bearing, and a design that respects internal models, prediction, resource limits, dual modes of processing, and multi-timescale reconstructive learning is standing on the firmest ground the science currently offers.

For konnectome the counsel is to build first and most confidently on this shared core, and to treat the places where frameworks still disagree as areas for cautious, revisable choices rather than firm foundations.


70.3.3 The open questions this outline hands forward, and the decisions that belong to the architect rather than to the survey

An outline like this one can survey the field, mark what is settled, and fence off what is contested, but it cannot make the final choices, because those choices depend on what a particular mind is being built to do, and they belong to the architect.

It is worth being explicit about the difference.

A survey reports what is known; an architect must decide, often before the science has finished, and must own the risk of deciding under uncertainty, which is a responsibility no survey can discharge on the architect's behalf.

Several open questions are hereby handed forward, unresolved on purpose.

There is the binding question, of how to get crisp, composable structure and rich learned grounding in the same system, which is the practical form of the symbolic-versus-connectionist seam.

There is the relevance question, of how a system decides what matters now without searching everything it knows, the frame problem in working clothes.

There is the control question, of how to make a system genuinely goal-directed and coordinated without smuggling in a little person who does the deciding.

There is the integration question itself, of what actually binds the faculties into one mind, and whether prediction, recurrence, a global workspace, or something not yet imagined is the real glue.

And there is the question of consciousness, of how much of the access, reportable, functional side to build in deliberately, and how to remain honest about the felt side that the science has not cracked.

The decisions these questions demand, which framework to lean on where the field is split, how much structure to hand-build against how much to let the system learn, where to place the boundary between fixed architecture and changeable content, are architectural decisions, and this outline deliberately does not pretend to settle them.

What it offers instead is the map: a catalogue of the processes a mind must reproduce, a set of frameworks read as constraints, a shared core that is safe to build on, and a clearly marked list of the deep problems still open.

The right way to close is the way the outline opened, with candour, saying plainly that no one yet possesses a complete, agreed account of how a whole human mind works, that this is the honest and even exciting state of the science, and that building konnectome well means treating that unfinished map not as a defeat but as the working charter for the next stretch of the journey.


SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ The sensory stream, as raw stimulus events from the environment, feeding perception.

◦ The current goal, as a maintained intention, feeding attention and control.

◦ Bodily and affective signals, as internal state readings, biasing every stage.

◦ Long-term memory contents, as stored records, available to retrieval on every cycle.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Overt actions, as motor commands, consumed by the environment.

◦ New memory traces, as encoded records of attended experience, consumed by the long-term stores.

◦ Updated goals and predictions, as internal signals, consumed by the next cognitive cycle.

◦ Reportable contents, as globally broadcast information, consumed by language and deliberate control.

• STATE.

◦ The perceptual interpretation currently settled on.

◦ The contents of working memory, about four chunks of currently active items.

◦ The active goal stack and control settings.

◦ The entire long-term memory, as the slowly changing background state of the whole system.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Attentional selectivity: how narrowly the gate filters the sensory stream.

◦ Working-memory capacity: about four chunks in the healthy adult.

◦ Control gain: how strongly goals bias competing processes against habit.

◦ Broadcast threshold: how much support an interpretation needs to win the workspace.

◦ Learning rates at each store, from fast episodic capture to slow skill tuning.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Iconic memory decay: under one second, bounding how long unattended sensory detail survives.

◦ Attentional blink: about 200 to 500 milliseconds, bounding how quickly attention can re-engage.

◦ Global broadcast and ignition: around 300 milliseconds after a stimulus, on the timescale of the P3b brain wave.

◦ A full perceive-decide-act cycle for a simple task: on the order of a few hundred milliseconds to about one second.

◦ The settling time of the whole-mind integration itself: REFUSED, because no accepted measurement of a unified integration time exists in the literature.

• MODES.

◦ Automatic mode: perception, habit, and well-learned skill run the cycle with little control; the default when predictions are being met.

◦ Deliberate mode: the workspace, working memory, and control dominate; triggered by novelty, conflict, error, or explicit intention.

◦ The detection of conflict or surprise is the switch from automatic to deliberate, and fluency restored is the switch back.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Selection failures: inattentional blindness, where the unattended never reaches memory.

◦ Capacity failures: overload of working memory collapsing reasoning and comprehension.

◦ Control failures: habit capture, distraction, and goal neglect.

◦ Binding failures: features or roles assigned to the wrong object or filler.

◦ Whole-system failures: the disorders of the previous chapter, read as parameters pushed outside their healthy range.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

Create a text variable called stimulus holding the current event in the world.
Create a text variable called goal holding what the agent is trying to notice.
Create a list variable called long term memory holding records that pair a cue with a suggested action.
Create an empty list variable called working memory with a capacity of four items.
Create an empty list variable called trace to record the journey of the thought.
Perceive: turn the stimulus into a set of features and add a note to the trace.
Attend: keep only the features that relate to the goal, and add a note to the trace.
Encode: add the attended features to working memory, dropping the oldest item if capacity is exceeded.
Retrieve: for each record in long term memory, if its cue matches an item in working memory, add its suggested action to a candidate list.
Add a note about the retrieval to the trace.
Decide: for each candidate action, calculate a score from its match strength, and choose the action with the highest score.
Add a note about the decision to the trace.
Act: publish the chosen action to the world, and add a final note to the trace.
Learn: add a new record pairing the attended cue with the chosen action to long term memory.
Print every note in the trace in order, showing one thought passing through the whole mind.

CODE SAMPLE:

# Create a text variable called stimulus holding the current event in the world.
stimulus = "a friend's worried face across a noisy room"
# Create a text variable called goal holding what the agent is trying to notice.
goal = "friend"
# Create a list variable called long_term_memory pairing cues with suggested actions.
long_term_memory = [("worried", "walk over and ask what is wrong"),
                    ("noisy", "ignore the background chatter"),
                    ("face", "make eye contact")]
# Create an empty list variable called working_memory with a capacity of four items.
working_memory = []
# Create a number variable called CAPACITY with value four.
CAPACITY = 4
# Create an empty list variable called trace to record the journey of the thought.
trace = []

# Perceive: turn the stimulus into a list of word features.
features = stimulus.replace("'s", "").split()
# Add a perception note to the trace.
trace.append("PERCEPTION: features " + str(features))
# Attend: keep the goal word and its two neighbours as the selected subset.
attended = [w for w in features if w in ("friend", "worried", "face")]
# Add an attention note to the trace.
trace.append("ATTENTION: selected " + str(attended))
# Encode: add each attended feature to working memory, honouring the capacity.
for item in attended:
    # Add the item to working memory.
    working_memory.append(item)
    # If working memory exceeds capacity, drop the oldest item.
    if len(working_memory) > CAPACITY:
        working_memory.pop(0)
# Add a memory note to the trace.
trace.append("WORKING MEMORY: holding " + str(working_memory))
# Retrieve: collect every stored action whose cue matches working memory.
candidates = [(cue, act) for cue, act in long_term_memory if cue in working_memory]
# Add a retrieval note to the trace.
trace.append("RETRIEVAL: candidates " + str([a for c, a in candidates]))
# Decide: score each candidate by how early its cue sits in working memory.
scored = [(CAPACITY - working_memory.index(cue), act) for cue, act in candidates]
# Choose the action with the highest score.
choice = max(scored)[1]
# Add a decision note to the trace.
trace.append("DECISION: chose " + choice)
# Act: publish the chosen action to the world.
trace.append("ACTION: " + choice)
# Learn: store the pairing of the situation with the chosen action.
long_term_memory.append(("worried friend", choice))
# Add a learning note to the trace.
trace.append("LEARNING: stored the episode for next time")
# Print every note in the trace, showing one thought crossing the whole mind.
for note in trace:
    # Print the note.
    print(note)

END OF COGNITION: A SYSTEMS APPROACH.
